The #1 state in artificial intelligence higher education is Texas—**21** schools in the Lone Star State offered **39** AI degree programs in 2025. Thanks to a constellation of factors, Texas is particularly strong in AI graduate studies. Public universities in Texas are supported by state incentives such as the [Governor’s University Research Initiative (GURI)](https://gov.texas.gov/business/page/guri) and the [Texas University Fund (TUF)](https://www.highered.texas.gov/research-funding-in-texas/research-funding-and-programs/). R1 universities are busy developing their own supercomputers & AI institutes (see UT Austin’s [Texas AI](https://ai.utexas.edu/)). And oil & gas companies are pumping money into advanced energy initiatives with AI applications (e.g. University of Houston’s [Energy Transition Institute](https://www.uh.edu/energy/eti/)).

It’s also not surprising to see California and New York in the top 5 states for artificial intelligence degrees. California has a long history of tech investment & startup funding, supported by top-level AI research at Stanford and schools within the UC System. New York is the home of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE), the [Empire AI](https://www.empireai.tech/) consortium, and the largest [fintech sector](https://www.technyc.org/nyc-tech-snapshot-2025) in the USA.

New York’s neighbor, Pennsylvania, is the seat of two massive university presences in artificial intelligence. Carnegie Mellon University (CMU) and the University of Pennsylvania account for the lion’s share of [AI graduate degree offerings in PA](https://www.mastersinai.org/degrees/pennsylvania/). Because of CMU, there’s now a dense [robotics & AI commercialization ecosystem](https://pittsburghregion.org/key-industries/ai-in-pittsburgh/) in Pittsburgh. The university is also spearheading the $20 million [NSF AI Institute for Societal Decision Making (NSF AI-SDM)](https://www.cmu.edu/ai-sdm/).

In Florida, it’s the big public universities that are helping to spur innovation (AI programs in the Sunshine State burgeoned from 3 programs in 2022 to 30 programs in 2025, a **900%** growth rate). In 2020, the University of Florida announced a $70 million [artificial intelligence partnership](https://news.ufl.edu/2020/07/nvidia-partnership/) with NVIDIA. In 2023, it distributed nearly [$19 million](https://ai.ufl.edu/about/building-an-ai-university/) in state funds to support AI projects in 10 colleges. And in 2025, it planned to inject $24 million into a upgrade of its [HiPerGator AI](https://ai.ufl.edu/research/hipergator/). But UF isn’t the only player in town. In 2024, the University of South Florida (USF) launched its $40 million [Bellini College of Artificial Intelligence, Cybersecurity and Computing](https://www.usf.edu/ai-cybersecurity-computing/).

But we also wanted to know which areas were punching above their weight! So we decided to analyze state growth rates in AI degree programs from 2022 to 2025. Iowa was an unusual standout—it had **1** AI degree program in 2022 and **11** programs in 2025 (**1,000%** growth rate). Due to the driving force of SD public universities, South Dakota had a similar story, growing from **1** AI degree program in 2022 to **9** programs in 2025, especially at the [undergraduate level](https://www.mastersinai.org/degrees/artificial-intelligence-degrees/) (**800%** growth rate). These statistics reflect the overall regional surge of AI higher education in the Midwest.

## Types of Universities Offering AI Programs

### Key University Type Statistics

* Research dollars = AI investment. In 2025, **47%** of U.S. universities offering degrees in artificial intelligence were classified as R1 institutions by the [Carnegie Classification of Institutions of Higher Education](https://carnegieclassifications.acenet.edu/). **16%** of U.S. universities offering degrees in AI were classified as R2 institutions.
* Public universities in the South offer **66%** of artificial intelligence degree programs within their region. But in the Northeast, it’s private universities that dominate, offering **73%** of AI degree programs within their region.
* As of 2022, [99](https://nces.ed.gov/fastfacts/display.asp?id=667) colleges were classified as Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCUs) by the U.S. Department of Education. However, only **5** HBCU schools currently offer undergraduate and/or graduate degrees in artificial intelligence. That’s just **5%** of HBCU schools with higher education programs in AI.

There is a clear correlation between research spending and AI education in the USA. To take just one example, in 2025, **16** universities in Texas attained R1 status. This designation is granted to schools that spend at least $50 million on research and award at least 70 research doctorates on average per year. It’s no accident that Texas R1 institutions have also developed a staggering **18** master’s degrees and **5** bachelor’s degrees in AI. It’s a similar story in Florida, Pennsylvania, Massachusetts, and New York—R1 universities in these states easily outpace their R2 and non-designated counterparts in offering AI programs.

Fascinatingly, different university systems are driving change. In Southern states such as Texas, Florida, North Carolina & Virginia and Midwest states such as Indiana & Ohio, public universities are the clear leaders in providing AI higher education programs. In the Northeast, it’s famous private universities in Pennsylvania, New York, and Massachusetts that offer the most choice. The Northeast has a dense cluster of private R1/R2 and Ivy League institutions with prestigious engineering & computer science departments. In contrast, the South and the Midwest are dominated by well-funded public research flagship and land-grant universities.

It’s a more challenging narrative for Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCUs). In 2025, only **5%** of HBCU schools had developed degrees in artificial intelligence and only one of them—Howard University—had achieved an R1 designation. The largest HBCU provider of AI programs in 2025 was North Carolina A&T State University, which only offered **2** bachelor’s programs and **1** master’s degree. In addition to being underfunded by decades, HBCUs lack the endowments, federal R&D dollars for AI centers, faculty, and MS/PhD ecosystems of R1 & R2 institutions. These are serious headwinds.

## Departmental Trends: Where AI Degrees Are Housed

### Key Departmental Statistics

* Although Departments of Computer Science and Colleges of Engineering still offer the lion’s share of AI programs at U.S. universities, artificial intelligence degrees within Schools of Business experienced an explosive **1,260%** increase from 2022 to 2025, jumping from just **5** programs to **68** business-focused programs in AI. The majority of these are [MBA in Artificial Intelligence](https://www.mastersinai.org/degrees/mba-in-artificial-intelligence/) programs.
* The South may hog the headlines, but the West has hidden engineering strengths in AI. In 2025, **23** programs in artificial intelligence were being offered by Colleges or Departments of Engineering in the West (**30.3%** of AI programs across all departments) and **30** programs in the Midwest (**25%** of AI programs across all departments).
* Departments of Math & Statistics and Informatics have also pivoted toward AI education, although program offerings remain limited. In 2025, Departments of Math & Statistics throughout the USA offered **27** undergraduate & graduate degrees in artificial intelligence. Similarly, Departments of Informatics offered **21** degrees in AI.

It makes sense that the vast majority of AI degrees have a technical parent. In 2025, **37%** of AI programs in the USA were being offered by Departments of Computer Science and **22%** by Colleges or Departments of Engineering. As always, it’s the South that leads the way. In 2025, computer science departments in the Southern region of the USA were responsible for **86** AI degree programs. Texas alone had **18** AI programs under the banner of computer science and Florida had **17**.

And while the Northeast has a diverse range of AI degree offerings from multiple departments, the West and the Upper Midwest are making names for themselves in AI engineering. For example, in Michigan, there are multiple [engineering-focused graduate degrees in AI](https://www.mastersinai.org/degrees/michigan/) at big public research universities (e.g. University of Michigan-Ann Arbor) and smaller private universities (e.g. Kettering). This trend probably reflects the Upper Midwest’s strengths in manufacturing and ag-tech and the region’s increasing need for 21st century engineers. Farther to the west, you’ll find plenty of engineering-focused AI programs within [California](https://www.mastersinai.org/degrees/california/).

But the real story is the astronomical rise of business-focused AI programs, including MBA offerings. Across every region of the country, Schools of Business have been scrambling to develop AI qualifications that will equip corporate leaders with strategic skills. You’ll now find **68** business AI degrees in over half of the states, with more programs coming on-board each year. Our guide to [MBA in Artificial Intelligence Programs](https://www.mastersinai.org/degrees/mba-in-artificial-intelligence/) has details on this phenomenon, including the dominance of schools in the Mid-Atlantic region like CMU Tepper and UPenn Wharton.

## AI Graduate Admissions: Requirements and Trends

### Key Graduate Admissions Statistics

* Admissions requirements for AI graduate degrees vary widely. In a random sampling of 75 AI master’s degrees from our database, **59%** listed specific undergraduate degree majors and/or skills prerequisites. However, **41%** did not require or specify an undergraduate major and/or skills.
* The GRE may be on the way out. In 2025, **62%** of master’s degrees in artificial intelligence in the United States did not require GRE scores for admission. **60%** of these “No GRE” programs in AI were offered online and **40%** were offered on-campus.
* A minimum 3.0 GPA is the standard requirement for an AI master’s degree across every type of school. In a random sampling of 75 AI master’s degrees from our database, **57** programs (**76%**) had a minimum GPA requirement of **3.0**. Only **14** schools had a minimum GPA requirement that was lower than 3.0.
* In 2025, a minimum 3.0 GPA was the requirement at **78%** of R1 and R2 universities. However, many R1 schools end up accepting students with much higher baseline GPAs.

Admissions standards for master’s degrees in artificial intelligence are typically dependent on the department that created them. For example, within a Department of Computer Science or a College of Engineering, it’s common to find AI degrees that are only open to applicants with an undergraduate major in a STEM field (e.g. computer science, math, physics, engineering, etc.) and skills in programming, math, statistics, calculus, and algorithms. In contrast, AI master’s degrees from Schools of Business, Colleges of Professional Studies, and interdisciplinary departments often welcome candidates with a bachelor’s degree in any major and little or no skills in programming.

In the past, the Graduate Record Examinations (GRE) test was a standard requirement for admissions to master’s and doctoral degrees in the USA. But COVID-19 changed the game. Many universities suspended the GRE requirement during the pandemic and eventually adopted a “No GRE” or test-optional policy going forward. Some decided the GRE was serving as a barrier to equity & diversity. Others made the decision to shift to a holistic review process. The result? Over half (**62%**) of master’s degrees in AI in the USA do not require GRE scores for admission. The minority that continue to insist on GRE scores are often interested in an applicant’s quantitative skills.

The standard minimum GPA requirement for a master’s degree in AI is a **3.0** GPA on any undergraduate work. This precept holds true for prestigious R1 & R2 universities, as well as small private colleges and state universities. But there is a sting in the tail. When we analyzed class profiles for some of the top graduate programs in AI, we found that the average GPA of successful applicants was often higher than **3.5**. At Rutgers, the [average GPA](https://www.cs.rutgers.edu/academics/graduate/m-s-program/admission-requirements) of a recent entering class for the MSCS in AI/Machine Learning was **3.6**. At Stanford, the [average GPA](https://www.cs.stanford.edu/admissions/masters-admissions-frequently-asked-questions) for the MS CS in Artificial Intelligence was **3.7**. As you might expect, computer science and engineering degrees in AI tend to have higher GPA standards than business degrees in AI.

## Online AI Degrees in 2025: Availability and Growth

### Key Online AI Degree Statistics

* Online is a popular delivery format for graduate programs in artificial intelligence, but a relatively rare format for undergraduate programs. In 2025, **51%** of master’s degrees in AI in the United States and **16%** of bachelor’s degrees in AI were offered online.
* Online offerings in artificial intelligence are rising rapidly. From 2022 to 2025, [online Master’s in AI](https://www.mastersinai.org/degrees/online-masters-in-artificial-intelligence/) programs experienced a **276%** growth (**42** programs to **158** programs). In the one-year span of 2024 to 2025, [online Bachelor’s in AI degrees](https://www.mastersinai.org/degrees/online-artificial-intelligence-degrees/) in AI experienced a **63%** growth (**19** programs to **31 programs**).
* Prestigious research universities are still more reluctant to offer online programs in AI. In 2025, **29%** of AI degrees at R1 universities, **37%** of AI degrees at R2 universities, and **49%** of AI degrees at universities without either Carnegie designation were being delivered in an online format.
* Private universities have a slight edge in distance learning. In 2025, **50%** of online AI degrees were being offered by private universities, **44%** were being offered by public universities, and **6%** were being offered by private for-profit universities in the USA.

Online learning in AI is on the rise, driven by market demand, employer acceptance, and changes in higher education habits brought on by COVID-19. This is especially noticeable at the graduate level, where online master’s degrees in artificial intelligence grew from **42** programs in **2022** to **158** programs in 2025. The majority of these programs (**42%**) can be found in Southern universities located in states such as Texas and Florida. We explore online master’s degrees in AI and profile the nation’s top offerings in our rankings of the [21 Best Online Master’s in Artificial Intelligence Programs](https://www.mastersinai.org/degrees/online-masters-in-artificial-intelligence).

Interestingly, although Midwestern and Western universities can’t compete with Southern universities on the graduate level, they are often more “online-friendly” to AI undergraduates. In 2025, **26%** of AI bachelor’s degrees in Western schools and **22%** of AI bachelor’s degrees in Midwestern schools were delivered online. In contrast, only **15.5%** of AI bachelor’s degrees in Southern schools and only **4.3%** of degrees in Northeastern schools were delivered online. And it’s not California that’s driving change in the West. It’s states like [Arizona](https://www.mastersinai.org/degrees/online-artificial-intelligence-degrees/) that are championing distance learning for AI undergraduates.

These trends indicate that access to AI higher education is being democratized outside traditional tech hubs and R1 institutions on the East & West Coast. For instance, it didn’t surprise us to learn that only **29%** of AI degrees within R1 universities are delivered in an online format (**67** programs out of **235** programs). R1 institutions pride themselves on developing in-person graduate education experiences and on-campus research opportunities through their AI institutes. It’s part of the reason their tuition costs are so high!

On the other hand, in 2025, **37%** of AI degrees in R2 institutions and **49%** of AI degrees in non-designated institutions were being offered online. If you want to know where distance learning in AI is really taking off, look to non-R1 universities in the South, Midwest, and Southwest.

## Conclusions: The State of AI Degree Programs in 2025

### Key Takeaways

* AI education is here to stay. Master’s programs in artificial intelligence grew from **116** programs in 2022 to **310** programs in 2025 (**167%** growth); 158 of these graduate programs in AI are now offered online (**51%**). From 2024-2025, bachelor’s programs in AI grew from **90** programs to **193** programs (**114%** growth); **31** of these undergraduate programs in AI are now offered online (**16%**).
* Research-focused institutions are leading the way in AI higher education. In 2025, **47%** of U.S. universities offering degree programs in AI were classified as R1 institutions and **16%** were classified as R2 institutions by the [Carnegie Classification of Institutions of Higher Education](https://carnegieclassifications.acenet.edu/) (**63%** in total). Having said that, non-designated universities are more proactive when it comes to distance learning, offering **49%** of all online AI degrees in the USA.
* Thanks to RI institutions in big states like Texas & Florida, the South is the region with the largest number of AI undergraduate & graduate programs in the USA, offering **38.4%** of all AI degrees. However, the Midwest is quietly making a name for itself in AI higher education, offering **23.9%** of all AI degrees in the country.
* Although technical departments like computer science continue to account for the majority of AI offerings, Schools of Business have woken up to the fact that AI knowledge is an integral part of management studies. From 2022 to 2025, AI degree programs within a School or College of Business went from **5** programs to **68** programs, a **1,260%** increase.

Artificial intelligence degrees are becoming a well-known factor in U.S. universities, both at the graduate level and the undergraduate level. Standalone degrees in AI are now joining AI concentrations in traditional majors like computer science and computer engineering. Business schools are pumping out MBA in AI programs. Even smaller Departments of Math and Informatics are jumping on the education bandwagon and beginning to develop quantitative-focused degrees in artificial intelligence.

However, the growth of AI higher education programs is not evenly spread across the country. Certain states are surging ahead while other areas are being left behind.

* College students who are fortunate to live in Texas and Florida can take advantage of a huge number of AI degree options, including some from prestigious R1 institutions with NSF-funded artificial intelligence institutes.
* Midwest students in Illinois, Indiana, and Michigan can look to their public flagship universities for AI education opportunities, especially in engineering disciplines. Similarly, California students can enroll in respected AI programs within the UC System.
* Intelligent students from Pennsylvania, New York, and Massachusetts can tap into the AI strengths of prestigious private schools like Carnegie Mellon, Columbia & MIT. Having said that, they will be competing with talented out-of-state applicants and paying a hefty tuition price for their education.

It’s a bleaker scenario for students living in AI educational deserts. Smaller state and private universities who lack endowments, money from public/private tech partnerships, and NSF funding often do not have the resources or expertise to develop in-depth artificial intelligence degree programs, especially at the graduate level. At HBCU schools, AI program offerings are extremely limited. And in places like Kansas, Arkansas, North Dakota, and New Mexico, there may only be one AI degree available within the entire state. Unless more funding and support is provided at city, state & regional levels, the gap between the “haves” and the “have nots” in AI higher education could continue to increase.

There are some bright spots on the horizon:

* U.S. universities are taking a more holistic approach to AI graduate program admissions, often omitting the GRE requirement and considering candidates without an undergraduate degree in a STEM field.
* There’s also been impressive growth in online AI degree programs at both the graduate and the undergraduate level. Although R1 universities are sometimes hesitant to commit to 100% online learning, R2 and non-designated universities are coming on strong.

The chance to earn a bachelor’s or master’s in AI remotely can reduce the barrier to entry for many students—especially those on a budget—but it doesn’t deal with the issue of prestige. An employer is more likely to pick a candidate with an on-campus computer science or AI degree from an R1 institution in Texas than an online AI degree from an obscure state school in West Virginia.

One solution is for universities to follow the lead of Upper Midwestern schools and develop expertise in a realm of AI that aligns with local industries (e.g. Michigan’s strengths in robotics, AI engineering, ag-tech & automotive AI). This approach helps to attract funding for programs. And it gives students a clear pipeline to employment after graduation.

The 2025 AI Degree Report from MastersinAI.org provides a comprehensive analysis of AI degree programs in the United States, covering bachelor's and master's degrees in AI, machine learning, and related fields. Key findings include:

**National Overview:**
- 304 universities now offer AI/ML degrees, with 310 master's programs and 193 bachelor's programs (503 total).
- Master's programs grew 167% from 2022 (116 programs) to 2025 (310 programs), adding 64.7 new programs per year on average.
- Bachelor's programs more than doubled from 90 programs in 2024 to 193 in 2025 (114.4% growth).
- 53% of programs are standalone AI degrees, 47% are AI concentrations/tracks within existing degrees.

**Regional Distribution:**
- The South leads with 38.4% of all AI degrees (193 programs at 113 schools), driven by Texas, Florida, and North Carolina.
- The Midwest is second with 23.9% (120 programs at 74 schools), emerging as a region to watch.
- The Northeast accounts for 22.7% (114 programs at 65 schools), including prestigious schools like Carnegie Mellon and MIT.
- The West lags at 15.1% (76 programs at 52 schools), though this may reflect naming traditions of incorporating AI into existing CS programs.

**State-Level Trends:**
- Texas is the national leader with 21 schools offering 39 AI programs (31 master's, 8 bachelor's).
- Pennsylvania punches above its weight with 16 schools offering 35 programs.
- Florida saw explosive growth from 3 programs in 2022 to 30 in 2025 (900% growth).
- Iowa and South Dakota saw the highest growth rates (1,000% and 800% respectively).
- Montana is the only state with zero AI bachelor's or master's programs.
- The top 5 states are Texas, California, New York, Pennsylvania, and Florida.

**University Types:**
- 47% of AI degree-offering universities are R1 institutions; 16% are R2.
- Public universities dominate in the South (66% of regional AI programs); private universities dominate in the Northeast (73%).
- Only 5% of HBCUs (5 schools) offer AI degrees, highlighting a significant equity gap.

**Departmental Trends:**
- Computer Science departments offer 37% of AI programs; Engineering departments offer 22%.
- Business schools saw explosive growth from 5 AI programs in 2022 to 68 in 2025 (1,260% increase), mostly MBA in AI programs.

**Admissions Requirements:**
- 59% of AI master's programs require specific undergraduate majors or skills prerequisites.
- 62% of AI master's programs do not require GRE scores (60% of these are online).
- A 3.0 GPA is the standard minimum requirement (76% of programs), though top schools often admit students with 3.5+ GPAs.

**Online AI Degrees:**
- 51% of master's programs and 16% of bachelor's programs are offered online.
- Online master's programs grew 276% from 2022 (42 programs) to 2025 (158 programs).
- R1 universities are more reluctant to offer online programs (29% of their AI degrees online) compared to non-designated universities (49% online).

**Key Takeaways:**
- The South leads in volume, but the Midwest is an emerging hub for AI engineering.
- Access to AI education is uneven, with "AI educational deserts" in states like Kansas, Arkansas, North Dakota, and New Mexico.
- Online programs are democratizing access, but prestige concerns remain.
- The report recommends universities align AI programs with local industries (e.g., Michigan's robotics and ag-tech) to attract funding and provide employment pipelines.

# B.S.E. in AI Curriculum

## Curriculum

## Overview

The AI degree provides the mathematical and algorithmic foundations of AI techniques, along with hands-on experience in programming as well as using AI tools and foundation models. Complementing these engineering skills with a broader perspective, students learn about intelligence from a cognitive science perspective, and they develop a sense of the issues (and solutions) required to responsibly develop AI to benefit society.  Finally, students choose a concentration, ranging from machine learning, to vision and language, to data and society, to robotics, to AI and health systems. Interested students can learn more about the courses below by visiting the [Penn Course Catalog](https://catalog.upenn.edu/courses/).

## Mathematics and Natural Science (7 CUs)

## Computing (5 CUs)

## AI Core (6 CUs)

Students choose at least one course unit from each of the following six categories:

##### Introduction to AI

##### Machine Learning

##### Signals & Systems

##### Optimization & Control

##### Vision & Language

##### AI Project *(must have AI development, 30% of grade from term project)*

## AI Electives (6 CUs)

In addition to the courses above, students will have an opportunity to take six AI courses selected from the list of approved courses below, along with the 1-year senior design sequence:

##### Machine Learning Electives

##### Optimization, Systems, and Control Electives

##### Other AI Electives

The above list will evolve as new courses are added to the program.

## AI Concentrations

The six AI elective courses can be structured along AI concentrations depending on the interests of the student. Concentrations are optional and consist of four courses in a specific theme. Only courses used in the AI Elective category may be counted towards a concentration.

## Senior Design (2 CU)

Rather than offering a specific course for senior design, AI majors will embed themselves into the ESE, CIS or other Penn Engineering senior design courses. This will enable AI students to apply their AI skills across many engineering challenges.

## Technical Electives (3 CU)

Three course units from Engineering, Math, Natural Science or from the list [here](https://advising.cis.upenn.edu/tech-electives/).

## General Electives (8 CUs)

##### **AI Ethics:** *Choose at least one of the following*

##### **Cognitive Science Elective:** *Choose at least one of the following*

## Frequently Asked Questions

## I’m thinking of applying to the University of Pennsylvania. When will I be able to apply for the AI undergraduate degree?

The application for prospective Penn students interested in the Artificial Intelligence Bachelor of Science in Engineering (AI BSE) program for a Fall 2025 start date will open in early August 2024.

For further details regarding the University of Pennsylvania’s admissions procedures, kindly refer to [https://admissions.upenn.edu](https://admissions.upenn.edu/).

## I’m joining Penn as an incoming first-year Engineering undergraduate student in Fall 2025. Can I declare an AI major?

Yes! Incoming first-year Engineering undergraduate students will be eligible to change their major to Artificial Intelligence. Beginning on August 26, incoming students can start the process by accessing the [Declare/Update Field of Study form](https://srfs.upenn.edu/registrar/forms).

## I’m currently a Penn student. How do I transfer into this program?

Current Penn Engineering students, including current first- and second-year M&T students are eligible to apply for transferring to the AI major.

These students will need to follow a two-step process:

Submit a 4-year academic plan to [buchkat@seas.upenn.edu](mailto:buchkat@seas.upenn.edu)

Submit the [Declare/Update Field of Study form](https://srfs.upenn.edu/registrar/forms)

All other students should follow the procedure outlined “**[Transfer Into Penn Engineering](https://ugrad.seas.upenn.edu/student-handbook/undergraduate-policies/transfer-in-to-penn-engineering/)**” page in the Penn Engineering Undergraduate Student Handbook.

BSE in AI students are permitted to pursue dual-majors within Penn Engineering, with the exception of CSCI, NETS and SSE.

Eligible BSE in AI students are permitted to pursue dual-degree programs or second majors in the College of Arts and Sciences, including the VIPER program. To determine eligibility, please contact [buchkat@seas.upenn.edu](mailto:buchkat@seas.upenn.edu).

Note that students seeking to declare the AI major must be able to graduate within 8 semesters in total (or 10 semesters for M&T students), otherwise the major change will not be approved.

## Is the AI undergraduate degree an online program?

No, Penn Engineering does not offer undergraduate online programs. The AI program is designed as a residential undergraduate bachelor’s program, emphasizing in-person instruction. For information regarding Penn Engineering’s online graduate degrees at the master’s level, please visit <https://online.seas.upenn.edu/>.

## What prerequisites do prospective students need for this program?

For details on prerequisites and recommendations when applying to Penn Engineering, please visit the [Office of Admissions](https://admissions.upenn.edu/academics/exploring-academics/penn-engineering) page.

Strong preparation in fundamental subjects, particularly Mathematics, is vital for any Penn Engineering degree program.

## What is the tuition for this program?

Tuition and financial aid policies are university-wide and not specific to individual programs. For more information, please visit [https://srfs.upenn.edu](https://srfs.upenn.edu/).

## What is the best way to receive updates about the AI degree program?

This website will provide the most up-to-date program information. Kindly continue to check back regularly for updates, and be sure to follow Penn Engineering AI on social media.

## I’m joining Penn as an incoming first-year Engineering and Management & Technology (M&T) undergraduate student in Fall 2025. Can I declare an AI major?

Yes! Incoming first-year Engineering and M&T undergraduate students will be eligible to change their major to Artificial Intelligence. Beginning on August 26, incoming students can start the process by accessing the [Declare/Update Field of Study form](https://srfs.upenn.edu/registrar/forms).

## Why Get an AI Degree?

There are many data-backed reasons why you may consider pursuing an AI bachelor’s degree:

* **Meaningful workplace differentiator:** Comparing similar workers who differ only in AI skills, PwC found that those with the AI skills commanded a [56% wage premium](https://www.pwc.com/gx/en/services/ai/ai-jobs-barometer.html).
* **Rapid salary growth potential:** The median salary for an AI professional is [$160,000](https://www.riseworks.io/blog/ai-talent-salary-report-2025), with the top 1% earning over $1,000,000. And wages are rising 2x faster in AI-exposed industries.
* **Developing hugely in-demand skills:** There is a [35 percentage point gap](https://financialservicesskills.org/news/skills-shortages-are-a-major-barrier-to-ai-driven-growth/) between AI skills and the availability of talent. [Lack of talent (46%)](https://www.workera.ai/blog/the-5-5-trillion-skills-gap-what-idcs-new-report-reveals-about-ai-workforce-readiness#:~:text=The%20AI%20talent%20crisis%20is,from%20the%20global%20market%20performance.) is the single biggest barrier to employer AI readiness, and over 90% of global enterprises risk running into critical skills shortages as early as this year.
* **Networking with potential employers:** Many of the best AI degree programs (e.g. [UC Berkeley](https://career.berkeley.edu/find-opportunities/internships/)) feature internships, co-ops or networking events. These offer brilliant opportunities to make valuable connections. Across all sectors, [62% of internships in the US convert to job offers](https://www.naceweb.org/talent-acquisition/internships/intern-offer-and-conversion-rates-fall-acceptances-rise), rising to 72% for in-person internships.
* **Cross-industry appeal:** An AI degree doesn’t commit you to working directly in AI. It will make you more employable across all sectors: [88% of all companies](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/quantumblack/our-insights/the-state-of-ai) report regularly using AI in at least one business function.
* **Early adoption:** AI is fast becoming ubiquitous, but you can be among the first to emerge with an AI bachelor’s degree. [UPenn was the first Ivy League school to offer an AI undergraduate degree](https://penntoday.upenn.edu/news/penn-engineering-launches-first-ivy-league-undergraduate-degree-artificial-intelligence), with the first cohort admitted in fall 2024.

## What Makes an AI Bachelor’s Degree Program Elite?

Lots of institutions are rushing to introduce AI programs, but quality is highly variable.

The best AI degrees combine a thoughtful curriculum with expert faculty, institutional prestige, affordable tuition and attainable admissions. In broad terms, the top AI bachelor’s degree programs will feature:

* R1 research status, with faculty **on the cutting edge** of AI developments
* A purpose-built AI curriculum that does not borrow too heavily from pre-existing courses and programs (as opposed to a hastily-assembled rebrand designed purely to meet growing demand)
* **Internship opportunities** and/or other collaborations with industry partners
* Elite computing facilities
* **Hands-on** labs and one or more capstone projects

Any AI degree that combines these features with total resident tuition below ~$50,000 offers a significant value. This guide will take you through the top 25 AI bachelor’s degree programs, taking into account all of the factors that make a program great.

## The Different Types of AI Degrees

Before you decide on an AI bachelor’s degree program, it’s **vital that you understand the different types of program you may encounter.**

Especially in comparison to more established majors, AI is an open-ended topic. Programs range from **highly technical** (working toward building AI systems) to **highly applied** (learning how to *use* AI, often within a particular industry).

Our list is focused on more technical AI degree programs. You can identify these by looking for courses like:

* Machine learning
* Deep learning
* Computer vision
* Neural networks
* Natural language processing
* Robotics

For example, AI majors at UC San Diego [have the choice of all these courses](https://cse.ucsd.edu/undergraduate/bs-artificial-intelligence-0) (and 30+ others).

But you may be looking for a non-technical AI degree. This is likely to be the case if you don’t have a background or strong interest in computing, but still want to leverage the AI boom to boost your opportunities and earning potential within a different field.

Examples of less technical AI programs include:

* [Artificial Intelligence in Business at Arizona State](https://wpcarey.asu.edu/information-systems-degrees/undergraduate)
* [BA in Artificial Intelligence Marketing and Design at Academy of Art University](https://www.academyart.edu/ai/communications-media-technologies-ba-ai/)
* [AI Governance minor at Lake Forest](https://www.lakeforest.edu/academics/majors-and-minors/artificial-intelligence)

Applied AI degrees have their place. The number of early-career job listings asking for AI skills has [almost doubled in the last year](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/04/29/entry-level-jobs-calling-for-ai-skills-nearly-doubled-from-a-year-ago-report.html). Which means the ability to work with AI (as opposed to building it) **is a valuable skill in the job market**.

But whichever route you take, it is critical that you know what you are signing up for, or else you will set yourself up for dissatisfaction.

## AI Degree vs AI Concentration

In this guide and in your own research, you will encounter lots of **computer science degrees with an AI concentration, focus, or track**. But are these the same thing as “AI degrees”?

Functionally, they may often be essentially the same. But there are some potential differences to be aware of:

**AI major**

* Highly likely to cover the key AI topics
* You’ll graduate with a degree in AI (very clear to employers)
* May borrow a lot from CS curriculum in practice
* Very new, so limited data on student experiences and outcomes

**Computer Science major with AI concentration**

* Often covers all of the same AI content as an AI major
* Potentially wider focus
* More data on proven graduate success
* “AI” may not show up on your final diploma

Our top 25 contains both kinds of programs, but each is marked clearly as either an outright AI program or an AI concentration.

[Program overview](https://compsci.rpi.edu/programs/bs-computer-science)

## Methodology

In order to rank the top AI degrees, we scored programs based on six weighted factors.

* Top weight (25%) went to **hands-on practice**, where we rewarded strong internship schemes, real-world projects, and capstone assessments.
* **Curriculum relevance** comprised 20% of the score for each program. This assessed each AI bachelor’s degree for “2026-readiness”: topics like generative AI and natural language processing, plus the use of modern tools.
* We also gave **affordability** 20% weighting. We adjusted this to make it a value-for-money indicator: programs judged to be delivering world-class quality were penalized less harshly for high tuition. We also made small regional adjustments to reward strong in-state value.
* **Academic quality** was worth 15%. Top marks went to institutions with impressive employer reputations and top-tier AI research.
* 10% of the final scores came from **focus on AI**. This penalized misleadingly named or marketed programs, crediting those with a clear and consistent AI-led curriculum.
* **Admissions** decided the final 10%. We did not want to unduly punish highly-selective institutions, but highly accessible programs get a slight edge. Credit was also given to practical elements like rolling admissions.

Estimated tuition figures are based on published per-year or per-semester tuition costs, extrapolated across the full four-year degree.

## How to Choose an AI Bachelor’s Degree

Your first step in choosing an AI degree is **devising a personal plan**. That means asking yourself some basic questions:

* Do I want to study in person or get [an online AI degree](https://programs.com/programs/online-ai-bachelor-degree-programs/)?
* Is there a particular state/region I want to study in?
* Am I looking for a more technical or applied AI degree?

You’ll also need to consider your **personal circumstances**. Think about the following:

* What is my high school GPA? Do I need to prioritize less selective schools?
* What costs am I able to take on? Will I be eligible for financial assistance?
* Am I looking to study full-time?

Before even getting into the substantive qualities of each AI bachelor’s degree program, these questions are likely to significantly trim down your shortlist.

#### Further study

While you don’t need to make firm decisions at this stage, you’ll also want to think about whether you may wish to pursue further education after you earn your bachelor’s degree. This could impact your choice of program. If you are keen on continuing in academia, you might wish to look at:

* **Combined/accelerated programs:** Some programs let you take a certain number of courses that count toward both a bachelor’s and a master’s degree, allowing you to earn them quicker and for a reduced overall cost. E.g. Arizona State, which allows students to [double-count nine credit hours](https://scai.engineering.asu.edu/accelerated-masters-in-robotics-and-autonomous-systems-ai/) toward an MS in Robotics and Autonomous Systems (AI).
* **Academic-slanted programs:** Some programs have more of an academic focus than others, giving more opportunities to conduct independent research. For instance, Columbia is unusual in that it gives you the [option of writing an undergraduate thesis](https://bulletin.columbia.edu/columbia-engineering/academic-departments-programs/computer-science/undergraduate-programs/computer-science-bs/).

## AI Degree Curriculum

Once you have your shortlist of practically viable candidates, you can start looking in earnest at program content. While there is no definitive “best” AI curriculum, top technical programs tend to share a rough structure along these lines:

#### Year 1 – Foundations

**Focus: Programming, math basics, and computational thinking.**

**Fall Semester**

* Introduction to Programming (Python or Java)
* Calculus I
* Discrete Mathematics I
* Introduction to Computer Systems
* First-Year Writing / Composition

**Spring Semester**

* Data Structures & Algorithms I
* Calculus II
* Linear Algebra (intro)
* Discrete Mathematics II
* Ethics in Technology (intro)

#### Year 2 – Core Computer Science & Math

**Focus: Building the technical backbone for AI.**

**Fall Semester**

* Data Structures & Algorithms II
* Probability & Statistics for Computing
* Computer Organization / Architecture
* Linear Algebra (advanced applications)
* General Education Elective

**Spring Semester**

* Software Engineering
* Database Systems
* Theory of Computation (intro)
* Numerical Methods or Optimization
* General Education Elective

#### Year 3 – Core AI & Machine Learning

**Focus: Core AI techniques and applied modeling.**

**Fall Semester**

* Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
* Machine Learning (supervised learning, regression, classification)
* Probability & Statistical Modeling (advanced)
* Human-Computer Interaction
* AI Lab I (project-based)

**Spring Semester**

* Deep Learning
* Natural Language Processing
* Computer Vision
* Reinforcement Learning (intro)
* AI Lab II (team-based project)

#### Year 4 – Specialization & Practice

**Focus: Advanced topics, research, and real-world application.**

**Fall Semester**

Advanced AI electives, e.g:

* Robotics
* Knowledge Representation & Reasoning
* AI for Healthcare / Finance
* AI Ethics & Policy
* Big Data Systems / Distributed Computing
* Generative AI
* Technical Elective
* Capstone Project I

**Spring Semester**

* AI Systems Design (deployment, scaling)
* Explainable AI / Trustworthy AI
* Technical Elective
* Internship or Research Practicum
* Capstone Project II

**Pro Tip:** Looking specifically at upper-division (third and fourth year) courses will be the most useful comparator when choosing an AI degree. They should be primarily populated by dedicated AI units, ideally with opportunities for internships and practical projects.

### 5 Things To Look For In An AI Program

Even if you think you already have a clear choice, it’s worth running through these factors as a final check. The best AI degrees should have:

* **Respected faculty:** Being taught by faculty who **have a track record of publishing AI research** is a sure sign of program quality. Courses taught by genuine subject-matter specialists are likely to be AI-led rather than merely AI-branded, and are also more likely to be kept up to date with new industry developments. For example, Danqi Chen is listed on the [Princeton faculty page](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/people/faculty) as an associate professor researching machine learning and natural language processing; she has numerous papers published within the last two years, including a [2025 paper on the surprising effectiveness of negative reinforcement in LLM reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.01347).
* **Opportunities for networking:** Programs that include internships are really valuable, not only for **providing workplace experience** but also for building industry connections. A good example is Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, where students typically work for a semester and a summer at [large firms like IBM, Microsoft, and Google](https://compsci.rpi.edu/student-resources/prospective-students). The best schools also provide other networking opportunities, like the [fall and spring career expos](https://csweb.rice.edu/academics/undergraduate-programs/opportunities) at Rice University.
* **Careers assistance:** Schools **should provide help and support** in making the next step post-graduation, whether that’s applying for jobs or further study. For instance, USC offers [advising appointments, workshops, resume reviews and interview prep](https://viterbicareers.usc.edu/students/), as well as a [dedicated jobs board](https://viterbicareers.usc.edu/students/handshake/).
* **Strong graduate outcomes:** Many institutions publish graduate outcomes data. When available, it is very valuable: if an AI degree program is demonstrably producing reliable, well-paid job opportunities, that is clearly a point in its favor. For instance, [94% of 2025 AI graduates from Carnegie Mellon are employed or in continuing education](https://www.cmu.edu/career/outcomes/post-grad-dashboard.html), with an average salary of $145,500.
  + Because so many AI programs are newly-offered, program-level data is rare for the time being, but you can still assess school-wide graduation rates and first destinations. For example, [82% of 2025 Berkeley grads](https://career.berkeley.edu/start-exploring/where-do-cal-grads-go/) across all majors are in work or continuing education, with a median salary of $100,000.
* **Good student reviews:** It’s easy to overlook anecdotal evidence when deciding on a program, but reviews and Reddit posts are invaluable. Official material is always bound to be promotional, and can sometimes be out of date. By contrast, sites like Rate My Professors provide honest feedback on current faculty from real students.
  + Searching for your desired program + “Reddit” on Google is likely to bring up relevant and helpful forum discussion. You may even be able to find [direct comparisons between schools](https://www.reddit.com/r/ApplyingToCollege/comments/1jddqpm/umd_csmachine_learning_vs_purdue_ai/) on your shortlist.

Remember to also consider factors that specifically apply to your individual preferences and circumstances, e.g. flexible admissions, delivery formats, thesis options etc.

## Who Should Get an AI Degree?

As with any bachelor’s degree, most applicants for an AI degree are likely to be recent high school graduates. But there are programs available that suit a variety of different circumstances:

* **High-school grads aiming for AI/ML roles:** If you’re coming out of high school with ambitions to be a machine learning engineer, AI software developer, or data analyst, an AI degree is your most directly relevant option. **Many programs will give you direct industry exposure** alongside your study.
* **“Traditional” computer science students:** With all of the hype, students who may otherwise have leaned toward a computer science major may now be wondering about an AI degree instead. There are plenty of excellent CS majors with a concentration in AI that give you elements of both. Just make sure the curriculum strikes the right balance for what you want to get out of it.
* **Career changers:** If you want to get into AI but you’re coming from a field with minimal relevance, a bachelor’s degree is an efficient way of gaining expertise, and demonstrating it to potential employers.
* **Aspiring academics:** AI research is evolving all the time, and some bachelor’s programs give you genuine exposure to that research. 4+1 programs can accelerate your route to a master’s, setting you on a path to a career in academia.
* **Career-focused non-technical applicants:** While the options on this list are unlikely to be right for you if you don’t have a STEM background or interest, some kind of applied AI degree program may be appropriate in helping you to get ahead in your chosen field.

### Do I Need a Degree to Get a Job In AI?

You don’t necessarily need an AI degree in order to get a job in the field. After all, dedicated AI bachelor’s degree programs are relatively new, and the vast majority of current practitioners therefore do not hold AI degrees.

On the other hand, the scarcity of graduates means a bachelor’s degree in AI is currently a **super-valuable differentiator**. That could change as more and more people earn the degree ([which is now offered at 193 US institutions](https://programs.com/resources/universities-offering-ai-programs/)), but for the time being, it’s a reasonably reliable pathway into a booming field.

Nevertheless, you may prefer to specialize later on in your education with an advanced degree. This can keep your options open. Possible alternative routes include:

* Computer science bachelor’s → AI master’s → **job in AI**
* Computer science bachelor’s → AI-adjacent graduate role + certifications (e.g. [AWS Certified AI Practitioner](https://aws.amazon.com/certification/certified-ai-practitioner)) → **job in AI**
* Entry-level tech role → progression to software engineering → **job in AI** (e.g. ML engineer)
* Non-technical bachelor’s → graduate role → AI self-study + certifications → begin to apply AI within your role → **job in AI**

But a good AI degree will both develop and certify your AI expertise in a single step, setting you on the most direct path to a career in AI. And if you’ve chosen a good program, employers will respect your degree even if you decide to pursue roles in another sector.

# Best Colleges for Artificial Intelligence (AI) Majors

Written By [Jennifer Stephan](/insights?author=6099476213b7a46675163310)

![Colorful (bright yellow, red, blue, and white) geometric figure with many lines and nested torii representing artificial intelligence (AI).](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/60747c1408a64f1d25ed83b2/1711931846839-J4P0KY9Z73G4BPW0HDHR/artificial-intelligence-programs)

From abstract patterns to real-world impact: where to study AI in college.

***Editor's Note:*** *This guide was originally published in March 2025 and has been substantially updated to reflect developments in AI education through August 2026.*

Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are now embedded in nearly every sector of the modern economy, from healthcare and finance to media, defense, education, and transportation. It is no surprise that students are increasingly asking whether they should major in AI.

Although interest in artificial intelligence is exploding, only a small number of U.S. colleges currently offer a standalone undergraduate major in AI. The vast majority of colleges prepare students for AI careers through computer science, engineering, data science, or interdisciplinary pathways rather than through a standalone AI degree.

Understanding the difference between a formal AI degree and an AI-focused pathway within another major is critical for families building a thoughtful college list. Below, we’ll clarify what students actually study in AI programs, where those programs exist, how they compare to computer science, and how to think strategically about preparing for a career in artificial intelligence.

## What You’ll Learn in This Article

By the end of this article, you’ll know:

* What AI is and why it matters for students today
* The colleges currently offering formal AI majors
* How AI compares to CS and other STEM majors (and how to choose)

Table of Contents

1. [What is Artificial Intelligence?](#what1)
2. [What Kind of Jobs Can You Get in AI? Is it A Growing Field?](#what2)
3. [What do Students Study When They Major in AI?](#what3)
4. [What Are Some Focus Areas Within an AI Degree?](#what4)
5. [Where Can You Get a Degree in AI?](#where)
6. [The Future of AI Majors at U.S. Colleges](#future)
7. [Do You Have to Major in Artificial Intelligence to be Prepared For Careers in AI?](#do)
8. [What Should You be Looking For in AI and CS Colleges?](#what5)
9. [What Other College Majors Besides AI and CS Can Prepare You For a Career in AI?](#what6)
10. [How do I Choose Between AI, CS, or Other STEM Majors?](#how)
11. [What Else is Valuable to Learn When Studying AI?](#what7)
12. [Are There Non-Technical Pathways to Contribute to AI?](#are)
13. [Continue Exploring](#continue)
14. [Frequently Asked Questions about AI Majors](#faq)

## What is Artificial Intelligence?

Artificial intelligence (AI) is a field of study that **uses technology to create machines that can perform tasks that typically require human intelligence**. AI uses mathematics, statistics, and computational logic to simulate human reasoning and decision-making. AI systems learn by identifying patterns and relationships in large amounts of data, often using algorithms to guide their analysis and decision-making.

## What Kind of Jobs Can You Get in AI? Is it A Growing Field?

There are **many career opportunities** in a **wide range of applications and domains**. Become a big data analyst, scientist or engineer, user experience (UX) designer or developer, researcher, AI engineer (machine learning, software, robotics, computer vision, natural language processing), business intelligence developer, AI ethicist, prompt engineer, AI product manager, and more! Work in exciting domains of financial services, healthcare, technology, media, marketing, government and military, national security, IoT-enabled systems, agriculture, gaming, and retail.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is a **rapidly growing field**, with high demand for skilled professionals due to its increasing adoption across industries and the rapid advancements in AI technology.

## What do Students Study When They Major in AI?

Typically, an AI degree includes:

* **Foundational math courses** such as calculus, probability and statistics, linear algebra, and discrete math;
* **Foundational computing concepts**, including introduction to programming, data structures, algorithm design, and programming languages;
* **Advanced computing concepts** like robotics, machine learning, signals and systems, big data, optimization and control, symbolic computation, computer graphics, human-computer interaction, decision-making, and vision, perception, and language processing; and
* **Related electives from the disciplines of ethics, social responsibility, cognitive science, linguistics, psychology, and philosophy**.

## What Are Some Focus Areas Within an AI Degree?

Students may be asked to focus their studies within the curriculum. Some examples of possible focus areas include:

### Robotics

Design, construct, and program physical machines capable of performing tasks autonomously or semi-autonomously.

### Computer vision

Enable computers to interpret and understand visual information from the real world.

### Language processing

Enable computers to understand human language as it's spoken and written.

### Machine learning

Develop algorithms which allow computers to learn from data and improve performance over time without explicit programming.

### Deep learning

Subset of machine learning which uses artificial neural networks with multiple layers to learn intricate patterns in large data sets.

### Data and society, including ethics

Study of  the societal impacts and ethical considerations surrounding the collection, analysis, and application of AI and data-driven technologies.

### Cognitive computing

Develop systems that mimic human thought processes, such as perception, reasoning, and decision-making.

### Neural networks

Work with computational models inspired by the structure and function of the human brain, utilized in various AI applications for pattern recognition and decision-making.

### Specialized domains such as healthcare, education, or transportation

Develop and apply AI techniques tailored to specific industries or fields, such as healthcare (medical diagnosis), education (personalized learning), or transportation (autonomous vehicles).

### Hardware

While most AI programs focus on software, some universities offer AI hardware specializations within their electrical and computer engineering or computer science programs, where students learn to design the advanced chips and computing systems that power AI.

**Quick Fact**  
Only a relatively small number of U.S. colleges currently offer a formal AI major — but many computer science programs allow students to specialize in artificial intelligence through tracks, concentrations, or interdisciplinary programs, and the number of formal AI majors is growing.

## Where Can You Get a Degree in AI?

1. ### [Bentley University](https://www.bentley.edu/) - [Artificial Intelligence for Innovation BS degree](https://www.bentley.edu/academics/undergraduate-programs/artificial-intelligence)

   This innovative degree combines AI with business. It includes critical reflection on AI’s ethical, social, and societal implications and encompasses computer programming/technology, math and data, human aspects (humanities and social sciences), and business.
2. ### [Carnegie Mellon University (CMU)](https://www.cmu.edu/) - [Bachelor of Science degree in Artificial Intelligence](http://coursecatalog.web.cmu.edu/schools-colleges/schoolofcomputerscience/artificialintelligence/) through the [School of Computer Science](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/)

   The curriculum includes coursework in computer science (CS), math, statistics, computational modeling, machine learning, symbolic computation, ethics and social responsibility. Students will have the computer science skills CMU students are famous for, with the added expertise in machine learning and automated reasoning needed to advance the field of AI.
3. ### [Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT)](https://www.mit.edu/) - [Bachelor of Science in Artificial Intelligence and Decision Making](https://catalog.mit.edu/degree-charts/artifical-intelligence-decision-making-course-6-4/)

   The curriculum includes coursework in computer science and math and courses in data-centric, model-centric, decision-centric, computation-centric, and human-centric areas of study. It also includes a communications-intensive course.

## The Future of AI Majors at U.S. Colleges

Families should keep an eye on colleges making bold new investments in AI, as these initiatives often bring new majors, research opportunities, and career pathways for undergraduates.

A December 2025 [*New York Times* article](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/12/01/technology/college-computer-science-ai-boom.html?smid=nytcore-ios-share) underscores this trend, noting that colleges nationwide are rapidly expanding AI-driven programs as student demand surges and employers seek graduates with both technical fluency and interdisciplinary training. Many institutions are rethinking the structure of their computer science departments altogether to accommodate new AI-focused pathways and research directions.

In 2023, my alma mater, [Johns Hopkins University](https://www.jhu.edu/), announced a major new [Data Science and AI Institute](https://engineering.jhu.edu/Datascience-AI/?utm_source=Inside+Higher+Ed&utm_campaign=382bfc575f-DNU_2021_COPY_03&utm_medium=email&utm_term=0_1fcbc04421-382bfc575f-199446093&mc_cid=382bfc575f&mc_eid=f3a4521741) — an extraordinary investment that will shape future undergraduate programs and opportunities.

And in March 2025, [Bowdoin College](https://www.bowdoin.edu/) received a $50 million gift to establish the [Hastings Initiative for AI and Humanity](https://www.bowdoin.edu/news/2025/03/announcing-the-hastings-initiative-for-ai-and-humanity.html), funding new faculty hires, faculty support, and expanded opportunities for student research and engagement.

The pace of institutional investment in AI accelerated even further in 2026. In May 2026, the [University of Southern California received a $200 million gift](https://www.forbes.com/sites/michaeltnietzel/2026/05/05/university-of-southern-california-receives-200-million-mega-gift-for-ai/?utm_campaign=ForbesMainFB&utm_source=ForbesMainFacebook&utm_medium=social&fbclid=IwY2xjawRr_CtleHRuA2FlbQIxMABicmlkETFQZ204SU1HSGR6T0RjNFhac3J0YwZhcHBfaWQQMjIyMDM5MTc4ODIwMDg5MgABHiHUlxgIUE3wTx-SLSBu9PPb1khXE2Fk2QF9kpkjloUPMVPeGpiHhMkh78xl_aem_YVdp6onc4f6_3d2lCoHeUQ) to support a major interdisciplinary AI initiative spanning engineering, health sciences, business, security, and the arts. USC announced a new [Bachelor of Science in Artificial Intelligence](https://viterbischool.usc.edu/news/2025/08/usc-viterbi-school-of-engineering-and-the-usc-school-of-advanced-computing-launch-an-undergraduate-degree-in-artificial-intelligence/) launching in Fall 2026. More universities are also introducing new undergraduate AI degrees. [Northwestern University announced a new AI major](https://www.mccormick.northwestern.edu/computer-science/academics/undergraduate/ai-major/) through its McCormick School of Engineering. Students may pursue it either as a Bachelor of Science in Engineering major or as a second major from any Northwestern undergraduate school. Kennesaw State University announced a new [Bachelor of Science in Artificial Intelligence](https://www.kennesaw.edu/news/stories/2026/ksu-launch-bachelor-science-artificial-intelligence-fall-2026.php) that combines a core computing foundation with interdisciplinary study through a required minor in an application area. Additionally, the University of Wisconsin–Madison is launching a new [College of Computing and Artificial Intelligence](https://cai.wisc.edu/) backed by more than $100 million in private gifts. These developments reflect how quickly universities are reorganizing around AI research, education, and workforce development.

Of the top 10 AI undergraduate programs in the U.S., only MIT and Carnegie Mellon offer formal AI majors. The rest prepare students through computer science programs with tracks, threads, concentrations, or minors to support specialization in AI.

## Do You Have to Major in Artificial Intelligence to be Prepared For Careers in AI?

**No!** Students can often be extremely well prepared through a typical undergraduate computer science degree (see our [complete guide to computer science admissions](/insights/college-application-process-for-cs-majors)) by making course selections to ensure they are learning key AI concepts.

Foundational math and computing concepts are not a concern because such courses are required for both CS and AI degrees. While the two degrees -CS and AI- may diverge at the upper levels and outside of core science, engineering, and math classes, in most BSCS degrees, students can choose how to fulfill many of their course requirements.

A student pursuing a BSCS degree who wants to become an expert in AI should choose these elective courses carefully to include important AI concepts like robotics, machine learning, signals and systems, big data, optimization and control, symbolic computation, computer graphics, human-computer interaction, decision-making, and vision, perception, and language processing. Similarly, they should use the freedom they have to select humanities, arts, and social sciences electives to include courses on ethics, social responsibility, cognitive science, linguistics, psychology, and philosophy.

Indeed, **of the ten** [**top AI undergraduate programs**](https://www.usnews.com/best-colleges/rankings/computer-science/artificial-intelligence)**, only CMU and MIT offer formal AI degrees.** Eight do not: [Stanford University](https://www.stanford.edu/), the [University of California, Berkeley](https://www.berkeley.edu/), [Georgia Institute of Technology](https://www.gatech.edu/), the [University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign](https://illinois.edu/), the [University of Washington, Seattle](https://www.washington.edu/), [Cornell University](https://www.cornell.edu/), [California Institute of Technology](https://www.caltech.edu/), and the [University of Texas at Austin](https://www.utexas.edu/)!

Some CS programs have a formal track, thread, concentration, or minor to support specialization in AI. Examples:

* Stanford’s Computer Science department offers [ten tracks](https://www.cs.stanford.edu/bachelors-compsci-tracks-overview), one of which is AI.
* GA Tech’s Computer Science department outlines seven [threads](https://catalog.gatech.edu/programs/computer-science-bs/#threadstext), one of which is Intelligence.
* At UT Austin students can pursue one of [seven concentrations](https://www.cs.utexas.edu/undergraduate-program/academics/concentrations), including [Machine Learning & Artificial Intelligence](https://www.cs.utexas.edu/concentrations/mlai).
* At [Case Western Reserve University](https://case.edu/), BSCS students may elect one of [six areas of specialization](https://engineering.case.edu/computer-and-data-sciences/academics/computer-science/bachelor-science), one of which is AI.
* [Duke University](https://duke.edu/) offers a [BS CS Concentration in AI and Machine Learning](https://cs.duke.edu/undergraduate/degrees/BS/concentrations/ai-ml).
* [UMass Dartmouth](https://www.umassd.edu/) has a [BS CS Concentration in AI](https://www.umassd.edu/programs/artificial-intelligence/).

## What Else is Valuable to Learn When Studying AI?

The 2024 Atlantic article, [Universities Have a Computer-Science Problem](https://www.theatlantic.com/technology/archive/2024/03/computing-college-cs-majors/677792/), raises good questions about the consequences of placing computer science within an engineering school or making it an independent college, as CMU, GA Tech, MIT, and Cornell have done and UC Berkeley recently announced it would do. It argues that CS students, including those studying AI, should not be isolated from other disciplines.

The author, [Washington University in St. Louis](https://wustl.edu/) Professor of Film & Media Studies and Professor of CS & Engineering Ian Bogost, poses a critical question, “whether computing ought to be seen as a superfield that lords over all others, or just a servant of other domains, subordinated to their interests and control?” The answer to this question has important implications for students and, of course, society at large! A stand-alone Computer Science department can define its own requirements, such as the extent to which a student will be broadly educated about the context of their work — or not.

That’s why these structural decisions matter. They point to a deeper question: How should we educate future technologists—not just in terms of skills, but in how they think and act? For an exploration of how interdisciplinary, ethics-centered programs are preparing students for an AI-shaped world, see my article [How Liberal Arts Engineering Degrees Prepare Students for an AI Future.](/insights/how-liberal-arts-engineering-degrees-prepare-students-for-an-ai-future)

Professor Bogost spoke with Charles Isbell, a former dean of Georgia Tech’s College of Computing and now the provost at the [University of Wisconsin-Madison](https://www.wisc.edu/), who warns that “setting up colleges of computing ‘absolutely runs the risk’ of empowering a generation of professionals who may already be disengaged from consequences to train the next one in their image.”

Likewise, a January 2025 [Chronicle of Higher Education article about AI](https://www.chronicle.com/article/flaws-in-ai-are-deciding-your-future-heres-how-to-fix-them?utm_source=Iterable&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=campaign_12331990_nl_Academe-Today_date_20250117) argues that the field “needs experts who deeply understand the specific domains they are designed to influence.” The author, [NYU](https://www.google.com/search?client=firefox-b-1-d&q=new+york+university) professor Rumi Chunara, goes on to say, “To create AI systems that truly serve humanity, we need experts from all fields, not just computer science, actively involved in their development.”

I am reminded that when I was a professor of CS at [Wellesley College](https://www.wellesley.edu/) in the 2000s, CS enrollments were at a nadir. It is hard to believe given the state of CS enrollments now, but the department struggled to fill CS classes, and CS students asked us for help talking with their parents about their choice to major in CS — parents were worried that their children would not have a job upon graduation due to outsourcing jobs to other countries.

In response, we created materials about our graduates’ job placement rates for students and the [valuable skills learned through a liberal arts education](https://hbr.org/2019/09/yes-employers-do-value-liberal-arts-degrees) to share with their parents: **oral and written communication, critical and quantitative thinking, advocacy, ethical judgment, and working effectively in teams.** We reassured them that the technical jobs that required these skills would not be the ones outsourced. Also, these skills would be valuable in any future field, including technical ones. If anyone needs evidence of this, look to MIT’s president, Sally Kornbluth, who has a BA degree in political science from [Williams College](https://www.williams.edu/)!

## Are There Non-Technical Pathways to Contribute to AI?

Absolutely. As NYU CS and Biostatistics professor Rumi Chunara [argues](https://www.chronicle.com/article/flaws-in-ai-are-deciding-your-future-heres-how-to-fix-them), “To create AI systems that truly serve humanity, we need experts from all fields, not just computer science, actively involved in their development.”

As AI becomes a more significant part of our society, there will undoubtedly be a **massive need for people of all skill sets and academic backgrounds who understand how AI works, its limitations, and how to use AI responsibly**. We are already seeing lawyers who specialize in AI, AI ethicists in business and medicine, non-technical AI researchers, experts in using AI for sales, marketing, and social media, AI artists and writers, prompt-engineers, and more.

Take particular notice of the Chinese start-up DeepSeek, which [employs “data omniscients” to improve the quality of the content of AI algorithms](https://www.scmp.com/tech/big-tech/article/3300820/deepseeks-small-team-liberal-arts-graduates-transforms-ai-text-generation-china?utm_medium=Social&utm_content=visual-style&utm_source=Facebook&utm_source=copy-link&utm_campaign=3300820&utm_medium=share_widget&fbclid=IwY2xjawI0HcZleHRuA2FlbQIxMQABHdoBIhL8AFjrZWR_eqA0vHXPkp9nosG0eMiQwKctgy0Z6z2sCWKG9T7lcQ_aem_A00MI_OicDVmFU_WnAeSeg) using their backgrounds in literature and social sciences.

## Frequently Asked Questions about AI Majors

### Is artificial intelligence a real undergraduate major?

Yes. While still relatively new, a growing number of U.S. universities now offer formal undergraduate degrees in artificial intelligence. Many others offer AI specializations within computer science, engineering, or data science programs.

### How is an AI major different from computer science?

Computer science provides a broad foundation in computing theory, systems, and programming. AI majors often focus more specifically on machine learning, data modeling, neural networks, and applied artificial intelligence systems.

### Is it better to major in AI or computer science?

In most cases, computer science remains the more flexible degree. AI majors can be excellent for students with a strong interest in machine learning and intelligent systems, but students should evaluate long-term adaptability and program structure carefully.

### Are AI majors harder to get into than computer science?

Currently, many AI majors are newer and may be less saturated than computer science. However, this may change as demand grows. Students should evaluate competitiveness at each institution individually.

### What math do you need for an AI major?

Students typically need strong preparation in calculus, linear algebra, probability, and statistics. Mathematical maturity is critical for success in advanced AI coursework.

Whether a student pursues a formal AI major or builds toward AI through computer science, the application strategy matters — and most families are navigating it without a clear inside view of how these programs evaluate candidates. args.summary:
This article from Lantern College Counseling provides a comprehensive guide for students interested in studying artificial intelligence (AI) at the undergraduate level. It clarifies that only a small number of U.S. colleges currently offer a standalone AI major, with most students preparing for AI careers through computer science, engineering, or data science programs with AI specializations.

**Key points covered:**

- AI majors typically include foundational math (calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics), computing concepts (programming, data structures, algorithms), advanced topics (machine learning, robotics, computer vision, natural language processing), and ethics/humanities electives.
- Focus areas within AI include robotics, computer vision, natural language processing, machine learning, deep learning, ethics, cognitive computing, neural networks, specialized domains, and hardware.
- **Colleges offering formal AI majors (as of August 2026):** Bentley University, Carnegie Mellon University, MIT, University of Pennsylvania, UC San Diego, Dakota State University, Drake University, Ferris State University, Illinois Institute of Technology, Indiana University-Bloomington, Keiser University, Long Island University, Purdue University (BS and BA options), University of South Florida (starting fall 2025), USC (starting fall 2026), Northwestern University, and Kennesaw State University.
- **Notable:** Of the top 10 AI undergraduate programs per U.S. News, only MIT and CMU offer formal AI majors. The rest (Stanford, UC Berkeley, Georgia Tech, UIUC, UW Seattle, Cornell, Caltech, UT Austin) prepare students through CS programs with AI tracks.
- Students do NOT need a formal AI major to work in AI; a well-chosen CS degree with AI-focused electives is often sufficient.
- Non-technical pathways (e.g., law, ethics, philosophy, liberal arts degrees) are also valuable for contributing to the AI field.
- The article discusses the importance of interdisciplinary education versus standalone computing colleges, citing experts who warn against isolating CS/AI students from other disciplines.
- Recent institutional investments include USC's $200M gift (2026), Bowdoin's $50M Hastings Initiative (2025), and UW-Madison's new College of Computing and AI.

Prepare for a career developing and improving the groundbreaking technology that promises to have a profound impact on every industry and area of life with Adelphi’s AI degree program.

## Why Earn a BS in Artificial Intelligence?

The age of artificial intelligence (AI) is here, as companies, organizations and governments worldwide are racing to create the technology to improve quality of life, enhance revenue and generate breakthrough solutions. Opportunities are abundant and growing for software engineers who can extend AI’s vast potential and use its algorithms responsibly in new applications. Our bachelor of science in artificial intelligence will allow students to get a headstart in this rapidly growing field.

## Why Earn Your BS in Artificial Intelligence at Adelphi?

* Learn to design, build and improve artificial intelligence algorithms from the multidisciplinary perspective of mathematics, statistics and computer science.
* Benefit from Adelphi’s long-held commitment to student success and the accessibility and expertise of the Department of Mathematics and Computer Science faculty.
* Learn in small classes of fewer than 25 students and enjoy extensive support in foundational AI degree courses in New York.

## Minors and Accelerated Degree Options

![](https://www.adelphi.edu/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/shutterstock_2283147071-740x494.jpg)  

### Minor in Artificial Intelligence

Artificial intelligence is changing nearly every industry, making an AI minor invaluable—no matter what your major is. Whether you are studying business, the sciences, communications or the humanities, you will get a head start in this rapidly growing field. Gain a competitive edge by learning from the multidisciplinary perspective of mathematics, statistics or computer science.

[Minor in Artificial Intelligence Requirements](https://catalog.adelphi.edu/preview_program.php?catoid=41&poid=22189&returnto=2493)

![](https://www.adelphi.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/Adelphi_MachineLearning-740x494.jpg)  

### Minor in Applied AI in Business

The era of AI has arrived and applications are ubiquitous across business functions and industries. This six-course minor will teach you how and when to responsibly apply generative and agentic AI to create value. You will work hands on with chatbots, build semiautonomous agents and discuss ethical considerations of AI’s use in business.

[Minor in Applied AI in Business Requirements](https://catalog.adelphi.edu/preview_program.php?catoid=41&poid=22186)

![](https://www.adelphi.edu/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/COACH_Teachers_2019_SG_47-740x494.jpg)  

### Scholar Teacher Education Program (STEP)

Students in this program are also eligible to enter STEP, which allows you to earn a master’s degree and prepare for teacher certification with one additional year, saving you time and tuition costs.

[Learn More about STEP](https://www.adelphi.edu/program/undergraduate/step/)

![STEM-Designated Badge](https://www.adelphi.edu/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/STEM-Designated-Badge.png)

This program is STEM-designated, offering specialized training in high-demand fields, and eligible international students can extend their OPT to 36 months.

[Adelphi’s STEM-designated Programs](https://www.adelphi.edu/international-services/employment-volunteering/opt/stem-designated-degree-programs/)
