You are tasked with summarizing the raw content of a webpage retrieved from a web search. Your goal is to create a summary that preserves the most important information from the original web page. This summary will be used by a downstream research agent, so it's crucial to maintain the key details without losing essential information.

Here is the raw content of the webpage:

<webpage_content>
[Explore Programs](/programs)

# The Latest AI in Education Statistics (2026)

AI is now ubiquitous in education.

[The vast majority of students](https://programs.com/resources/students-using-ai/), teachers, researchers, administrators, and other education professionals have used AI tools at least once.

[Generative AI](https://programs.com/resources/generative-ai-in-cybersecurity/) can have significant benefits for teachers and students. However, there are legitimate concerns about potential drawbacks. And most wish they had more support or guidance on how to use or teach AI.

So is AI ultimately helpful in the world of education? Or is it a net negative? What tools are students and teachers turning to, how are they using them, and what do they think of it all?

This article covers over 125 statistics, trends, and surveys on the state of AI’s current impact on education.

## Editor’s picks

* The global AI education market will be worth **$136.79 billion** by 2035.
* **30%** of K-12 students use AI tools at least once per day.
* **53%** of K-12 students use AI for help with homework, while **51%** of university students use AI to save time.
* **65%** of students agree that the way they’re assessed is changing due to generative AI.
* Just **7%** of schools worldwide have AI guidance, and of those that do, **40%** have only informal guidance.
* **60%** of educators use AI, with education leaders the most likely to do so.
* **43%** of teachers buy AI tools with their own money, and **89%** prefer these tools to cost less than $10 per month.
* **59%** of educators would like “train the trainer” programs to help them teach AI.
* **82%** of students think knowing how to use AI properly is important for their future.
* **88%** of teachers think genAI will positively affect their students’ careers.
* Teachers who regularly use AI save an average of **6 weeks** per school year.
* **81%** of educators lack the time to develop an AI training curriculum, and **75%** lack the knowledge to do so.

## AI education market size statistics

### The AI education market is valued at an estimated $9.58 billion ([Precedence Research](https://www.precedenceresearch.com/ai-in-education-market))

AI is already being used in education at scale.

The largest deployment segment is cloud, with 57% of the market share. The largest component segment is solution (72%), the largest technology segment is machine learning (64%), and the largest application segment is learning platform and virtual facilitators (47%).

Expect to see even more use cases in the future.

### The AI education market will be worth $42.48 billion in 2030 ([The Business Research Company](https://www.thebusinessresearchcompany.com/report/ai-in-education-global-market-report#))

That’s based on a projected compound annual growth rate of 41.5%, an increase from the 40.9% forcecast between 2025 and 2026.

### The AI education market will be worth $136.79 billion by 2035 ([Precedence Research](https://www.precedenceresearch.com/ai-in-education-market))

That’s based on a market of $7.05 billion in 2025 with a compound annual growth rate of 34.52%. Precedence Research called that CAGR “remarkable.”

### The US AI education market is worth $2.73 billion ([Precedence Research](https://www.precedenceresearch.com/ai-in-education-market))

North America is the largest sector of the global AI education market.

### By 2035, the US AI education market will be worth $39.83 billion ([Precedence Research](https://www.precedenceresearch.com/ai-in-education-market))

That’s based on a CAGR of 34.8%, a little higher than the CAGR for the global AI education market.

## K-12 student use of AI statistics

### Over half of US students aged 13 to 17 have used AI for research purposes ([Pew Research](https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2026/02/24/how-teens-use-and-view-ai/))

The top reason for using AI is to search for information (57%). This is followed by help with schoolwork (54%), fun or entertainment (47%), and summarizing articles, books, or videos.

### 15% of students admit they use ChatGPT without permission from their teacher ([Walton Family Foundation](https://www.waltonfamilyfoundation.org/chatgpt-used-by-teachers-more-than-students-new-survey-from-walton-family-foundation-finds?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

It’s somewhat common for educational institutions to ban the use of AI tools. But that doesn’t stop many students from using them. There are presumably more students who use AI tools without permission who are not willing to admit it, too.

### 30% of students use AI daily ([Microsoft](https://cdn-dynmedia-1.microsoft.com/is/content/microsoftcorp/microsoft/bade/documents/products-and-services/en-us/education/2025-Microsoft-AI-in-Education-Report.pdf))

This figure is likely to increase as AI tools become more powerful and commonplace.

### 96% of younger students think digital learning tools are fun ([New Schools](https://www.newschools.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/Gallup-Ed-Tech-Use-in-Schools-2.pdf))

Engaging younger students is crucial. Digital learning tools, including those powered by AI, can be a great resource for improving student engagement.

### Around 1 in 3 educational institutions offer students AI training ([Amazon](https://assets.aboutamazon.com/95/62/8ab96f0a4127acd0a2e31ce59db2/amazon-accelerating-ai-skills-through-education-survey-tennessee.pdf))

Of those institutions, just 19% incorporate AI skills training. That means just 5.89% of educational institutions offer AI skills training to students.

## Differences in which students use AI tools

### 95% of students now use AI ([HEPI](https://www.hepi.ac.uk/reports/student-generative-ai-survey-2026/))

AI use is now borderline universal among students. As many as 94% report using generative AI to help with assessed work.

Although relatively low, the proportion of students directly including AI-generated text in assessed work continues to increase. As of 2026, this figure stands at 12%, up from 8% in 2025 and 3% in 2024.

### Students in grades 11 to 12 are twice as likely to use ChatGPT as students in grades 7 to 8 ([Pew Research](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2024/05/15/a-quarter-of-u-s-teachers-say-ai-tools-do-more-harm-than-good-in-k-12-education/sr_24-05-15_ai-in-class_3/))

A little under a quarter of students in grades 11 and 12 (24%) reported using ChatGPT. In grades 9 and 10, that figure is 17%; in grades 7 and 8, 12%. Note that these figures are for students who’ve heard of ChatGPT. Those who haven’t were excluded.

### Just 1% of university students and faculty in China never use AI tools ([Technology Review](https://www.technologyreview.com/2025/07/28/1120747/chinese-universities-ai-use/))

The pervasiveness of AI tools in China’s universities might be a reflection of the country’s high optimism toward AI in general. That’s interesting, considering [multiple research](https://www.tortoisemedia.com/data/global-ai) [projects have China lagging behind the US](https://hai.stanford.edu/news/global-ai-power-rankings-stanford-hai-tool-ranks-36-countries-in-ai) in terms of AI capacity, investment, deployment, etc.

### Students who study 3+ hours per weeknight are 11% more likely to have used an AI chatbot ([Quizlet](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/quizlets-state-of-ai-in-education-survey-reveals-teachers-are-surprise-ai-champions-301884427.html))

61% of students who reported studying for one or two hours per weeknight said they’d used ChatGPT or a similar tool. 72% of students who study three or four hours per night said they’d used these tools.

### Black students are 12% more likely to use generative AI to get help with their homework compared to White students ([Common Sense Media](https://www.commonsensemedia.org/sites/default/files/research/report/2024-the-dawn-of-the-ai-era_final-release-for-web.pdf))

59% of Black students use generative AI for homework help. 47% of White students do the same. Black students are also more likely to use generative AI to get advice on a personal issue (25% compared to 14%) and help them write code (17% compared to 7%).

## Why students use AI

### Around 1 in 3 students use AI tools to help them get started on work, the most popular use case ([Microsoft](https://cdn-dynmedia-1.microsoft.com/is/content/microsoftcorp/microsoft/bade/documents/products-and-services/en-us/education/2025-Microsoft-AI-in-Education-Report.pdf))

AI can be a great tool for beating writer’s block or introducing yourself to a new topic.

Other popular use cases for AI among students are summarizing information (33%), getting answers more quickly than through other means (33%), receiving initial feedback on schoolwork (32%), helping with studying (30%), improving writing (28%), and making projects more visually appealing (25%).

### 51% of university students use AI to save time ([HEPI](https://www.hepi.ac.uk/reports/student-generative-ai-survey-2026/))

This isn’t unique to students. Saving time is one of the most common reasons people in general use AI. One [recent survey](https://www.adeccogroup.com/our-group/media/press-releases/ai-saves-workers-an-average-of-one-hour-each-day) found the average worker saves 1 hour per day thanks to AI. 5% of workers said AI saves them between 3 and 4 hours per day.

### 50% of university students use AI to improve the quality of their work ([HEPI](https://www.hepi.ac.uk/reports/student-generative-ai-survey-2025/))

Improving work is another common use case for AI among students. This also extends to the workplace. [One study](https://www.cnbc.com/2025/09/12/iwg-report-gen-z-employees-are-coaching-older-colleagues-to-use-ai.html) from June 2025 found that 76% of office workers think AI helps their careers. That figure rises to 87% among Gen Z office workers.

It also extends to teachers. For example, 74% of [teachers say](https://news.gallup.com/poll/691967/three-teachers-weekly-saving-six-weeks-year.aspx) AI improves the quality of administrative work. Interestingly, [research by Gallup](https://news.gallup.com/poll/691967/three-teachers-weekly-saving-six-weeks-year.aspx) finds that teachers who use AI more frequently are more likely to report that it improves the quality of their work.

### 44% of students use AI for research, the most common use case ([Quizlet via PR Newswire](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/quizlets-state-of-ai-in-education-survey-reveals-teachers-are-surprise-ai-champions-301884427.html))

AI tools can be excellent research aides. That use was followed by summarizing information (38% of students) and generating study guides or study materials (33%).

### Around 2 in 3 teachers say students use generative AI to write assignments ([Forbes](https://www.forbes.com/advisor/education/it-and-tech/artificial-intelligence-in-school/))

According to teachers, students are most likely to use AI to generate essays or other written assignments. 31% of teachers say students use AI chatbots during exams (including using the voice feature), to translate text (29%), and to generate code (28%).

### 59% of teenagers use generative AI to search for information or facts ([Common Sense Media](https://www.commonsensemedia.org/sites/default/files/research/report/commonsensemedia_generationai.pdf))

That made research the most common reason teenage students use AI.

Here’s the full list:

Help with homework (55%)  
Creating new images (39%)  
Brainstorming ideas (38%)  
Writing tasks (33%)  
Searching for personal advice (23%)  
Companionship (8%)  
Something else (5%)  
Don’t use AI (12%)  
Not sure (1%)  
  
Students interested in using AI effectively can benefit from structured learning paths, such as [associate’s](https://programs.com/programs/cybersecurity-associate-degree/) and [bachelor’s degree programs in cybersecurity](https://programs.com/programs/cybersecurity-bachelors-degrees/), which often teach foundational AI, data literacy, and ethical use of generative technologies.

### 67% of kids and teenagers are regular users of AI companions ([Common Sense Media](https://www.commonsensemedia.org/sites/default/files/research/report/commonsensemedia_generationai.pdf))

Broken down further, 69% of 15 to 17-year-olds use chatbots often/sometimes. That’s 4% higher than 12 to 14-year-olds (65%).

Boys (70%) are more likely to use AI than girls (64%).

## Changes in the use of AI in education

### The number of students who are regular users of genAI tools has increased by 17% since 2023 ([AIPRM](https://www.aiprm.com/ai-in-education-statistics) and [Tyton Partners via Illinois Department of Education](https://education.illinois.edu/about/news-events/news/article/2024/10/24/ai-in-schools--pros-and-cons))

In 2023, a survey by Tyton Partners found that 27% of students regularly used generative AI tools. By 2025, that figure had increased to 44%.

### 94% of students use generative AI for university assessments ([HEPI](https://www.hepi.ac.uk/reports/student-generative-ai-survey-2026/))

In 2024, a narrow majority (53%) of university students in the UK used genAI tools while completing their assessments. In 2025, that figure leaped to 88%, and has cotnued to rise to 94% in 2026.

### 65% of university students say the way they are assessed has changed a lot because of generative AI ([HEPI](https://www.hepi.ac.uk/reports/student-generative-ai-survey-2026/))

Generative AI tools have revolutionized how schoolwork is assessed. AI tools can assess work themselves, but also necessitate different assessment procedures due to how they can be used by students to cheat.

### 133% more university students believe their institution’s staff are well-equipped to work with AI than in 2024 ([HEPI](https://www.hepi.ac.uk/reports/student-generative-ai-survey-2025/))

In 2024, just 18% of university students thought their institution’s staff were well-equipped to work with AI tools. By 2025, that had increased to 42%.

## Rules surrounding the use of AI in education

### Teachers are 3.8x more likely to allow students to use ChatGPT than to catch them using it when it is forbidden ([Walton Family Foundation](https://www.waltonfamilyfoundation.org/chatgpt-used-by-teachers-more-than-students-new-survey-from-walton-family-foundation-finds?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

38% of teachers allow their students to use ChatGPT, while 10% say they’ve caught their students using it when not allowed.

### Just 13% of universities around the world have institutional guidance or policies regarding AI tools ([UNESCO](https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/unesco-survey-less-10-schools-and-universities-have-formal-guidance-ai))

The lack of institutional guidance regarding AI extends to the workplace. One [survey](https://www.adeccogroup.com/our-group/media/press-releases/ai-saves-workers-an-average-of-one-hour-each-day) found that just one-quarter of workers have received training on how to apply AI at work.

### And only 7% of schools have guidance or policies ([UNESCO](https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/unesco-survey-less-10-schools-and-universities-have-formal-guidance-ai))

The lack of institutional guidance is even more stark in elementary, middle, and high schools. Structured programs such as [AI degree programs](https://programs.com/resources/universities-offering-ai-programs/) can help students and educators gain the skills and knowledge needed to use AI effectively and responsibly.

### Of the education institutions that *did* have guidance, 40% reported that guidance was informal ([UNESCO](https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/unesco-survey-less-10-schools-and-universities-have-formal-guidance-ai))

By informal, we mean not written down. Instead, the institutional guidance or policies regarding AI use were communicated orally. Not having clear, written policies or guidance can lead to confusion.

### 5% of university students feel aware of their institution’s AI guidelines and believe they are comprehensive ([Digital Education Council](https://www.digitaleducationcouncil.com/post/what-students-want-key-results-from-dec-global-ai-student-survey-2024))

Even fewer institutions have guidelines that are comprehensive and effectively communicated to students.

### Approximately 3 in 4 local US policymakers demand more AI regulation ([Stanford University](https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-index/2025-ai-index-report/public-opinion))

There’s a widespread appetite for AI regulation. According to [Pew Research](https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2025/04/03/how-the-us-public-and-ai-experts-view-artificial-intelligence/#regulation-and-responsible-ai), 58% of adults and 56% of AI experts are more worried that the US government won’t go far enough when regulating AI, rather than go too far.

### All 50 states have introduced legislation on AI ([NCSL](https://www.ncsl.org/technology-and-communication/artificial-intelligence-2025-legislation))

Lawmakers are working to keep up with the rapidly evolving field of AI. DC, Puerto Rico, and the Virgin Islands also introduced legislation on AI in 2025.

## How education professionals use AI

### 3 in 5 educators use AI tools ([Forbes](https://www.forbes.com/advisor/education/it-and-tech/artificial-intelligence-in-school/))

Interestingly, less experienced teachers are more likely to have adopted AI than teachers with more than 10 years of experience. This could be a reflection of age, as younger people are more likely to have less teaching experience and are more likely to use AI.

### 99% of education leaders have used AI at least once for school-related tasks ([Microsoft](https://cdn-dynmedia-1.microsoft.com/is/content/microsoftcorp/microsoft/bade/documents/products-and-services/en-us/education/2025-Microsoft-AI-in-Education-Report.pdf))

While almost every education leader has tried AI tools at least once, far fewer use AI regularly.

### And 53% of education leaders use AI daily, compared to 36% of teachers ([Microsoft](https://cdn-dynmedia-1.microsoft.com/is/content/microsoftcorp/microsoft/bade/documents/products-and-services/en-us/education/2025-Microsoft-AI-in-Education-Report.pdf))

Education leaders are more likely to use AI tools regularly compared to teachers (especially compared to the general population). According to [research by Exploding Topics](https://explodingtopics.com/blog/ai-workforce-research), only 35.49% of people use AI tools daily.

### Almost 1 in 3 educators use AI to brainstorm ideas, the most common use case ([Microsoft](https://cdn-dynmedia-1.microsoft.com/is/content/microsoftcorp/microsoft/bade/documents/products-and-services/en-us/education/2025-Microsoft-AI-in-Education-Report.pdf))

AI tools can be a helpful way for professionals to explore different ideas.

Other popular use cases for educators are creating lesson plans (29% of educators use AI for this), simplifying complex topics (24%), identifying ways to help students improve (24%), and personalizing student feedback or instructions (23%).

### 35% of teachers want data on student progress and personalized instruction in an AI tool ([New Schools](https://www.newschools.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/Gallup-Ed-Tech-Use-in-Schools-2.pdf))

These are the two most commonly cited features that teachers want in an AI tool. That student data should be immediately accessible and actionable. Instruction should be personalized based on each individual student’s skill level.

Other commonly cited features are engaging students with learning (30% of teachers want this), ease of use (30%), cost (26%), aligned with relevant standards (26%), and improving student learning outcomes (25%).

The fact that improving student learning outcomes is relatively low on the list of teacher priorities is interesting, especially as a failure to improve student outcomes is the most commonly cited reason for school districts stopping use of a new digital learning tool. Indeed, just 38% of teachers believe AI tools improve student learning outcomes a great deal.

### 65% of history and social studies teachers use digital learning tools to teach at least half their class, the highest percentage of any teacher ([New Schools](https://www.newschools.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/Gallup-Ed-Tech-Use-in-Schools-2.pdf))

14% of history and social studies teachers use digital learning tools to teach all of their classes.

### While just 42% of reading teachers say the same, the lowest percentage ([New Schools](https://www.newschools.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/Gallup-Ed-Tech-Use-in-Schools-2.pdf))

Just 9% of reading teachers use digital learning tools to teach all of their classes.

For comparison, 53% of English and language teachers use digital learning tools to teach at least half of their classes. The figure is 50% for science teachers, 50% for math teachers, and 46% for special education teachers.

### Over 1 in 3 teachers use AI to prepare to teach ([Gallup](https://news.gallup.com/poll/691967/three-teachers-weekly-saving-six-weeks-year.aspx))

Preparing to teach is the most common task for which teachers use AI. As we discuss below, 80% of teachers say AI saves them time when preparing to teach.

46% of teachers say they never use AI to prepare to teach. And just 3% use it every day to prepare to teach.

Meanwhile, 33% use AI at least once per month to make worksheets, and 28% to modify materials to meet student needs.

### 94% of teachers seek input on new digital learning tools from other teachers ([New Schools](https://www.newschools.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/Gallup-Ed-Tech-Use-in-Schools-2.pdf))

Teachers are the most trusted resource for information on new digital learning tools among teachers, principals, and administrators. For comparison, 85% of teachers seek information from their school or district, 84% look up information online, 58% research social media, and 55% ask their students.

### 27% of teachers only use free AI tools ([New Schools](https://www.newschools.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/Gallup-Ed-Tech-Use-in-Schools-2.pdf))

Infrequent users of AI are far more likely to use only free tools. Of teachers who use AI once or less per week, 40% use only free tools. Among teachers who use AI daily, 24% only use free tools.

### Almost half of all teachers purchase AI tools with their own money ([New Schools](https://www.newschools.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/Gallup-Ed-Tech-Use-in-Schools-2.pdf))

Unsurprisingly, teachers who use AI tools daily are almost twice as likely to do this (46%) as teachers who use AI tools once per week (28%).

It’s not just teachers who feel they need to buy their own AI tools. According to [research by Exploding Topics](https://explodingtopics.com/blog/ai-workforce-research), 29% of employees pay for their own AI, often without the knowledge of their boss.

### 87% of teachers use at least one AI tool to make their job easier ([Amazon](https://assets.aboutamazon.com/95/62/8ab96f0a4127acd0a2e31ce59db2/amazon-accelerating-ai-skills-through-education-survey-tennessee.pdf))

The most common use of AI tools by teachers is grading, according to this survey from Amazon. That’s followed by administrative tasks, then personalizing learning.

### 59% of educators would be interested in programs that “train the trainer” ([Amazon](https://assets.aboutamazon.com/95/62/8ab96f0a4127acd0a2e31ce59db2/amazon-accelerating-ai-skills-through-education-survey-tennessee.pdf))

In other words, a majority of educators are interested in learning how to train their students in AI skills. [Computer science and data science degrees](https://programs.com/programs/) can equip educators with the knowledge and skills to confidently integrate AI into their classrooms.

### 51% of educators use AI for educational games, the most common use ([Forbes](https://www.forbes.com/advisor/education/it-and-tech/artificial-intelligence-in-school/))

AI educational games are becoming increasingly common, with a majority of educators already using them.

Other common uses of AI are adaptive learning platforms (43% of educators use them), automated feedback or grading (41%), chatbots for supporting students (35%), and intelligent tutoring systems (29%).

## Which AI tools do students and teachers use?

### Globally, approximately 9 in 10 students use ChatGPT ([Digital Education Council](https://www.digitaleducationcouncil.com/post/ai-adoption-is-nearly-universal-among-students-but-confidence-is-not))

That makes ChatGPT the most popular AI tool among students, at least in the 35 countries surveyed by the Digital Education Council. That survey included over 27,000 students.

### 56% of students have used an AI search engine, the most commonly used AI tool ([Common Sense Media](https://www.commonsensemedia.org/sites/default/files/research/report/2024-the-dawn-of-the-ai-era_final-release-for-web.pdf))

AI-powered search engines were followed by chatbots (51% of students have used one), image generators (34%), and video generators (22%).

One in five students uses AI search engines daily. Just 11% say the same about chatbots.

## What people think of AI’s impact on education

### 71% of teachers and 65% of students believe ChatGPT will be an essential tool for their success in college and at work ([Walton Family Foundation](https://www.waltonfamilyfoundation.org/chatgpt-used-by-teachers-more-than-students-new-survey-from-walton-family-foundation-finds?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

In part, this could be due to the [rise in remote learning and work](https://www.bls.gov/opub/btn/volume-13/remote-work-productivity.htm). According to an [October 2025 survey](https://www.resume.org/majority-of-gen-z-workers-use-chatgpt-to-slack-off-at-work/), 60% of Gen Z workers who use AI tools talk to those tools as much or more than they talk to their coworkers. Almost half say their AI tools know them better than their boss.

### Over half of public K-12 teachers believe that AI tools in the classroom will cause equal or greater harm than benefit ([Pew Research](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2024/05/15/a-quarter-of-u-s-teachers-say-ai-tools-do-more-harm-than-good-in-k-12-education/sr_24-05-15_ai-in-class_1/))

25% of teachers thought AI tools would bring more harm than benefit, and 32% thought they would bring an equal amount of harm and benefit. Just 6% said AI tools would bring more benefit than harm.

### 54% of people trust AI won’t discriminate or show bias ([Stanford University](https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-index/2025-ai-index-report/public-opinion))

That’s a decrease from 2022, according to the Stanford Institute of Human-Centered AI.

### 48% of students worldwide worry they aren’t adequately prepared for an “AI-enabled workplace” ([Digital Education Council](https://www.digitaleducationcouncil.com/post/what-students-want-key-results-from-dec-global-ai-student-survey-2024))

As AI becomes more important in the workplace, students are rightfully becoming more concerned with being adequately prepared to utilize AI tools. [According to Gallup](https://www.gallup.com/workplace/691643/work-nearly-doubled-two-years.aspx), the use of AI at work nearly doubled between 2024 and 2025, with 40% of US employees now using AI a few times a year or more.

Daily AI use also doubled, from 4% to 8% of employees.

### And 58% think they don’t have enough AI knowledge and skills ([Digital Education Council](https://www.digitaleducationcouncil.com/post/what-students-want-key-results-from-dec-global-ai-student-survey-2024))

A majority of students worry about their lack of AI expertise, which is perhaps unsurprising considering how few educational institutions provide clear guidance on AI use.

### Around 4 in 5 students believe knowing how to use AI responsibly and efficiently is important for their future ([Microsoft](https://news.microsoft.com/source/2026/06/24/microsofts-new-ai-in-education-report-highlights-widespread-adoption-and-increasing-demand-for-support/))

In part, this is because experts think AI will significantly change the landscape of work, making some jobs obsolete and others look very different. [Research suggests](https://news.stanford.edu/stories/2018/05/artificial-intelligence-workplace) that about half of all US workers are in industries that are vulnerable to disruption by AI in the short term.

### 72% of students aged 9-17 want support with learning AI ([Microsoft](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/education/products/copilot-in-education))

It’s clear that the relative lack of AI guidance and education in many schools isn’t because of student disinterest.

### 42% of students want to use digital learning tools more often ([New Schools](https://www.newschools.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/Gallup-Ed-Tech-Use-in-Schools-2.pdf))

Interestingly, that’s far less than what teachers, principals, or administrators would think.

Teachers, for example, estimated that 64% of students would want to use digital learning tools more. Principals put that figure at 73% and administrators 66%.

### Over 4 in 5 educators think the lack of AI teaching resources is a problem ([Amazon](https://assets.aboutamazon.com/95/62/8ab96f0a4127acd0a2e31ce59db2/amazon-accelerating-ai-skills-through-education-survey-tennessee.pdf))

Educators, many of whom are worried about their own job security in the face of AI, are well-placed to understand how problematic a lack of AI education is for students.

There’s also the question of helping young people learn how to use AI properly and responsibly. “It’s irresponsible to not teach it,” one [Texas superintendent told the New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/04/14/us/schools-ai-teachers-writing.html) in early 2025. “We have to. We are preparing kids for their future.”

### 93% of experts who trained educators on AI reported teachers having negative views of AI ([RAND](https://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RRA956-31.html))

Negative views of AI are fairly common among educators. Of 14 trainers interviewed by RAND, 13 reported encountering at least one teacher with negative views of AI.

### 81% of K-12 computer science teachers think AI should be a part of foundational computer science education ([Economic Graph](https://economicgraph.linkedin.com/content/dam/me/economicgraph/en-us/PDF/ai-and-the-global-economy.pdf))

However, less than half of K-12 CS teachers feel properly equipped to teach AI.

### 68% of university students believe using AI is essential in today’s world ([HEPI](https://www.hepi.ac.uk/reports/student-generative-ai-survey-2026/))

AI is rapidly becoming more widespread. It was estimated that over 378 million people [would use AI](https://www.edge-ai-vision.com/2025/02/global-ai-adoption-to-surge-20-exceeding-378-million-users-in-2025/) as of 2025, more than three times the number of global AI users in 2020.

### 7 in 10 educators agree that using ChatGPT for assignments is considered plagiarism ([Neuroscience News](https://neurosciencenews.com/chatgt-student-writing-23821/#:~:text=Despite%20ChatGPT%27s%20capabilities%2C%2070%25%20of,9%20out%20of%2032%20courses.))

There’s a difference between using AI to aid in schoolwork and using it to complete schoolwork for you. Teachers are worried about students becoming overreliant on AI and not actually learning the material they are supposed to be learning.

For example, one teacher in Massachusetts [told the New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/04/14/us/schools-ai-teachers-writing.html) that about half his middle school students use AI problem-solvers, like Google Lens. While some only use the tools for homework, he’s caught others using AI to complete quizzes.

### 41% of teenagers think generative AI will have both positive and negative effects on their lives ([Harvard](https://www.gse.harvard.edu/ideas/usable-knowledge/24/09/students-are-using-ai-already-heres-what-they-think-adults-should-know))

This reflects a broader trend among people who are often uncertain about the effect AI will have on their lives. [According to Pew Research](https://www.pewresearch.org/science/2025/09/17/how-americans-view-ai-and-its-impact-on-people-and-society/), 38% of Americans are equally as excited as concerned about the increased use of AI in daily life.

### 73% of university students and researchers think AI is effective for research ([Zendy](https://curated-unify.zendy.io/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/AI-in-Research-Survey-Report.pdf))

39.6% of students and researchers (including academics and faculty) think AI is “very effective” for research.

### Around 9 in 10 university students and researchers think AI tools should cost under $10 per month ([Zendy](https://curated-unify.zendy.io/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/AI-in-Research-Survey-Report.pdf))

AI costs vary widely. Personal accounts might be free or come with a relatively cheap monthly subscription.

But many tools have more costly professional or institutional subscriptions, which can be prohibitive for teachers, especially as many have to use their own money to buy AI tools, as we discuss below. University students in particular often have to be careful about their spending, so it’s unsurprising they would prefer cheaper AI tools.

### 65% of teachers are worried about plagiarism due to AI use ([Forbes](https://www.forbes.com/advisor/education/it-and-tech/artificial-intelligence-in-school/))

Plagiarism is the most common AI-related fear among teachers. It’s followed by a reduction in human interaction (62%), data privacy and security (52%), job displacement for teachers (30%), unequal access to AI resources (30%), and automation of manual tasks (23%).

### 94% of teachers think students need at least some education in AI ([Forbes](https://www.forbes.com/advisor/education/it-and-tech/artificial-intelligence-in-school/))

Just 1% of teachers believe there’s no need for AI education.

## How different people view AI in education

### Teachers of older students are almost twice as likely to view AI negatively as teachers of younger pupils ([Pew Research](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2024/05/15/a-quarter-of-u-s-teachers-say-ai-tools-do-more-harm-than-good-in-k-12-education/sr_24-05-15_ai-in-class_2/))

35% of teachers believe AI will bring more harm than benefit when it comes to educating high school students. For middle school teachers, this figure is 24%; for elementary school teachers, 19%.

### And they’re 2.24x more likely to be sure about their opinion about AI ([Pew Research](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2024/05/15/a-quarter-of-u-s-teachers-say-ai-tools-do-more-harm-than-good-in-k-12-education/sr_24-05-15_ai-in-class_2/))

Just 21% of high school teachers said they were unsure about what they thought of AI being used in schools. Middle school teachers were also fairly certain, with 28% saying they were unsure. But 47% of elementary school teachers (almost half) reported being unsure of their thoughts on AI.

### People in China are 2.13x more likely to be optimistic about AI compared to people in the US ([Stanford University](https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-index/2025-ai-index-report/public-opinion))

In the US, 39% of people believe AI-powered services and products offer more benefits than drawbacks. That’s similar to other Western nations like Canada (40%) and the Netherlands (36%). And it’s an increase in optimism from 2022.

But it’s a much smaller percentage than in China, where a stunning 83% of people believe AI brings more good than harm. Other countries in the region are similarly optimistic, like Indonesia (80%) and Thailand (77%).

### Education leaders are 48% more likely than teachers to claim they know a lot about AI ([Microsoft](https://cdn-dynmedia-1.microsoft.com/is/content/microsoftcorp/microsoft/bade/documents/products-and-services/en-us/education/2025-Microsoft-AI-in-Education-Report.pdf))

Almost three-quarters of education leaders (72%) said they know a lot about AI. That makes leaders far more confident than teachers (44%) and students (41%).

### Education leaders are 1.5x as likely as teachers to believe that AI is integrated into their school or district’s curriculum ([Microsoft](https://cdn-dynmedia-1.microsoft.com/is/content/microsoftcorp/microsoft/bade/documents/products-and-services/en-us/education/2025-Microsoft-AI-in-Education-Report.pdf))

There’s an interesting disconnect between how education leaders and teachers view AI integration in their schools and school districts. The vast majority of education leaders, 82%, believe AI is integrated in their area. But just 54% of teachers agree.

### And they are 1.4x more likely to think AI literacy should be an essential part of basic education ([Microsoft](https://cdn-dynmedia-1.microsoft.com/is/content/microsoftcorp/microsoft/bade/documents/products-and-services/en-us/education/2025-Microsoft-AI-in-Education-Report.pdf))

A little over three-quarters of education leaders (76%) agree that AI literacy is essential to a basic education, but only 54% of teachers agree.

### Students are 25% less likely to be excited or optimistic about AI in education than teachers ([Quizlet via PR Newswire](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/quizlets-state-of-ai-in-education-survey-reveals-teachers-are-surprise-ai-champions-301884427.html))

50% of teachers are excited or optimistic about AI, but just 39% of students feel the same.

### LGBTQ+ students are 11% more likely to say generative AI will have a “mostly negative” impact on them ([Harvard](https://www.gse.harvard.edu/ideas/usable-knowledge/24/09/students-are-using-ai-already-heres-what-they-think-adults-should-know))

A little over one-quarter (28%) of LGBTQ+ students think generative AI will have a “mostly negative” impact on their lives. That’s significantly more than among cisgender and/or straight students, of whom just 17% say the same.

## Changes in how people view AI in education

### 70% of nations surveyed saw an increase in residents who think AI offers more benefits than drawbacks between 2022 and 2024 ([Stanford University](https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-index/2025-ai-index-report/public-opinion))

Researchers at the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI surveyed people in 26 nations. Of those, 18 nations saw an increase in positive views toward AI between 2022 and 2024.

### AI optimism grew by 4% between 2022 and 2024 in the US ([Stanford University](https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-index/2025-ai-index-report/public-opinion))

In 2022, 35% of the US was optimistic about AI. Two years later, that figure increased to 39%. Optimism in the US lags behind other countries around the world, especially those in East Asia. But it’s similar to other Western nations like Canada.

### But excitement about the increased use of AI in daily life declined by 8% between 2020 and 2025 ([Pew Research](https://www.pewresearch.org/science/2025/09/17/how-americans-view-ai-and-its-impact-on-people-and-society/))

Pew Research presents a slightly less optimistic picture of how Americans perceive AI. In 2020, 37% were more concerned than excited about the increased use of AI in daily life, and 18% were more excited than concerned. The remaining 45% were an equal mix of excited and concerned.

Fast forward to 2025, and half of Americans say they were more concerned than excited, 38% were an equal mix, and just 10% were more excited than concerned. Put another way: 57% think the societal risks of AI are high, while just 25% think the benefits of AI are high.

## Benefits of AI in education

### Over 4 in 5 teachers state that AI cuts time spent making worksheets, assignments, etc. ([Gallup](https://news.gallup.com/poll/691967/three-teachers-weekly-saving-six-weeks-year.aspx))

Producing educational materials is one area in which AI can save significant time. For context, 81% of teachers say AI saves them time when completing administrative work, 80% when preparing to teach, 79% when grading, 74% when modifying materials to meet the needs of students, 65% when supplementing teaching, 63% when analyzing patterns in student learning or achievement, and 60% when providing personal tutoring.

These figures are all for teachers who use AI tools for the relevant task at least once per month.

### Squirrel AI improved student question accuracy rates by 15% ([World Economic Forum](https://www.weforum.org/stories/2025/01/how-ai-and-human-teachers-can-collaborate-to-transform-education/))

In this case study, an AI tool helped students improve their accuracy when completing quizzes.

### Students in Australia who used an AI chatbot saw their grades increase by 10% ([Microsoft](https://news.microsoft.com/source/asia/2025/03/24/macquarie-university-students-exam-scores-up-by-nearly-10-per-cent-thanks-to-new-ai-powered-chatbot/))

Similarly, an Australian study gave students access to Microsoft Copilot. The AI tool helped them increase their grades.

### Students in Indiana who used AI saw a 40% reduction in the time it took to complete their work ([Indiana University](https://cdn-dynmedia-1.microsoft.com/is/content/microsoftcorp/microsoft/final/en-us/microsoft-product-and-services/microsoft-education/downloadables/IU-Copilot-Report-Initial-analysis.pdf))

In a study conducted with Microsoft, students in Indiana were allowed to use AI to help with their schoolwork. Their grades increased by 10%, and the time it took them to complete their work decreased by 40%, a significant difference. However, students said they felt like the work they completed with AI was less their own work.

### Around 9 in 10 teachers think generative AI will positively impact students’ future careers ([Amazon](https://assets.aboutamazon.com/95/62/8ab96f0a4127acd0a2e31ce59db2/amazon-accelerating-ai-skills-through-education-survey-tennessee.pdf))

Based on this study, teachers are significantly more optimistic about the impact of genAI on their students than the [population in general](https://www.pewresearch.org/science/2025/09/17/how-americans-view-ai-and-its-impact-on-people-and-society/).

### 16% of the total productive capacity that could be unlocked in the US by generative AI lies in the education, health, and social work sectors ([Economic Graph](https://economicgraph.linkedin.com/content/dam/me/economicgraph/en-us/PDF/ai-and-the-global-economy.pdf))

Experts think generative AI will unlock substantial boosts to productivity. A 2024 [analysis by EY](https://www.ey.com/en_us/ai/productivity-potential-gen-ai), for example, estimated that productivity gains brought by generative AI will increase GDP by 2.5% by 2033, which the company says would be worth some $650 billion.

A significant proportion of that potential increase is set to come from the education sector.

### 34% of university students would put in more effort if their exams were at least partially assessed by AI ([HEPI](https://www.hepi.ac.uk/reports/student-generative-ai-survey-2025/))

However, this is only slightly more than the 29% who would actually put in less effort.  
  
Interestingly, [research suggests](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2666920X25000591) that students are more likely to prefer AI graders when they are dissatisfied with the current system. This is especially true for students who receive low grades. Students receiving high grades, however, generally prefer to stick with human graders.

### 47% of students say AI has a positive impact on their learning ([Quizlet](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/quizlets-state-of-ai-in-education-survey-reveals-teachers-are-surprise-ai-champions-301884427.html))

Interestingly, this is [far less](https://www.aiprm.com/ai-in-workplace-statistics/) than the proportion of employees who think AI has helped them at work. Perhaps that’s because “learning” is a little more personal, requiring more human input than many common work-related tasks.

### Around 2 in 5 students and teachers believe AI has created a more equitable education system ([Quizlet](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/quizlets-state-of-ai-in-education-survey-reveals-teachers-are-surprise-ai-champions-301884427.html))

Bias when grading is a [widespread problem](https://www.edutopia.org/article/implicit-bias-grading/) in education. AI could help solve for implicit biases, which humans often struggle to overcome.

### 48% of teachers think AI tools will help students recover from pandemic learning loss ([Quizlet](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/quizlets-state-of-ai-in-education-survey-reveals-teachers-are-surprise-ai-champions-301884427.html))

COVID had a significant negative impact on student outcomes. In some parts of the country, students in 2025 were [almost a full year behind](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/02/11/briefing/covid-learning-losses.html) typical pre-COVID reading levels.

[According to the Annie E. Casey Foundation](https://www.aecf.org/blog/pandemic-learning-loss-impacting-young-peoples-futures), the decline in learning throughout the pandemic “amounted to decades of lost progress.” Experts worry this loss could [translate to significant economic losses](https://hanushek.stanford.edu/sites/default/files/Hanushek%2BStrauss%202024%20Pandemic%20Learning%20Losses.pdf), as entire cohorts of students graduate with a relatively weaker education than their predecessors. But AI has the potential to help recover from pandemic learning loss.

### 55% of teachers say AI improves educational outcomes ([Forbes](https://www.forbes.com/advisor/education/it-and-tech/artificial-intelligence-in-school/))

This figure may increase as AI tools become more capable, and more institutions provide adequate training and guidance on how to use them.

### Almost 6 hours a week is saved by teachers who regularly use AI tools in their work ([Gallup](https://news.gallup.com/poll/691967/three-teachers-weekly-saving-six-weeks-year.aspx))

Here, “regularly” means at least once per week. The time saved is based on estimates provided by the teachers themselves. Over the course of a standard school year, this amounts to six weeks saved annually.

## Barriers to AI in education

### Around 3 in 5 students are concerned about the potential unfairness of AI evaluations ([Digital Education Council](https://www.digitaleducationcouncil.com/resource-library-items/ai-in-higher-education-global-survey-2026))

While AI has the potential to help counteract human biases, [AI tools can have biases of their own](https://www.chapman.edu/ai/bias-in-ai.aspx). Biases can occur during data collection, data labeling, model training, and deployment.

### 65% of school administrators say they stopped using a digital learning tool ([New Schools](https://www.newschools.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/Gallup-Ed-Tech-Use-in-Schools-2.pdf))

Almost two-thirds of school districts stop using a digital learning tool after piloting or adopting it. The most common reason for this was that the tool failed to improve student learning outcomes.

### Just 18% of school administrators think their district offers a lot of evidence-based information about AI tools ([New Schools](https://www.newschools.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/Gallup-Ed-Tech-Use-in-Schools-2.pdf))

This is particularly problematic, as it places the onus of researching information on AI on teachers, who are already overworked and potentially unfamiliar with AI.

### 81% of educators cite time constraints as a major challenge preventing them from developing an AI training curriculum ([Amazon](https://assets.aboutamazon.com/95/62/8ab96f0a4127acd0a2e31ce59db2/amazon-accelerating-ai-skills-through-education-survey-tennessee.pdf))

Educators are often overworked as it is, and lack the time to properly develop an AI curriculum. They would likely benefit from a prepared curriculum or courses on how to prepare one. According to [one survey by RAND](https://www.nea.org/nea-today/all-news-articles/survey-teachers-work-more-hours-week-other-working-adults), teachers work an average of 53 hours a week, seven more than the typical working adult.

### Three-quarters of educators say they are held back by a lack of knowledge on how to develop or access an AI curriculum ([Amazon](https://assets.aboutamazon.com/95/62/8ab96f0a4127acd0a2e31ce59db2/amazon-accelerating-ai-skills-through-education-survey-tennessee.pdf))

Most teachers lack sufficient familiarity with AI to develop a curriculum. In order to properly teach their students how to use AI, they need support.

### High-poverty school districts are 53% less likely to have AI-trained teachers ([RAND](https://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RRA956-31.html))

67% of low-poverty districts have trained teachers on AI use, but just 39% of high-poverty districts have done the same.

### 78.6% of district leaders to a DIY approach to developing AI training for their school district ([RAND](https://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RRA956-31.html))

11 of 14 district leaders interviewed by RAND did this. Why? Perhaps to ensure their district’s training was personalized. But there is also widespread suspicion of people professing to be experts in AI.

For example, one district leader told RAND that “there are people that are claiming to have the best practices and are making money hand over fist.” The leader said “a lot” of the AI workshops they attended left them feeling that it had been “a waste of time and money.”

### 36% of university students say their institution doesn’t encourage them to use AI ([HEPI](https://www.hepi.ac.uk/reports/student-generative-ai-survey-2026/)

The same proportion (36%) agrees that their institution encourages them to use AI tools.

### Around 2 in 5 university students currently receive AI skills training ([HEPI](https://www.hepi.ac.uk/reports/student-generative-ai-survey-2026/))

This is concerningly low, considering how many people agree that AI skills are important – and are becoming more important – in the workplace.

# 25 AI in Education Statistics to Guide Your Learning Strategy in 2026

By Lindsey Seril

Last updated on June 13, 2026

Originally published on July 15, 2025

Artificial intelligence is no longer a peripheral tool in education. It is woven into how students study, how teachers plan lessons, and how institutions make decisions. In 2026, the conversation has shifted from whether to use AI to how to use it well.

These statistics come from primary research from 2025 and 2026 by Microsoft, McKinsey, Pew Research Center, and other credible institutions. They reveal what's actually happening in classrooms, corporate training programs, and online learning platforms right now.

Whether you are an educator, an administrator, or a policymaker, these figures offer a grounded picture of where AI in education stands right now.

Feel free to jump to the topic you're most interested in:

* [Statistics on student and teacher AI adoption](#adoption)
* [Statistics on AI education market growth and adoption](#growth)
* [Statistics on AI's impact on learning outcomes](#outcomes)
* [Statistics on AI in corporate training](#corporate)
* [Statistics on personalized learning benefits](#personalized)
* [Statistics on the future of AI in education](#future)

## AI adoption and usage statistics

### 1. 85% of teachers and 86% of students used AI during the 2024-25 school year.

AI adoption in K-12 education has reached near-universal levels among both educators and students. In the United States, student use of AI for school-related purposes jumped 26% since last school year, while educator use rose 21% over the same period. This rapid, simultaneous adoption across both groups signals a fundamental shift in how teaching and learning happen day to day. The most common applications include research and content gathering (44%), creating lesson plans (38%), summarizing information (38%), and generating classroom materials (37%). [1, 2]

### 2. Teachers who use AI tools at least weekly save an average of 5.9 hours per week, the equivalent of six full weeks per school year.

This finding, from the Gallup-Walton Family Foundation survey of more than 1,000 teachers, represents a meaningful reduction in the administrative burden that has long contributed to teacher burnout and attrition. The most common time-saving applications include lesson planning, grading support, generating classroom materials, and drafting communications to parents. When teachers get hours back in their week, they can redirect that time toward direct student interaction and the relational work that no AI can replace. [3]

### 3. 92% of higher education students now use generative AI in some form, up from 66% in 2024.

The Higher Education Policy Institute's annual survey of UK students found that AI use surged more in a single year than in all prior years combined. Nearly 9 in 10 students (88%) acknowledged using generative AI tools for tests in 2025. This pace of adoption has outrun most institutional policy frameworks, creating a significant governance gap that universities are now racing to close. [4, 5]

### 4. 69% of teachers say AI tools have improved their teaching methods and skills.

A 2025 EdWeek survey found that beyond saving time, AI is actively improving how teachers teach. 59% of teachers said AI had enabled more personalized instruction, and high school teachers are the most active adopters, with 69% reporting generative AI use, compared with 42% of elementary teachers and just 33% of pre-K teachers. This gradient reflects the greater availability of AI tools designed for secondary and post-secondary content. [6, 7]

![Downloadable how-to guides, research, and white papers designed for better online learning](https://www.engageli.com/hs-fs/hubfs/Downloadable%20how-to%20guides%2c%20research%2c%20and%20white%20papers%20designed%20for%20better%20online%20learning%20(3).png?width=750&height=422&name=Downloadable%20how-to%20guides%2c%20research%2c%20and%20white%20papers%20designed%20for%20better%20online%20learning%20(3).png)

## Market growth and adoption statistics

### 5. The global AI in education market was valued at $7.05 billion in 2025 and is projected to reach $136.79 billion by 2035.

The global AI in education market was valued at approximately $7.05 billion in 2025 and is projected to reach $136.79 billion by 2035, growing at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of roughly 35%. To put that trajectory in perspective, the broader global learning and development market already exceeds $350 billion, and AI is increasingly the engine driving its expansion.

In July 2025, Microsoft announced an investment of more than $4 billion specifically in AI education initiatives, targeting schools, community colleges, and nonprofits through its newly launched Microsoft Elevate Academy. That commitment underscores how seriously major technology companies now view education as a strategic AI deployment frontier. [8, 9]

### 6. 86% of education organizations now use generative AI, which is the highest adoption rate of any industry.

While education has historically lagged behind other sectors in technology adoption, AI implementation has been remarkably swift. Educational institutions can deploy AI tools quickly to address immediate challenges like creating quiz questions, generating lesson plans, and providing feedback. The high adoption rate, documented in IDC research cited in Microsoft's 2025 AI in Education Report, demonstrates that AI tools are meeting real needs in educational practice. [1]

### 7. The Asia-Pacific region shows the fastest AI education market growth at 48% compound annual growth rate.

The region's explosive growth stems from large, rapidly expanding populations with growing educational needs and cultural attitudes that highly value educational achievement. Many Asia-Pacific countries are investing heavily in educational technology as part of broader economic development strategies, creating substantial demand for scalable, effective AI solutions. [10]

### 8. Only 20% of universities have a formal AI policy in place, even as 56% of students and educators believe their institution is unprepared to manage AI.

A February 2026 Coursera survey of more than 4,200 students and educators across five countries found that AI adoption has dramatically outpaced governance. At the K-12 level, the gap is just as wide: as of December 2024, only 31% of U.S. public schools had a written AI policy, according to U.S. Department of Education data. Institutions that close this gap first will be better positioned to capture the benefits of AI while managing its risks. [5, 11]

## Learning outcomes and effectiveness statistics

### 9. 80% of students globally say AI has positively supported their learning experience.

The Coursera AI in Higher Education Report, released in February 2026, found that four in five students report AI has improved their academic performance. 70% believe AI will improve exam performance and the overall quality of higher education, and 63% say they use AI for less than half of their academic tasks, suggesting most students are using it as a supplement rather than a replacement for their own thinking. [5]

### 10. Students using an AI tutor scored significantly higher than those in traditional classes, according to a randomized controlled trial.

A peer-reviewed randomized controlled trial published in *Scientific Reports* in June 2025 found that an AI tutor outperformed traditional in-class learning, with an effect size between 0.73 and 1.3 standard deviations. Students using the AI tutor not only achieved substantially higher post-test scores than their peers in traditional active learning environments, but did so in less time. The AI group’s median time on task was 49 minutes, compared with 60 minutes for in-class learners. This represents one of the strongest experimental results to date on the effectiveness of AI tutoring. [5]

### 11. Students in AI-enhanced active learning programs achieve 54% higher test scores than those in traditional environments.

The improvement spans multiple subjects (mathematics, science, language arts, and social studies) and appears on standardized assessments designed independently of AI-enhanced learning. AI systems excel at identifying and addressing knowledge gaps before they compound into larger problems, ensuring students have solid foundations before advancing to more complex concepts. [13]

### 12. AI-powered active learning generates 10 times more engagement than traditional passive learning methods.

AI enables interactive experiences regardless of class size or format, transforming passive lecture-based learning into participatory experiences. Students in AI-enhanced environments participate more in discussions, ask more questions, and spend additional time with course materials outside class. The technology facilitates real-time adjustments based on student engagement levels. [13]

### 13. AI-powered assessment tools provide feedback that is 10 times faster than traditional methods.

Immediate feedback allows students to correct misconceptions while material remains fresh in their minds, significantly improving learning effectiveness. AI enables continuous micro-assessments rather than periodic major tests, providing more accurate pictures of student understanding and enabling timely interventions when students need additional support. [14]

### 14. 95% of college faculty believe generative AI will increase students' overreliance on these tools, and 90% say it will diminish critical thinking skills.

A January 2026 national survey by the American Association of Colleges and Universities found that faculty concerns about AI are running high. 73% of faculty reported having personally handled academic integrity issues related to student AI use, and 83% predicted AI will decrease students' attention spans. These concerns are not a reason to avoid AI, but they are a clear signal that intentional pedagogical design matters enormously. [15]

## AI in corporate training statistics

### 15. Businesses collectively spend $400 billion on training annually, yet 74% of companies report they are not keeping up with their organization's demand for new skills.

Research from the Josh Bersin Company, published in February 2026, found that despite massive investment in learning and development, most organizations are falling behind. AI is now reshaping this market from the ground up, enabling personalized, adaptive training at a scale and speed that traditional content libraries and instructor-led programs cannot match. [16]

### 16. AI-powered corporate training leads to a 57% increase in learning efficiency.

Employees complete training programs faster while demonstrating superior mastery and better retention when tested weeks or months later. Most importantly, they apply new skills more effectively in actual work situations. AI optimizes learning experiences by focusing on areas where each person needs development rather than covering material they already know. [9]

### 17. 66% of education and business leaders say they would not hire someone without AI literacy skills.

Microsoft's 2025 AI in Education Report found that AI fluency has become a baseline hiring requirement across industries. Upskilling employees in AI is now the top workforce strategy for 47% of leaders over the next 12 to 18 months. 54% of global educators and 76% of global education leaders view AI literacy as an essential component of basic education for every student. [1]

### 18. 77% of global workers express willingness to retrain or learn new AI-related skills.

Workers recognize that AI tools make jobs more efficient and effective, leading to increased productivity and job satisfaction. They understand that AI literacy is becoming a competitive advantage, with employers increasingly seeking candidates who can work effectively with AI systems. This willingness represents a significant shift from historical resistance to technological change. [17]

## Personalized learning through AI statistics

### 19. AI-powered personalized learning increases student engagement rates by up to 60% and learning efficiency by 57%.

When AI tailors learning paths to individual students, the results compound across multiple dimensions simultaneously: engagement rises, time-to-mastery falls, and retention improves. 74% of adult learners report greater motivation in AI-enhanced courses due to personalized experiences, and 67% of students agree that AI helps them study faster or more efficiently. [9]

### 20. 75% of students feel more motivated in personalized AI learning environments compared to 30% in traditional classrooms.

Personalized learning experiences tailored to individual interests, learning styles, and knowledge levels help students feel more competent and confident. Students gain greater autonomy over their educational experiences, exploring topics that interest them and progressing at their own pace rather than following rigid, predetermined paths. [14]

### 21. Schools implementing AI-powered personalized learning observed a 12% increase in student attendance and a 15% reduction in dropout rates.

AI-powered early warning systems analyze multiple data points such as declining grades, reduced participation, irregular attendance, and changes in engagement to identify at-risk students before they disengage entirely. Early identification enables educators to provide targeted support, and when educational content aligns with individual interests and learning styles, students find school more relevant and worthwhile. [14]

### 22. Students achieve 70% better course completion rates with AI-personalized learning compared to traditional approaches.

AI bridges differences in learning styles, cultural backgrounds, and prior educational experiences, which is particularly valuable in global educational contexts with diverse student populations. AI-powered collaboration tools also help overcome language barriers and communication challenges that can impede international learning programs. [18]

## Future trends for AI in education statistics

### 23. The OECD's Digital Education Outlook 2026 warns that performing a task with AI does not automatically lead to learning.

The OECD's landmark 2026 report on digital education found that students with access to general-purpose AI chatbots produced higher-quality outputs than peers, but this advantage disappeared and sometimes reversed in exams when access was removed. Educational AI tools designed with intentional pedagogical purpose, by contrast, showed sustained improvements. The report argues that learning to work with AI, and to know when not to, is now a foundational skill alongside reading and mathematics. [19]

### 24. Students in low-income and rural areas are the least likely to report that their schools allow or integrate AI use.

A Gallup survey cited by NPR in August 2025 found that the AI opportunity is not being distributed equally. Globally, 24.7% of the working-age population in the Global North now uses generative AI tools, compared with only 14.1% in the Global South. UNESCO's 2025 survey of higher education institutions found that around 70% of institutions in Europe and North America have or are developing AI guidance, compared with just 45% in Latin America and the Caribbean. Closing this equity gap is as important as any other challenge in AI education policy. [20, 21, 22]

### 25. Workers using AI tools could add $7.9 trillion to the global economy, but only if AI literacy scales across the entire workforce.

The economic impact comes from productivity improvements as workers learn to leverage AI tools effectively in their specific roles. Education and training play crucial roles in realizing this potential: widespread AI literacy is necessary for the productivity gains to scale. 92% of business leaders expect to boost AI spending over the next three years, reflecting a broad consensus that the investment in AI-enabled learning is not optional. [23]

## AI in education FAQs

### What is AI in education?

AI in education refers to artificial intelligence technologies that enhance teaching, learning, and administrative processes. This includes personalized learning systems that adapt to individual student needs, automated grading and feedback tools, intelligent tutoring systems, and predictive analytics that help identify at-risk students. AI also assists teachers with content creation, lesson planning, and administrative tasks.

### How effective is AI compared to traditional teaching methods?

Research demonstrates significant advantages for AI-enhanced education. Students in AI-powered learning environments achieve 54% higher test scores, show 30% better learning outcomes, and experience 10x more engagement compared to traditional methods. A 2025 randomized controlled trial published in Scientific Reports found AI tutoring outperformed in-class active learning with an effect size between 0.73 and 1.3 standard deviations. AI also improves completion rates by 70% and reduces dropout rates by 15% while simultaneously increasing student motivation.

### What are the main benefits of AI in education?

Key benefits of AI in education include personalized learning experiences that adapt to individual needs, immediate feedback that accelerates learning, improved student engagement and motivation, better learning outcomes and test scores, significant time savings for teachers (nearly six weeks per year for weekly AI users), early identification of at-risk students, and more efficient corporate training programs (57% increase in learning efficiency).

### How can educational institutions implement AI effectively?

Successful AI implementation in educational institutions involves starting with specific use cases like automated grading or content creation, ensuring proper teacher training and support, maintaining focus on pedagogical goals, protecting student privacy and data security, and measuring outcomes to demonstrate value. The OECD's 2026 Digital Education Outlook recommends moving beyond general-purpose AI tools toward purpose-built educational AI that is designed to produce durable learning gains, not just better task outputs. Platforms like Engageli provide comprehensive solutions that integrate multiple AI capabilities.

### What does the future hold for AI in education?

The AI education market is projected to grow from $7.05 billion in 2025 to $136.79 billion by 2035. Key trends include increased personalization, more sophisticated assessment tools, better integration with existing educational systems, expanded use in corporate training, and AI-powered collaboration tools for global learning experiences. 92% of business leaders plan to increase AI spending, indicating continued rapid adoption. The most pressing challenge ahead is equity: ensuring that the benefits of AI in education reach students in low-income, rural, and under-resourced communities at the same rate as those in well-funded institutions.

#### Driver: Increasing demand for personalized learning experiences

Adoption in education is being driven by the need for personalized learning pathways, scalable infrastructure, and data-informed instruction. Implementations are deploying cloud-native platforms, adaptive learning engines, and real-time analytics to enhance engagement and improve outcomes. For example, GetCourse leveraged cloud compute and storage to scale its platform, while Century Tech's AI-powered solution enabled personalized instruction and reduced teacher workload. These implementations reflect a broader market shift toward intelligent automation, student-centric pedagogy, and operational agility.

#### Restraint: Reluctance among institutions to replace traditional teaching/learning methods.

Adoption of AI in education continues to grow, yet institutional hesitation to overhaul traditional teaching models and concerns over data privacy, cybersecurity, and regulatory compliance remain significant barriers. Vendors recognize these challenges, with reports from Microsoft, EDUCAUSE, and AWS Education highlighting GDPR, FERPA, and escalating cyber threats as primary concerns. In response, leading providers are implementing privacy-first architectures, secure cloud infrastructures, and transparent AI governance frameworks, prominently featured in their offerings and whitepapers. Additionally, faculty enablement, ethical AI deployment, and robust governance structures are critical to mitigating risk, fostering trust, and driving adoption of AI-powered educational solutions.

#### Opportunity: Adaptive Tech Unlocks Immersive Experiences

AI presents significant opportunities to transform education through adaptive technologies, generative content creation, and immersive learning tools. Institutions are integrating virtual tutors, automated assessments, and AR/VR-enhanced instruction to support self-paced learning and improve accessibility. Stride’s use of generative AI to create interactive storytelling apps for K–12 learners exemplifies how vendors are enabling creative engagement, digital literacy, and personalized content delivery. These innovations position institutions to expand reach, attract diverse learners, and differentiate through intelligent education ecosystems.

#### Challenge: Misuse of AI tools for unethical academic practices

The rise of generative AI has amplified concerns around academic integrity, with tools increasingly misused for plagiarism and content manipulation. Vendors are vocal about these risks, with Microsoft, Turnitin, and other academic integrity platforms developing plagiarism detection engines, usage monitoring tools, and ethical AI guidelines to safeguard learning environments. Institutions face the challenge of balancing innovation with accountability, ensuring AI-enhanced learning does not compromise ethical standards. This issue is prominently reflected in vendor events, product updates, and policy briefings, driving the creation of AI literacy programs, student integrity protocols, and transparent governance models to promote responsible AI adoption.

## AI in Education Market Report Summary (Published Nov 2024, MarketsandMarkets)

**Market Size & Forecast:**
- 2023: USD 1.78 billion
- 2024: USD 2.21 billion (projected)
- 2030: USD 5.82 billion (forecasted)
- CAGR (2024-2030): 17.5%
- Report covers 2019-2030

**Key Trends & Drivers:**
- Growth is driven by digital transformation, demand for personalized learning, and adoption of e-learning platforms.
- Key technologies include machine learning, NLP, generative AI, and adaptive learning engines.
- Content generation tools are the fastest-growing software type (projected CAGR 19.1%).
- Generative AI is the fastest-growing technology segment.
- Personalized learning & content management dominates application segments with 34.5% market share in 2024.

**Regional Insights:**
- North America holds the largest market share (43% in 2024).
- Asia Pacific is the fastest-growing region, driven by government-led digital initiatives and public-private partnerships.

**Market Dynamics:**
- Drivers: Demand for personalized learning, rising e-learning adoption.
- Restraints: Institutional reluctance to replace traditional teaching methods.
- Opportunities: Adaptive/immersive tech, AI-powered assessment systems, virtual tutors.
- Challenges: Misuse of AI for unethical academic practices (plagiarism).

**Key Players:** Major companies include Microsoft, IBM, Google, Alibaba Cloud, AWS, Duolingo, Carnegie Learning, DreamBox Learning, Khan Academy, Pearson, OpenAI, and Grammarly. Duolingo is identified as a 'Star' player; Grammarly as an 'Emerging Leader'.

**Recent Developments (2024):**
- Oct 2024: Pearson expanded partnership with ServiceNow for workforce development.
- Aug 2024: IBM partnered with University of Wollongong India.
- May 2024: Khan Academy & Microsoft partnered to provide free AI teaching assistant (Khanmigo).
- Apr 2024: Alibaba Cloud partnered with Hanyang University (South Korea).
- Jan 2024: Arizona State University collaborated with OpenAI to integrate ChatGPT.

**End Users:** K-12 segment dominates; EdTech companies are the fastest-growing institutional end-user segment.

**Commercial Use Cases Highlighted:** GetCourse (Alibaba Cloud), Century Tech (Epsom & Ewell High School), Google Cloud (Malaysia's Ministry of Education), Stride (Amazon Bedrock for K-12 AI storytelling).

# K-12 Artificial Intelligence Market Set to Explode in U.S. and Worldwide by 2024

![Little black boy and teacher making a robot for school science project](data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSI1NzBweCIgd2lkdGg9Ijg0MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=)
