## 1 Introduction

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is changing the education system offering transformative possibilities to overcome persistent challenges and improve learning outcomes. AI applications like adaptive learning platforms, intelligent tutoring systems, and automated administrative tools are helping to personalize education addressing individual student needs while empowering educators with actionable insights. For example, with their scoping review Su and Yang [[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44217-026-01816-z#ref-CR1 "Su J, Yang W. Artificial intelligence in early childhood education: a scoping review. Comput Educ Artif Intell. 2022;3:100049.")] reported that AI significantly improves teaching and learning in early child education and enhance learning and development among young children. AI systems can analyze vast amounts of data to customize content delivery, identify learning gaps, and provide timely interventions, making education more efficient and effective. Besides, it promotes students’ mathematical reasoning and positive attitudes towards mathematics [[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44217-026-01816-z#ref-CR2 "Lee D, Yeo S. Developing an AI-based chatbot for practicing responsive teaching in mathematics. Comput Educ. 2022;191:104646.")].

As the global focus shifts towards achieving inclusive and equitable education (aligned with Sustainable Development Goal 4), leveraging AI to address disparities in developing regions has become a critical area of interest. These regions often have limited technological infrastructure, inadequate teachers training, and socio-economic barriers contribute to the spreading educational gap that hinder access to AI-driven solutions. For instance, a lack of reliable internet connectivity and affordable devices restricts the adoption of AI tools, leaving rural and underserved communities behind [[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44217-026-01816-z#ref-CR3 "Mizumoto A, Eguchi M. Exploring the potential of using an AI language model for automated essay scoring. Res Methods Appl Linguistics. 2023;2(2):100050.")]. Moreover, the gap in digital literacy among both students, parents and educators poses a significant obstacle to leveraging AI effectively in the classroom [[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44217-026-01816-z#ref-CR4 "Iku-Silan A, Hwang G-J, Chen C-H. Decision-guided chatbots and cognitive styles in interdisciplinary learning. Comput Educ. 2023;201:104812.")].

AI offers potential alternative solutions to these and unforeseen problems. For example, AI-powered chatbots and conversational agents can deliver real-time feedback to students in remote areas, bridging gaps in teacher availability [[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44217-026-01816-z#ref-CR2 "Lee D, Yeo S. Developing an AI-based chatbot for practicing responsive teaching in mathematics. Comput Educ. 2022;191:104646."), [4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44217-026-01816-z#ref-CR4 "Iku-Silan A, Hwang G-J, Chen C-H. Decision-guided chatbots and cognitive styles in interdisciplinary learning. Comput Educ. 2023;201:104812.")]. Moreover, AI-enabled platforms can facilitate teacher training, ensuring educators are equipped with the necessary skills to adapt to modern pedagogies [[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44217-026-01816-z#ref-CR3 "Mizumoto A, Eguchi M. Exploring the potential of using an AI language model for automated essay scoring. Res Methods Appl Linguistics. 2023;2(2):100050.")]. In recent years, AI’s potential has expanded in education and other industries significantly with advancements in technologies such as machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, big data, internet of things, image processing, virtual reality, augmented reality, speech recognition, computer vision [[5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44217-026-01816-z#ref-CR5 "Rashid AB, Kausik MAK. AI revolutionizing industries worldwide: A comprehensive overview of its diverse applications. Hybrid Adv. 2024;7:100277.")]. Tools like ChatGPT, built on sophisticated models like GPT-4, exemplify how AI can support personalized learning by generating customized educational materials, quizzes, and interactive activities [[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44217-026-01816-z#ref-CR3 "Mizumoto A, Eguchi M. Exploring the potential of using an AI language model for automated essay scoring. Res Methods Appl Linguistics. 2023;2(2):100050.")]. After evaluating impact on teaching and learning Alam [[6](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44217-026-01816-z#ref-CR6 "Alam A. Employing adaptive learning and intelligent tutoring robots for virtual classrooms and smart campuses: reforming education in the age of artificial intelligence. In Advanced computing and intelligent technologies: Proceedings of ICACIT 2022. Springer; 2022. pp. 395–406.")] concluded the beneficial effect on both the quality of instruction and on the learning outcomes of students. Furthermore, AI-powered analytics can help policymakers optimize resource allocation, addressing systemic issues like teacher shortages and uneven distribution of educational resources.

Along with the challenges reflected, AI has pressing concern on ethical implications of deploying it in education. Issues such as data privacy, algorithmic bias, and unequal resource distribution exacerbate existing inequalities rather than alleviating them [[7](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44217-026-01816-z#ref-CR7 "Yu PK. The algorithmic divide and equality in the age of artificial intelligence. Fla L Rev. 2020;72:331.")]. For example, AI systems trained on datasets from high-income countries may fail to address the unique educational needs of learners in developing contexts, leading to culturally insensitive content or exclusionary practices [[8](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44217-026-01816-z#ref-CR8 "Daher W, Diab H, Rayan A. Artificial intelligence generative tools and conceptual knowledge in problem solving in chemistry. Information. 2023;14(7):409.")]. Additionally, the high costs associated with AI implementation strain the already limited budgets of educational institutions in the developing regions [[9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44217-026-01816-z#ref-CR9 "Folorunso A, et al. A policy framework on AI usage in developing countries and its impact. Global J Eng Technol Adv. 2024;21(01):154–66.")].

Generally, it is evident that AI in education offers several advantages, especially on personalized learning, where students can receive tailored content based on their individual needs and learning styles. It also assists efficient administrative tasks, like grading and scheduling, allowing educators to focus more on teaching. Besides, AI tools can provide real-time feedback and support for students, enhancing learning outcomes. In developing countries, AI has the potential to bridge gaps in access to quality learning resources, offering students in remote access opportunities for personalized education. However, there are disadvantages, including concerns about data privacy, high dependency that may reduce human interaction and critical thinking, and a risk of biases if AI algorithms are not properly designed. Moreover, challenges such as limited access to technology, internet infrastructure, and the need for teachers training in developing countries may hinder AI’s effective implementation, potentially exacerbating existing inequalities. This review aims to address these gaps by examining the tradeoffs through generating evidences, providing insights into how AI can be harnessed to transform education in developing regions. The review is intended to get answers for the following research questions (RQ):

*   **RQ1**: What is the effectiveness of AI technologies in improving educational outcomes in developing regions?

*   **RQ2**: What are the primary barriers to the adoption and integration of AI in the education systems of developing regions?

*   **RQ3**: How do emerging AI innovations (e.g., virtual reality, generative AI) address educational challenges particularly in developing regions?

*   **RQ4**: What are the ethical implications of using AI in education in developing regions, and how can these concerns be addressed?

*   **RQ5**: What are the best practices for integrating AI technologies into educational policy and practice in developing regions?

## 2 Methodology

### 2.1 Review design and classification

#### 2.1.1 Review approach

The review employed appropriate methodologies to explore the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in transforming educational practices in developing regions. Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guideline was used for the systematic component to synthesize empirical evidence on the application of AI in education. For the review purpose, a comprehensive search of peer-reviewed studies published between 2020 and 2024 was conducted. The studies focus on AI applications such as adaptive learning platforms, intelligent tutoring systems, and AI-powered assessment tools aimed at improving student outcomes, teacher support, and overall educational equity in developing regions. The review critically assessed the impact of these AI applications, with a particular focus on challenges related to infrastructure, digital literacy, and socio-economic barriers. Bibliometric visualizations (word cloud and co-occurrence networks) and term frequency analyses were performed on the final included corpus, with procedures detailed in Subsect. [2.6](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44217-026-01816-z#Sec13).

Furthermore, the review also gave emphasis on cutting-edge AI technologies that enhance educational practices in low-resource settings. It was employed in the analysis by examining the latest innovations in AI, including generative AI, immersive learning environments, and AI-driven content creation tools. This component identifies emerging technologies that offer transformative potential in education and investigates how they could address the unique challenges faced by developing regions, such as the lack of access to trained educators, infrastructure limitations, and language barriers.

#### 2.1.2 Study classification and methodological limitations

Consistent with the title, this study is classified as a systematic scoping review rather than a full systematic review. While PRISMA guidelines were followed for search reporting and study selection, the following elements of a full systematic review are absent: (a) protocol registration (e.g., PROSPERO), (b) quantitative risk-of-bias assessment (e.g., ROBINS-I, AMSTAR-2), and (c) meta-analysis or statistical synthesis of effect sizes. These omissions are deliberate and appropriate given the review’s objectives. A scoping review is indicated when the aim is to map emerging evidence, identify key concepts and gaps, and synthesize heterogeneous study designs across a broad research area—precisely the case here, given the nascent state of AI-in-education research in developing regions. Findings should therefore be interpreted as thematic and descriptive rather than causally conclusive.

### 2.2 Inclusion and exclusion criteria

The inclusion and exclusion criteria are indicated in Table [1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44217-026-01816-z#Tab1).

**Table 1 Inclusion and exclusion criteria of literatures for the study**

[Full size table](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44217-026-01816-z/tables/1)

### 2.3 Search strategy

A comprehensive search strategy was employed to capture all relevant studies, ensuring a thorough review of both empirical research and cutting-edge technological innovations. The search was conducted only in English language, and it was completed in July 2024. The review followed PRISMA guidelines [[10](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44217-026-01816-z#ref-CR10 "Shamseer L, Moher D, Clarke M, Ghersi D, Liberati A, Petticrew M, Shekelle P, Stewart LA. Preferred reporting items for systematic review and meta-analysis protocols (PRISMA-P) 2015: elaboration and explanation. BMJ. 2015;349. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1186/2046-4053-4-1
                  
                .")] to ensure transparency and reproducibility. However, the review protocol was not registered in PROSPERO or other registries, which is acknowledged as a limitation. Given the inclusion of both peer-reviewed and grey literature, and the emphasis on emerging technologies, the study is best described as a systematic scoping review rather than a full systematic review.

#### 2.3.1 Databases searched

The review utilized a range of academic and multidisciplinary databases known for their coverage of educational, technological, and health-related research: ScienceDirect, Scopus, and Google Scholar. Google Scholar was additionally used to identify grey literature such as reports, policy briefs, and non-published conference proceedings.

#### 2.3.2 Search terms and Boolean operators

Search strings combined specific keywords, synonyms, and Boolean operators to maximize relevant results. Core examples included:

*   “Artificial Intelligence application” OR “AI in Education” AND “developing countries”.

*   “AI in education” OR “Educational technology” AND “Developing regions”.

*   “AI applications in Education” OR “AI in Educational outcomes” AND “Developing countries”.

*   “AI in education” OR “Education improvement” AND “Developing regions”.

*   “Personalized learning” AND “AI” AND “Low-resource settings”.

#### 2.3.3 Detailed search strings, dates, and initial hits per database

To ensure reproducibility and transparency in accordance with PRISMA guidelines, Table[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44217-026-01816-z#Tab2) presents the exact search strings, search dates, database-specific filters, and the number of initial records retrieved from each source. All searches were conducted on July 15, 2024.

**Table 2 Database-specific search strings, filters, dates, and initial hit counts**

[Full size table](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44217-026-01816-z/tables/2)

### 2.4 Study selection

The study selection process was conducted in a systematic manner to ensure the inclusion of relevant and high-quality studies, following the PRISMA guidelines (Fig.[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44217-026-01816-z#Fig1)). The process involved two main stages:

1.   1.
Title and abstract screening – Two independent reviewers screened all retrieved studies to identify those that likely met the inclusion criteria.

2.   2.
Full-text review – Studies that passed the initial screening were evaluated in detail for methodology, findings, and relevance to the review objectives.

Disagreements between reviewers were resolved through consensus discussions and/or consultation with a third reviewer. A PRISMA flow diagram was used to document the study selection process, visually capturing the number of studies retrieved, screened, included, and excluded, along with reasons for exclusion. This transparent approach ensured reproducibility and reliability, adhering to systematic review methodology standards.

**Fig. 1**

![Image 7: Fig. 1](https://media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1007%2Fs44217-026-01816-z/MediaObjects/44217_2026_1816_Fig1_HTML.png)

[Full size image](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44217-026-01816-z/figures/1)

Processes for database search of publications for systematic reviews

The substantial reduction from 2,102 initial records to 29 included studies (1.4% retention) reflects the rigorous application of inclusion and exclusion criteria (Table [1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44217-026-01816-z#Tab1)). The primary drivers of exclusion were: studies conducted exclusively in developed regions without relevance to developing country challenges (_n_ = 1,042; 49.6% of exclusions), non-educational applications (_n_ = 398; 18.9%), methodological gaps or lack of measurable outcomes (_n_ = 211; 10.0%), and duplicate records (_n_ = 312; 14.8%). Notably, a parallel search for high-income countries using identical terms yielded over 8,000 records for the same period, confirming that the modest final sample reflects the emergent state of empirical AI-in-education research in developing regions rather than a methodological limitation. The 29 studies constitute a curated, evidence-rich corpus that prioritizes relevance and rigor over exhaustive but unfocused inclusion.

### 2.5 Data extraction

The data extraction process aimed to capture all pertinent details related to the use of AI in education within developing regions and its transformative impact on educational practices. Table[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44217-026-01816-z#Tab3) summarizes the extracted studies covering a wide range of regions including South Asia, Sub-Saharan Africa, Southeast Asia, the Middle East, and high-income countries. Reported AI interventions span adaptive learning systems, intelligent tutoring systems (ITS), ChatGPT, virtual mentors, smart classrooms, AI-powered teacher training, and radiology-specific applications. The documented educational impacts emphasize personalization of learning, improved student engagement and motivation, enhanced teacher efficiency, curriculum relevance, and expanded access in low-resource settings. At the same time, recurring barriers to adoption include infrastructure deficits, high costs, limited teacher training, ethical concerns such as privacy and bias, cultural resistance, and risks of over-reliance on technology.

**Table 3 Studies involved with basic information used in the review**

[Full size table](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44217-026-01816-z/tables/3)

Building on this extracted evidence, the following bibliometric and text-mining procedures used to analyze patterns, themes, and co-occurrences across the included studies, providing the foundation for the Results section.

### 2.6 Bibliometric and text-mining procedures

To complement the systematic review, bibliometric and text-mining analyses were conducted to explore keyword trends, word cloud visualizations, and co-occurrence networks. These procedures ensured transparency and reproducibility of the visualizations presented in Sect. [3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44217-026-01816-z#Sec14).

_Data sources and corpus_

*   Analyses were conducted on the final set of 29 included studies following full-text screening and eligibility confirmation.

*   For the “frequency of key terms over time,” trends were cross-checked against the broader set of screened records to avoid idiosyncratic effects of a small corpus. However, the visualizations and clusters reported are based on the final 29 studies.

_Software and tools_

*   _Word cloud generation_: Conducted with an online word cloud creator, with stop words removed and frequency weighting applied.

*   _Co-occurrence networks and clustering_: Performed using VOSviewer (v1.x) with full counting and LinLog/modularity for community detection.

*   _Keyword frequency and term tracing over time_: Computed using Bibliometrix (R package; biblioshiny module) for tokenization and frequency tables, cross-validated with manual extraction from author keywords and titles.

_Text fields and term types_

*   _Primary sources_: Author keywords and titles from the 29 studies.

*   _Secondary sources_: Abstracts, when author keywords were absent or insufficient.

*   _Preprocessing_: Lowercasing, removal of general stop words, lemmatization of common AI terms (e.g., “chatbots” → “chatbot”), and merging of synonyms (e.g., “ITS” and “intelligent tutoring systems”).

_Parameter settings_

*   _Minimum occurrences_:

    *   Word cloud: ≥ 2 mentions across the corpus.

    *   Co-occurrence network: ≥ 2 co-occurrences across documents.

    *   Frequency plots: ≥ 1 occurrence per year bin.

*   _Counting method_: Full counting in VOSviewer; author keywords prioritized, supplemented by titles and abstracts where necessary.

*   _Clustering and layout (VOSviewer)_: LinLog layout, association strength normalization, modularity optimization for cluster detection. Cluster labels were assigned manually based on dominant term sets.

*   _Inclusion logic_: Only terms directly relevant to AI in education and developing regions were retained; generic terms (e.g., “study,” “method”) and bibliographic noise were excluded.

It is important to note that the bibliometric and text-mining components (word cloud, co-occurrence network, frequency plots) are employed as descriptive and exploratory aids rather than inferential statistical tools. Their primary purpose is to visually map thematic patterns and identify term co-occurrence trends within the included corpus, thereby complementing the qualitative synthesis. All analytical claims presented in Sect. The key insights and recommendations focus on the important role of artificial intelligence (AI) in addressing challenges in education and healthcare. A significant point is the focus on equity and accessibility, where AI is increasingly seen as a tool to bridge the digital divide and reduce inequalities in these sectors. AI interventions have emerged as a transformative force in education, addressing systemic challenges and improving the quality of learning experiences. The key themes were derived from a systematic screening of 29 peer-reviewed articles. Each article was analyzed for explicit mentions of AI interventions, tools, and applications relevant to educational contexts. These keywords and phrases were then grouped into thematic clusters based on shared functions, target audiences, and technological domains. For example, terms like _adaptive learning systems_, _intelligent tutoring systems (ITS)_, and _AI-powered teacher training_ were grouped under AI for Personalized and Professional Learning, while _radiology-specific diagnostics_ and _clinical decision-making tools_ formed the AI in Health Education cluster. This is a systematic scoping review published in Discover Education (July 2026) examining the opportunities and barriers of AI in transforming education in developing regions. The review synthesized evidence from 29 eligible studies (from an initial pool of 2,102 records) published between 2020-2024.

**Key Findings:**
- AI-powered tools (adaptive learning systems, intelligent tutoring platforms, generative AI like ChatGPT) showed positive effects on personalized learning, teacher efficiency, and student engagement in 62% of studies (18/29).
- Technical barriers (infrastructure deficits, high costs, limited internet access) were reported in 26% of studies; ethical/human challenges (data privacy, algorithmic bias, resistance to change) in 22%; and educational system challenges (lack of teacher training, outdated curricula) in 19%.
- Only 17% of studies (5/29) reported outcomes beyond a single academic term, and none used randomized controlled designs, indicating a weak evidence base for long-term effectiveness.
- Emerging innovations like generative AI for culturally relevant content and virtual labs for STEM education remain underutilized (14.8% of studies).
- Region-specific insights: Low-resource settings prioritize basic access tools (voice assistants, mobile platforms), while higher-resource developing regions focus on personalized learning systems.

**Research Questions Addressed:** Effectiveness of AI technologies, primary barriers to adoption, emerging AI innovations, ethical implications, and best practices for integration.

**Methodology:** PRISMA-guided systematic scoping review (not registered in PROSPERO). Searched ScienceDirect, Scopus, and Google Scholar. Included bibliometric analyses (word clouds, co-occurrence networks) and thematic synthesis.

**Conclusions:** AI holds transformative potential for education in developing regions, but requires substantial investments in infrastructure, teacher training, culturally localized AI tools, and robust ethical frameworks. Without context-specific strategies, AI risks deepening existing educational inequities.

# 10 questions every school should ask about AI data privacy

Protect student information with these 10 essential questions about AI data privacy in schools. Learn about compliance, data security, and best practices.

[Stephanie Howell](#author-bio) • Feb 4, 2026

AI Literacy Safety & Policy

![Four security and privacy commitments displayed as rounded button badges with icons: Privacy first, Certified secure, Always…](https://6lm1nym0g4umrrdy.public.blob.vercel-storage.com/blog/key-questions-ai-data-privacy-schools-before-implementation.jpg)

[Get started](https://app.schoolai.com/sign-up)Get a custom demo for your school

[Get started](https://app.schoolai.com/sign-up)Get a custom demo for your school

## Key takeaways

* Schools must assess what student data AI tools collect, why it's needed, and who can access it, particularly given that [85 to 86%](https://www.edweek.org/technology/rising-use-of-ai-in-schools-comes-with-big-downsides-for-students/2025/10) of teachers and students are now using AI tools
* Strong data-security measures (encryption, access controls, and auditing) are non-negotiable in an environment where [education faces over 4,300 cyberattacks](https://deepstrike.io/blog/data-breaches-education-2025) per organization weekly
* Legal compliance with FERPA, COPPA (including [2025 amendments](https://www.nea.org/sites/default/files/2025-06/5.1-ai-policy-overview-of-federal-regulations-final.pdf)), state laws, and vendor accountability is essential
* Clear policies on data ownership, retention, and deletion reduce risk and liability
* Ongoing staff training and parent transparency build trust and ensure responsible AI use

The rapid integration of AI tools in schools has reached unprecedented levels, with [85% of teachers and 86% of students](https://www.edweek.org/technology/rising-use-of-ai-in-schools-comes-with-big-downsides-for-students/2025/10) using them during the 2024-25 school year. While these technologies hold great promise for enhancing education, they also raise critical concerns about AI data privacy in schools.

Before you integrate [AI technology](https://schoolai.com/blog/revolutionizing-learning-10-leading-benefits-of-ai-in-education) into your educational environment, it's essential to ask key questions to ensure student data is protected and that privacy laws are followed. School administrators and technology coordinators must balance innovation with their ethical and legal responsibility to safeguard sensitive student data, guided by comprehensive [data protection policies](https://schoolai.com/privacy).

Without proper vetting and oversight, AI systems may collect excessive data, create security vulnerabilities, or use student information in ways families never intended. With these risks in mind, the following 10 questions provide a clear framework for evaluating AI tools responsibly.

## 1. What student data will the AI tool collect and why?

Understanding the scope of student data collection is your first line of defense in safeguarding AI data privacy in schools. [AI tools in education](https://schoolai.com/blog/exploring-ais-role-in-modern-education) typically gather information across six main categories, each with distinct privacy implications:

* **Personally Identifiable Information (PII)** – names, email addresses, student IDs, photos/avatars
* **Academic Performance Data** – grades, test scores, assignment submissions, participation metrics
* **Behavioral and Engagement Data** – classroom interactions, time-on-task, responses to materials
* **Learning Analytics** – content-interaction patterns and knowledge gaps, used to [personalize homework](https://schoolai.com/blog/using-ai-personalize-homework-assignments) or enhance [science instruction](https://schoolai.com/blog/enhancing-science-education-ai-tools)
* **Communication Logs** – chat discussions, feedback exchanges
* **Assistive Technology Data** – information about learning difficulties and accommodations

The principle of data minimization (collecting only what's necessary) protects both student privacy and your district's liability. Under FERPA, all of this information qualifies as "education records," triggering specific protection requirements and parent rights.

Key questions to ask vendors or internal teams:

* Is every data point essential to the learning goal?
* Could the same insights be achieved with de-identified data?
* Who, inside and outside the district, can access raw student information?

## 2. How will the data be stored, secured, and encrypted?

Student data protection demands specific technical standards that separate serious vendors from those cutting corners.

Essential security requirements include:

* **Encryption** must protect student information both at rest and in transit.
* **Access controls** should include role-based permissions, multi-factor authentication, and comprehensive audit logs.
* Vendors should conduct regular penetration tests and vulnerability assessments.

The [Federal Trade Commission's enforcement action](https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2025/12/ftc-takes-action-against-education-technology-provider-failing-secure-students-personal-data) against Illuminate Education revealed that the company exposed personal information of more than 10.1 million students, including email addresses, dates of birth, and health-related information, due to inadequate security practices, including storing student data in plain text until at least January 2022.

Ask pointed questions:

* How do you manage and rotate encryption keys?
* Do third-party subcontractors ever access raw student data?
* What are your results from recent security assessments?

## 3. Does the vendor comply with FERPA, COPPA, GDPR, and relevant state laws?

Compliance frameworks serve as guardrails, keeping AI data privacy in schools safe. The regulatory landscape has evolved significantly, with the [Federal Trade Commission finalizing amendments](https://www.nea.org/sites/default/files/2025-06/5.1-ai-policy-overview-of-federal-regulations-final.pdf) to COPPA in January 2025 to address evolving digital practices and enhance children's online privacy protections.

[SchoolAI](https://schoolai.com/privacy) maintains strict compliance with FERPA, COPPA, and GDPR, ensuring that student data is protected according to the highest standards. Our platform is designed with privacy-first principles, giving schools the confidence that their AI implementation meets all regulatory requirements.

Key compliance requirements include:

* **FERPA** limits disclosure of education records without parental consent.
* **COPPA** requires parental consent for data collection from children under 13, with new 2025 amendments requiring separate consent for third-party data sharing and mandatory data retention policies.
* **GDPR** applies if you serve international students or use global providers and enforces principles like purpose limitation and data minimization.
* More than [128 state student privacy laws](https://studentprivacycompass.org/state-guidance-on-the-use-of-generative-ai-in-k-12-education/) have been enacted across the United States, creating varying requirements.

## 4. Who owns student data, and how is it shared?

School districts should retain complete ownership of all student data, including any AI-generated outputs derived from that data. Research reveals troubling practices among educational technology vendors: [60% of school apps](https://publicinterestprivacy.org/ai-laws/) send student data to third-party advertising platforms, and only 14% of schools enable parents to consent to technology use.

Contracts should explicitly prohibit vendors from:

* Reselling student data
* Using it to train unrelated AI models
* Sharing it with third parties without explicit permission

## 5. What is the data retention and deletion policy?

Written retention schedules protect both student privacy and district liability. The [updated COPPA amendments](https://www.nea.org/sites/default/files/2025-06/5.1-ai-policy-overview-of-federal-regulations-final.pdf) require operators to retain children's personal information only as long as necessary to fulfill the purpose for which it was collected and prohibit retaining such information indefinitely.

Critical retention policy questions:

* How long is student data kept after contract termination?
* How long are backup copies maintained?
* Can the district trigger immediate deletion on request?
* How is deletion verified and documented?

Comprehensive [audit logs](https://ncce.org/securing-student-data-best-practices-for-k-12-schools/) should document every step of data-lifecycle management.

## 6. How will parent/student consent and transparency be managed for AI data privacy in schools?

Consent is a bridge of trust between schools and families. However, research reveals significant gaps in current practices, with [most parents unaware](https://edtech.law/issue/no-consent/) of the applications their children use, and schools claiming they can consent on behalf of parents, limiting families' effective authority over educational data.

Best practices include:

* **Opt-in** requires explicit agreement before any data collection begins.
* **Opt-out** assumes consent unless families decline.

Communicate in plain language:

* Educational purpose and benefits
* Specific data collected
* How to opt out
* Contact information for questions

Provide notifications in families' home languages and start conversations early. Be aware that parents seeking to opt out often face undesirable consequences and may forgo efforts to learn about platforms out of fear of retaliation or concern about their children being ostracized.

## 7. How does AI mitigate bias and promote equity?

AI bias can disadvantage students based on race, gender, income, or learning differences. Recent research demonstrates concerning patterns, with [predictive algorithms commonly used](https://www.aera.net/Newsroom/Study-Algorithms-Used-by-Universities-to-Predict-Student-Success-May-Be-Racially-Biased) by colleges and universities showing racial bias against Black and Hispanic students, incorrectly predicting failure for Black and Hispanic students at rates of 19% and 21%, respectively.

Causes of bias include skewed training data, proxy variables, and historical inequities.

Vendor requirements:

* Diverse, representative training datasets
* Regular fairness audits
* Human oversight for high-stakes decisions

Link these evaluations to existing district equity and inclusion policies, and adopt practices for [ethical AI in classrooms](https://schoolai.com/blog/strengthening-ethical-ai-in-classrooms-improvements-to-historical-figure-spaces).

## 8. How does the algorithm provide transparency and explainability?

Transparency = understanding how the model works. Explainability = understanding why the AI made a specific recommendation.

Request documentation such as:

* Model cards (intended use, limitations, performance)
* Impact-assessment summaries
* Accessible explanations of decision pathways

Ask vendors:

* Can teachers see feature-importance scores?
* How are algorithm updates documented and communicated?
* What processes exist for challenging or overriding AI decisions?

The importance of transparency has been reinforced by the [U.S. Department of Education's](http://www.ed.gov/about/news/press-release/us-department-of-education-issues-guidance-artificial-intelligence-use-schools-proposes-additional-supplemental-priority) 2025 guidance, which emphasizes principles for responsible AI adoption, including attention to user privacy and the need to engage affected stakeholders, particularly parents, in AI implementation decisions.

## 9. What ongoing monitoring, breach response, and compliance reviews are in place?

Given that [ransomware attacks against schools](https://www.k12dive.com/news/first-dip-ransomware-attacks-quarters-since-2024-comparitech/804339/) rose 23% year over year in the first half of 2025, with average ransom demands of $556,000, robust monitoring is essential.

A "minimum viable monitoring stack" should include:

* Automated alerts for unusual data-access patterns
* Anomaly-detection systems for security incidents
* Regular user-access recertification
* Scheduled compliance reviews

Strong incident-response protocols feature 72-hour breach-notification timelines and clear escalation paths. Internally, designate staff to monitor privacy compliance and vendor relationships.

Schools should follow [comprehensive data breach](https://www.nea.org/professional-excellence/student-engagement/tools-tips/student-and-educator-data-privacy) response procedures, including immediate reporting to leadership, containing the breach, preserving evidence, and supporting investigations.

## 10. How will staff and students be trained for responsible AI use?

AI tools without training are like handing car keys to someone who's never driven. Alarmingly, [less than half of teachers](https://www.edweek.org/technology/rising-use-of-ai-in-schools-comes-with-big-downsides-for-students/2025/10) (48%) have participated in any training or professional development on AI provided by their schools or districts. Among teachers who received training, fewer than a third received guidance on using AI tools effectively, and only 17% learned how to monitor and check AI systems.

The training gap extends to students, with [less than half of students](https://www.edweek.org/technology/rising-use-of-ai-in-schools-comes-with-big-downsides-for-students/2025/10) (48%) reporting that someone at their school provided information about AI use. Few students received guidance on school AI policies (22%), AI risks (17%), or basic AI literacy (12%).

Comprehensive training should include:

* Provide [AI literacy programs](https://schoolai.com/blog/ai-literacy-educators-building-strong-foundations-teaching) for educators.
* Include privacy obligations under FERPA, COPPA, and state laws.
* Teach strategies for identifying and mitigating bias.
* Offer age-appropriate digital-citizenship lessons for students.
* Embed AI literacy into onboarding and ongoing professional-development pathways.

## Protecting student data while embracing innovation

Implementing AI in education doesn't have to mean compromising student privacy. By asking these 10 critical questions, schools can harness the transformative potential of AI while safeguarding data privacy and maintaining the trust of students, families, and communities. The framework presented here provides a roadmap for responsible AI adoption that balances innovation with protection.

As AI technology and privacy regulations continue to evolve, ongoing vigilance remains essential. Regular policy reviews, staff training, and transparent communication with families will ensure your AI implementation remains secure, compliant, and effective.

Ready to implement AI with confidence? [Discover how SchoolAI](https://app.schoolai.com/sign-up) provides FERPA and COPPA-compliant AI tools designed specifically for education, with robust data protection, transparent policies, and comprehensive support for responsible AI adoption in your school.

#### Frequently Asked Questions

Schools can ensure FERPA and COPPA compliance by auditing AI vendors, verifying data protection agreements, and confirming that tools collect only the minimum data needed for instruction. They should obtain required parental consent, especially for students under 13, and maintain clear breach-response protocols. Regular privacy training for staff, ongoing compliance checks, and transparent communication with families strengthen adherence to both regulations.

Schools can audit and mitigate bias by using diverse training data, conducting regular fairness reviews, and comparing AI outputs across student groups. Human oversight in high-stakes decisions reduces reliance on algorithmic judgments alone. Tools like model cards and impact assessments increase transparency, while involving students, families, and educators in policy development ensures systems align with district equity goals and support fair outcomes for all learners.

Successful AI integration begins with structured professional development that builds educator understanding of AI uses, limitations, privacy requirements, and ethical considerations. Hands-on practice helps teachers effectively incorporate tools. For students, AI instruction should be age-appropriate and embedded in digital citizenship lessons, covering how AI works, its risks and benefits, and responsible use. Interactive projects and discussions build critical thinking and prepare students for an AI-driven world.

*Refreshed and updated September 10th, 2025.*

### Key Takeaways:

* **FERPA protects the privacy of student education records, and the stakes are rising.** Educational institutions face an average of 2,507 cyberattack attempts per week, and breaches have impacted over 1.8 million students in the U.S. since 2020. Much of this data belongs to minors, making protection a top priority.
* **2025 brought stricter enforcement and new transparency requirements.** The Department of Education stated that schools and state agencies must now demonstrate proactive protections and were required to submit compliance documentation by April 2025.
* **FERPA violations often happen unintentionally.** Common examples include sharing recommendation letters without authorization, accidentally sending confidential emails to the wrong recipients, and granting vendors access to student records without proper consent.
* **Experts warn that FERPA still lacks clear cybersecurity requirements.** As schools rely on hundreds of ed-tech tools, the next wave of enforcement will likely combine transparency mandates with explicit technology and security obligations.

When we think about digital transformation and massive migration to the cloud, the private sector likely comes to mind. However, educational institutions are increasingly leveraging digital platforms for student records and academic activities (though some may be slower to adopt).  

For the education sector, since much of the data held and processed belongs to minors, protecting student data is a top priority. 

The key issue here is trust, especially between institutions and students. Thus, the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA) was created to help set rules and guidelines around data and privacy protection.   

Established in 1974, FERPA is a federal law in the United States that protects the privacy of student education records and setting the standard for protecting sensitive student data.  

FERPA requires educational institutions that receive federal funding to have robust security measures in place — including physical security controls, network security mechanisms, and procedural safeguards to ensure comprehensive data protection.  

### What are the key principles of FERPA and who do they apply to?

FERPA is comprised of several core principles designed to protect the privacy and security of student education records: 

* **Privacy**: Protects students’ educational records by restricting the use and disclosure of that data. The objective is to ensure students’ rights to their information and apply rules on the release of academic records.
* **Access**: Establishes the rights of parents and eligible students to access and review their education records, ensuring transparency and allowing for corrections if inaccuracies are found.
* **Directory Information**: While most information in a student’s education record is protected by FERPA, there’s some information termed “directory information” that can be disclosed without consent, unless the student or parent opts out.
* **School Official**: Allows schools to share student records without consent to school officials with legitimate educational interests.

 FERPA applies to all schools receiving funds under an applicable program of the U.S. Department of Education, including public and private elementary and secondary schools and post-secondary institutions. 

### Individual rights under FERPA

 FERPA grants students and their parents several rights concerning their educational records, including: 

* **Right to Access**: Students and parents have the right to review or obtain copies of their educational records.
* **Right to Amend**: If students or parents believe that information in the records is inaccurate, they have the right to request amendments.
* **Right to Control Disclosure**: Students and parents can control the disclosure of certain data from their educational records.
* **Right to File a Complaint**: If they believe their rights under FERPA have been violated, students and parents may file a complaint with the U.S. Department of Education.

### What important cybersecurity statistics are there for the education sector?

As educational institutions continue to embrace digital technologies, they also face skyrocketing cybersecurity threats. Understanding the current landscape of cyber threats and challenges in protecting sensitive data is crucial for schools and universities.  

The following stats shed light on the magnitude of these challenges and emphasize the urgent need for robust cybersecurity measures to protect educational infrastructure. 

**Escalating threats**: Educational institutions are seeing an [alarming average](https://er.educause.edu/articles/sponsored/2023/9/three-cybersecurity-facts-campus-leaders-should-know) of 2,507 cyberattack attempts each week in 2023. This significant number highlights the urgent need for robust security protocols to protect sensitive data. 

**Persistent ransomware**: [Two-thirds of educational organizations](https://www.sophos.com/en-us/press/press-releases/2022/04/ransomware-hit-66-percent-of-organizations-surveyed-for-sophos-annual-state-of-ransomware-2022) have faced ransomware attacks, with a recovery of all data in only 4% of cases. The financial impact is also severe, with an average remediation cost of $1.42 million per incident. 

**Staffing c****hallenges**: Recruiting skilled cybersecurity personnel [continues to be a major hurdle](https://www.chronicle.com/article/higher-eds-hiring-challenges-are-getting-worse) for 62% of education administrators, emphasizing the need for comprehensive training and development programs in cybersecurity. 

**Dramatic impact**: The far-reaching effects of cyber threats have impacted [over 1.8 million students](https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-23-105480) in the U.S. since 2020, showcasing the extensive consequences of these security breaches. 

### What are some examples of FERPA violations?

Understanding and adhering to FERPA regulations is a crucial step for educational institutions in protecting student privacy. FERPA violations can occur in various forms, often unintentionally, through mishandling of student information.  

The following examples illustrate common scenarios where FERPA compliance may be breached. 

**Unauthorized disclosures** 

* Unauthorized sharing of a student’s recommendation letter with potential employers
* A vendor is granted access to student records without proper authorization
* Contracts with vendors who perform data mining on student information without consent

**Improper release of information**  

* Releasing educational records to parents of students aged 18 or over without the student’s approval
* Confidential information about students shared by school officials with unauthorized parties, including the media and on social networks

**Communication** **mishaps** 

* School officials accidentally sending confidential emails to unintended recipients
* Public postings of student grades with identifiable information
* Discussing sensitive student details over the phone without verifying the caller’s identity

### **What’s new under FERPA in 2025?**

The Department of Education has doubled down on enforcement and transparency. Regulators are making it clear that compliance is no longer a box-checking exercise.

Schools and state agencies are now expected to demonstrate proactive protections as opposed to reactive response.

* In April 2025, the Department of Education [issued a Dear Colleague letter](https://www.mcguirewoods.com/client-resources/alerts/2025/4/department-of-education-issues-guidance-on-student-privacy-and-parental-rights-imposes-reporting-requirements-for-state-educational-agencies) emphasizing that student “gender support plans” belong in the education record and cannot be hidden from parents. It also underscored the need to share safety-related information, issue annual privacy notices, and treat military recruiters like any other recruiter unless parents opt out.

* By April 30, 2025, SEAs and LEAs [were required to submit documentation](https://www.osba.org/us-department-of-education-seeks-assurances-of-ferpa-compliance) demonstrating compliance with these mandates.

* Mid-year, prior guidance related to using financial aid information for research [was officially rescinded](https://studentprivacy.ed.gov/topic/family-educational-rights-privacy-act-ferpa).

A growing body of commentary in mid-2025 noted that [FERPA lacks clear cybersecurity requirements](https://publicinterestprivacy.org/fixing-ferpa-cybersecurity/) even though schools rely on hundreds of ed-tech tools. Experts urge lawmakers to modernize FERPA with vendor security obligations to better protect student data.

Looking ahead, institutions should prepare for potential cybersecurity-specific mandates that extend FERPA beyond privacy into the realm of digital risk, especially as vendor ecosystems grow more complex. The next wave of FERPA enforcement will likely combine transparency requirements with explicit technology and security obligations.

This thorough discovery and identification process is crucial for educational institutions aiming for FERPA compliance.
2. **Monitor and classify s****tudent** **data for risk**: After identifying student data, it’s equally important to monitor its usage, sharing patterns, and access logs. This continuous monitoring can quickly and accurately detect risks from inappropriate permissions, risky sharing, and unauthorized access. Concentric AI handles this process autonomously, alleviating the burden on IT and security teams, who often lack those resources in the education sector. Plus, our solution classifies data based on its sensitivity and significance, enabling institutions to apply suitable data protection measures and implement data retention policies.
3. **Remediate d****ata** **risk issues**: The final step is to tackle any data risk issues that emerge. Concentric’s Risk Distance™ analysis leverages deep learning to compare each data element with baseline security practices used by similar data to detect risk — without relying on rules and policies. ## Abstract

This study examines how Chinese and Western news media covered artificial intelligence (AI) privacy issues in higher education from 2019 to 2024. News articles were retrieved from Nexis Uni. First, non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) was employed to identify core AI privacy topics in university teaching, administration, and research. Next, a time trend analysis investigated how media attention shifted in relation to key events, including the COVID-19 pandemic and the emergence of generative AI. Finally, a sentiment analysis was conducted to compare the distribution of positive, negative, and neutral reporting. The findings indicate that AI-driven proctoring, student data security, and institutional governance are central concerns in both Chinese and English media. However, the focus and framing differ: some Western outlets highlight individual privacy rights and controversies in remote exam monitoring, while Chinese coverage more frequently addresses AI-driven educational innovation and policy support. The shift to remote education after 2020 and the rise of generative AI from 2023 onward have intensified discussions on AI privacy in higher education. The results offer a cross-cultural perspective for institutions seeking to reconcile the adoption of AI with robust privacy safeguards and provide a foundation for future data governance frameworks under diverse regulatory environments.
