## China K‑12 Content & Platform Market Outlook (2026-2034):

The China K‑12 content & platform market is positioned for robust expansion throughout the forecast period, propelled by continued government investments in educational digitalization initiatives and the nationwide rollout of AI education mandates beginning in 2025. The Ministry of Education's commitment to upgrading the Smart Education of China platform into the world's largest digital education database will further enhance resource accessibility across all regions. Additionally, the strategic pivot of major EdTech companies toward AI-powered intelligent hardware and quality-oriented education following regulatory reforms is creating new revenue streams, while increasing parental demand for personalized learning experiences and corporate partnerships with technology giants are accelerating innovation in educational content delivery and platform capabilities.

## Impact of AI:

AI is fundamentally reshaping China's K‑12 content and platform landscape by enabling unprecedented personalization and efficiency in education delivery. AI-powered systems provide intelligent tutoring, automated grading with step-level precision, and adaptive learning pathways that adjust to individual student needs in real-time. Major EdTech providers have developed proprietary educational large language models demonstrating superior accuracy in subject-specific applications, with reported learning efficiency improvements of 300%. The Chinese government's mandate for nationwide AI education beginning September 2025, establishment of 184 AI education bases, and integration of AI capabilities into the national smart education platform underscore artificial intelligence's central role in modernizing China's educational ecosystem and preparing students for an increasingly technology-driven future.

## Market Dynamics:

### Key Market Trends & Growth Drivers:

***Government-Led National Digital Education Infrastructure and Smart Platform Expansion***

The Chinese government has elevated educational digitalization to a national strategic priority, fundamentally transforming how educational content and platforms are delivered across the country. At the core of this initiative is the Smart Education of China platform, which has evolved into the world's largest high-quality digital education repository since its launch in 2020. By the end of 2023, the platform had connected 519,000 educational institutions across China, benefiting 18.8 million teachers and 293 million learners, with over 100 million registered users from 200 countries and 36.7 billion cumulative visits. The platform's success demonstrates the positive multiplier and spillover effects of digital technology in education. Building on this foundation, the Ministry of Education declared 2025 as the inaugural year of smart education and launched the National Education Digitalization Strategic Plan 2.0 in May 2025, which aims to further improve content quality, incorporate educational resource sharing mechanisms, and establish a comprehensive national resource center. In 2024, The Chinese Ministry of Education officially kicked off the comprehensive application of the Smart Education of China platform in primary and secondary schools, focusing on three major tasks: expanding pilot programs in Guangdong and Hainan by fully integrating high-quality resources from all platforms at all levels, expanding programs in ethnic minority areas in middle and western China to improve effectiveness and support the improvement of quality through digitalized education, and promoting the sharing of high-quality digital resources in eastern China by mobilizing stakeholders in Beijing, Shanghai, and Jiangsu. This infrastructure development driven by the government is creating unparalleled opportunities for content providers and platform developers while guaranteeing equal access to quality educational resources across urban and rural divides. The Ministry's commitment to streamlining access to public education services, including easier cross-provincial student transfers and teacher qualification certifications, alongside launching a national lifelong education platform, further expands the addressable market beyond traditional K-12 boundaries, positioning digital education infrastructure as a cornerstone of China's broader educational transformation and economic modernization strategy.

***Artificial Intelligence (AI) Integration Enabling Personalized Adaptive Learning Experiences***

The integration of AI into K-12 educational content and platforms represents a paradigm shift in how learning is delivered and experienced in China. Educational technology companies have invested heavily in developing proprietary large language models specifically designed for educational applications, enabling capabilities that were previously impossible with traditional digital learning tools. These AI systems provide intelligent tutoring that adapts to individual student learning patterns, automated grading with detailed feedback on problem-solving steps, real-time performance analytics that identify knowledge gaps, and personalized content recommendations that optimize learning pathways. The penetration rate of AI adaptive learning in China's K-12 education sector is rising owing to policy benefits, technology maturity, and strong demand from customers seeking high-quality educational resources and institutions eager to be equipped with innovative teaching tools. Major EdTech providers have achieved significant breakthroughs in AI capabilities, with companies like TAL Education Group developing MathGPT, a specialized AI model that outperforms general-purpose models like GPT-4 in mathematical education applications. In January 2024, TAL Education Group unveiled its Xueersi xPad Flagship Model at CES 2024, featuring proprietary MathGPT Education LLM that provides intelligent guided learning, adaptive difficulty levels, and personalized recommendations through interactive AI elements including image recognition and real-time AI voice assistant. The Chinese government has further accelerated AI adoption by mandating AI education for all primary and secondary school students beginning September 1, 2025, with Beijing spearheading the program as a pilot, and designating 184 schools as AI education bases nationwide, thereby supporting the China K‑12 content & platform market growth.

***Blended Learning Model Adoption and Cloud-Based Platform Proliferation***

The Chinese K-12 education market is experiencing a fundamental transformation in learning delivery models, with blended learning approaches that combine traditional face-to-face instruction with online digital content becoming increasingly mainstream across public schools, private institutions, and supplementary education providers. This hybrid model addresses multiple stakeholder needs simultaneously: students benefit from personalized pacing and flexible access to content, teachers gain powerful tools for differentiated instruction and real-time assessment, schools achieve cost efficiencies and expanded curriculum offerings, and parents receive greater transparency into their children's learning progress and performance analytics. Cloud-based deployment has emerged as the preferred technology architecture for educational platforms, offering scalability that allows systems to accommodate fluctuating user loads during peak examination preparation periods, cost-effectiveness by eliminating the need for expensive on-premises infrastructure, accessibility enabling students to learn from any location with internet connectivity, and continuous updates that ensure users always have access to the latest content and features. The market expansion reflects growing customization of online education services facilitated by cloud computing technologies that enable sophisticated data analytics and personalized learning pathways. Traditional online course providers are pivoting toward more tech-driven approaches, offering quality-oriented education including coding, speech training, and skill-based learning rather than exam-focused tutoring, aligning with government policy preferences following the Double Reduction reforms. Companies like Zuoyebang have successfully adapted by equipping smart tablets with AI applications that allow students to have assignments graded, corrected, or improved by AI tutors, while Huohua Siwei has shifted toward quality education offerings. The proliferation of cloud-based platforms is also enabling innovative business models including subscription services, freemium offerings with premium upgrades, pay-per-course options, and institutional licensing arrangements that provide flexible monetization pathways for content and platform providers while accommodating diverse customer preferences and purchasing power across China's economically diverse regions. Edtech sector is also flourishing owing to the heightened focus on technologically advanced learning procedures and rise in government investments in education and research. The Chinese government announced a massive $52 billion investment in research and development for 2024, up a full 10% from the previous year and representing the largest percentage increase of any major funding area, including military spending.

### Key Market Challenges:

***Regulatory Uncertainty and Ongoing Policy-Driven Market Disruption***

The China K‑12 content and platform market operates within a highly dynamic and sometimes unpredictable regulatory environment that poses significant challenges for businesses operating in this space. The most impactful regulatory intervention came in July 2021 with the introduction of the "Double Reduction" policy, which fundamentally reshaped the industry landscape by banning for-profit tutoring for core academic subjects during weekends, national holidays, and vacation periods for students in compulsory education. The policy mandated that after-school tutoring institutions register as non-profit entities, prohibited them from listing on stock exchanges or accepting foreign investment, and severely restricted their ability to raise capital or expand operations. The impact was devastating for traditional EdTech companies, with billions of dollars in market value wiped off major players like New Oriental, TAL Education Group, and Yuanfudao overnight. Companies have been forced to pivot rapidly toward alternative business models including smart hardware devices, quality-oriented education offerings like coding and arts training, vocational education, and adult learning, but these transitions require substantial new investments and expertise in unfamiliar market segments. The regulatory environment remains fluid, with ongoing policy adjustments and implementation guidelines issued at national and provincial levels, making it difficult for businesses to develop stable long-term strategies. Furthermore, enforcement varies across regions, creating additional complexity for companies operating nationwide.

***Digital Infrastructure Disparities and Unequal Access to Technology Resources***

Despite China's remarkable progress in building digital education infrastructure and the government's substantial investments in connectivity and devices, significant disparities persist between urban and rural areas that create barriers to equitable market development and limit the addressable population for K-12 content and platform providers. Essential educational resources including high-speed broadband internet, personal computing devices, digital-ready classroom facilities, and technology-capable teachers remain heavily concentrated in developed eastern urban centers and first-tier cities, while many rural schools, particularly in western provinces, ethnic minority regions, and remote mountainous areas, struggle with inadequate infrastructure and limited technological capacity. According to educational research, there are notable disparities in educational levels between urban and rural areas as well as among different regions in China, with essential resources such as qualified teachers, modern teaching facilities, and financial investments concentrated in developed areas and urban centers. This creates a multi-tiered market where premium digital education products and services can achieve high penetration in affluent urban markets but face adoption challenges in less developed regions where they might deliver the greatest marginal educational benefit. The digital divide extends beyond mere infrastructure to encompass teacher training and digital literacy, as many educators in rural schools lack experience with advanced educational technologies and may be reluctant to adopt new tools without adequate professional development support. Students from less privileged socioeconomic backgrounds also face disadvantages in accessing online learning resources, as they may lack personal devices, reliable home internet connections, or parental support for technology-mediated learning. The government has initiated programs to bridge these gaps, including the Smart Education of China platform's focus on expanding pilot programs in ethnic minority areas and efforts like Alibaba's "Cloud Youth" initiative that brings digital tools to underserved regions, but progress remains uneven.

***Data Privacy Concerns and Platform Security Requirements***

As K-12 content and platform providers increasingly leverage artificial intelligence, big data analytics, and personalized learning technologies, they collect and process vast amounts of sensitive student information including academic performance data, learning behavior patterns, personal preferences, demographic information, and in some cases biometric data from face recognition or voice analysis systems. This creates significant challenges related to data privacy, security, and appropriate use of student information, particularly given heightened global awareness of digital privacy issues and China's evolving regulatory framework governing data protection and cybersecurity. The Chinese government has implemented strict data sovereignty requirements mandating that student data be stored within national borders on domestic servers, requiring foreign platform providers to establish local data centers or partner with domestic entities, adding complexity and cost to market entry. Parents, educators, and policymakers express growing concerns about potential misuse of student data, inadequate protection against data breaches, unauthorized sharing of information with third parties, and the long-term implications of comprehensive digital profiles being created for children from an early age. These concerns are amplified by high-profile data security incidents in other sectors and international controversies surrounding educational technology and student privacy. Platform providers must navigate complex compliance requirements including obtaining appropriate parental consent, implementing robust security measures to protect against unauthorized access, ensuring data minimization by collecting only information necessary for educational purposes, providing transparency about data usage and retention policies, and establishing secure mechanisms for data deletion when students or parents request removal. The security infrastructure required to meet these standards represents significant ongoing investment, particularly for smaller companies with limited resources. Additionally, platform providers face concerns about screen time and potential negative impacts of excessive technology use on children's physical health, social development, and psychological well-being, leading some parents to resist adoption regardless of educational benefits. Education authorities and schools must balance enthusiasm for digital innovation with responsibility to protect students, creating procurement processes that carefully evaluate platforms' privacy and security practices alongside pedagogical effectiveness. As AI systems become more sophisticated and data collection more comprehensive, these concerns are likely to intensify, requiring proactive engagement from platform providers to build trust through transparent practices, robust security measures, and demonstrated commitment to ethical use of student data, while policymakers continue refining regulatory frameworks to protect children in an increasingly digital educational environment.

# China K-12 Content & Platform Market Summary (IMARC Group Report)

## Market Overview
The China K-12 content & platform market reached **USD 15,941.44 Million** in 2025 and is projected to reach **USD 45,835.75 Million** by 2034, growing at a **CAGR of 12.45%** during 2026-2034.

## Key Growth Drivers
1. **Government-Led Digital Education Infrastructure**: The Smart Education of China platform has become the world's largest digital education repository. By end of 2023, it connected 519,000 educational institutions, benefiting 18.8 million teachers and 293 million learners, with 36.7 billion cumulative visits. The Ministry of Education declared 2025 the inaugural year of smart education and launched the National Education Digitalization Strategic Plan 2.0 in May 2025.

2. **AI Integration**: AI is enabling personalized adaptive learning experiences with intelligent tutoring, automated grading, and adaptive learning pathways. Major EdTech firms (e.g., TAL Education's MathGPT) have developed proprietary educational LLMs. The government mandated AI education for all K-12 students beginning September 1, 2025, designating 184 schools as AI education bases nationwide.

3. **Blended Learning Adoption**: Cloud-based platforms are proliferating, supporting scalable, cost-effective, accessible digital learning. The Chinese government announced a $52 billion investment in R&D for 2024 (10% increase YoY).

## Key Market Challenges
- **Regulatory Uncertainty**: The July 2021 "Double Reduction" policy banned for-profit tutoring for core academic subjects, forcing major EdTech companies to pivot toward smart hardware, quality education, vocational training, and adult learning.
- **Digital Infrastructure Disparities**: Significant urban-rural gaps persist in broadband access, devices, and technology-capable teachers.
- **Data Privacy & Security**: Strict data sovereignty requirements, parental consent mandates, and concerns over student data misuse create compliance burdens.

## Market Segmentation (2026-2034)
- **By Component**: Content Solutions (digital courseware, e-textbooks, video lectures, test prep, gamified/AR-VR content) and Platform Solutions (LMS, SIS, adaptive learning platforms, collaboration tools)
- **By Subject Area**: STEM, Language & Literature, Social Studies & Humanities, Arts & Music, Physical Education & Health
- **By Deployment Mode**: Cloud-based, On-premises, Hybrid
- **By Grade Level**: Primary (Grades 1-5), Middle (Grades 6-9), High (Grades 10-12)
- **By Learning Model**: Synchronous, Asynchronous, Blended Learning
- **By Business Model**: Subscription-based, Freemium, Pay-Per-Course, Institutional Licensing
- **By End User**: Public Schools, Private Schools, Tutoring/After-school Institutions, Individual Learners & Parents
- **By Region**: North China, East China, South Central China, Southwest China, Northwest China, Northeast China

## Competitive Landscape
Highly dynamic market with established education giants pivoting post-Double Reduction toward AI-powered hardware and quality education. Key recent development: In August 2025, TAL Education's Xueersi AI Thinkie 1-on-1 Super Educational Intelligence received a 4+ rating from the China Academy of Information and Communications Technology, the highest industry level for AI-powered personalized learning products.

<webpage_content>
IN-DEPTH / [IN-DEPTH](https://www.globaltimes.cn/In-depth/index.html)

From primary to high schools, students showcase AI-powered projects, highlighting China's long-term AI education drive nurturing next generation of innovators

Preparing tomorrow's minds

By Liang Rui Published: Jul 05, 2026 10:07 PM

Teenage contestants take part in a robotics competition for primary and secondary school students in Fuyang, East China's Anhui Province on May 16, 2026. Photo: VCG

  
The atmosphere at an AI-themed forum in Beijing this June felt different from the usual technology conferences. Instead of executives in suits unveiling the latest products, seven primary and secondary school students from across China took turns stepping into the spotlight. A primary school participant was too young to have fully mastered typing on a keyboard, yet each student confidently presented an AI-powered solution designed to tackle real-world challenges.   
  
How can someone with a broken arm still enjoy racing games? How can visually impaired women "see" their makeup? How can pollutants in rivers be remotely monitored and analyzed in real time? These were functioning AI projects created by children whose average age was under 15 - members of what many now call China's "first generation of AI natives."  
  
The showcase came as China continues to expand AI education nationwide. In May 2025, the Ministry of Education released two landmark guidelines introducing AI literacy and generative AI education for primary and secondary schools.  
  
More recently, on June 29, the Ministry of Education said that China's State Council has issued the outline plan for the development of the education sector during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), calling for AI education across every stage of schooling and greater efforts to strengthen students' AI literacy.  
  
The country's growing emphasis on AI education has also attracted international attention. In late May, Newsweek published an article titled "China's Kids Are Getting an Edge With AI," noting that AI is playing an increasingly significant role in Chinese education, with a heavy push from a government that is keen not only to get children to use AI to improve their performance, but also to master the technology behind it.  
  
An industry expert told the Global Times that the steady investment in AI education is beginning to produce visible results, with more students applying AI as a means of solving practical problems. At the same time, educators stressed that technological capability must be guided by correct values.  
  
**Turning curiosity into innovation**  
  
Among the youngest presenters was Jin Yihong, a primary school student from Shanghai and an avid video game enthusiast. He began his presentation with a photograph showing his right arm in a cast after a fracture.  
  
"If your hand looked like this," he asked the audience, "would you still be able to play video games?"  
  
The personal experience sparked an unexpected journey. During an AI education course, Jin learned about the world's 1.3 billion people living with disabilities, a community he had rarely thought about before.  
  
"My teacher introduced me to a friend living with Wilson's disease," Jin recalled. "His body can't properly process copper, making it difficult for him to control his limbs."  
  
Inspired by the encounter, Jin decided to build an accessible racing game for people with rare diseases, visual impairments and limited mobility.  
  
The project evolved steadily, from a simple 2D obstacle-avoidance game to an early version controlled by foot movements, before eventually becoming a fully immersive 3D racing game.  
  
"I still can't type very well," Jin said with a smile. "But with voice input, I can still create all of this using AI."  
  
His comments unintentionally captured one of AI's most transformative impacts: lowering the barriers to creativity and enabling children to turn ideas into reality long before mastering traditional technical skills.  
  
After Jin sent the game to the friend with Wilson's disease, he received an encouraging response: "I'd like to give it a try."  
  
At another public event in 2025, a participant born with cerebral palsy tested the game and told him he could "play it all day," while also offering suggestions on introducing different accessibility levels for players with varying physical conditions.  
  
The experience changed Jin in unexpected ways. "It made me pay much more attention to accessibility in everyday life," he said. "Now if I see a bicycle blocking a path for visually impaired people, I'll move it out of the way."  
  
A similar desire to solve real-world problems motivated You Xiaopeng, a sixth-grade student from Central China's Hunan Province.  
  
His team developed an AI-powered real-time makeup assistant designed specifically for visually impaired women.  
  
"The idea came from one of our female teammates, who noticed the challenges visually impaired people face," You explained. "Research identified three major obstacles: they cannot observe makeup demonstrations, cannot evaluate the final results themselves, and often struggle with inaccessible tools and environments. So instead of creating an AI that simply tells users how they look, we wanted one that teaches them how to apply makeup."  
  
Another primary school student from Beijing presented an AI-powered robotic system for river monitoring. Equipped with an AI agent, the robot can patrol waterways remotely, monitor water quality, collect environmental data in real time and automatically analyze the information, making environmental monitoring both smarter and more efficient.  
  
As the reporter observed, the forum also featured a youth AI innovation exhibition showcasing more than a dozen student projects, including smart pet collars, AI-enabled home automation systems, intelligent shared bicycle dispatching solutions and AI-assisted rehabilitation devices.  
   

An AI intelligent robot gives lessons to students at a school in Southwest China's Chongqing Municipality on April 16, 2025. Photo: VCG

  
**Building an AI-literate generation**  
  
The students who took center stage at the forum are not isolated prodigies. Behind their projects lies a rapidly expanding, nationwide effort to introduce AI literacy into China's basic education system, with the goal of making AI education accessible not only to exceptional students but to every child.  
  
"AI education requires two complementary approaches," the Global Times learned from Lu Yu, deputy dean of the School of Educational Technology at Beijing Normal University and secretary-general of Beijing's expert committee on AI education for primary and secondary schools. "We need programs that identify and cultivate top talent. While, at the same time, we need universal AI education so that many more students have the opportunity to encounter AI, develop an interest in it and eventually allow truly creative minds to emerge."  
  
In reality, AI education in Chinese schools did not begin overnight. Guangzhou in South China's Guangdong Province introduced citywide AI literacy education as early as 2022, followed by Shenzhen in Guangdong in 2023 and Shanghai in 2024. Beijing was set to roll out universal AI education across all primary and secondary schools beginning in September 2025, requiring every student to receive no fewer than eight class hours of AI instruction each academic year, according to media reports.  
  
Scaling such a program, however, has proved to be a challenge. "AI literacy is not yet a nationally standardized subject like mathematics or physics," Lu said. "The biggest question was how to make sure every school, not just a handful of model schools, could actually teach it."  
  
Rather than asking individual schools to design courses from scratch, Beijing developed a centralized support system. According to Lu, the city has produced more than 160 sets of teaching resources, including presentation slides, lesson plans, programming examples and AI tools, all freely available to teachers. It has also organized large-scale teacher training programs and established a dedicated expert committee to provide ongoing academic support.  
  
Beijing's education authorities announced that AI literacy courses now cover more than 1,400 primary and secondary schools, reaching approximately 1.83 million students across the municipality, according to the Beijing Daily on July 2.  
  
"The term 'AI agent' has arguably become even more familiar in primary and secondary schools than it is on many university campuses," Lu said.  
  
China's systematic approach has drawn growing international attention.  
  
"Beijing can kind of set out the agenda for what tools are going to be used, what curricula are going to be established. We don't really have an equivalent of that here, besides funding priorities or maybe some executive orders that kind of establish the importance of something," Priten Soundar-Shah, a Harvard-trained educator, was quoted by the Newsweek in May as saying.  
  
In January, the Financial Times also highlighted the message that science as the key to national progress continues to echo through classrooms and homes in China.  
  
According to the People's Daily in December 2025, China has a talent pool of 220 million skilled professionals, including more than 72 million highly skilled workers. The country is home to nearly 20 million scientists and engineers and sees more than five million students graduate in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) disciplines every year - the largest annual STEM talent output in the world.   
  
****Beyond technology****  
While the achievements are encouraging and policy support continues to grow, AI education remains a work in progress. Behind the success stories lie challenges that cannot be overlooked.  
  
"In many classrooms today, AI is simply replacing existing teaching tools," Lu said. "Teachers use it to answer questions, explain difficult concepts or prepare teaching materials. That's useful, but fundamentally it's still doing traditional tasks with more advanced technology."   
  
True AI education, he argued, should go much further.  
  
Rather than focusing solely on improving classroom efficiency, AI should help cultivate students' creativity, critical thinking and problem-solving abilities while encouraging them to explore how the technology works and how it can be applied responsibly.  
  
To achieve that goal, Lu has proposed a three-dimensional framework for generative AI education.  
  
The first dimension is generation: understanding how generative AI creates content and the principles behind it. The second is application: learning to use AI creatively and appropriately across different scenarios. The third, and in his view the most important, is responsibility.  
  
Ultimately, Lu believes a well-designed AI curriculum should serve two purposes simultaneously: introducing students to AI, while also addressing long-standing challenges in traditional classroom teaching.  
  
"China has made remarkable progress in expanding AI education nationwide," Lu said. "But achieving genuinely high-quality teaching and learning remains a long-term task."  
  
Chu Zhaohui, a research fellow at the National Institute of Education Sciences, told the Global Times that if education becomes excessively digitized - or relies on AI in one-directional ways - students may gradually lose opportunities for independent exploration, develop greater dependence on digital systems and become increasingly passive in the learning process.  
  
While AI promises personalized learning, Chu cautioned that it may also reduce students' opportunities to make choices, solve problems independently and cultivate resilience through trial and error.  
  
"Also, if educators rely on AI too rigidly, they may gradually become spokespersons for AI models rather than independent educators capable of exercising their own professional judgment and creativity," Chu said.  
  
"No external tool, however advanced or efficient, can replace the development of human intelligence and character," Chu emphasized. "Whether to use AI, how much to use it and in what ways it should be used ought to remain decisions made by educators and learners themselves."  
  
That perspective resonates strongly with Mi Qi, principal of the High School Affiliated to Renmin University of China.  
  
Mi acknowledged that the emergence of large language models and increasingly capable AI agents can make it seem as though every student now has access to an all-knowing tutor.  
  
"But cognitive development doesn't happen because someone simply receives the correct answer," he said. "Children's brains develop through exploration. It is during the process of thinking, making mistakes and discovering solutions that the brain's internal structures continue to evolve."  
  
"We hope children will continue to explore, invent and innovate," he said. "But their work should always look toward the future, contribute to our country's development and benefit the shared future of humanity. Schools and teachers must remain committed to nurturing people, regardless of how technology changes."  
  
Encouragingly, the children growing up with AI are proving to be far from passive recipients of the technology.  
  
After an AI-led failure, You Xiaopeng learned not to blame himself or trust AI blindly. "AI can't make me understand or make decisions," he said, "what it can do is make it easier to turn my ideas into reality."

Here is the raw content of the webpage:

<webpage_content>
# What Is China’s AI+Education Action Plan? A Breakdown for Educators and Policymakers

### U.S. and China Are Converging on the Same AI Education Goals

[David PBL Ross](https://substack.com/@davidpblross)

In mid-April, China launched a national action plan that will embed AI across its education system and impact learning on a generational scale.

While the plan centers on education policy, its broader aim is clear: future-proof China’s workforce in an era of intense global AI competition.

This announcement came around the same time as OpenAI’s publication of its [Industrial Policy for the Intelligence Age: Ideas to Keep People First](https://cdn.openai.com/pdf/561e7512-253e-424b-9734-ef4098440601/Industrial%20Policy%20for%20the%20Intelligence%20Age.pdf)). The document advances a similar goal: aligning education policy with workforce development in the AI era.

The Chinese Ministry of Education, alongside four other ministries, released the “[AI+Education Action Plan](http://www.moe.gov.cn/fbh/live/2026/77927/wj/).” This document, which builds on the earlier “[Outline of the Plan for the Construction of China into an Education Powerhouse (2024–2035)](https://cset.georgetown.edu/wp-content/uploads/t0645_education_powerhouse_plan_EN.pdf)”, mandates the integration of AI as early as kindergarten and continues with lifelong learning support.

According to the plan, it “aims to systematically advance artificial intelligence talent cultivation, application innovation, foundational infrastructure, and ecosystem development. It seeks to build an education system suited for the intelligent era and achieve deep integration of AI and education by 2030.” (*Note: I used a [custom bot](https://chatgpt.com/g/g-alAgm5I8k-english-mandarin-curriculum-crafter) I programmed to translate Chinese educational research and policy documents into English*).

The authors of the plan list four guiding principles:

* prioritizing human development
* emphasizing competency development
* focusing on practical applications
* ensuring AI is used for positive and ethical purposes

The guiding principles of the Chinese action plan do not vary significantly from those cited in the OpenAI plan, which I analyzed a week ago in this [blog](https://davidpblross.substack.com/p/what-openais-industrial-policy-means). In my analysis, I identified these four features as central to OpenAI’s advocacy:

* AI as foundational infrastructure
* An open economy that generates shared prosperity
* AI literacy for all
* Research and innovation are democratized

For the remainder of this analysis, we’ll turn our attention to the operational details of the Chinese plan, which can serve as a laudable discussion starter for U.S. policy groups focused on similar goals.

**Lifelong learning of AI literacy**

The Chinese plan seeks to createa comprehensive AI education system across all stages of formal and informal learning. This programming begins in kindergarten, proceeds through secondary school, elevates vocational learning to a more central role, is intensified in higher education, and continues for the duration of a Chinese citizen’s working career, regardless of the field.

In education, AI courses must be fully implemented to cultivate computational and intelligent thinking in K-12 education. In higher education, AI will be incorporated into general foundational curricula across the disciplines. In vocational education, programs will be upgraded to align with industrial transformation. In lifelong education, equal access to AI learning resources will be ensured.

Both nations are quietly redefining the purpose of schooling, from academic sorting to workforce alignment. This shift is apparent in a review of the [policy documents](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/white-house-ai-education-plan-aligns-jffs-vision-resources-0xjlc) released by the White House last summer.

**Infrastructure Development**

China already has a national-scale education platform that functions as a shared digital learning and services infrastructure ([Smart Education of China](https://csmartedu.cn/)), which [UNESCO describes](https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/smart-education-platform-china-laureate-unesco-prize-ict-education) as a “one-stop” platform for teachers, learners, and families across basic, vocational, and higher education.

The new element in this action plan is the decision to create dedicated AI infrastructure for education. The Ministry of Education said it will build a National Education Intelligent Computing Service Platform, which indicates a national need for centralized computing support for AI-enabled education.

UNESCO and other organizations describe smart education platforms as important public infrastructure for equitable access to digital learning. This movement is finding fertile ground in the AI-forward nation of Estonia, which is receiving assistance via OpenAI’s [country program](https://openai.com/global-affairs/openai-for-countries/).

**Teacher Development and Pedagogy**

OpenAI’s industrial policy document calls for the repositioning of teaching. Education is not being automated out of existence — it is being redefined.

Despite fears of automation, the OpenAI report consistently reinforces the idea that teaching is fundamentally about establishing and maintaining relationships between learner and teacher. AI’s role is to offer cognitive support (tutoring) as well as administrative relief for time-consuming and onerous tasks.

The Chinese action plan adopts a similar philosophy: Teachers’ digital literacy and AI competencies will be comprehensively enhanced to support innovative teaching models empowered by AI. Chinese teachers will be encouraged to innovate in pedagogy while using AI. (*Note: In July I will be working in an elite Chinese school and plan to report on how this process is developing.*)

The plan encourages AI-powered personalized learning, intelligent tutoring, data-driven instruction, and it will promote “future classrooms” and smart learning environments. This focus on future classrooms is not theoretical. I am once again organizing a study tour for a group of Chinese administrators from the Beijing National Day School leadership development program. This year, they only want to see one program: [Alpha School.](https://alpha.school/)

In February of 2024, the Chinese Ministry of Education selected 184 primary and secondary schools as [AI education pilot sites](https://english.www.gov.cn/news/202412/03/content_WS674e4959c6d0868f4e8ed9ae.html) with the purpose of testing new models, curricula, resources, and teacher training for AI education. This was not a small experiment: the 184 schools were meant to become exemplary cases for broader national rollout. The ministry linked the pilot work to a wider push to build AI literacy across primary and secondary education.

The pilot schools were required to lead curriculum development, enrich instructional resources, support teacher training, and experiment with practical AI applications in teaching and learning.

This new action plan pushes that pilot into a more structured attempt to develop scalable demonstration models.

**Safety and Governance**

In early April, Anthropic announced the launch of [Mythos](https://red.anthropic.com/2026/mythos-preview/), Anthropic’s most powerful AI model to date. It is a general-purpose system with dramatically advanced capabilities in cybersecurity, coding, and reasoning that is so potent at identifying and exploiting software vulnerabilities that Anthropic chose not to release it publicly, instead giving access to a limited group of tech companies to use it defensively to shore up the world’s critical software before bad actors gain access to similar capabilities.

With the arrival of Mythos, the need to foreground [data security](https://www.nbcnews.com/tech/security/anthropic-claude-mythos-ai-hackers-cybersecurity-vulnerabilities-rcna273673) has rapidly drawn the full attention of policy makers in the U.S. and China. One goal of the new policy will be enhanced protection of students’ Personally Identifiable Information. Ideally, the two AI superpowers can find common ground and lead a policy initiative that creates international standards.

In the meantime, China is prepared to focus on its own needs by creating acomprehensive safety framework that will include:

* AI content review mechanisms
* data and privacy protection systems
* risk monitoring and early warning mechanisms
* and regulations to prevent misuse such as fraud, academic misconduct, and data leakage.

**Industry Partnerships**

In December of last year, Sal Khan wrote an [op-ed](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/12/27/opinion/artificial-intelligence-jobs-worker-training.html) in the New York Times in which he described the need to dramatically and quickly increase the AI competency of all learners, teachers, and workers. He suggested that high-tech companies dedicate a portion of their revenue to this process.

Chinese technology companies operate in a different political and governance system that quite frankly has the power to mandate this type of support. The action plan promotes collaboration between universities, enterprises, and research institutes with the purpose of accelerating the transformation of research into educational tools.

This is not unlike last summer’s [policy statements](https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Americas-AI-Action-Plan.pdf) from the White House**.** The basic idea is that the US government should not try to build AI literacy alone; instead, it should coordinate with industry for tools and funding, universities for research and curriculum design, and schools/districts for implementation so AI education reaches students and teachers at scale.

Industry can supply AI tools, expertise, and money, but also helps define what practical AI literacy looks like in real workplaces. In the White House’s September 2025 announcement, companies were invited to support curriculum development, teacher training, student engagement, and R&D so that AI education could be useful, current, and connected to career pathways. [Early versions](http://en.moe.gov.cn/news/press_releases/202601/t20260120_1427027.html) of a similar policy are already in place in China and are likely to be accelerated by the action plan.

**Final Thoughts**

A quick scan of current media coverage reveals a near-universal anxiety about the changes AI will force upon society. The very nature of work and learning are about to change in ways we can only imagine.

If you read this post with a discerning eye and then turn your gaze to the other writers who spend time analyzing the convergence between industrial and education policy you will notice a second convergence.

The policy solutions demonstrate a policy convergence across geopolitical rivals.

Experts are calling for a system-level transformation both here and in China. This transformation focuses on:

* Universal AI literacy for learners and workers
* Deep integration of AI into teaching and infrastructure
* State-led ecosystem building with industry and higher education
* Strong emphasis on safety, ethics, and governance

The convergence is striking. Rival nations, competing fiercely in AI development, are advancing nearly identical blueprints for education. That should tell us that this is not a passing reform cycle. It is a structural shift.

Time and tide may wait for no one — but in this case, neither will artificial intelligence. Education systems now face a simple choice: adapt with intention, or be reshaped by forces beyond their control.

In mid-April 2026, China launched a national "AI+Education Action Plan" issued by the Ministry of Education alongside four other ministries, mandating AI integration across the education system from kindergarten through lifelong learning, with a goal of deep AI-education integration by 2030. The plan builds on the earlier "Outline of the Plan for the Construction of China into an Education Powerhouse (2024–2035)." It has four guiding principles: prioritizing human development, emphasizing competency development, focusing on practical applications, and ensuring ethical AI use.

The plan's six key areas include:
1. **Lifelong AI literacy** - AI courses from K-12 through higher education, vocational training, and lifelong learning.
2. **Infrastructure development** - A National Education Intelligent Computing Service Platform to complement China's existing Smart Education of China platform.

4. **Safety and governance** - A comprehensive framework including AI content review, data/privacy protection, risk monitoring, and anti-misuse regulations.
5. **Industry partnerships** - Collaboration between universities, enterprises, and research institutes to accelerate AI education tools.
6. **Pilot scaling** - Building on 184 primary/secondary schools selected as AI education pilot sites in February 2024.

# Case Study: Duolingo’s AI-Powered Language Learning Revolution

* by [Valerio Zanini, CPIT, CST](https://www.5dvision.com/post/author/valeriozanini-5d/ "Posts by Valerio Zanini, CPIT, CST")

Technology is deeply embedded in Duolingo’s DNA. The company consistently invests to deliver a fun, engaging, and effective learning journey, all while staying true to its mission: to create the best education in the world and make it accessible to everyone. Their partnership with OpenAI to integrate GPT-4 is one of the most impactful applications of generative AI in education, proving how AI can simultaneously boost learning outcomes and business performance.

This case study on Duolingo, the leading mobile language learning platform with over 500 million users, showcases a successful AI integration in education. After its adoption, the company saw a 51% surge in Daily Active Users, exceeding 40 million, and achieved record Q4 revenue. Duolingo’s success stems from its strategic AI use, transforming learning and driving growth.

Duolingo faced several critical challenges that traditional language learning methods couldn’t adequately address:

**Conversation Practice Gap:** True proficiency in a language requires conversation, ideally with a native speaker, something not everyone has access to. Traditional language learning apps, including Duolingo’s earlier versions, focused heavily on vocabulary and grammar exercises but failed to provide meaningful conversational practice, leaving learners unprepared for real-world interactions.

**Content Creation Scalability:** With fewer than 1,000 employees and over 21 million daily users, Duolingo needed to prioritize ruthlessly with resources to develop the best education in the world. Building, updating, and maintaining courses took considerable time, with most courses releasing new content only a few times per year.

**Market Competition and Growth Pressure:** With approximately 56% of the online language learning market, Duolingo needed to innovate to maintain its leadership position and continue attracting users in an increasingly competitive landscape.

## Solution Adopted

Duolingo implemented a comprehensive AI strategy centered around OpenAI’s GPT-4 integration, launching **Duolingo Max** as their premium AI-powered subscription tier with several key features:

**1. GPT-4 Powered Conversation Practice:** Duolingo Max introduced “Roleplay,” which allows learners to practice real-world conversation skills with AI characters in the app. Learners can discuss vacation plans, order coffee at a café in Paris, or go furniture shopping, with the AI providing responsive and interactive conversations where no two conversations are exactly alike.

The company also developed **Video Call with Lily**, enabling users to have voice conversations with AI characters, bridging the critical gap between lesson completion and real-world speaking confidence.

**2. Intelligent Answer Explanations:** “Explain My Answer” provides AI-powered, contextual feedback on accuracy and complexity of responses, along with tips for future conversations. The feature uses GPT-4 to deliver detailed explanations rather than simple “correct/incorrect” feedback.

**3. AI-Driven Content Creation:** CEO Luis von Ahn highlighted the transformative impact: “*Gen AI is allowing us to make the content for all of our subjects mostly, close to 100%, automatically. So that allows us to just have a lot more content that is made a lot faster and much cheaper*“.

**4. Enhanced Learning Infrastructure:** Duolingo implemented AI across their content creation pipeline, where Learning Designers plan themes and grammar, then use AI to generate multiple sentence variations, allowing human experts to focus on curation and quality control rather than manual content creation.

## Outcomes

Duolingo’s AI implementation delivered remarkable results across multiple business metrics:

**Explosive User Growth:**

* Daily Active Users reached over 40 million with a 51% year-over-year increase in 2024
* DAUs continued growing at 40% in Q2 2025, reaching 47.7 million users
* Monthly Active Users soared to 130.2 million in Q1 2025, a 33% year-over-year increase

**Subscription Revenue Surge:**

* Paid subscribers rose to 10.9 million, a 37% year-over-year gain, with quarterly revenue growing to $252.3 million, up 41% from Q2 2024
* The company hiked its full-year guidance to between $1.01 billion and $1.02 billion, up from a prior range of $987 million to $996 million
* Max represents about 5% of total subscribers with strong early adoption helping drive top-line growth

**Enhanced User Engagement:**

**Operational Efficiency:**

AI cost reductions improved gross margins via lower API/token expenses, enabling pricing experiments to enhance profitability

# Duolingo’s Transformation Into Learning Platform | Case Study

![AI-powered language learning app transforming into a scalable and profitable platform - Case Study by Cognitute](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/62bcfa42079bd468c6f9294f/695c980dfbb9929e13b2d571_22-COG-03-0048-copy.webp)

# **How an AI-Powered Language App Transformed into a Scalable, Profitable Learning Platform Introduction**

Duolingo’s journey from a freemium language-learning app to an AI-first global education platform is a compelling case of [business transformation](https://www.cognitute.org/consulting-services/business-transformation). In recent years, the company has pivoted strategically not just growing its user base, but fundamentally rethinking how it builds content, delivers learning, and monetizes. For leadership teams navigating disruption in education or tech more broadly, Duolingo’s evolution offers rich lessons in strategy, operations, and innovation.

## **How Duolingo’s Journey Began**

**‍**When Duolingo launched in 2011 (publicly available soon after), it was built around a simple but powerful premise: democratize language learning through mobile-first, gamified lessons. Over the years, it grew rapidly thanks to its freemium model offering a free tier supported by ads, and a paid “Super” subscription for more features.

By the early 2020s, Duolingo had become one of the most downloaded education apps globally, but it faced several significant challenges:

* **Monetization limits:** While millions of users engaged with the free app, converting them into paying customers was hard, and subscription penetration remained modest.
* **Content scale and creation bottlenecks:** Developing new language courses manually was time-consuming, resource-intensive, and constrained by contract content creators.
* **Competitive pressure:** The edtech space was becoming more crowded, with rivals offering personalized, AI-driven learning. As [McKinsey has noted](https://www.cognitute.org/), online education providers must “take bold action” to sustain growth.
* **Operational inefficiencies:** Balancing gamification, user engagement, and content quality at scale required constant iteration and investment.

In essence, Duolingo had scale, but its growth engine was still constrained by human-generated content and a freemium monetization model that capped its margin potential.

## **Key Challenges Driving the Need for Transformation**

Several interlocking pressures made transformation not just desirable, but necessary:

1. **Scaling content faster than traditional processes would allow.** Creating high-quality lessons for dozens of languages and expanding into non-language domains (e.g., math, music) posed a bottleneck.
2. **Improving user engagement and retention.** To grow its paid base, Duolingo needed deeper, more meaningful learning experiences, not just repetitive drills.

**3. Raising monetization efficiency.** Conversion from free to paid users, and creating higher-value tiers, would require more differentiated offerings.

**4. Reducing operating costs over the long run.** Reliance on contractors and manual content creation threatened scalability and cost structure.

**5. Positioning for the future of edtech.** As AI began to reshape how content is created and personalized, Duolingo needed to lead, not lag.

## **The Transformation in Strategy, Operations, and Marketing Shift**

### **A) Strategic Pivot: Becoming AI-First**

In 2025, Duolingo publicly articulated an “AI-first” strategy.

* The company committed to using AI not just for content generation, but for hiring, performance reviews, and operational decision-making.
* It announced a phased reduction in contractor roles, with repetitive tasks being automated via AI so that employees could focus on higher-value, creative work.
* Crucially, Duolingo launched **Duolingo Max**, its premium subscription tier powered by AI, which includes features like video-call conversation practice with AI characters and “Explain My Answer” feedback, built on large language models.

### **B) Product & Ecosystem Reinvention**

* **Personalization engine:** Duolingo leveraged its AI “Bird Brain” engine (internal name) to adapt lessons dynamically to each user’s performance and pacing.
* **Content scale:** With generative models, Duolingo accelerated course creation. Reports suggest it developed 148 new language courses in under a year using AIsomething that would have taken far longer with traditional methods.
* **Expanded subject offering:** The company articulated ambitions beyond just languagesto math, music, and even chesspowered by AI personalization.

**Assessment innovation:** The Duolingo English Test (DET) incorporated AI-driven item generation and scoring, raising both throughput and quality. Duolingo also paid attention to fairness and equity in its AI use.

### ‍ **C) Operational Transformations**

‍

* **AI in workforce design:** Automating tasks handled by contractors freed up resources. According to CEO Luis von Ahn, headcount would only grow if AI could not efficiently automate the work.
* **Efficiency and leanness:** Teams were encouraged to run “f-r-AI days” (fun-AI days) to experiment with AI-based productivity tools.
* **Cost structure:** By using AI for content and operations, Duolingo aimed to reduce recurring content costs and scale margin. Analysts have noted that the AI-first shift may improve gross margins over time.

### **D) Commercial & Marketing Shift**

* **Monetization via tiering:** The Max subscription, with advanced AI-driven features, is positioned as a premium value tier, helping increase average revenue per user (ARPU).
* **Retention & engagement:** AI-powered interactive features drove higher engagement, making the app more “sticky” and converting free users into paying ones.
* **Narrative and brand:** Duolingo leaned into “AI tutor” positioning in its marketing, highlighting how tech personalizes learning.
* **Global reach and scale:** AI allowed more cost-efficient localization and creation of new language courses, helping expand to new geographies and segment.

## **4) Outcomes: Measuring the Impact**

### **A) Usage & Reach**

* In Q2 2024, Duolingo reported **103.6 million monthly active users (MAUs)**, up from 74.1 million a year earlier (+40%).
* Daily active users (DAUs) grew to **34.1 million**, +59% year-over-year.
* By Q4 2024, estimates suggest ~116.7 million MAUs.

### **B) Monetization & Profitability**

* In Q2 2024, Duolingo’s **total GAAP revenue** was $178.3 milliona 41% increase over Q2 2023.
* Adjusted EBITDA in that quarter was $48.1 million, more than doubling from $20.9 million a year earlier, signaling strong operating leverage.
* For FY2023, Duolingo reported $531.1 million in revenue, up 44% from $369.5 million in 2022.
* At the end of Q1 2024, **paid subscribers** stood at 7.4 million, up 54% from 4.8 million a year before.

Free cash flow and operating cash also improved significantly; for Q2 2024, net cash from operations was $62.4 million (+68% YoY), and non-GAAP free cash flow was $54.9 million (+60%).

### ‍ **C) Forecast & Strategic Momentum**

* On May 1, 2025, Duolingo raised its full-year 2025 revenue guidance to **$987 million–$996 million**, citing strong demand for its AI-powered Max subscription.
* The company’s “AI-first” shift is also beginning to resonate with investors: higher engagement, new content, and scalable unit economics are strengthening its long-term monetization narrative.

## **Strategic Diagnosis**

Here are the key success factors behind Duolingo’s transformation:

1. **AI as a lever, not a gimmick:** Duolingo’s use of AI is deeply integratedfrom content creation to personalization to operationsrather than simply a buzzword.
2. **Product-led monetization:** Instead of pushing ads or lowering prices, Duolingo created value through a premium, differentiated tier (Max) that justifies higher pricing.
3. **Scalable content creation:** Generative AI unlocked a previously limited rate of course rollout, expanding Duolingo’s addressable content universe quickly.
4. **Operational discipline:** Through automation, Duolingo reallocated human effort to specialized, creative tasks, improving productivity and margins.
5. **Learning business fundamentals:** Duolingo’s transformation resonates with broader trends in edtech; McKinsey research points to the necessity of bold structural moves in online education to sustain growth.
6. **Thoughtful AI ethics:** As Duolingo scales AI in testing (e.g., its English Test), it is also focused on responsible AI practices, ensuring fairness and quality.

## **Risks, Responses & Governance**

No transformation of this magnitude is without risk. Duolingo has faced:

* **Backlash over AI-first strategy:** The announcement to reduce contractor roles and rely more on AI sparked internal and public debate. Duolingo clarified that full-time roles would not be cut, and that automation would free humans for more creative work.
* **Quality concerns:** As more content is generated via AI, there’s potential for lower linguistic nuance or cultural mismatches.
* **Regulatory and equity risks:** With AI-powered tests (like DET), Duolingo is under scrutiny for maintaining test fairness and validity.
* **Execution risk:** Scaling AI effectively requires engineering capabilities, good data, and disciplined feedback loopsareas where missteps could undermine the strategy.

But many of these risks are explicitly addressed in Duolingo’s strategy. Its internal “f-r-AI days” encourage experimentation and risk mitigation, and its growing focus on AI governance (especially for testing) suggests a mature approach.

## **Strategic Lessons for Leadership Teams**

For senior leaders in education, technology, or platform businesses, Duolingo’s transformation offers several strategic take-aways:

1. **Make automation your growth engine:** Use AI to unlock scalable content and performance that humans alone cannot sustain.
2. **Monetize around value, not just volume:** Premium tiers succeed when they deliver real, differentiated valueDuolingo Max is a prime example.
3. **Design for long-term economics:** Transforming your cost base (contractors, operating manual tasks) pays off when you embed AI deeply.
4. **Balance innovation with ethics:** As you scale generative AI, embed guardrails (fairness, test validity, user trust) from day oneespecially when your product has educational impact.
5. **Experiment aggressively, but govern responsibly:** Encourage innovation (Duolingo’s “f-r-AI days”) while ensuring that AI adoption is governed and aligned with company values.

**Build your learning flywheel:** More users → more data → better personalization → higher conversion → more revenue. That virtuous cycle is at the heart of Duolingo’s transformation.

## **Conclusion**

Duolingo’s reinvention is not merely a story of growthbut of structural change. By pivoting to an AI-first strategy, rethinking its product architecture, and driving operational discipline, it has reshaped its value proposition for both learners and investors. For leaders navigating digital disruption, Duolingo offers a powerful example of how to transform a consumer-scale platform into a sustainable, high-margin, mission-driven business.

## Abstract

**Introduction:**

Although generative artificial intelligence (AI) is ubiquitous, there is little research on how it supports self-efficacy (learners’ belief that they can perform at a particular level on a specific task). The purpose of these studies was to investigate self-efficacy development in a generative AI-based language learning experience.

**Methods:**

In two studies, learners (*N* = 385) of French/Spanish used AI-based features offering conversation practice and on-demand explanations in a mobile app (Duolingo) for 1 month. Before and after using the features, learners reported their self-efficacy and other perceptions.

**Results:**

In Study 1, learners who had already used the features felt significantly more prepared to use French/Spanish in real-life situations after 1 month, as did learners in Study 2 who used the features for the first time. Learners in Study 2 also felt significantly more prepared to share their opinions and navigate a city, and reported significantly higher self-efficacy for speaking and understanding grammar and mistakes. Across studies, the majority of learners agreed that the AI-based features effectively supported learning, and reported using their learning outside the app.

**Discussion:**

These results provide the first evidence of enhanced language learning self-efficacy after use of generative AI, building on findings from classroom interventions.

## 1 Introduction

Learning a language is challenging, and supporting learners’ motivation during the language learning process is critical ([Albalawi and Al-Hoorie, 2021](#ref2)). Motivation for learning results from how much learners *value* learning, as well as their *expectancy* that learning will lead to specific outcomes ([Vu et al., 2022](#ref70)). One type of expectancy is *self-efficacy*, learners’ belief in the ability to perform at a particular level on a specific task ([Bandura, 1994](#ref6)). Self-efficacy plays an important role in theories of learning, and studies across a variety of educational domains, including language learning, reveal significant correlations between self-efficacy, performance, and behaviors that support learning ([Zimmerman, 2000](#ref84); [Goetze and Driver, 2022](#ref27)).

Classroom interventions have successfully increased students’ language learning self-efficacy with communication-focused tasks, constructive feedback that highlights learners’ success, and explicit teaching of language learning strategies ([Raoofi et al., 2012](#ref60); [Graham, 2022](#ref28)). Although generative AI models such as ChatGPT are well-positioned to provide real-time communication practice that could increase self-efficacy, there is little research on this topic ([Han, 2024](#ref29); [Law, 2024](#ref40)). This study aims to help fill this gap in the research literature.

## 2 Self-efficacy in language learning

Self-efficacy plays an important role in learning theory ([Zimmerman, 2000](#ref84); [Wigfield and Eccles, 2000](#ref75)). Individuals form self-efficacy beliefs based on their past performance, and these self-efficacy beliefs exert a strong influence on behaviors such as learning goals and strategies, which impact subsequent performance ([Talsma et al., 2018](#ref67)). Performance is thought to influence self-efficacy, and self-efficacy is thought to influence performance ([Vu et al., 2022](#ref70)), in a mutually reinforcing cycle (see [Figure 1](#fig1)).

Figure 1

![Figure 1](https://www.frontiersin.org/files/Articles/1499497/xml-images/feduc-10-1499497-g001.webp)

Theoretical relationship between motivation (including self-efficacy), behavior, and performance.

Consistent with these theories, empirical evidence from a variety of countries in Africa, Asia, Europe, the Middle East, and North America suggests that self-efficacy plays an important role in second language learning. Self-efficacy correlates with actual task performance in a variety of domains ([Honicke and Broadbent, 2016](#ref32)), including second language learning ([Yang and Lian, 2023](#ref79); [Young Kyo, 2022](#ref80)), with a larger effect size than for other motivational variables ([Schneider and Preckel, 2017](#ref63); [Goetze and Driver, 2022](#ref27)). Longitudinal data show that when learners’ self-efficacy increases, performance tends to increase as well ([Bernacki et al., 2015](#ref9); [Vu et al., 2022](#ref70)). Self-efficacy is also correlated with goal-directed behaviors that promote learning ([Zimmerman, 2000](#ref84)). For example, high self-efficacy learners tend to use more language learning strategies ([Raoofi et al., 2012](#ref60); [Wang and Sun, 2020](#ref73)).

What cultivates language learning self-efficacy? Although most research on this topic is correlational, a number of classroom interventions in Asia, Europe, the Middle East, and North America have increased students’ self-efficacy. These interventions feature communication-focused tasks such as writing and speaking activities ([Abdelhalim, 2024](#ref1); [Leeming, 2017](#ref42); [Mills, 2009](#ref50); [Goetze and Driver, 2022](#ref27)), constructive feedback that highlights students’ success ([Xu et al., 2022](#ref78); [Li et al., 2023](#ref44)), and explicit teaching of learning strategies ([Chen, 2022](#ref13); [Milliner and Dimoski, 2024](#ref49)). Taken together, these studies suggest that new interventions with these same elements could support the development of language learning self-efficacy.

## 3 Generative AI to support self-efficacy

Given the prominence of communication-focused tasks in interventions that support self-efficacy, it is possible that real-time conversation practice provided by generative AI could enhance self-efficacy as well. Research conducted prior to the release of Open AI’s GPT in Asia, Europe, the Middle East and North America found that chatbots simulating human interaction can enhance motivational constructs related to self-efficacy, such as speaking confidence and willingness to communicate in the language ([Du and Daniel, 2024](#ref17); [Xiao et al., 2023](#ref77)). However, experimental evidence on ChatGPT and other recent generative AI is still limited ([Han, 2024](#ref29); [Law, 2024](#ref40)).

One practically relevant context for investigating the impact of learning experiences supported by generative AI is widely used language learning apps ([Tommerdahl et al., 2024](#ref69)), which have recently incorporated this new technology ([Godwin-Jones, 2024](#ref26)). Although rigorous research on language learning apps is limited, several apps have demonstrated efficacy relative to a control group ([Tommerdahl et al., 2024](#ref69)). In particular, three apps have been investigated in multiple experimental studies: Rosetta Stone, Memrise, and Duolingo.

When the application Rosetta Stone is combined with classroom instruction, studies in China ([Bai, 2024](#ref5); [Fan, 2023](#ref20)) and the US ([Harper et al., 2021](#ref31)) find that this leads to better learning outcomes than classroom instruction alone. Memrise, a vocabulary learning app, leads to comparable or better learning outcomes than classroom instruction in China ([Wang et al., 2023](#ref71)), Iran ([Shamshiri et al., 2023](#ref64)), and Vietnam ([Nguyen et al., 2023](#ref53)). Duolingo, a language learning app studied in over 300 articles ([Shortt et al., 2023](#ref65)), produces learning outcomes that are comparable to or better than classroom instruction in China ([Qiao and Zhao, 2023](#ref58)), Colombia ([García Botero et al., 2021](#ref24)), Russia ([Pichugin et al., 2023](#ref57)), and the US ([Rachels and Rockinson-Szapkiw, 2018](#ref59)). Duolingo also yields learning outcomes that are comparable to or better than other language learning apps, in Russia ([Pichugin et al., 2023](#ref57)) and the US ([Kessler et al., 2023](#ref37)), and is effective when used by learners outside of formal education settings in various countries ([Jiang et al., 2021](#ref35); [Jiang et al., 2024b](#ref34)). Duolingo is highly relevant to many learners, as the most downloaded digital language learning product in the world ([Statista, 2024](#ref66)). Moreover, motivating learners is a key component of Duolingo’s research-based teaching method. Many different elements, such as short lessons, celebrations of learner success, rewards for accuracy and continued app use, and social features work in concert to increase learners’ expectancy of positive learning outcomes ([Freeman et al., 2023](#ref21)).

The present research focuses on Duolingo, with the following rationale: (1) A greater number of studies have demonstrated Duolingo’s learning efficacy, compared to other apps. (2) These studies suggest that Duolingo learning outcomes are comparable to learning outcomes in other apps and classrooms, (3) in settings both within and outside of formal schooling. (4) The app’s widespread use increases the relevance of any research conducted on it, and (5) Duolingo’s teaching method grounded in research on learning and motivation is well suited to supporting the development of self-efficacy.

Several Duolingo features that use Open AI’s GPT-4 ([OpenAI, 2023b](#ref56)) were released as part of a higher subscription tier[1](#fn0001) ([Duolingo Team, 2023](#ref19)). In the “Roleplay” feature ([Figure 2](#fig2)), learners practice written or spoken real-world conversation with characters whose live responses are generated by GPT-4, in scenarios like taking a taxi to the airport. Learners are offered translation hints, helpful phrase suggestions, feedback on accuracy, and tips for future conversations, all of which are generated live by GPT-4. In Duolingo’s “Explain My Answer” feature ([Figure 3](#fig3)), learners can optionally tap on a button after certain exercises to enter a chat, where GPT-4 is used to generate an explicit explanation of why the learners’ answer was right or wrong, along with examples or further clarification.
