Duolingo’s AI-enabled learning experiences contain the same core elements that have been shown to enhance self-efficacy in the classroom: communication-focused tasks, constructive feedback that highlights learners’ success, and explicit teaching of language learning strategies. These similarities, in addition to the focus on motivation in Duolingo’s teaching method ([Freeman et al., 2023](#ref21)), suggest that the experiences provided by the AI-based features may enhance learners’ self-efficacy. However, there is no experimental evidence to date that demonstrates an increase in self-efficacy after using Duolingo, or any other language learning app that incorporates generative AI.

## 4 Research questions and overview of the studies

The goal of the current research is to explore the development of language learning self-efficacy in learning experiences supported by generative AI. A total of 385 learners in the Duolingo French and Spanish courses used AI-based features for 1 month. These learners took a survey before and after using the features, to answer the following exploratory Research Questions:

*RQ1*. Are there significant increases in learners’ self-efficacy for language skills after 1 month of using AI-based features?

*RQ2*. What percentage of learners believe that AI-based features effectively support language learning?

*RQ3*. Do learners use what they learned from AI-based features outside the app, and if so, how?

The present research also investigated AI-based feature novelty. Economic and computational models of human decision-making hypothesize that novelty has a high value, because gathering new information could benefit future decisions ([Wittmann et al., 2008](#ref76)). Consistent with these theories, research in psychology demonstrates that novelty leads to enhanced attention ([Kagan, 2009](#ref36)) as well as better learning and memory ([Barto et al., 2013](#ref7)), and research in marketing suggests that customers’ perceived value of novel products is higher ([Blut et al., 2023](#ref10); [Sánchez-Fernández and Iniesta-Bonillo, 2007](#ref62); [Leroi-Werelds, 2019](#ref43)). Novelty effects are prevalent in perceptions of technology: Technologies with higher perceived novelty are associated with more positive attitudes and higher intentions of use ([Wells et al., 2010](#ref74)). In interactions with pre-GPT chatbots, learners report higher interest in language learning when the chatbot was novel ([Fryer et al., 2017](#ref22); [Fryer et al., 2019](#ref23)). Research in business and medicine also suggests that reduced cost of products and medicines can lead to more positive perceptions ([Blut et al., 2023](#ref10); [Lee et al., 2020](#ref41); [Wang et al., 2013](#ref72)). On the other hand, research in economics demonstrates that people value things that they own more (the “endowment effect”; [Marzilli Ericson and Fuster, 2014](#ref46)), suggesting that cost associated with ownership could also lead to positive perceptions.

To determine whether AI-based feature novelty and cost could impact learners’ self-efficacy, Study 1 was conducted with pre-existing subscribers who had already been using the AI-based features, while Study 2 was conducted with learners who had been using the free version of Duolingo and were granted complimentary access to the features.

## 5 Study 1

### 5.1 Methodology

#### 5.1.1 Participants

The participants were 280 pre-existing subscribers who met the following inclusion criteria:

They consented to be contacted by Duolingo for research purposes.

They were enrolled in the French or Spanish course for English speakers (the subscription was only offered in those courses at the time of the study).

They completed no more than the first or second section of the “basic” (*Common European Framework of Reference* A1 level; [Council of Europe, 2001](#ref14)) course content, in line with the majority of subscribers at the time of the study.

Their average daily app use was between 15 minutes (the time to complete several Duolingo lessons) and 27 minutes (the 75th percentile of subscribers’ daily app usage).

They were using Duolingo on iOS (the subscription was only available on this platform at the time of the study).

They were located in one of six English-speaking countries (the subscription was only available in those countries at the time of the study).

They self-reported their age as 18 or older.

#### 5.1.2 Research tools

##### 5.1.2.1 Background questionnaire

The background questionnaire asked participants’ age, as well as their reasons for learning the language, knowledge of the language prior to using Duolingo, and use of other programs/apps besides Duolingo to learn the language. The full questionnaire and questionnaire response data can be found in [Appendices A, B](#SM1), respectively.

##### 5.1.2.2 Pre-survey: self-efficacy

The pre-survey (for full text, see [Appendix A](#SM1)) collected data on participants’ self-efficacy in the language they were learning. Rather than drawing on another published scale, 17 different items were developed to assess self-efficacy on a wide range of different language skills and language use scenarios that could be relevant to learning on Duolingo. In line with previous research on self-efficacy, these were statements of confidence in one’s own ability to achieve a performance goal ([Talsma et al., 2018](#ref67)). Each statement was rated on a 6-point bipolar Likert-type scale.

While data were collected on all 17 items, subsequent user experience research found that the following seven statements were most relevant to Duolingo learners’ use of the Roleplay and Explain My Answer features. To increase statistical power, only responses to these items were analyzed to answer RQ1:

I feel prepared to use French/Spanish in real-life situations.

I feel prepared to use French/Spanish to ask for directions and navigate a new city.

I feel prepared to use French/Spanish to share my opinions with others.

I’m confident in my ability to understand French/Spanish grammar.

I’m confident in my ability to understand the mistakes I make in French/Spanish.

I’m confident in my ability to understand spoken French/Spanish.

I’m confident in my ability to speak in French/Spanish.

##### 5.1.2.3 Post-survey: self-efficacy and perceptions of the AI-based features

The post-survey (for full text, see [Appendix A](#SM1)) included the same 17 self-efficacy statements as on the pre-survey, as well as 18 additional items developed to assess participants’ perceptions of the AI-based features.

Sixteen of the 18 items referred to a wide range of different language skills and language use scenarios relevant to learning on Duolingo. While data were collected on all these items, the analysis to answer RQ2 focused on the following eight statements for the same reasons as mentioned above (maximizing relevance and statistical power):

Duolingo Max prepares me for real-world situations.

Duolingo Max helps me learn from my mistakes.

Duolingo Max helps me understand conversations.

Duolingo Max helps me understand grammar.

Duolingo Max helps me learn to speak.

“Roleplay” prepares me to use French/Spanish in real-world situations.

“Explain My Answer” helps me better understand grammar.

“Explain My Answer” helps me learn from my mistakes.

Duolingo Max was the name of the subscription at the time of the study.

One of the 18 items asked about learners’ experiences using their learning outside the app, and another elicited general feedback on the study experience. We only analyzed answers to the former, which was relevant to RQ3:

Have you used what you learned with Duolingo Max outside of the app? (Yes/No).

[*Only displayed if ‘Yes’ was selected*] Please describe the situation (optional).

#### 5.1.3 Data collection procedure

Data were collected between August 30, 2023 and November 17, 2023 on a rolling basis. [Figure 4](#fig4) shows the steps of the study and the number of participants involved, described in more detail below.

Figure 4

![Figure 4](https://www.frontiersin.org/files/Articles/1499497/xml-images/feduc-10-1499497-g004.webp)

Study 1 Steps with numbers of participants at each step.

Based on a power analysis with a small estimated effect size (0.2), the aim was for 150 participants to complete the full, month-long study. To reach our target sample size, emails soliciting participation were sent in multiple recruitment waves to 1,421 subscribers who met inclusion criteria 1–6 (see Participants section). As the subscriber population was skewed towards Spanish learners at the time of the study, 1,030 of invited subscribers were in the Spanish course for English speakers, and 391 were in the French course for English speakers.

Participants were asked to complete the background questionnaire. Those who were 18 years or older were invited to take the pre-survey, and then use Duolingo for 30 days. During the 30 days they were asked to use Duolingo for at least 15 minutes per day, including AI-based features such as Roleplay and Explain My Answer, and to complete at least 15 Roleplays by the end of the 30 days. Participants received weekly reminder emails summarizing their app usage, and were excluded when there was no chance of them meeting minimal usage requirements (using the app for at least 20 days by the end of the study, average app usage excluding Roleplays above 12 minutes per day, more than 8 Roleplays in total).

After the 30 days, participants were invited to take the post-survey if they had been active for at least 25 days, completed at least 15 Roleplays, and had at least 12 minutes of app usage per day on average. If they had less usage (active for 20–24 days, completed 8–14 Roleplays, at least 12 minutes usage per day), they were given an additional 5 days to use the app and then invited to the post-survey. Participants who had even less app usage (active for 20–24 days, completed 8–14 Roleplays, less than 12 min usage per day) were partially compensated $15 and not invited to take the post-survey.

After completing the post-survey, participants received $40 as promised in the initial invitation email, as well as a surprise complimentary 31-day subscription extension.

*Treatment attrition* (participants not meeting app usage requirements) was 40%. The background questionnaire responses of excluded participants and those who completed the study were similar (see [Tables B1, B2](#SM1)), and these groups did not differ significantly in pre-survey self-efficacy responses (*p* > 0.05 in Mann–Whitney U tests; see [Tables C1, C2](#SM1)).

#### 5.1.4 Data analysis

To answer RQ1, participants’ responses to the self-efficacy items were analyzed to see if there was a change from the pre-survey to the post-survey. Likert scale ratings were converted to a binary “disagree” or “agree” rating (“strongly disagree,” “disagree,” or “slightly disagree” = 0, “slightly agree,” “agree,” or “strongly agree” = 1). Although we acknowledge shortcomings of binarizing Likert scale data (e.g., data loss and possible error rate inflation, [Royston et al., 2006](#ref61)), there is precedent for this approach when the response can be considered binary ([Harpe, 2015](#ref30)). A logistic regression analysis was conducted to determine if participants were more likely to agree with a self-efficacy statement on the post-survey than the pre-survey, given their pre-survey responses and app usage:

Post-survey response ~ Intercept + Pre-survey response + number of Roleplays completed + number of Explain My Answers shown.

We mean-centered app usage predictors, and checked that multicollinearity, sample size requirements, and linearity of the logit assumptions held. Since we conducted a separate logistic regression for each of the 7 self-efficacy statements, we corrected for multiple comparisons ([Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995](#ref120)).

To answer RQ2, participants’ responses to the feature perception items were analyzed. As in the RQ1 analysis, the Likert scale ratings were converted to a binary “disagree” or “agree” rating, and the percentages of participants who agreed with each statement were calculated. A one-sided binomial test was used to check if each percentage was significantly greater than 80%.

To answer RQ3, the percentage of “yes” responses to the question about using learning outside the app was calculated, and themes were identified in learners’ descriptions of using learning outside the app. Following recent use of large language models for thematic analysis ([Morgan, 2023](#ref52); [Moorhouse and Kohnke, 2024](#ref51)), Glean’s “AI Summarization” feature ([Glean, 2024](#ref25)), which used GPT-4 ([OpenAI, 2023b](#ref56)), GPT-3.5-Turbo ([OpenAI, 2023a](#ref55)), and text-embedding-ada-002 ([OpenAI, 2022](#ref54)), was given the following two prompts to identify themes appearing in 10% of participants’ responses: (1) “I need to know the most common situations in which Duolingo learners used what they learned outside the app. Here is a document with learner descriptions of these situations; each bullet point represents one learner’s description. Can you write a summary of the main themes in these learner descriptions, making sure that each theme appears in the descriptions of at least 10 learners?” (2) “Thank you! Can you please provide evidence for each theme summarized above, by citing 3 learners’ descriptions that contain the theme?”

Glean produced a set of themes with examples (see [Tables C6, E6](#SM1)). To reduce inaccuracy and insufficient nuance ([Morgan, 2023](#ref52)), a research assistant checked that all Glean-generated themes could be matched with at least 10 learner descriptions, and that Glean-generated text did not contain any hallucinations. Any inaccuracies were removed.

### 5.2 Results

#### 5.2.1 Learners’ self-efficacy increased significantly

To answer RQ1, we first calculated descriptive statistics of self-efficacy ratings. Of the 15–45% of learners who disagreed with the statements on the pre-survey, 39–69% changed their rating to “agree” on the post-survey (see [Figure 5](#fig5)). Of the 55–85% of learners who agreed with the statements on the pre-survey, 88–97% still agreed on the post-survey (see [Figure 6](#fig6)). Taken together, these results suggest that many participants maintained or adopted positive self-efficacy beliefs (see [Table C3](#SM1)). Indeed, regression analyses (see [Table 1](#tab1)) showed that participants who disagreed with the statement “I feel prepared to use French/Spanish in real-life situations” on the pre-survey were significantly more likely to agree with it on the post-survey (Intercept Coefficient = 0.79, *z* = 2.56, *p* < 0.05). Participants who initially agreed with this statement were still likely to agree with it on the post-survey (Pre-survey Coefficient = 1.44, *z* = 3.18, *p* < 0.01).

However, participants were not significantly more likely to agree with the other six self-efficacy statements on the post-survey (see [Table 1](#tab1)). Although participants who initially agreed with these statements were still likely to agree with them on the post-survey (Pre-survey Coefficients all p < 0.01 or *p* < 0.001 in these regression models; see [Table 1](#tab1)), participants who initially disagreed with them did not demonstrate significant increases in their self-efficacy on the post-survey (*p* > 0.05 for Intercept Coefficients in these regression models; see [Table 1](#tab1)).

Participants’ average days active (*M* = 31.24, *SD* = 2.11, range = 24–36) and daily average minutes of app usage (*M* = 30.92, *SD* = 15.28, range = 13–99) suggests that they did slightly more than required to stay in the study (see [Table B3](#SM1)). However, Roleplay and Explain My Answer feature use did not significantly predict self-efficacy ratings on the post-survey (relevant coefficients in all regressions were not significantly different from 0; see [Table 1](#tab1)).

#### 5.2.2 Learners believed AI-based features were effective

To answer RQ2, we calculated the percentage of participants who agreed with statements about AI-based feature efficacy. Agreement rates were significantly above 80% for all eight statements (see [Table C5](#SM1)) and 7 of 8 statements had agreement rates numerically above 90% (see [Figure 7](#fig7)), suggesting that participants thought the features helped them meet a variety of learning goals.

Figure 7

![Figure 7](https://www.frontiersin.org/files/Articles/1499497/xml-images/feduc-10-1499497-g007.webp)

Agreement rates for 8 statements on the post-survey in study 1 (*N* = 153). “Duolingo Max” was the name of the higher subscription tier at the time of the study.

#### 5.2.3 Learners used what they learned outside the app

To answer RQ3, we analyzed the percentage of learners who said they used what they learned outside the app, as well as themes across these situations. Of the 153 participants, 111 (73%) said they used what they learned with the AI-based features outside the app, and 95 (86%) of the 111 provided descriptions of real-life situations in which they used the language. [Table 2](#tab2) lists the human-verified themes in these participants’ responses (see [Table C6](#SM1) for Glean-generated text). Participants described a large variety of real-world contexts, suggesting that many participants used their language skills outside the app and believed they were transferring their learning to real life contexts. Moreover, the fact that so many participants practiced their learning outside the app gave them the ability to truly test their language skills, strengthening the validity of their self-reported self-efficacy ratings and perceptions of the AI-based features.

## 6 Study 2

### 6.1 Methodology

#### 6.1.1 Participants

The participants were 302 learners who met the same criteria as the learners in Study 1, except that they did not currently have paid access to the AI-based features as part of a subscription, and their location was not restricted to English-speaking countries.

#### 6.1.2 Research tools

Study 2 used the same research tools as in Study 1.

#### 6.1.3 Data collection procedure

1,111 Duolingo learners who met the eligibility criteria were invited to the study: 555 in the French course for English speakers, and 556 in the Spanish course for English speakers. The same data collection window and procedure applied as in Study 1, except that participants were granted complimentary access to the subscription after completing the pre-survey, so they could use it for the study. [Figure 8](#fig8) shows the study steps with numbers of participants.

Figure 8

![Figure 8](https://www.frontiersin.org/files/Articles/1499497/xml-images/feduc-10-1499497-g008.webp)

Study 2 steps with numbers of participants at each step.

There was less treatment attrition in Study 2 (19%), compared to 40% in Study 1. Participants who completed the study tended to be older (19% 18–34 years, 81% 35+ years) than those excluded from the study (27% 18–34, 73% 35+), but other background questionnaire responses in these groups were similar (see [Tables D1, D2](#SM1)), and their pre-survey self-efficacy statement responses did not differ significantly (*p* > 0.05 in Mann–Whitney U tests; see [Tables E1, E2](#SM1)).

#### 6.1.4 Data analysis

The same analyses were used as in Study 1, except that the first prompt to Glean was slightly different. In the portion of the prompt which specified that each theme should be present in 10% of learner responses (“…making sure that each theme appears in the descriptions of at least 10 learners”), “10 learners” was changed to “12 learners” to account for the larger sample size in Study 2.

### 6.2 Results

#### 6.2.1 Learners’ self-efficacy increased significantly

To answer RQ1, we calculated descriptive statistics and conducted regression analyses on self-efficacy statement ratings. Of the 29–46% of learners who initially disagreed with the statements, 61–79% changed their rating to “agree” on the post-survey (see [Figure 9](#fig9)), and of the 54–79% of learners who agreed with the statements on the pre-survey, 93–98% still agreed on the post-survey (see [Figure 10](#fig10)), suggesting that most participants maintained or adopted positive self-efficacy beliefs (see [Table E3](#SM1)).

Figure 9

![Figure 9](https://www.frontiersin.org/files/Articles/1499497/xml-images/feduc-10-1499497-g009.webp)

Post-survey agreement for participants who disagreed on the pre-survey in Study 2.

Figure 10

![Figure 10](https://www.frontiersin.org/files/Articles/1499497/xml-images/feduc-10-1499497-g010.webp)

Post-survey agreement for participants who agreed on the pre-survey in Study 2.

Regression analyses confirmed this interpretation. For participants who initially disagreed on the pre-survey, there was a significant increase in self-efficacy for 6 of 7 statements: “I feel prepared to use French/Spanish in real-life situations” (Intercept Coefficient = 1.04, *z* = 3.88, *p* < 0.001), “I feel prepared to use French/Spanish to ask for directions and navigate a new city” (Intercept Coefficient = 1.66, *z* = 4.27, *p* < 0.001), “I feel prepared to use French/Spanish to share my opinions with others” (Intercept Coefficient = 1.33, *z* = 5.01, *p* < 0.001), *“*I’m confident in my ability to speak in French/Spanish” (Intercept Coefficient = 0.94, z = 4.04, *p* < 0.001), “I’m confident in my ability to understand French/Spanish grammar” (Intercept Coefficient = 0.70, z = 2.99, *p* < 0.01), and “I’m confident in my ability to understand the mistakes I make in French/Spanish” (Intercept Coefficient = 0.81, *z* = 2.53, *p* < 0.05). Participants who initially agreed with these same statements were still significantly more likely to agree with them on the post-survey: They felt prepared to use French/Spanish in real-life situations (Pre-survey Coefficient = 1.95, *z* = 4.26, *p* < 0.001), to ask for directions and navigate a new city (Pre-survey Coefficient = 1.74, *z* = 3.58, *p* < 0.01), and to share opinions with others (Pre-survey Coefficient = 1.29, *z* = 3.05, *p* < 0.01). They also felt confident in their ability to speak in French/Spanish (Pre-survey Coefficient = 2.86, *z* = 4.58, *p* < 0.001), understand French/Spanish grammar (Pre-survey Coefficient = 2.19, *z* = 5.06, *p* < 0.001), and understand the mistakes they made in French/Spanish (Pre-survey Coefficient = 3.35, *z* = 5.03, *p* < 0.001).

However, participants who initially disagreed with the statement “I am confident in my ability to understand spoken French/Spanish” did not demonstrate a significant increase in their self-efficacy on the post-survey (*p* > 0.05 for the Intercept Coefficient; see [Table 3](#tab3)), although participants who initially agreed with the statement were still likely to agree with it on the post-survey (Pre-survey Coefficient = 2.19, *z* = 5.48, *p* < 0.001). Taken together, these results suggest a significant increase in self-efficacy for a variety of language skills after using the AI-based features.

To answer RQ3, we calculated the percentage of learners who said they used what they learned outside the app, as well as themes reported across the use situations. Of the 232 participants, 145 (63%) said they used what they learned with the AI-based features outside the app, and 121 (83%) of the 145 provided descriptions of the real-life situations. These percentages suggest that like in Study 1, participants perceived transfer of learning from the app to use of language skills in real-life.

[Table 4](#tab4) lists themes in participants’ responses (see [Table E6](#SM1) for Glean-generated text). The “Travel,” “Workplace communication,” “Educational support and settings,” “Daily errands and services,” “Family interaction,” and “Casual conversations” themes correspond to the Study 1 themes “Travel,” “Workplace communication,” “Education and tutoring,” “Service and retail,” “Social interactions,” and “Conversations with native speakers.” Other themes showed significant overlap across studies: social media and texting in the theme “Casual conversations” from Study 2 is similar to the “Remote correspondence” theme in Study 1, and the theme “Cultural engagement” in Study 2 was present for some learners in Study 1 who mentioned using media.

## 7 Discussion

The goal of the present studies was to assess changes in self-efficacy of French and Spanish learners who engaged in learning experiences enabled by generative AI. Study 1 investigated whether there were significant increases in pre-existing, paying subscribers’ self-efficacy for language skills, after using Duolingo AI-based features for 1 month. Learners’ perceptions of the features’ efficacy and self-reported transfer of learning outside the app were also analyzed. Study 2 evaluated the same outcomes in learners who were given 1 month of complimentary access to the AI-based features.

### 7.1 Increases in learners’ self-efficacy

Participants who engaged in learning experiences enabled by the AI-based features showed significant increases in their self-efficacy, especially when the AI-based features were novel. In Study 1, self-efficacy for using French/Spanish in real-life situations increased significantly. In Study 2, learners showed a significant increase in self-efficacy for using French/Spanish in real-life situations, as well as for the specific situations of navigating a new city and sharing opinions with others. The learners in Study 2 also showed significant increases in self-efficacy for speaking in French/Spanish, understanding French/Spanish grammar, and understanding mistakes in French/Spanish.

These results represent the first evidence that language learning self-efficacy increases significantly after app-based learning experiences that use generative AI, consistent with learners’ expectation that generative AI in language apps can help them with personalized conversation practice and error correction ([Yuen and Schlote, 2024](#ref81)). The findings in this study are consistent with evidence that technology-assisted learning experiences prior to ChatGPT support language learning self-efficacy ([Zhang, 2022](#ref82)), including studies in China ([Liu, 2020](#ref45)), Iran ([Babakhani and Tabatabaee-Yazdi, 2023](#ref4); [Dong et al., 2022](#ref16)), and the US ([Zheng et al., 2009](#ref83)). More broadly, these findings build on previous international research showing that language learning self-efficacy can be increased through interventions with communication-focused tasks, constructive feedback that highlights learner success, and explicit teaching ([Raoofi et al., 2012](#ref60); [Chen, 2022](#ref13); [Goetze and Driver, 2022](#ref27)). Taken together with the present results, this literature suggests that other AI-enabled learning experiences that effectively leverage communication-focused tasks, constructive feedback, and explicit teaching should also be able to increase learners’ self-efficacy. More research with other AI-based tools is needed to test this hypothesis.

args.summary:
This is an original research article published in Frontiers in Education on February 6, 2025, investigating how generative AI features in the Duolingo language learning app affect learners' self-efficacy. The study involved 385 French/Spanish learners who used AI-based features (Roleplay for conversation practice and Explain My Answer for on-demand explanations) for one month.

**Methods:** Two studies were conducted. Study 1 involved 153 pre-existing subscribers who had already been using the AI features. Study 2 involved 232 learners who were given complimentary access to try the features for the first time. Participants completed pre- and post-surveys measuring self-efficacy across 7 key language skills.

**Key Findings:**
- In Study 1, learners who already used the features felt significantly more prepared to use French/Spanish in real-life situations after one month.
- In Study 2 (first-time users), learners showed significant increases in self-efficacy for 6 of 7 measures: feeling prepared for real-life situations, navigating a city, sharing opinions, speaking confidence, understanding grammar, and understanding mistakes.
- Across both studies, over 90% of learners agreed the AI-based features effectively supported learning.
- 73% (Study 1) and 63% (Study 2) of participants reported using what they learned outside the app, in contexts such as travel, workplace communication, conversations with native speakers, and daily errands.

**Conclusion:** These results provide the first evidence that generative AI-based language learning experiences can enhance self-efficacy, building on classroom intervention research. The AI features contained elements shown to support self-efficacy: communication-focused tasks, constructive feedback, and explicit teaching of language learning strategies.

# Business Case Study: Duolingo — Gamifying Education and Building a Habit-Forming Empire

![Md. Jubair Hasan](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fill:64:64/1*JhZnXpeL4pen5LT992GHgg.jpeg)

![]()

## 1. Introduction: The Gamification of Human Capital

In the annals of modern educational technology, few entities have achieved the ubiquity, cultural resonance, and financial velocity of Duolingo, Inc. As of late 2025, the Pittsburgh-based language learning platform has transcended its utility-based origins to become a global lifestyle brand, boasting over 135 million Monthly Active Users (MAUs) and surpassing the critical milestone of 50 million Daily Active Users (DAUs). What began as a computer science project at Carnegie Mellon University has evolved into a multi-billion dollar enterprise that effectively disrupted a centuries-old industry characterized by high barriers to entry, exorbitant costs, and rigid pedagogical structures.

This case study provides a comprehensive, expert-level analysis of Duolingo’s ascent, dissecting the intricate convergence of behavioral economics, generative artificial intelligence, and “unhinged” brand marketing that powers its growth engine. Unlike traditional competitors such as Rosetta Stone or Babbel, which adhered to legacy subscription models or academic formalism, Duolingo pioneered a “freemium” ecosystem that leveraged the psychological mechanics of mobile gaming to solve the “motivation problem” inherent in self-directed learning. By transforming education into a habit-forming loop — anchored by the “Streak” — Duolingo has not only captured the largest market share in digital language learning but has also fundamentally redefined the unit economics of the sector.

The report delves deeply into the company’s fiscal trajectory, analyzing its transition from a venture-backed growth vehicle to a highly profitable public company with Adjusted EBITDA margins approaching 30% in 2025. It scrutinizes the strategic pivot toward an “AI-First” methodology, exemplified by the rollout of Duolingo Max and the algorithmic generation of content, which has allowed the firm to scale its course offerings at an unprecedented rate while managing operational costs. Furthermore, we examine the Duolingo English Test (DET), a high-margin, disruptive business unit that challenged the monopolistic hold of TOEFL and IELTS, democratizing access to higher education for millions of students in the Global South.

Through a granular investigation of its organizational architecture — characterized by autonomous “vertical teams,” a culture of relentless A/B testing, and rituals like “Grease Week” — this study illuminates how Duolingo maintains the velocity of a startup despite its massive scale. Ultimately, this report argues that Duolingo’s competitive moat is constructed not merely of data, but of attention, having successfully repurposed the addictive algorithms of social media for the accumulation of human capital.

## 2. Origins and Philosophical Foundations: From CAPTCHA to the Green Machine

## 2.1 The Roots of Human Computation

To understand the strategic DNA of Duolingo, one must first examine the intellectual history of its co-founder and CEO, Luis von Ahn. A professor of computer science at Carnegie Mellon University, von Ahn was a pioneer in the field of “human computation,” a discipline focused on harnessing human brainpower to solve problems that computers — at the time — could not. His first major breakthrough was the invention of the CAPTCHA (Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart), a security mechanism designed to distinguish human users from malicious bots by asking them to decipher distorted text.

While CAPTCHA was a commercial success, sold to Google, von Ahn was troubled by the sheer magnitude of human time “wasted” solving these puzzles — estimated at approximately 500,000 hours per day globally. This inefficiency birthed his second major innovation: reCAPTCHA. This system utilized the same security infrastructure to digitize human knowledge. When Optical Character Recognition (OCR) software failed to decipher a word from an archival text due to fading or blurring, reCAPTCHA would serve that word to a human user as a security challenge. The user’s input, verified by consensus, would then digitize the word. This brilliant dual-purpose model — extracting value (book digitization) from a necessary friction (security verification) — became the philosophical bedrock for Duolingo.

![]()

## 2.2 The Failed B2B Translation Model

When Duolingo launched in 2011/2012, its business model was a direct spiritual successor to reCAPTCHA. The premise was a “fair trade” exchange: users would receive high-quality language education for free, and in return, they would translate the internet. As users progressed through the curriculum, they were presented with sentences from the web to translate as part of their practice exercises. Duolingo then aggregated these translations and sold them to corporate clients, such as CNN and BuzzFeed, effectively operating as a B2B translation service powered by crowdsourcing.

To ensure quality control from a workforce of “amateur” learners, Duolingo employed a sophisticated consensus algorithm. Beginners were assigned simple syntactic structures, while advanced users tackled complex semantic nuances. Multiple users translated the same passage, and the system used statistical variance to determine the “correct” translation. While technically innovative, this model faced significant scalability challenges. The demand for translations did not perfectly align with the learning progression of users, and the revenue potential of translation services paled in comparison to the burgeoning app economy. Consequently, the company executed a decisive pivot away from B2B services to a consumer-centric “freemium” model, realizing that the users themselves — not their labor — were the true asset.

## 2.3 The Robin Hood Mission and Market Expansion

A defining characteristic of Duolingo’s corporate strategy is its adherence to a social mission: “To develop the best education in the world and make it universally available”. This is not merely a philanthropic tagline but a strategic wedge. Von Ahn, raised in Guatemala, observed that high-quality education in developing nations was often a luxury good, reinforcing socioeconomic stratification. By offering its core product for free, Duolingo obliterated the barrier to entry, allowing it to aggregate a user base of unparalleled size and diversity.

This massive Top of Funnel (ToF) serves two critical business functions that competitors like Babbel or Rosetta Stone (which rely on hard paywalls) cannot replicate:

## 3. The Engine of Growth: Behavioral Economics and the Hook Model

Duolingo’s primary innovation is not pedagogical; it is psychological. Recognizing that the hardest part of self-directed learning is staying motivated, the company engineered its product to mimic the addictive loops of social media and mobile gaming. This strategy is a textbook application of the Hook Model, a framework developed by Nir Eyal consisting of four phases: Trigger, Action, Variable Reward, and Investment.

![]()

## 3.1 Phase 1: The Trigger (External and Internal Nudges)

The first step in the habit-forming loop is the trigger. Duolingo has mastered the art of the External Trigger through its push notification strategy.

## 3.2 Phase 2: The Action (Frictionless Engagement)

The “Action” phase requires the user to perform a behavior in anticipation of a reward. Duolingo minimizes the friction of this action to near-zero.

## 3.3 Phase 3: Variable Reward (The Dopamine Dispenser)

Borrowing directly from B.F. Skinner’s research on operant conditioning, Duolingo utilizes Variable Rewards to maintain engagement. If a reward is predictable, the brain eventually habituates to it and releases less dopamine. If the reward is unpredictable, engagement spikes.

## 3.4 Phase 4: Investment (The Sunk Cost Lock-In)

The final phase involves the user putting something *into* the product — time, data, or effort — which increases the product’s value to them and the likelihood of their return.

## 4. Organizational Architecture: The Green Machine

Duolingo’s ability to innovate at the speed of a startup, despite having over 800 employees and a multi-billion dollar valuation, is a result of its unique organizational structure and engineering culture.

## 4.1 Vertical Teams and Metric Ownership

Unlike traditional corporate structures that organize by function (e.g., Engineering, Design, Marketing), Duolingo organizes its workforce into Vertical Teams or “Pods.” Each pod is cross-functional, containing engineers, product managers, designers, and data scientists, and is focused on moving a *single* specific metric.

## 4.2 A Culture of Experimentation

Duolingo operates as a data science company first and an education company second. The company runs over 750 A/B tests per quarter.

## 4.3 Grease Week and Technical Debt Management

The rapid pace of A/B testing inevitably leads to “spaghetti code” and technical debt. To mitigate this, Duolingo instituted a ritual known as “Grease Week”.

## 4.4 The Hole vs. A-hole Talent Strategy

A core tenet of Duolingo’s hiring philosophy, established by Von Ahn, is the principle: “It is better to have a hole than an a-hole”. This adage dictates that the company would rather leave a critical role vacant for months (or even a year) than hire a highly qualified individual who does not fit the culture or exhibits toxic behavior. This rigorous adherence to cultural fit has resulted in high employee retention rates and a collaborative environment that supports the cross-functional pod structure.

## 5. Technology and AI Strategy: The AI-First Pivot

Long before the Generative AI boom of 2023, Duolingo was deeply integrated with machine learning. However, the emergence of Large Language Models (LLMs) like GPT-4 precipitated a major strategic pivot in 2024 and 2025.

## 5.1 Birdbrain: The Personalization Engine

Duolingo’s proprietary AI model, Birdbrain, is the invisible hand guiding the user experience. It creates a personalized model of every user’s proficiency and every exercise’s difficulty.

## 5.2 Duolingo Max and GPT-4 Integration

In March 2023, Duolingo announced a partnership with OpenAI to launch Duolingo Max, a new premium subscription tier powered by GPT-4.6 This tier introduced two flagship features designed to address the platform’s historical weakness: lack of conversational practice and deep grammatical explanation.

## 5.3 The AI-First Content Strategy

In 2025, Duolingo radically restructured its content creation pipeline. Previously, the company relied on thousands of contractors to hand-craft sentences and translations. The “AI-First” strategy replaced much of this manual labor with Generative AI tools, overseen by human experts.

## 6. Business Model Deep Dive: Monetizing the Free User

Duolingo’s financial success is a testament to the viability of the freemium model when executed at massive scale. The company has diversified its revenue streams to reduce reliance on any single source.

## 6.1 Subscription Revenue (Super amp; Max)

The core revenue driver is subscriptions, accounting for over 80% of total revenue in 2025.

## 6.2 The Duolingo English Test (DET)

The DET represents a strategic “Blue Ocean” move. The standardized testing market was a duopoly controlled by ETS (TOEFL) and the British Council (IELTS), characterized by high fees ($200+), physical testing centers, and slow results.

## 6.3 Advertising and In-App Purchases (IAP)

## 7. Financial Performance: A Quantitative Analysis (2024–2025)

The fiscal years 2024 and 2025 marked Duolingo’s maturation from a growth stock to a profitable compounder.

## 7.1 Explosive Top-Line Growth

## 7.2 Profitability and Margin Expansion

Duolingo has defied the “growth at all costs” stereotype of tech companies.

## 8. Strategic Expansion: Beyond Language to the Everything App

Duolingo’s long-term vision is to decouple its teaching method from language learning and apply it to all subjects that require memory and repetition.

## 8.1 Mathematics and Music

In late 2023, Duolingo integrated Math and Music courses directly into the main app (rather than standalone apps), a strategy fully realized by 2025.

## 8.2 Strategic Pivot 2026: Teaching Better

In Q3 2025, management announced a subtle but significant pivot. While user growth (DAU) remains a priority, the focus shifted towards “Teaching Better” and deepening engagement for advanced learners.

## 9. Risks and Challenges

## 9.1 The Efficacy Ceiling and Competition

Despite its success, a persistent critique is that Duolingo is a game first and a teacher second. Serious learners often “graduate” from Duolingo to use tutors, textbooks, or immersive platforms like Speak or TalkPal, which focus heavily on AI conversation. If Duolingo Max cannot bridge this gap, the company risks churning its most valuable (high LTV) users.

## 9.2 Geopolitical Risk: The China Factor

China is Duolingo’s second-largest market by DAU and its fastest-growing region in 2025. This exposure carries significant risk. The Chinese regulatory environment for ed-tech is volatile, and any geopolitical tension or regulatory crackdown (e.g., data privacy laws, restrictions on foreign content) could instantaneously sever a major growth artery. The company has mitigated this by minimizing paid marketing in the region, relying on viral partnerships like the one with Luckin Coffee.

## 9.3 Valuation Volatility

In 2025, Duolingo’s stock experienced significant volatility, dropping ~46% from its highs despite strong earnings. This reflects Wall Street’s anxiety over two factors:

## 9.4 Visa Acceptance for DET

While DET is accepted by thousands of universities, it is *not* yet accepted for student visas in key markets like the UK and Australia. These governments maintain strict “SELT” (Secure English Language Test) lists that favor IELTS and PTE. This regulatory bottleneck limits the DET’s total addressable market, as students in these regions often opt for IELTS to satisfy both university and visa requirements with a single test.

## 10. Conclusion: The Attention Economy Winner

Duolingo creates a compelling case study in the power of product-led growth and behavioral design. It did not win the language learning market by having the best curriculum; it won by solving the problem of motivation. By treating education as an attention economy product — competing with TikTok and Instagram rather than textbooks — it built a habit-forming engine that competitors have failed to replicate.

The company’s evolution from a crowdsourced translation tool to an AI-powered educational conglomerate demonstrates exceptional strategic agility. The 2025 pivot to “AI-First” content creation and the expansion into Math and Music suggest that Duolingo aims to become the operating system for all casual learning.

However, the path forward requires navigating the “Uncanny Valley” of AI education — proving that an app can not only entertain but truly teach complex proficiency. With the upcoming CFO transition to Gillian Munson signaling a focus on operational discipline, Duolingo is positioned not just as a high-growth tech stock, but as a mature, diversified platform with the potential to dominate the global education market for decades to come.

Recommendation: For observers and investors, the key metric to watch in 2026 is not just DAU growth, but the Max penetration rate and retention at advanced levels. Success here will prove that Duolingo has successfully crossed the chasm from a fun game to a serious educational imperative.

As of late 2025, Duolingo has over 135 million Monthly Active Users (MAUs) and 50 million Daily Active Users (DAUs), originating from a Carnegie Mellon University project by Luis von Ahn.

### Key Origins & Philosophy
- Luis von Ahn pioneered "human computation," inventing CAPTCHA and reCAPTCHA (sold to Google).
- Duolingo initially launched as a B2B translation service (crowdsourced translations from learners), but pivoted to a consumer "freemium" model.
- Social mission: "To develop the best education in the world and make it universally available."

### Growth Engine: Behavioral Economics (Hook Model)
1. **Trigger**: Masterful push notifications (e.g., passive-aggressive owl reminders).
2. **Action**: Frictionless engagement (5-minute lessons, mobile-first design).
3. **Variable Reward**: Gamification features (XP, badges, leaderboards, Streak system) using operant conditioning.
4. **Investment**: Sunk cost lock-in (Streak freezes, in-app purchases, social features).

### Organizational Architecture
- **Vertical Teams/Pods**: Cross-functional teams focused on single metrics.
- **A/B Testing**: Over 750 tests per quarter.
- **Grease Week**: Ritual for paying down technical debt.
- **Hiring Philosophy**: "Better to have a hole than an a-hole" — prioritizing culture fit over qualifications.

### AI & Technology Strategy
- **Birdbrain**: Proprietary AI personalization engine modeling user proficiency and exercise difficulty.
- **Duolingo Max**: Premium tier powered by GPT-4 (launched March 2023) featuring AI conversation practice and deep grammar explanations.
- **AI-First Content Strategy (2025)**: Replaced manual contractor content creation with Generative AI tools overseen by human experts.

### Business Model & Monetization
- **Subscriptions**: Super and Max tiers account for 80%+ of revenue.
- **Duolingo English Test (DET)**: Disruptive "Blue Ocean" move challenging TOEFL/IELTS duopoly with lower fees, remote proctoring, and faster results.
- **Advertising & In-App Purchases** for free users.

### Financial Performance (2024-2025)
- Strong top-line growth with margin expansion; Adjusted EBITDA margins approaching 30%.
- Q3 2025 Net Income includes a one-time ~$222M tax benefit release.

### Strategic Expansion
- Math and Music courses integrated into main app (2023-2025).
- **Pivot 2026**: Shift toward "Teaching Better" and deepening engagement for advanced learners.

### Risks & Challenges
- **Efficacy Ceiling**: Risk that serious learners "graduate" to tutors or other platforms.
- **Geopolitical Risk**: China is the second-largest market; regulatory volatility.
- **Valuation Volatility**: Stock dropped ~46% from highs despite strong earnings.
- **Visa Acceptance**: DET not yet accepted for student visas in UK and Australia.

### Conclusion
Duolingo succeeded not by having the best curriculum, but by solving the motivation problem using behavioral design and attention economy principles. The key metric to watch in 2026 is Max penetration rate and retention at advanced levels.

## Part 3: Advancing Academic Success in Gateway Courses

In the fall of 2019 when Renick called Magliozzi to say, “I have an idea,” Magliozzi had enough wisdom to say “yes” before Renick even finished his thought.

Once again with Dr. Page serving as lead research partner, GSU set out to apply Mainstay’s technology as a virtual Teaching Assistant (TA) to address a significant student success issue: high DFW (drop, fail, or withdrawal) rates in large gateway courses, starting with American Government — a required course at all public institutions in Georgia.

Professor Michael Evans, the senior lecturer overseeing the course, noted that while students typically received email reminders, the direct and personalized text messages from TA Pounce were more impactful. They offered not just reminders, but also readiness assessments through practice quizzes and crucial academic nudging tailored to students’ immediate needs.

In that first semester, students who engaged with Pounce achieved significantly higher academic performance. Those in the treatment group scored grades of B or above at rates 16% higher than their counterparts who did not receive success coaching.  Moreover, first-generation students in the treatment group earned an overall grade 11 points higher than similar students in the control group.

The Wall Street Journal highlights this success in their article “[How Data Is Changing the College Experience](https://www.wsj.com/articles/data-college-metrics-apps-11660832149),” where they discuss GSU’s strategic use of AI enhanced chatbots like Pounce. In it, Renick shares that “overall, students who received chatbot messaging were more likely to earn an A or B in the class than those who didn’t receive messages. First-generation students receiving messages earned final grades about 11 points higher than similar students not receiving messages. That’s a full letter grade better. It’s leveling the playing field.”

Moreover, the effectiveness of Pounce extends beyond academic performance; it also provides critical emotional support to students. One first-generation student shared their experience in [the same Wall Street Journal article](https://www.wsj.com/articles/data-college-metrics-apps-11660832149), stating, “*I needed to talk to someone, but didn’t know who. TA Pounce was particularly beneficial for underrepresented students and those historically at a higher risk of dropping the class. For students from underrepresented minorities, those first in their family to attend college, or coming from low-income backgrounds, Pounce is more than a technological tool—it’s a constant, accessible source of guidance that’s always ready to help, at any hour.

Here's how AI agents automate campus tasks, which use cases deliver the most impact, and how to deploy them in your institution.

## **AI Agents for Education: How They Automate Campus Tasks**

AI agents for education are intelligent systems that interact with students, parents, and staff through chat, voice, or messaging to handle the operational tasks that keep campuses running. They go beyond scripted FAQ bots by understanding natural language, maintaining conversation context, accessing institutional databases, and taking actions like enrolling students, scheduling appointments, or sending deadline reminders.

Here's where they deliver the most value across the campus.

### **Admissions and Enrollment Automation**

This is where AI agents have the most proven track record in education. The admissions funnel involves hundreds of repetitive interactions: application status questions, deadline reminders, document requirements, financial aid inquiries, campus visit scheduling, and yield management communications.

Georgia State University's Pounce is the gold standard example. Deployed in 2016 to combat summer melt (students accepted but who fail to register for fall), Pounce texted reminders about critical steps like completing financial aid, submitting documents, and registering for orientation. The chatbot handled 185,000 interactions in its first summer with just 1% staff intervention. Summer melt dropped from 19% to 9%, and enrollment increased by 3.3%.

The impact was so significant that the U.S. Department of Education awarded Georgia State's National Institute for Student Success a $7.6 million grant to study and scale AI chatbot deployment across partner institutions.

For institutions looking to automate enrollment inquiries, platforms like [FwdSlash](https://www.fwdslash.ai/) offer pre-built templates including a [course fee enquiry AI agent](https://www.fwdslash.ai/ready-to-use-ai-agent/course-fee-enquiry-ai-agent), an [online course enquiry and lead capture agent](https://www.fwdslash.ai/ready-to-use-ai-agent/online-course-enquiry-and-lead-capture-ai-agent), and a [student course enrollment agent](https://www.fwdslash.ai/ready-to-use-ai-agent/student-course-enrollment-ai-agent). These can be customized with your institution's specific programs, deadlines, and requirements and deployed in minutes.

### **Student Support and Campus FAQ**

Every institution gets the same questions thousands of times a semester. "When is the add/drop deadline?" "Where is the registrar's office?" "How do I request a transcript?" "What meal plans are available?" "How do I connect to campus Wi-Fi?"

AI agents handle these instantly, 24/7, across website chat, WhatsApp, and mobile apps. This is especially critical for evening and weekend inquiries when campus offices are closed but students still need answers.

Maryville University's AI assistant Max answers thousands of student questions each month and resolves the majority without human intervention. This frees advising staff to focus on complex cases that require personal attention and relationship building.

[FwdSlash](https://www.fwdslash.ai/) lets you [build a student support chatbot with a custom knowledge base](https://www.fwdslash.ai/blog/how-to-build-an-ai-chatbot-with-a-custom-knowledge-base) by uploading your student handbook, course catalog, campus policies, and FAQ documents. The AI agent learns your institution's specific information and answers questions accurately. There's also a dedicated [EdTech student support AI agent](https://www.fwdslash.ai/ready-to-use-ai-agent/edtech-student-support-ai-agent) template ready to deploy.

### **Academic Tutoring and Course Assistance**

AI tutoring is one of the fastest-growing use cases in education. Modern AI tutors don't just give answers. They engage in Socratic dialogue, scaffold difficult concepts, generate practice problems based on real-time course performance, and adapt to each student's learning pace.

Georgia State's course-level Pounce chatbot showed remarkable results. Students receiving AI-powered text messages about assignments, academic supports, and course content were more likely to earn a B or higher. First-generation students in the program earned final grades 11 points higher than their peers who didn't receive the messages.

Arizona State University has deployed ChatGPT-powered tutors that offer personalized learning support. The University of Toronto's Rotman School's "All Day TA" answered 12,000 questions in a single semester. Instructure's IgniteAI Agent, launched in March 2026, helps teachers automate grading rubrics and lesson organization so they have more time for direct student interaction.

40% of education platform students now engage weekly with AI learning assistants. For institutions building out AI tutoring, [FwdSlash](https://www.fwdslash.ai/) lets you create [AI agents trained on specific course material](https://www.fwdslash.ai/blog/how-to-create-industry-specific-knowledge-bases-for-ai-agents) so students get accurate, curriculum-aligned responses.

### **Campus Visit and Event Management**

Every campus visit is a conversion opportunity. But scheduling, confirmations, reminders, and follow-ups consume significant staff time, especially with admissions teams stretched to breaking point.

AI agents manage the entire visit lifecycle. Scheduling happens through natural conversation rather than clunky web forms. Confirmations and reminders go out automatically. Pre-visit preparation materials are personalized based on the student's interests (programs, housing, financial aid). Post-visit follow-up happens promptly while the experience is fresh.

For students who can't visit in person, AI agents schedule virtual meetings, coordinate with student ambassadors, and ensure no interested prospect falls through the cracks. This is particularly valuable during the enrollment cliff when every prospective student interaction matters more than ever.

### **Financial Aid and Scholarship Guidance**

Financial aid is one of the most confusing and anxiety-inducing parts of the college experience for students and parents. AI agents can answer common FAFSA questions, explain aid packages, guide students through verification requirements, and send deadline reminders for critical financial aid steps.

This is exactly what drove Georgia State's success with Pounce. The chatbot's financial aid reminders were a key factor in reducing summer melt by 10 percentage points. Students who missed financial aid deadlines often lost their spots entirely. Proactive AI reminders prevented this at a scale that human advisors couldn't match.

The AI doesn't replace financial aid counselors for complex situations. It handles the repetitive questions ("When is my aid disbursed?" "What documents do I still need to submit?" "Am I eligible for work-study?") and escalates complicated cases to human staff with full context.

### **Employee and HR Support**

Campus operations aren't just about students. Faculty and staff generate thousands of HR-related inquiries annually: benefits questions, leave policies, payroll issues, onboarding procedures, and policy clarifications.

AI agents trained on your institution's HR policies handle these inquiries instantly, reducing the load on HR departments that are often understaffed. FwdSlash offers an [internal HR policy FAQ AI agent](https://www.fwdslash.ai/ready-to-use-ai-agent/internal-hr-policy-faq-ai-agent) and an [employee feedback collection agent](https://www.fwdslash.ai/ready-to-use-ai-agent/employee-feedback-collection-ai-agent) that can be deployed for campus staff.

### **Mental Health Triage and Wellness Check-ins**

This is an emerging and sensitive use case. AI agents can serve as low-barrier triage points, offering immediate coping strategies for common stressors (exam anxiety, homesickness, time management) and seamlessly escalating high-risk cases to human counselors.

Deakin University's Genie includes a unique focus on monitoring student well-being through supportive interactions. The agent checks in with students proactively and flags concerning patterns for human follow-up.

AI should never replace professional mental health services. But as a first-touch resource that's available at 2 AM when counseling centers are closed, it fills a critical gap. Institutions deploying mental health AI must ensure clear escalation protocols and human oversight are built in from day one.

## **How to Deploy AI Agents at Your Institution**

### **Start With Admissions and Enrollment**

This is the highest-impact, most proven starting point. Build an AI agent that answers the questions your admissions team handles hundreds of times daily: application requirements, deadlines, program information, financial aid basics, and campus visit scheduling.

[FwdSlash](https://www.fwdslash.ai/) offers education-specific templates including the [course enquiry and lead capture agent](https://www.fwdslash.ai/ready-to-use-ai-agent/online-course-enquiry-and-lead-capture-ai-agent) and [student enrollment agent](https://www.fwdslash.ai/ready-to-use-ai-agent/student-course-enrollment-ai-agent) that you can customize with your institution's programs and deploy on your website within hours.

### **Train on Your Institutional Data**

Upload your student handbook, course catalog, admissions FAQ, financial aid guides, housing information, and campus policies. Connect your website URL or sitemap so the agent can learn from your existing web content. [FwdSlash's training tools](https://www.fwdslash.ai/blog/how-to-train-an-ai-chatbot) make this straightforward for non-technical staff.

The more specific your training data, the more accurate and helpful the agent becomes. Generic responses hurt more than they help when students have specific questions about your programs and policies.

### **Deploy Across Student Touchpoints**

Students communicate through different channels at different times. Deploy your AI agent on your admissions website, student portal, and messaging platforms like WhatsApp. FwdSlash supports multi-channel deployment from a single dashboard.

Make sure the AI is prominent on high-traffic pages: admissions landing pages, financial aid pages, course catalog pages, and the student services section.

### **Measure Retention and Engagement Impact**

Track metrics that matter for education: enrollment conversion rates, summer melt reduction, student satisfaction scores, staff time saved, inquiry resolution rates, and campus visit scheduling rates. Georgia State tracked Pounce's impact rigorously through randomized controlled trials, which is what led to the $7.6 million DOE grant.

AI agents [improve accuracy over time](https://www.fwdslash.ai/blog/how-ai-chatbots-improve-response-accuracy-over-time) as they learn from more student interactions. Regular review of conversation logs helps identify gaps in your knowledge base.

### **Ensure Compliance**

Education AI must comply with FERPA (Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act) for student data protection, GDPR for international students, and emerging AI regulations like the EU AI Act. Build compliance into your deployment from the start, including data handling policies, audit trails, and clear disclosures when students are interacting with AI.

## **Common Mistakes to Avoid**

**Deploying without training on your actual data.** A chatbot that gives generic answers about "college" instead of specific answers about your institution's programs, deadlines, and policies will frustrate prospective students and damage trust. Train on your content.

**Ignoring the** [**human handoff**](https://www.fwdslash.ai/blog/ai-chatbots-vs-human-agents)**.** Complex financial aid situations, academic advising for students on probation, mental health concerns, and disability accommodations all require human expertise. AI should handle volume; humans should handle complexity and sensitivity.

**Treating AI as an IT project instead of a student success initiative.** The institutions seeing the best results (Georgia State, Deakin, Maryville) treat AI agents as student success tools owned by admissions, student services, and academic departments, not as technology experiments.

**Launching without measuring.** Georgia State's success was validated through rigorous randomized controlled trials. Track enrollment conversion, summer melt, student satisfaction, and staff time savings from day one so you can prove ROI and build the case for expansion.

**Forgetting about equity.** AI agents should improve access for all students, especially first-generation, low-income, and working students who can't always call during business hours. Please follow these guidelines to create your summary:

1. Identify and preserve the main topic or purpose of the webpage.
2. Retain key facts, statistics, and data points that are central to the content's message.
3. Keep important quotes from credible sources or experts.
4. Maintain the chronological order of events if the content is time-sensitive or historical.
5. Preserve any lists or step-by-step instructions if present.
6. Include relevant dates, names, and locations that are crucial to understanding the content.
7. Summarize lengthy explanations while keeping the core message intact.

When handling different types of content:

- For news articles: Focus on the who, what, when, where, why, and how.
- For scientific content: Preserve methodology, results, and conclusions.
- For opinion pieces: Maintain the main arguments and supporting points.
- For product pages: Keep key features, specifications, and unique selling points.

Your summary should be significantly shorter than the original content but comprehensive enough to stand alone as a source of information. Aim for about 25-30 percent of the original length, unless the content is already concise.

   "key_excerpts": "First important quote or excerpt, Second important quote or excerpt, Third important quote or excerpt, ...Add more excerpts as needed, up to a maximum of 5"
}
```

We're not just going back to the Moon, we're going forward to the Moon, Commander Jane Smith stated during the pre-launch press conference."
}
```

Example 2 (for a scientific article):
```json
{
   "summary": "A new study published in Nature Climate Change reveals that global sea levels are rising faster than previously thought. Researchers analyzed satellite data from 1993 to 2022 and found that the rate of sea-level rise has accelerated by 0.08 mm/year² over the past three decades. This acceleration is primarily attributed to melting ice sheets in Greenland and Antarctica. The study projects that if current trends continue, global sea levels could rise by up to 2 meters by 2100, posing significant risks to coastal communities worldwide.",
   "key_excerpts": "Our findings indicate a clear acceleration in sea-level rise, which has significant implications for coastal planning and adaptation strategies, lead author Dr. Emily Brown stated. The rate of ice sheet melt in Greenland and Antarctica has tripled since the 1990s, the study reports. Without immediate and substantial reductions in greenhouse gas emissions, we are looking at potentially catastrophic sea-level rise by the end of this century, warned co-author Professor Michael Green."  
}
```

*Georgia State, Morgan State and the University of Central Florida will pilot chatbots designed to support students in critical undergraduate math and English courses.*

ATLANTA — The U.S. Department of Education (DOE) has awarded the [National Institute for Student Success](https://niss.gsu.edu) (NISS) at Georgia State University a $7.6 million grant to study how chatbots can improve student outcomes in foundational college math and English courses.

Building on previous studies that demonstrate AI-enhanced chatbots increase grades and retention rates among lower-income and first-generation students, the NISS will deploy chatbot technology in first-year math and English courses at Georgia State and its associate degree-granting institution Perimeter College, and at partner schools [Morgan State University](https://www.morgan.edu) in Maryland and the [University of Central Florida](https://www.ucf.edu).

The DOE’s highly competitive Postsecondary Student Success Program supports innovative approaches with the potential to improve national student outcomes. The NISS grant will fund the piloting and scaling of text-based chatbots in critical first-year courses at the partner universities as well as support an evaluation team of national scholars to assess the work.

The goal of introducing chatbots into these courses, according to Tim Renick, the founding executive director of the NISS and the project lead for the grant, is to provide more personalized and timely supports for the students in the courses. The chatbot is designed to complement the efforts of course instructors — answering basic student questions about course material, reminding students of upcoming assignments, and offering encouragement and tips when they struggle.

“Because of their schedules, students with jobs and families currently are less likely to attend after-class tutoring and study sessions,” Renick said. “The chatbots we are developing can support students 24/7, answer questions after hours and keep students on track in these challenging courses.”

Georgia State’s use of artificial intelligence-enhanced chatbot technology dates to 2016, when it piloted a program aimed at reducing “summer melt,” a term describing the phenomenon of high school graduates accepted to college failing to register for fall classes. By communicating with students over the summer through text message reminders and two-way question-and-answer capabilities, Georgia State reduced summer melt from 19 percent to 9 percent, according Renick.

During the first summer, the Pounce chatbot interacted with incoming first-year students 185,000 times, an impossible feat for even the most robustly staffed admissions office.

Georgia State has since expanded the use of the Pounce chatbot for enrollment-related communications to around 40,000 students on its Atlanta and Perimeter College campuses, and in 2021 developed a course-related Pounce, designed for students in first-year political science and economics courses critical to many majors.

[Lindsay Page, the Annenberg Associate Professor of Education Policy](https://vivo.brown.edu/display/lpage2) at Brown University, designed and led experimental studies to assess Georgia State’s use of the Pounce chatbot. All of these trials have shown the benefit of chatbot communication for students. For example, the studies focused on course [chatbots in political science and economics](https://edworkingpapers.com/sites/default/files/ai22-564.pdf) found that receiving direct text messages about class assignments, available academic supports and course content increased the likelihood students would earn a course grade of B or higher and reduced the likelihood of students dropping the course.

“We are grateful to have this opportunity to build on our strong research-practice partnership with the NISS and Georgia State,” said Page, who will lead a team of scholars from Brown, Harvard, Stanford and the Brookings Institution to evaluate the implementation and impact of the newest classroom chatbots. “This project will provide a unique opportunity to dramatically scale course-specific chatbots to additional academic subjects, students and campus contexts, and to deeply investigate how best to incorporate these tools in service of improved learning outcomes for students.”

The NISS and its partners at Morgan State and the University of Central Florida hope to show that chatbots integrated into core math and English courses result in higher grades in those foundational courses, setting students up for better performance in later courses and, ultimately, a degree.

“Far too many of our students find themselves struggling in gateway math and English courses,” said Dr. Ryan Maltese, Associate Vice President for Student Success and Retention at Morgan State. “By incorporating faculty-driven assistive technology directly into the classroom, our students will be able to engage their course materials at any time, in digitally native spaces that they have come to expect as a part of their everyday lives. Morgan State University is proud to be a partner in this innovative work that will help shape the future of higher education, and we look forward to working with our colleagues at GSU and UCF on this trailblazing initiative.”

“Student success is a top priority at UCF, and we’re excited to elevate our use of this promising technology to positively impact student outcomes,” said Dr. Ryan Goodwin, Interim Chief of Staff and Assistant Vice President for Strategy and Innovation at the University of Central Florida. “We are excited to work with our partners at Georgia State University and Morgan State University at the forefront of the student success movement to make an even greater impact on our students.”

Performing well in their first college math and English courses has an outsized impact on a student’s later academic success, according to Renick. A student who passes the courses during their initial 12 months at Perimeter College, for example, is nine times more likely to graduate.

"It’s not just because they are required courses,” Renick said. “It’s because the skills that students are learning in those courses are disproportionately impactful on how they’ll do in subsequent courses. If you can strengthen your composition skills by getting a good grade in an introductory English course, then you’re more likely to do well in your history class or your psychology class.”

By fall 2024, researchers will begin piloting the chatbots in courses at each location with the aim of demonstrating the effectiveness of the tool across a variety of demographic profiles served by each institution.

***Research involving a Georgia State University course using a chatbot to keep students connected showed improved grades and retention rates.***

ATLANTA—Georgia State’s pioneering, artificial intelligence-enhanced chatbot “Pounce” is well established as an institutional tool for helping incoming students navigate the thorny world of finances, registration and just getting started in college. Now, Georgia State is showing student performance jumps when classes employ the chatbot to keep them connected.

Receiving direct text messages about their class assignments, academic supports and course content increased the likelihood students would earn a B or higher and, for first-generation students, increased their likelihood of passing the class. First-generation students receiving the messages earned final grades about 11 points higher than their peers.

“Eleven points is more than a full letter grade, and a full letter grade can be the difference between students holding onto their HOPE Scholarship and Pell Grant awards or not,” said Timothy M.  Renick, the founding executive director of the [National Institute for Student Success](https://niss.gsu.edu) at Georgia State. “These are exceptional results from a fairly light-touch initiative.”

![Timothy M. Renick seated at a table.](https://news.gsu.edu/files/2019/05/Renick-800-660x720.jpg)

Timothy M. Renick, founding executive director of the National Institute for Student Success.

An AI-enhanced text messaging tool in use at Georgia State since spring 2016, the institution-level Pounce chatbot is just one of myriad efforts by the university to support students as they progress through college. Georgia State’s student success efforts have made it a national leader in graduating students from diverse backgrounds and reduced the average time it takes to earn a degree by almost a full semester.

In 2021, the chatbot was integrated for the first time into course content. A group of 500 students in one of Georgia State’s largest courses — political science 1101 — was selected to participate in a randomized controlled trial led by [Lindsay Page, the Annenberg Associate Professor of Education Policy](https://vivo.brown.edu/display/lpage2) at Brown University. Half of the students were selected to receive messages related to the class from the chatbot, and half did not receive the messages.

Page and colleagues Katharine Meyer of Brown and Tyler Walsh of Georgia State presented the findings last week, in a talk titled “Let’s Chat: Chatbot Nudging for Improved Course Performance,” during a conference of the [Association for Education Finance and Policy](https://aefpweb.org) in Denver.

The study was conducted in coordination with [Michael Evans](https://politicalscience.gsu.edu/profile/michael-evans/), senior lecturer in [political science](https://politicalscience.gsu.edu) at Georgia State and the faculty coordinator for the course, taken by about 3,000 students each semester to satisfy degree requirements in American government. Students participating in the fall 2021 trial were taking the course fully online.

Evans said the course typically has a relatively high rate of what are known as DFWs (students receiving a grade of D, F or withdrawing) — around 15 percent prior to the COVID-19 pandemic and as high as 25 percent since the onset.

“It’s a challenge because a lot of times students are just learning how to be college students,” Evans said. “We get every type of student, in terms of their preparation.”

Students already get email reminders about assignments, quizzes and exams, but Evans said students receiving text messages from the “PolsPounce” chatbot were getting an extra, direct reminder as well as the opportunity to text questions back, through PolsPounce, to their professor. Some reminders were targeted to students who didn’t have much time left to complete a reading assignment by the deadline. Students were also reminded when an exam was coming up and given an opportunity to take a short practice quiz to gauge their preparedness.

“Clearly this was having a bigger impact than just the emails, and part of that was because they were receiving the message,” Evans said. “I did not expect we’d get this overwhelming evidence that the chatbot is this effective.”

According to Page’s study results, students who received the PolsPounce messages earned grades of B or above at a rate 16 percent higher than those not on the chatbot.

The average final grade in the class for first-generation students in the control group was 64, while similar students receiving the messages earned a final grade an average of 11 points higher.

Among students who were not in their first year of college, those who received the chatbot messages were more likely to pass the class and less likely to drop their other Georgia State classes. They also did better in their other classes, earning fall term grade point averages 0.28 points higher.

Students participating in the study who displayed lower academic performance in high school were more likely to attend supplemental instruction, more likely to earn a B or higher in the class and complete more credits for the semester if they received the chatbot messages.

“While we’ve seen that students from all kinds of different demographic groups benefit, what we’ve seen consistently is that students who struggle the most overall benefit the most from the chatbot intervention,” Renick said. “Students who are low income, the first in their families to go to college or from underrepresented minorities often lack a support system at home or familiarity with how to get help in college. They are the ones to benefit the most by having this tool in their hand 24/7.”
