## Why Adopt AI In Corporate Training?

By now, almost all companies have realized why they must keep their workforce skilled and ready for the future. Corporate training is a critical investment in people, performance, and staying competitive, especially now that AI has started making its way into L&D. From tailoring learning paths to automating assessments, AI is helping organizations change how they deliver, track, and design training to create smarter and more personalized learning experiences. Companies like IBM, Amazon, and Walmart are already using AI to upskill teams, boost engagement, and drive performance.

According to **eLearning Industry's 2026 research**, only 7.5% of L&D buyers say AI is fully integrated into their learning environments, while 45% are still planning adoption. Meanwhile, 42% of learning technology vendors already offer fully integrated AI capabilities, highlighting that many organizations are still in the implementation phase rather than the optimization phase.

But what makes AI so important to corporate training? For starters, AI can learn from data and make intelligent decisions in real time. Unfortunately, traditional training methods can't do that. In L&D, this means personalized learning journeys, predictive insights, and automation leading to smarter and more effective training. Specifically, AI can analyze a learner's behavior, role, performance, and preferences to recommend the right content at the right time. Plus, it can take care of repetitive admin tasks, freeing up training professionals' time and allowing them to focus on strategy. Lastly, with predictive analytics, [AI tools](https://elearningindustry.com/directory/software-categories/ai-tools "AI Tools") can spot skill gaps, predict learning outcomes, and even suggest when an employee might need extra help before their performance drops.

Below, we'll examine some companies that have succeeded in using AI for their corporate training needs and how they've seen better results in profit, productivity, and learning outcomes.

![Cover of The AI Expectation Gap In Learning Tech 2026: What L&D Leaders Want From AI Platforms Vs. What Vendors Are Building](https://cdn.elearningindustry.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/The-AI-Expectation-Gap-In-Learning-Tech-2026-Report-Cover-Img.webp)
![Cover of The AI Expectation Gap In Learning Tech 2026: What L&D Leaders Want From AI Platforms Vs. What Vendors Are Building](https://cdn.elearningindustry.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/The-AI-Expectation-Gap-In-Learning-Tech-2026-Report-Cover-Img.webp)

#### The AI Expectation Gap In Learning Tech 2026: What L&D Leaders Want From AI Platforms Vs. What Vendors Are Building

## 6 Companies That Have Successfully Implemented AI In Corporate Training Programs

### 1. IBM: Personalized Learning

With a company the size of IBM, with more than 250,000 employees globally, you can imagine how challenging it is to keep everyone trained and well-skilled. And since traditional learning methods weren't enough to prepare the workforce for the future, IBM decided to bring AI to the center of its corporate training program. So, IBM created [Watson](https://www.ibm.com/watson "IBM Watson to watsonx"), its own AI platform. Instead of just offering generic online courses, IBM decided to use Watson to offer personalized learning tailored to each employee's skills, goals, and needs.

How does it work? Watson analyzes data such as job roles, past training, and performance, and uses that information to deliver smart learning paths. For example, if someone wants to get a promotion as a team leader or sharpen their communication skills, Watson figures out the best path to get them there. It even performs skills gap analyses to show where employees stand and what they need to learn next. Then, based on that data, the system suggests relevant courses, resources, and certifications. The [results](https://blogs.psico-smart.com/blog-how-is-artificial-intelligence-transforming-the-training-and-development-management-software-industry-15350#:~:text=They%20implemented%20an%20AI%2Dpowered,in%20today's%20dynamic%20business%20landscape. "How is artificial intelligence transforming the training and development management software industry?")? IBM saw a significant reduction in training time and a boost in employee satisfaction and course completion rates.

**Our research** found that 65% of L&D buyers rank personalized learning as the most valuable AI capability, making it the highest-priority use case. Yet only 44% of vendors are actively investing in personalization, suggesting that organizations using AI to deliver adaptive learning paths may gain a competitive advantage.

### 2. Walmart: AI-Powered VR Training

With over 2 million employees worldwide and thousands of stores to manage, Walmart faces a huge challenge when it comes to training, and that's because retail employees need to be prepared for numerous scenarios. But how do you train that many people in so many different roles in a way that's both effective and engaging? Walmart found the answer in AI-powered Virtual Reality training.

With the [help of STRIVR](https://www.strivr.com/customers/walmart "Walmart cuts training time by 96% with immersive learning"), Walmart used AI-powered VR training across its training academies and stores. These VR modules place employees in realistic, immersive scenarios, like dealing with impatient customers. The AI analyzes employee performance, such as where they look, how quickly they react, and how they make decisions. Based on that, the system offers personalized feedback, helping each person improve where they need it most. Ultimately, it resulted in a [15% improvement](https://corporate.walmart.com/news/2018/09/20/how-vr-is-transforming-the-way-we-train-associates "How VR is Transforming the Way We Train Associates") in employee performance and a 95% reduction in training time. This means a more confident workforce that recalls information faster and actually participates in training.

### 3. Amazon: Training On AI Robots

For Amazon to be able to deliver packages so fast around the world, there's a big network of fulfillment centers and more than 1.5 million employees who need to be trained fast and efficiently. As you can understand, traditional training methods wouldn't be up to this task, so Amazon resorted to AI. In Amazon's fulfillment centers, [AI-powered robots](https://www.aboutamazon.com/news/operations/how-amazon-deploys-robots-in-its-operations-facilities "How Amazon deploys collaborative robots in its operations to benefit employees and customers") and automation systems are used for sorting and packaging items. While these take care of a lot of the heavy lifting, humans still need to manage these robots.

To make it happen, Amazon has created training modules that teach warehouse staff how to safely interact with robots. These modules are also AI-enhanced, adjusting to each employee's progress and offering extra help if someone needs it. For instance, if a worker is dealing with a system error, the AI can walk them through it with real-time support and visual guides. The AI also tracks how long tasks take, accuracy rates, and even movement patterns to spot areas for improvement. With that data, the system can suggest personalized training programs. Overall, this approach has led to a [75% boost](https://www.virtasant.com/ai-today/ais-influence-on-corporate-cultures-insights-from-amazon-sprintit-and-hp "Enterprise AI Adoption: Insights from Amazon, SprintIT, HP") in employee engagement and a 40% increase in task fulfillment time.

### 4. Unilever: AI-Based Recruitment

Starting a new job in a company as big as Unilever can feel overwhelming. There's a lot to learn, from HR policies to internal systems and the pressure to become productive as soon as possible. That's where [Unabot](https://bernardmarr.com/the-amazing-ways-how-unilever-uses-artificial-intelligence-to-recruit-train-thousands-of-employees/ "The Amazing Ways How Unilever Uses Artificial Intelligence To Recruit & Train Thousands Of Employees") comes in, Unilever's friendly AI assistant designed to help new hires settle in smoothly. Unabot is built on Microsoft's Bot Framework and uses Natural Language Processing (NLP), allowing it to understand how people typically ask questions. From instructions on how to set up one's ID or checking employee benefits to learning about the company's values, Unabot's got every answer. It gets the info from official company guidelines, policy docs, onboarding schedules, and even questions from past employees, so the answers are tailored specifically to Unilever's culture and structure.

As of 2023, Unabot was active in 36 countries. Its launch has really been well-received by the employees. In the areas where it's been introduced, 36% of the workforce has given it a try, and 80% think it's useful enough to keep using it. Because it's [so successful](https://aiexpert.network/case-study-revolutionizing-operations-with-ai-at-unilever/#:~:text=Furthermore%2C%20the%20introduction,within%20the%20organization. "Case Study: Revolutionizing Operations with AI at Unilever"), there are plans to roll it out globally across all 190 markets Unilever operates in.

### 5. McDonald's: Training With Voice-Activated AI Systems

McDonald's is one of the biggest fast-food chains in the world, so getting its employees trained quickly is a must. With thousands of locations and millions of customers every day, McDonald's faces a challenge regarding new hires: how to onboard them efficiently while making sure they provide great customer service. As part of its L&D strategy, McDonald's adopted an AI-powered training simulator to make onboarding smoother and boost real-time learning. Specifically, they introduced [voice-activated AI systems](https://litslink.com/blog/ai-in-learning-8-use-cases-of-using-ai#:~:text=McDonald%E2%80%99s%20uses%20voice%2Dactivated%20AI%20training%20systems%20to%20guide%20new%20employees%20through%20their%20initial%20tasks. "AI in Learning: 8 Use Cases of Using AI to Enhance Employee Skills") that help new employees through tasks like making burgers, taking orders, and keeping things clean, all with step-by-step guidance.

What makes this special is that the system is smart. It analyzes interactions with customers to spot common issues, patterns, and trends in how employees serve customers, and areas where the staff could do better. The data is then used to optimize training courses, so new hires learn not just how to do their jobs but also how to excel in their roles. [This approach](https://www.hrdconnect.com/casestudy/inside-mchire-how-ai-helped-mcdonalds-drop-time-to-hire-by-65/#:~:text=Time%2Dto%2Dhire%20reduced,to%20the%20previous%20system "Inside 'McHire': How AI reduced McDonald's time-to-hire by 65%") has led to a 65% reduction in time-to-hire and a 20% increase in the number of candidates finishing the process.

### 6. Google: Monitoring Performance

Google has created a strong internal learning system that leverages AI to keep people engaged and always one step ahead when it comes to tech and industry trends. At the core of this is Grow, Google's own learning platform. When it started, it had all sorts of courses, from 3D printing to Rubik's Cube tricks, but in 2025, they decided to change it a bit, and now it focuses mainly on AI-related skills.

Powered by AI analytics, Google's system [monitors how employees are performing](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/ai-driven-career-development-how-machine-learning-can-w-phr-mba-wn5sc/ "AI-Driven Career Development: How Machine Learning Can Map Out Your Next Promotion") and engaging with their learning. It suggests personalized courses, workshops, and hands-on projects, tailored not just to what someone is currently doing but also to what's going to be popular in the industry in the future. So, the main goal is to keep everyone ready for whatever challenges come next. This has boosted internal skills and made everyone focus on the learning opportunities most relevant to their roles. While Google hasn't shared specific results, the [internal feedback](https://www.deel.com/blog/employee-development-at-google/#:~:text=Program%20%7C%20Source%3A%20YouTube-,The%20key%20to%20Google%27s%20L%26D%20success,-Let%E2%80%99s%20look%20at "How Google's Innovative Training and Development Programs Empower Employees") shows that employees really value the platform, as it allows them to grow both personally and professionally.

## Conclusion

AI is here, and it's pretty clear it's changing how organizations approach L&D. AI adoption is changing how L&D teams work. **According to our research**, 22% of organizations report significant changes to roles and team structures due to AI, while another 33% report moderate changes, indicating that successful AI adoption often requires both organizational and technological transformation.

As we've seen from the above companies that made it, the key is starting with clear goals and small actions. You don't need a big budget or a complete system change to begin. Just identifying your challenges is enough. From there, you can find the AI system that will address your corporate training program's issues. In the future, no L&D strategy will succeed without AI implementation, so why not take the lead and begin now?

1. **IBM**: Created Watson AI to offer personalized learning paths for 250,000+ employees, analyzing job roles, past training, and performance to deliver smart learning paths and skills gap analyses. Resulted in reduced training time and improved employee satisfaction and course completion rates.

2. **Walmart**: Used AI-powered VR training (with STRIVR) to train 2 million+ employees in realistic scenarios. The AI analyzes performance metrics like gaze, reaction time, and decision-making. Achieved a 15% improvement in employee performance and 95% reduction in training time.

3. **Amazon**: Deployed AI-powered robots in fulfillment centers with training modules that adjust to employee progress. AI tracks task times, accuracy rates, and movement patterns to suggest personalized training. Led to a 75% boost in employee engagement and 40% increase in task fulfillment time.

4. **Unilever**: Created "Unabot," an AI assistant built on Microsoft's Bot Framework using NLP, to help onboard new hires across 36 countries. As of 2023, 36% of the workforce tried it, and 80% found it useful. Plans to roll out globally across 190 markets.

5. **McDonald's**: Implemented voice-activated AI training simulators guiding new employees through tasks and analyzing customer interactions to optimize training. Resulted in a 65% reduction in time-to-hire and 20% increase in candidates completing the process.

6. **Google**: Developed "Grow," an internal learning platform using AI analytics to monitor employee performance and engagement, suggesting personalized courses and workshops focused on AI-related skills. Internal feedback indicates employees highly value the platform.

The article concludes that AI adoption is changing L&D teams, with 22% of organizations reporting significant changes to roles and team structures due to AI, and another 33% reporting moderate changes. The key is starting with clear goals and small actions.

Key data points: 65% of L&D buyers rank personalized learning as the most valuable AI capability, but only 44% of vendors are actively investing in it.

# The Impact of AI on Corporate Training

* Share This: [Share The Impact of AI on Corporate Training on Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fcpc.tsu.edu%2Fblog%2F2025%2F02%2F03%2Fthe-impact-of-ai-on-corporate-training%2F "Click to share on Facebook")[Share The Impact of AI on Corporate Training on LinkedIn](http://www.linkedin.com/cws/share?token&isFramed=false&url=https%3A%2F%2Fcpc.tsu.edu%2Fblog%2F2025%2F02%2F03%2Fthe-impact-of-ai-on-corporate-training%2F "Click to share on LinkedIn")[Share The Impact of AI on Corporate Training on X](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?text=The+Impact+of+AI+on+Corporate+Training&url=https%3A%2F%2Fcpc.tsu.edu%2F%3Fp%3D4270 "Click to share on Twitter")

*[The Impact of AI on Corporate Training](https://ivyexec.com/career-advice/2024/the-impact-of-ai-on-corporate-training/) was originally published on [Ivy Exec](https://ivyexec.com).*

Alright, let’s get real here. [The future is now](https://ivyexec.com/classes/the-future-is-now-practical-ai-computer-vision-and-emerging-technologies), and innovative technologies like artificial intelligence (AI) don’t surprise anyone.

The adoption of [AI in business](https://ivyexec.com/classes/the-business-and-application-of-artificial-intelligence) isn’t big news anymore. You can notice it applied by companies to the right and left, whether in digital transformation, competitor analytics, or marketing. And it’s here to stay. In fact, [95% of employees](https://www.unleash.ai/artificial-intelligence/95-of-employees-believe-ai-will-have-a-positive-impact-in-2024/) believe AI will positively impact business in 2024. Meanwhile, [72% of HR leaders](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/future-ai-corporate-training-mda-training/) think it will substantially modify the realm of learning and development (L&D) in the workplace.

Why is AI significant for corporate training, and how does it influence how employers educate and train their workforce?

This article explores how AI can [transform your corporate training](https://ivyexec.com/career-advice/2023/transforming-training-sessions-the-path-to-engaging-and-impactful-learning) and provides a list of AI tools with examples of businesses already using them.

So, put your seatbelt on and enjoy the read.

## AI’s Benefits for Corporate Learning

First and foremost, let’s look at artificial intelligence through the lens of its capabilities for educational activities and training initiatives in the workplace. Below are the six things AI can do for your company and your employees.

### 👉 Cost Reduction And Time Efficiency

“The cost-saving potential is one of the most valuable advantages of AI in workplace training for employers,” claims Jim Pendergast, Senior Vice President at [altLINE Sobanco](http://altline.sobanco.com/). He explains, “Unlike traditional classroom training, it doesn’t require investing in a dedicated physical space, salaries for trainers or coaches, printed handouts, and other materials.”

Actually, organizations using AI for employee learning and development reduce training costs [by 30%](https://www.reworked.co/learning-development/can-you-trust-ai-to-revolutionize-corporate-training/).

If you embrace [continuous employee learning](https://ivyexec.com/career-advice/2023/the-imperative-of-continuous-employee-learning-a-priority-for-executive-level-leaders) (most probably, you do), the ongoing preparation and training process can involve too much time, effort, and human and financial resources. With artificial intelligence, you automate all time-consuming administrative and organizational tasks and put corporate training on autopilot.

### 👉 Effective Content Creation

AI has spurred the [use of technology in executive education](https://ivyexec.com/career-advice/2022/why-the-use-of-technology-in-executive-education-is-the-order-of-the-day/) and employee L&D overall by bringing content generators to the arena of corporate training.

Jerry Han, CMO at [PrizeRebel](http://prizerebel.com/), emphasizes the effectiveness of such tools in educating the staff. He mentions, “Today, companies train employees with AI-generated surveys, quizzes, videos, animations, etc. This way, L&D leaders improve operational efficiency and productivity. Moreover, they get high-quality training materials for L&D programs because AI eliminates human error in producing content.”

Jerry Han provides a list of tools used to create educational content for employees:

* Text → ChatGPT
* Text to video → HourOne.ai
* Video → Synthesia
* Infographic → Venngage
* Checklist → ChecklistGenerator.ai
* Animation → Animaker AI
* Course → Thinkific
* Quiz → Vevox AI Quiz Generator
* Survey → QuestionPro QxBot

Of course, you can find more of them as AI-driven content creators invade the Internet spaces at breakneck speed.

### 👉 Streamlined Onboarding Training

Employers actively utilize AI to [onboard new hires](https://ivyexec.com/career-advice/2023/successfully-onboard-new-hires-to-your-companys-culture) and streamline their mentorship.

“AI-powered solutions aimed at hiring, onboarding, and training new employees are indispensable tools in the HR tech stack,” claims Max Wesman, Founder & COO of [GoodHire](http://goodhire.com/). “AI platforms for HRs (take HRPad or Leena.ai) and conversational AI bots (Botbot.ai or Eggheads.ai) revolutionize mentoring processes during onboarding. They empower companies to deliver a positive employee experience to their recruits who become more engaged and productive at work,” he adds.

[Research proves](https://www.nber.org/papers/w31161) that a conversational AI assistant increases the productivity of novice and low-skilled workers by 34%.

HR tech integrations like AI recruitment tools can indeed navigate [the future of hiring](https://ivyexec.com/career-advice/2024/the-future-of-recruitment-hiring-trends-for-2024) and onboarding. Artificial intelligence for onboarding training is a win-win for all parties: HR managers, organizations, and employees.

### 👉 Personalized Learning Experience

What should you do when a one-size-fits-all approach doesn’t work in [learning and development](https://ivyexec.com/career-advice/2023/the-importance-of-continuous-learning-and-professional-development-for-career-advancement)?

You can turn to AI for corporate training personalization.

Personalized corporate training is an educational approach addressing employees’ learning requirements and preferences.

Personalized learning with AI is:

* **Flexible** (flexibility in schedules, availability round-the-clock)
* **Motivational** (personalized nudges, aka motivators or persuasive tactics that work individually)
* **Adaptive** (adjustable learning plan, difficulty level, content, and pace)
* **Learner-centered (**learner profiles based on the learning styles – reading, writing, auditory, visual, or kinesthetic learner)
* **Inclusive** (accessible for employees with disabilities, employees coming from various backgrounds and cultures, or employees speaking different languages)

Ryan Hammill, Co-Founder and Executive Director of the [Ancient Language Institute](https://ancientlanguage.com/) notes, “Importantly, artificial intelligence diminishes geographic and linguistic limitations imposed on international companies. AI tools for corporate training don’t tie employees to only one location or language for learning the material. They get trained from around the globe, choosing their preferred time zones and languages.”

### 👉 Higher interactivity and engagement with gamification

What if your employees are inactive and disengaged during workplace training? For instance, AI can offer personal certificates or awards for [employee appreciation](https://ivyexec.com/career-advice/2022/need-to-update-your-employee-appreciation-efforts-try-these-17-tactics).

Consider the following examples of gamified L&D powered by artificial intelligence:

* Game-based quizzes
* Gamified learning management systems (LMS)
* Augmented reality (AR) simulators
* Virtual reality (VR) games
* Corporate training scenarios in [the Metaverse](https://ivyexec.com/classes/rise-of-the-metaverse-in-the-era-of-digital-transformation)

Developers like Edverse, Hivelance, or Antier build immersive virtual environments in the Metaverse, offering even more benefits of AI for corporate training: interactivity and employee engagement.

Robert Kaskel, Chief People Officer at [Checkr](https://checkr.com/) mentions, “In the face of employee inactivity and disengagement during workplace training, leveraging the power of artificial intelligence through gamified learning experiences presents a transformative solution. AI-driven platforms not only enhance interactivity but also elevate employee engagement by providing personalized certificates and awards, thereby creating a dynamic and motivating learning environment.”

### 👉 Real-time Data Analysis And Employee Insights

Artificial intelligence analyzes the employee’s performance data and adjusts the learning pathway accordingly. [Creating value from data](https://ivyexec.com/classes/creating-value-from-data-artificial-intelligence-and-beyond), AI can tailor the training modules and resources to employees based on their experience, level of knowledge, and personal preferences in the type of content (visual, audial, textual).

Artificial intelligence monitors real-time performance and provides dynamic [employee feedback](https://ivyexec.com/career-advice/2019/giving-employee-feedback/) on tasks and achievements. An AI-driven training system also generates instant performance reports, gives a comprehensive view of the learners’ progress, and allows them to see the gaps instantly. At this rate, they can return to those modules or topics and work on them once again.

## AI Tools for Workplace Learning and Development

You can harness the power of [generative AI in online learning platforms](https://ivyexec.com/classes/the-impact-of-generative-artificial-intelligence-in-online-learning-platforms) like these:

* Axonify
* KEA
* Knowingo
* Cognispark.ai
* Docebo
* EdCast
* Zoomi

**Note:** Beware of [business mistakes made by AI tools](https://ivyexec.com/career-advice/2023/5-worst-business-mistakes-ai-tools-have-made).

“Privacy and data security breaches are not rare in AI systems,” forewarns Volodymyr Shchegel, VP of Engineering at [Clario](https://clario.co/). “That is why when relying on AI for workplace training, make sure to clarify whether the tool has all the defensive measures that prioritize data protection like encryption, masking, loss prevention, or others,” he recommends.

In addition, it’s also crucial to promote privacy awareness among employees who share their personal information with AI for learning (full name, date of birth, email, job title, professional history, education, etc.).

## 7 Use Cases of AI in Corporate Training

See how different companies leverage artificial intelligence to train employees.

### ◾ Bank of America

The financial institution combines [AI with the Metaverse](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2023-07-13/bank-of-america-is-using-the-metaverse-ai-to-train-its-hires) to train new hires via immersive learning scenarios. These can be tough conversations with customers or other work-related situations.

But not only “newbies” engage with AI for workplace training. The bank’s “oldies” also rehearse customer talks with AI coaches.

### **◾** Kiehl’s

The brand used [Docebo](https://www.docebo.com/customers/global-learning-platform/) for corporate learning with AI, focusing on employees’ personalized training experiences.

### ◾ Care.com

The AI assistant [MeBeBot](https://www.mebebot.com/how-care-com-uses-mebebots-ai-intelligent-assistant/) helped the company with instructions and guidance for new employees. It answered the frequently asked questions about the brand’s tech platform and its peculiarities.

### ◾ Pristyn Care

The healthcare company implemented artificial intelligence for corporate training with [Meera AI](https://biovoicenews.com/pristyn-care-launches-ai-powered-medical-trainer-mira-ai-to-standardize-healthcare-training/). It offers engaging learning modules across over a dozen medical categories to train care coordinators.

### ◾ BESTSELLER

The international fashion brand [BESTSELLER](https://www.synthesia.io/case-studies/bestseller) created 250+ AI videos for their employee training courses with Synthesia.io, saving 50% of classroom time.

### ◾ Roadsurfer

The company leveraged [Zavvy’s AI system](https://www.zavvy.io/case-studies/roadsurfer) to develop a robust program for training new hires. Interactive exercises, quizzes, and automatic reminders created by artificial intelligence are only a couple of things that drive corporate training at Roadsurfer.

### ◾ Air Methods

The medical helicopter company adopted an [aviation training system built with AI](https://belitsoft.com/custom-elearning-development/personalized-e-learning-action). As a result, they personalized the training course, reduced costs, and cut the onboarding program from ten to five days.

## Conclusion

[AI will continue shaping the business world](https://ivyexec.com/classes/how-will-ai-shape-the-world-of-business) even more drastically than you can imagine. As you have seen above, it hasn’t left corporate training untouched either.

As an employer or business leader, you should stay tuned and get ready to embrace a revolutionary approach to educating your employees with artificial intelligence.

Let AI help you and your team learn and develop daily.

By [Ivy Exec](https://ivyexec.com)

# Ep. 183: Voices of Student Success: AI Tool Provides Predictive Analytics Data

*Inside Higher Ed*’s Voices of Student Success discusses how AI can be leveraged to improve predictive analytics and provide insight into workforce outcomes data for a two-year college.

By   [Ashley Mowreader](/author/ashley-mowreader)

November 25, 2025

This series of Voices of Student Success focuses on the use of generative artificial intelligence in higher education and how technology can support student success goals.

Central New Mexico Community College is deploying a new AI-powered predictive analytics tool, [CampusLens](https://www.campusworksinc.com/campuslens/), part of CampusWorks, to improve data visibility in student retention, early alerts and career outcomes.

In the latest episode of Voices of Student Success, Tracy Hartzler, president of Central New Mexico Community College, discusses the risks with taking on new tools, the college’s approach to change management and the need for more responsive data.

Hosted by *Inside Higher Ed* [Student Success reporter](https://www.insidehighered.com/news/student-success) **Ashley Mowreader**, this episode is sponsored by TimelyCare.

# How Predictive Analytics Supports Higher Ed Student Success

![How Predictive Analytics Supports Higher Ed Student Success Beyond Enrollment-Blog](https://multimedia.liaisonedu.com/images/How_Predictive_Analytics_Supports_Higher_Ed.format-webp.webp)

With AI forecasting tools like Liaison Othot, institutions gain a clear view of each student’s journey, enabling them to provide personalized support when it matters most.

## Table of Contents:

## Key Takeaways

Predictive analytics empowers higher education institutions to identify student risks early, anticipate needs, and provide timely, personalized support.

AI forecasting tools like Othot analyze student data to improve retention, engagement, and overall academic success.

By leveraging predictive insights, institutions can proactively allocate resources, enhance student satisfaction, and drive better long-term outcomes.

Data-driven strategies not only support individual students but also help institutions refine policies, curricula, and student services for continuous improvement.

The journey to student success doesn’t end at enrollment—it’s just the beginning. For higher education institutions, helping students thrive academically, socially, and emotionally throughout their college experience is essential. Predictive analytics is transforming how institutions approach this challenge, offering AI-powered insights that identify risks, anticipate needs, and guide timely interventions. The [use of predictive analytics in education](https://www.liaisonedu.com/data-readiness-checklist-for-predictive-ai-in-higher-education-infographic/) is no longer a far-off, futuristic concept but a practical tool that enhances student engagement, satisfaction, and long-term outcomes.

## Unlocking the Power of Predictive Analytics in Higher Ed

Predictive analytics leverages historical and real-time data to forecast future outcomes. In higher education, this means analyzing student performance, behavior, and engagement to identify patterns that signal success—or potential struggles. With AI forecasting tools like [Liaison’s Othot platform](https://www.liaisonedu.com/othot-analytics-liaison/), institutions gain a clear view of each student’s journey, enabling them to provide personalized support when it matters most.

From predicting which students are likely to excel to identifying those at risk of dropping out, predictive analytics equips institutions with actionable insights. This data-driven approach ensures that support systems are proactive, not reactive, creating an environment where every student has the opportunity to achieve their aims.

## The Benefits of AI-Driven Predictive Analytics in Higher Education

AI-powered predictive analytics is transforming how higher education institutions support student success. By leveraging data insights, institutions can anticipate challenges, provide timely interventions, and improve student outcomes. Institutions can then tailor their outreach efforts, offering timely tutoring, relevant campus activities, or counseling services. Here are some of the other benefits:

By harnessing AI forecasting tools, higher education institutions not only strengthen student outcomes but also build a proactive support system that [enhances engagement](https://www.liaisonedu.com/transforming-student-engagement-how-ai-is-personalizing-the-community-college-experience/), satisfaction, and long-term success.

## Data-Driven Strategies for Continuous Improvement

Predictive analytics not only supports individual students but also informs broader institutional strategies. By analyzing trends across the student body, higher education leaders can identify systemic challenges and implement solutions that benefit all students. For example, if data reveals that a particular course has a high dropout rate, institutions can take steps to revise the curriculum, provide additional resources, or train faculty to offer better support.

AI forecasting tools also enable scenario-based analysis, allowing institutions to test different strategies and predict their outcomes before implementation. This continuous refinement helps institutions remain agile and responsive to student needs, ultimately driving better outcomes across the board.

## Empowering Student Success With Predictive Analytics

As higher education evolves, the need for data-driven strategies becomes increasingly clear. Predictive analytics offers a powerful solution to one of the sector’s most pressing challenges: how to improve student outcomes throughout their college journey. By leveraging AI forecasting tools, institutions can not only anticipate challenges but also provide timely, personalized support that helps students thrive.

Partner with Liaison to harness the power of predictive analytics at your institution. From AI-driven forecasting to proactive support systems, Liaison’s solutions help you turn data into action and drive meaningful outcomes. # PREDICTIVE ANALYTICS IN HIGHER EDUCATION: A COMPARATIVE STUDY OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE APPROACHES ACROSS MULTIPLE COHORTS

## Authors

## Keywords:

## Abstract

Predicting student success in higher education is critical for enhancing retention, enabling timely interventions, and improving the overall quality of the study process. This paper is about evaluation and comparing several artificial intelligence approaches on the same dataset of cohorts, covering multiple generations and great number of students, including both graduates and non-graduates. A range of AI tools is applied with respect of the known large language models (LLMs) using natural language prompts in order to predict academic outcomes, final grade point average, dropout risk etc. Prompts were designed to identify at-risk students, to show key predictors of success based on data available, as well as compare quality cross generations. Outputs were evaluated in terms of predictive accuracy, interpretability and applicability for decision making processes in higher education. Obtaining reliable information about adding more data into the dataset for more accurate forecasting was also considered. The paper shows that prompt-based AI can generate actionable insights from large datasets from higher education with no extensive coding or specialized technical expertise. Some AI platforms emphasized quantitative precision, whereas others highlighted qualitative explanations and contextual risk factors, illustrating the complementary strengths of different approaches. Cohort-level analysis revealed meaningful trends across all the generations of students that were analyzed, including fluctuation in graduation rates and performance clusters linked to curriculum changes. For sure, the forecasting accuracy is different across different tools, but consistent patterns emerged regarding critical early courses, as well as the important engagement indicators. This study contributes to the growing body of research on AI in higher education by demonstrating a systematic comparison of multiple prompt-based tools on the same dataset. It highlights both the opportunities and limitations of natural-language AI for predictive analytics in higher education, emphasizing the balance between performance, interpretability, and ease of use. The results suggest that combining predictive accuracy with transparent explanations can support more informed interventions, enhance program evaluation, and ultimately improve student outcomes. Furthermore, the study anticipates that different AI tools will not only vary in predictive strength but also offer distinct recommendations for improving forecasting accuracy. These insights are expected to inform future methodological choices and guide the design of more effective, adaptive educational analytics frameworks.

# Learning Analytics and Predictive Modeling: Enhancing Student Success through Data-Driven Insights

## Authors

* Samuel Abiodun Oyedotun   Wellspring University   Author
* Otega Prosper Ejenarhome   Delta State University   Author
* Godfrey Perfectson Oise   Department of Computing, Wellspring University, Edo State   Author

## DOI:

 <https://doi.org/10.70882/josrar.2025.v2i3.77>

## Keywords:

 Academic Performance Prediction, Explainable AI (SHAP), Learning Analytics, Predictive Modeling, Student Engagement

## Abstract

In the evolving landscape of data-informed education, predictive modeling has become a powerful tool for identifying students at risk of academic failure or withdrawal. This study investigates the use of learning analytics techniques to predict student outcomes using the Open University Learning Analytics Dataset (OULAD), a comprehensive, publicly available dataset that includes demographic profiles, continuous assessment records, and detailed interaction logs from a virtual learning environment (VLE). By integrating and preprocessing these data sources, the authors developed a comprehensive set of behavioral and temporal features, with particular focus on total click activity, which acts as a proxy for student engagement. The prediction task was framed as a binary classification problem: distinguishing students who completed a course (pass or distinction) from those who failed or withdrew. Although the specific classification algorithm is not explicitly identified, the trained model achieved a classification accuracy of 71% and an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC) of 0.79, indicating a reasonably high level of discriminative ability. A key strength of the study is its use of SHAP (Shapley Additive Explanations) values to interpret the model’s output, offering transparency into how individual features influenced prediction results. The analysis showed that engagement-related features, especially VLE click counts, had the greatest predictive power, while demographic variables such as gender and age contributed little, suggesting a reduced risk of bias from protected attributes. These findings underscore the practical value of interpretable predictive models in supporting early warning systems and learner support strategies in higher education. Additionally, the study addresses important ethical considerations by emphasizing fairness, privacy, and the need for explainable AI. While some methodological limitations remain, such as the lack of algorithm disclosure and validation details, the research provides valuable insights into designing transparent, ethical, and actionable learning analytics tools.

args.summary: This research article, published in the Journal of Science Research and Reviews (JOSRAR) on July 10, 2025, investigates the use of learning analytics and predictive modeling to predict student academic outcomes using the Open University Learning Analytics Dataset (OULAD). The authors—Samuel Abiodun Oyedotun, Otega Prosper Ejenarhome, and Godfrey Perfectson Oise—developed behavioral and temporal features focusing on VLE click activity as a proxy for student engagement. The binary classification task (completion vs. fail/withdraw) achieved 71% accuracy and a ROC-AUC of 0.79. Key findings include: (1) engagement-related features (especially VLE click counts) had the greatest predictive power, (2) demographic variables (gender, age) contributed little, suggesting reduced bias risk, and (3) SHAP (Shapley Additive Explanations) values were used for model interpretability. The study emphasizes the practical value of interpretable predictive models for early warning systems in higher education and addresses ethical considerations including fairness, privacy, and explainable AI. The specific classification algorithm is not disclosed, and validation details are limited.

# Using AI to predict student success in higher education

##### [Denisa Gándara](http://www.denisagandara.com/) and [Denisa Gándara headshot](http://www.denisagandara.com/) [Denisa Gándara](http://www.denisagandara.com/) Associate Professor, Department of Educational Leadership and Policy - The University of Texas at Austin Hadis Anahideh hadis anahideh headshot Hadis Anahideh Assistant Professor - University of Illinois Chicago

##### More On

[Education Access & Equity](https://www.brookings.edu/topics/education-access-and-equity/) [Education Policy](https://www.brookings.edu/topics/education-policy/) [Education Technology](https://www.brookings.edu/topics/education-technology/) [Higher Education](https://www.brookings.edu/topics/higher-education-2/) [K-12 Education](https://www.brookings.edu/topics/k-12-education/)

As AI tools become increasingly [accessible](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3387/14/6/127), higher education [leaders](https://www.educause.edu/ecar/research-publications/2024/2024-educause-ai-landscape-study/introduction-and-key-findings) are rapidly adopting strategies and practices aimed at integrating these technologies into college operations. One of the most common uses of AI in higher education is [student success prediction](https://www.mdpi.com/2504-2289/8/12/187). Prediction algorithms use data, such as students’ [demographics](https://www.civitaslearning.com/), [student ID swipes](https://www.othot.com/blog/advanced-analytics-prompt-new-paradigm-student-success), [prior academic achievements](https://eab.com/resources/blog/student-success-blog/the-promises-and-perils-of-student-success-predictive-modeling/), and [financial need](https://ocelot.ai/articles/how-to-enhance-the-student-experience/), to project whether a student will be successful if admitted and enrolled. These tools may also help identify specific challenges faced by students, enabling the institution to intervene with additional supports. Predictions from these models can inform decisions across a range of areas—from [financial aid disbursement](https://www.highereddive.com/news/colleges-enrollment-algorithms-aid-students/692601/) to targeted [outreach](https://www.civitaslearning.com/blog/using-predicitve-analytics-to-support-college-students/) to students in need of support.

AI implementation in higher education brings critical ethical [concerns](https://hechingerreport.org/predictive-analytics-boosting-college-graduation-rates-also-invade-privacy-and-reinforce-racial-inequities/), particularly regarding transparency, privacy, and fairness. One central question is whether these algorithms are biased against certain groups of students, such as racial/ethnic minorities or students from rural backgrounds. In [our work](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/23328584241258741), we define bias in prediction algorithms as cases where algorithms produce incorrect predictions at disproportionately higher rates for racially minoritized groups compared to others. This happens because prediction algorithms identify patterns in historical data and propagate those patterns from historical inequalities into its future predictions, reinforcing those inequities.

Research from other social sectors suggests that models used to predict outcomes reflect this type of bias. For instance, in [criminal justice](https://us.macmillan.com/books/9781250074317/automatinginequality), predictive policing algorithms have disproportionately targeted minority communities, while in [health care](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aax2342), predictive models have sometimes underestimated the severity of health risks for non-white patients.

In education, similar risks of perpetuating social inequities arise. If racially minoritized students in the dataset have historically been less likely to complete college, the algorithm may predict that future students from the same racial groups—or of those with other features strongly correlated with race—are also less likely to complete college, even if those features are not explicitly about race. For example, socioeconomic status, school district, or neighborhood demographics may correlate with race, and these correlations might lead to biased predictions. While our study focused on race, such biases can occur based on other social characteristics associated with college student success, such as rural background, gender, and socioeconomic status.

[Our study](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/23328584241258741) aimed to answer two key questions: (1) To what extent are algorithms used to predict college student success racially biased? and (2) Can we effectively reduce bias using statistical techniques?

## Why race? The role of race in algorithmic predictions

Our study focused on race for several reasons. First, persistent disparities in educational outcomes across racial groups combined with differences in the spread of performance within groups can lead to biased predictions. When this occurs, historical underperformance can lead the algorithm to overgeneralize from group-level trends, failing to adequately capture the variation within racially minoritized groups. This dynamic contributes to the higher error rates observed in our results.

Second, key measures commonly used in predictive algorithms are statistically [associated](https://www.brookings.edu/articles/race-gaps-in-sat-scores-highlight-inequality-and-hinder-upward-mobility/) with race. For example, [research](https://psycnet.apa.org/doiLanding?doi=10.1037%2Fa0034376) has shown that college entrance exams like the SAT and ACT are more accurate predictors of performance for white and Asian students than for Black and Hispanic students. Unless specific actions are taken to account for these group-level differences, predictive models that are trained based on these scores may confound racial disparities with predictions of student performance.

Finally, factors that could be particularly important to the success of racially minoritized students—such as campus climate or family support—are often excluded from prediction models because related data are not collected, or they are not accessible to the entities designing prediction algorithms. The exclusion of such context-specific factors can further distort predictions for minoritized groups, compromising fairness and accuracy.

## Evidence of bias in student success predictions

To investigate racial bias in student success predictions, we trained several predictive models using common variables from the Educational Longitudinal Study of 2002 (ELS), a large, nationally representative dataset. Our models were trained to predict college success, defined as earning a bachelor’s degree within eight years of high school graduation for students who ever attended a four-year university. Our predictive variables included features commonly associated with student success, including students’ social characteristics (e.g., native language, family composition, and parental education), academic performance indicators (e.g., standardized test scores, first-year GPA, and college credits earned), and high school–level variables (e.g., urbanicity and whether the school was public or private).

When we compared the model predictions to actual outcomes, distinct patterns emerged across racial groups. First, Black and Hispanic students were more likely to be *incorrectly* predicted to fail when they actually graduated (known as false negatives). As shown in the figure (left panel), Black and Hispanic students were falsely predicted to fail 20% and 21% of the time, respectively, compared to 12% for white students and 6% for Asian students.

Meanwhile, white and Asian students were more likely to be incorrectly predicted to succeed (known as false positives). Among “failing” students who did not attain a bachelor’s degree within eight years, the predicted probability of success varied significantly by racial group (see right panel). Estimates of success were overly optimistic for white and Asian students (61% and 68% estimated probability of success, respectively). Conversely, the model estimates only a 32% probability of success for Hispanic students and 39% for Black students in similar circumstances.

## Mitigating bias: Pre-processing vs. in-processing techniques

The results underscore the need for fairness-aware predictive modeling to address algorithmic bias in college student success predictions. To that end, we evaluated four different bias-mitigation strategies, categorized into two main approaches: pre-processing and in-processing.  Pre-processing involves modifying the data before it is fed into the model to reduce inherent biases, such as reweighting the importance of underrepresented groups or altering feature distributions to achieve parity across groups. In contrast, in-processing incorporates fairness constraints directly into the training process.

Our findings revealed that while no single technique fully eliminates disparities, in-processing methods—those that adjust the model during training — tend to perform better than those that manipulate the data beforehand. For example, the baseline model inaccurately predicted failure for 21% of Hispanic students who actually succeeded. By applying in-processing techniques, this error rate was reduced to approximately 2%, demonstrating a significant improvement. However, the effectiveness of each method varied depending on the racial or ethnic group in question and the fairness criteria applied. These findings highlight the need for tailored approaches, as the most effective bias-mitigation strategy may depend on the specific context, data, and target population as well as institutional goals.

## Broader implications

As colleges and universities strive to better serve students through data-informed strategies, it is critical to design predictive models with an awareness of their potential social consequences. Models that ignore racial bias risk penalizing groups that have long faced educational disadvantages, such as those related to [school segregation](https://www.civilrightsproject.ucla.edu/research/k-12-education/integration-and-diversity/the-unfinished-battle-for-integration-in-a-multiracial-america-2013-from-brown-to-now/National-Segregation-041624-CORRECTED-for.pdf), [teacher bias](https://www.educationnext.org/power-of-teacher-expectations-racial-bias-hinders-student-attainment/), and [disparities in school funding](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.3102/00028312221079297). Recognizing these historical systemic patterns and incorporating fairness measures are crucial to reducing bias in model outcomes and promoting equitable student support.

Biases can have different implications depending on the use case. In admissions, for instance, biased models could unjustly limit access for racially minoritized students by predicting lower chances of success. When used to recommend courses or majors, they could fuel educational tracking along racial lines, limiting opportunities for students of color in advanced courses. However, when applied to identify students for support interventions, these models could lead to inefficient spending by sending resources to minoritized students who are inaccurately predicted to fail, while overlooking the needs of white and Asian students who may actually be more at risk of failure.

**In our paper, we offer a set of** recommendations to support the fair use of predictive analytics to enhance college student success. Among our recommendations are the following:

## Conclusion

As colleges and universities integrate AI into their strategies for supporting student success, it is essential to balance the potential benefits of these technologies with a commitment to fairness, transparency, and ethical responsibility. Predictive models, when designed and monitored thoughtfully, could help identify students who may benefit from additional support and institutional barriers to student success.

However, without careful attention to the historical biases that may shape data and algorithms, these tools can inadvertently reinforce educational inequities, such as by denying admission to qualified students or steering them into less rigorous courses or majors based on their social characteristics. Our findings underscore the importance of developing AI systems that are responsive to the needs of all students.

args.summary: This Brookings Institution article (April 17, 2025) by Denisa Gándara and Hadis Anahideh examines racial bias in AI-based predictive algorithms used for student success in higher education. The authors define bias as algorithms producing incorrect predictions at disproportionately higher rates for racially minoritized groups. Using data from the Educational Longitudinal Study of 2002 (ELS), they trained models to predict bachelor's degree completion within eight years and found significant racial disparities: Black and Hispanic students were falsely predicted to fail (false negatives) 20% and 21% of the time, compared to 12% for white and 6% for Asian students. Conversely, white and Asian students were more likely to be incorrectly predicted to succeed (false positives). The study evaluated bias-mitigation strategies, finding that "in-processing" techniques (adjusting the model during training) outperformed "pre-processing" methods (modifying data beforehand). For example, in-processing reduced false negative rates for Hispanic students from 21% to approximately 2%. The authors provide recommendations for fair use of predictive analytics, emphasizing the need for transparency, fairness-aware modeling, and recognition of historical systemic inequities in education.

--- SOURCE 7: China's AI Education Experiment - by Lily Ottinger ---
URL: https://www.chinatalk.media/p/chinas-ai-education-experiment

SUMMARY:
<summary>
# China's AI Education Experiment

The article explores China's ambitious government-led push to integrate artificial intelligence into its K-12 education system, driven by the Ministry of Education's (MOE) goal to universalize basic AI access in primary and secondary schools by 2030. The MOE's May 2025 white paper on "intelligentizing" education outlines four main use cases: **(1) teacher task reduction** (AI-assisted grading, lesson planning), **(2) improving rural schools** (digital education support, AI literacy lessons), **(3) analyzing student biometrics** (facial expression monitoring, attention tracking, mental health screening), and **(4) helping students with disabilities**.

## Key Motivations
The Party prioritizes AI in education because improving the education system is extremely popular with Chinese families. Chinese households spend an average of 17.1% of annual income on education (vs. 1-2% in US/Japan), and the poorest quartile devotes 56.8% of income. However, only 30.6% of China's population has ever attended high school, and roughly 40% of middle school graduates don't go on to high school. The system is fundamentally zero-sum — universities are overwhelmingly urban, and less than 5% of elite university students come from rural families despite 65% of children having rural hukou.

## Structural Challenges
Rural education faces severe resource depletion: elite schools systematically attract talent from periphery areas, leaving rural schools with teacher shortages (senior teachers are only 6.8% of all teachers in China vs. 26% in the US with 20+ years experience), oversized classrooms (56+ students), and severe funding constraints. Local governments bear ~85% of education spending, and poorer counties have less to spend. A 2025 study found 82% of rural children aged 6-36 months had at least one developmental delay.

## Implementation Barriers
- **Funding**: MOE white papers are unfunded mandates that signal priorities but provide no money. Schools are instructed to "strengthen overall planning of funds" but budgets are already stretched thin.
- **Device access**: Rural areas face a shortfall of 8.5 million computers. Historical scandals (schools forcing families to buy overpriced tablets) and concerns about screen time and addiction have hindered device distribution.
- **Private sector costs**: iFlytek's smart classroom software cost one school ¥1,744,000 (~US$254,000). Even the Bengbu city contract covering 875 schools worked out to roughly ¥800 per student per year.
- **Data privacy**: At least 63% of primary/secondary students have dealt with spam calls from data leaks. Student data protection relies on non-mandatory recommendations. Schools routinely pressure parents to sign expansive data agreements.
- **Teacher incentives**: Rural teachers' careers are centrally managed with forced transfers, reducing motivation to integrate AI. The "County-managed, school-hired" system is widely resented.

## Key Concerns
The article notes that while computer-assisted learning has shown some benefits, AI cannot address root causes of educational inequality — the gaokao system, hukou-based restrictions, centralization of resources, and early childhood developmental delays. The mental health surveillance use case is particularly worrying, as the structure of boarding schooling itself (with 47.3% of boarding students suffering from acute pessimism and 63.8% feeling lonely) is a major source of psychological harm. Meanwhile, wealthy urban students already enjoy AI-guided learning tools, potentially widening rather than narrowing the gap.
</summary>

# Summary of National AI Initiative Act Article (WashU Law)

This article from Washington University School of Law discusses the **National AI Initiative Act**, passed as part of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2021 (signed into law January 2021). The Act represents a coordinated federal strategy for U.S. leadership in AI development, governance, and risk management, with a focus on civil rights, security, and trustworthy AI systems.

## Key Framework Components:

1. **Advance U.S. Leadership in AI R&D**: Established the National AI Initiative Office within OSTP, funds AI research institutes, and supports international collaboration. Created the National AI Advisory Committee (NAIAC).

2. **Promote Trustworthy AI Systems**: Directs NIST to develop frameworks, standards, testbeds, and guidelines for ethical, transparent, and reliable AI systems. Includes standards for performance, safety, fairness, and oversight committees.

3. **Prepare the Workforce**: Encourages K-12 and higher education AI training, scholarships/fellowships for AI research, and public-private workforce development partnerships.

4. **Coordinate Federal AI Activities**: Creates interagency working groups and the National AI Initiative Office to oversee shared policies, reduce duplication, and report to Congress.

## Implementation:

- Federal agencies involved include DOD, NSA, DOE, NSF, and OSTP.
- Created the **National AI Research Resource (NAIRR)** Task Force, which released a final report calling for advanced computing resources, curated datasets, and user support for researchers, with strong data privacy and ethics controls.
- States have also passed their own AI regulations and formed alliances with industry and academia.

## Economic Impacts:

The Act has spurred investments in AI research, job growth, startup support, and cross-sector collaboration (healthcare, manufacturing, finance, law). Workforce training and grants level the playing field for small firms.

## Significance:

The Act serves as a model for future technology legislation in the U.S. and internationally, setting benchmarks for ethical, trustworthy AI and coordinated government approaches.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This USCC research working group paper analyzes China's open AI strategy and its implications for U.S.-China competition. It identifies two mutually reinforcing feedback loops: a digital loop (open model diffusion driving community iteration and adoption) and a physical loop (AI deployment across China's manufacturing base generating real-world data that feeds back into model improvement). Key findings include: (1) China's open-source approach has resulted in rapid global uptake—Alibaba's Qwen models account for the largest ecosystem on Hugging Face with over 100,000 derivatives; (2) Chinese labs have narrowed performance gaps with top Western models despite compute constraints, with DeepSeek R1 and subsequent models approaching frontier performance; (3) Chinese models cost a fraction of U.S. prices—Kimi K2.5 costs four times less than OpenAI's GPT-5.2 while achieving similar benchmark scores; (4) Beijing has built institutional infrastructure designating data as a formal factor of production and permitting enterprises to carry data assets on their balance sheets; (5) The shift toward small, specialized models for industrial deployment plays to China's strengths, as open ecosystems produce these most efficiently. The paper argues that U.S. export controls targeting advanced semiconductors for frontier training do not adequately address the physical loop of deployment-driven data creation, meaning China may build AI advantages rooted in its physical economy that compound independently of access to cutting-edge hardware. Beijing's AI+ Initiative, robotics industrial policy, and draft 15th Five-Year Plan all reflect a strategy organized around deployed AI rather than frontier scale.
</summary>

China has opted to go all in on an open-source approach to AI. Southeast Asia (Indonesia, Malaysia, Philippines, Thailand, Vietnam) and LATAM/Sub-Saharan Africa (Mexico, Argentina, Chile, Colombia, Nigeria) focus on building core capacity.

URL: https://ised-isde.canada.ca/site/ised/en/canadas-national-artificial-intelligence-strategy-ai-all

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## Canada's National Artificial Intelligence Strategy: AI for All

This document outlines Canada's new national AI strategy, released in 2025-2026, which aims to build a responsible, safe, and sovereign AI industry that serves all Canadians. The strategy is built on three core values: **Trust, Opportunity, and Sovereignty**, connected through **Adoption**.

### Key Context & Current State of AI in Canada
- Canada's digital sector employs ~800,000 workers and contributes $140B+ to GDP, with 150,000 jobs directly linked to AI.
- Over 3,500 Canadian firms are developing AI, raising $37B+ in venture capital.
- Only **12% of Canadian businesses** use AI (mid-2024 to mid-2025), versus Nordic leaders (29-42%), Germany (26%), and France (18%).
- Canada ranked **44th of 47 countries** on AI training/literacy and 42nd of 47 on trust in AI systems.
- Only 24% of Canadians have received any AI training.
- Generative AI alone could add $187B annually to the Canadian economy by 2030.

### The Six Pillars of the Strategy

**Pillar 1: Protecting Canadians and Safeguarding Democracy**
- Updating privacy and online safety laws to combat deepfakes, algorithmic bias, and online harms.
- Establishing a Canadian AI Safety Institute and introducing mandatory transparency measures for AI systems.
- Strengthening cybersecurity for critical infrastructure.

**Pillar 2: Empowering Canadians**
- Building an AI-skilled nation through foundational literacy in schools, post-secondary, and workforce training.
- Goal: Create over 250,000 new AI-relevant jobs by 2031.
- Supporting Indigenous leadership in AI, ensuring cultural and linguistic protection.
- Ensuring AI reflects Canadian identity, French language, and inclusion of diverse communities.

**Pillar 3: Powering AI Adoption for Shared Prosperity**
- Target: **60% of Canadian businesses (especially SMEs) adopting AI by 2034**.
- Launching AI "missions" starting with healthcare (e.g., CHARTWatch system at St. Michael's Hospital reduced unexpected deaths by 26%).
- Transforming public service delivery with AI, maintaining human-in-the-loop oversight.
- Supporting sector-specific applications in agriculture (e.g., Croptimistic, Vivid Machines, EarthDaily), healthcare, energy, manufacturing, and mining.

**Pillar 4: Building the Canadian Sovereign AI Foundation**
- Development of sovereign compute infrastructure: Canada needs 5.5 GW of AI compute by 2030.
- Leveraging Canada's clean grid (83% renewable/low-emission) and cold climate for sustainable data centres.
- Unlocking data as a strategic national asset, starting with healthcare data (VITAL platform).
- "Build-partner-buy" approach to infrastructure, ensuring Canadian control and governance.

**Pillar 5: Scaling Canadian Champions**
- Unlocking growth capital and using government as a strategic anchor customer for Canadian AI companies.

**Pillar 6: Building Trusted Partnerships and Global Alliances**
- Strengthening AI partnerships with like-minded democracies (G7, etc.).
- Canada has signed 20 new economic/defence partnerships in the past year (11 explicitly advancing AI cooperation).
- Secured nearly $100B in foreign investment commitments.

### Priority Sectors
Five sectors where Canada will concentrate investment: healthcare, energy, agriculture, manufacturing, and natural resources/mining, with dual-use applications aligned with national security.

### Notable Quotes
- **François-Philippe Champagne (Minister):** "Canadians want safe, reliable, and sovereign AI. They want the best tools to build a prosperous future guided by our values. That is our plan. This is Canada's AI for All moment. Let's seize it."
- The strategy states: "Trust is the north star of this strategy. Prosperity and sovereignty in this era belong to nations that can leverage trust to adopt, build, and govern AI on their own terms."
- "AI must also work for all Canadians, not the other way around."

### Key Statistics
- 11,000+ submissions received during national consultation from 28-member AI Strategy Task Force.
- Canadian AI employs 150,000 people across 3,500+ companies.
- 78% of non-adopting firms say they don't see how AI benefits their goods/services.
- Data centres using renewable energy reduce operating emissions by up to 90%.
- 80% of Canadian workers in a 7-country OECD survey said AI improved their performance.
- Croptimistic's AI soil mapping and EarthDaily's invasive species detection can increase crop yield and quality by up to 50%.
- Amii trains 125,000+ students annually in AI and has reached 1,000+ K-12 teachers across 400+ schools.
- CHARTWatch AI system: 26% drop in unexpected patient deaths after implementation.
- Maya HTT: 200+ industrial AI deployments increasing production line throughput by 17% average, creating/maintaining 1,000+ jobs.
</summary>

Let's seize it." — Minister, "Trust is the north star of this strategy. I was skipping most of my lectures and classes at University, I was just doing competitions." - Alexander Guschin, "When you solve one dozen of competitions, it's much easier to solve the next dozen." - Alexander Guschin, "I found out that when you teach, you need to figure it out, you need to understand it if you want to come and explain people... the best way to learn something is to teach." - Alexander Guschin, "I'm designing a problem for the whole semester so they need to build a classifier... we are building a platform where these classifiers can get data from and then we'll have them competing with each other." - Alexander Guschin, "There are some things that almost all competition winners do: they explore data carefully, they try to do EDA, they try to understand the domain, and build a careful validation.
