## Fully Comprehensive Findings

### 1. University AI Programs and Frameworks

#### 1.1 United States Undergraduate AI Programs

**Carnegie Mellon University (CMU):**
- CMU offers a Bachelor of Science in Artificial Intelligence program through the School of Computer Science. [6]
- In 2018, CMU's School of Computer Science offered the nation's first bachelor's degree in AI. [7]
- U.S. News and World Report ranks CMU No. 1 in artificial intelligence (2025 ranking). [7]
- CMU offers over 25 programs at all levels surrounding AI. [7]
- For the Class of 2025, six months after graduation, 91% were employed or in grad school, with an average salary of $160,688. [6]
- Recent employers include Amazon, Google, Jane Street, and NVIDIA. [6]
- The curriculum emphasizes building AI systems that reason, think through human problems, and are used for ethical and social good. [6]
- CMU's School of Computer Science (SCS) created the world's first machine learning academic department in 2006. [10]
- Graduate programs: MS in AIE, MSAII, MSCV, MIIS, MSML, AIM (AI Systems Management), MSR. [10]

**Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT):**
- MIT offers a Bachelor of Science in AI and Decision Making, covering algorithms, reasoning, and computational cognitive science. [8]
- MIT's Schwarzman College of Computing was launched in 2019 with a $350M gift (part of $1B commitment), 50 new faculty positions, aims to bring computing/AI to all fields, emphasizes responsible AI and U.S. global competitiveness. [12]
- MIT's president described this as an effort to reshape MIT for the AI era, ensuring computing "reshapes our world… for the good of all." [12]
- MIT CSAIL is one of the leading AI research labs globally.

**Stanford University:**
- Stanford offers a Symbolics Systems major with an AI concentration; located in Silicon Valley, offering proximity to tech employers. [8]
- Stanford is "right in Silicon Valley's backyard, giving students the opportunity to rub elbows with potential employers, mentors, and thought leaders pioneering the field." [8]
- Stanford's Institute for Human-Centered AI (HAI) was launched in 2019, is an interdisciplinary institute across all 7 Stanford schools, co-directed by John Etchemendy and Fei-Fei Li, focuses on AI research/education/policy guided by human values. [12]
- Stanford HAI stresses a "diversity of thought" and close collaboration between technologists and social scientists. [12]
- Stanford offers MS CS with AI specialization (on-campus, 1.5 years) and Online MS CS – AI. Home to the Stanford Artificial Intelligence Lab (SAIL) since 1963. Some graduates earn $331k+ per annum. [10]

**University of Pennsylvania:**
- UPenn was the first Ivy League school to offer an AI undergraduate degree, with the first cohort admitted in fall 2024. [8][14]
- The BSE in AI curriculum provides the mathematical and algorithmic foundations of AI techniques, along with hands-on experience in programming as well as using AI tools and foundation models. [7]
- The AI Project component requires AI development with at least 30% of grade from a term project. [7]
- Students learn about intelligence from a cognitive science perspective, and develop a sense of the issues (and solutions) required to responsibly develop AI to benefit society. [7]
- BSE in AI students cannot dual-major in CSCI, NETS, or SSE but may pursue dual-degree programs in the College of Arts and Sciences. [7]

**UC San Diego:**
- Ranked #1 in the top 25 AI bachelor's programs in the US for 2026 (AI, BS, $85,836 resident tuition). [8]
- Jacobs School of Engineering offers AI/ML courses for Engineering majors, including robotics, deep learning, and data mining. [8]

**Georgia Institute of Technology:**
- Ranked #2 in top 25 AI bachelor's programs (CS BS with AI/ML Threads, $42,048 resident). [8]
- Hosts NSF AI Institute for Advances in Optimization (AI4OPT). [10]
- Offers on-campus MSCS and highly acclaimed Online MSCS (OMSCS) with AI, ML, and robotics specializations. Received $20M NSF grant for Nexus supercomputer. [10]

**UC Berkeley:**
- Ranked #3 in top 25 AI bachelor's programs (CS BA/BS with AI/ML Track, $54,408 resident). [8]
- Home to the Berkeley Artificial Intelligence Research Lab (BAIR). [10]
- Offers MSCS (research-focused, MS/PhD pathway) and MEng (professional). [10]

**UT Austin:**
- Ranked #4 (CS BS with AI/ML Focus, $47,064 resident). [8]
- Austin has become "an outpost of Silicon Valley" - many are calling it "Silicon Hills." [8]

**Other Notable US Programs:**
- Virginia Tech (#5, CS BS with AI/ML Focus, $55,736 resident). [8]
- Harvard's Kempner Institute (2022): $500M donation from Chan Zuckerberg Initiative, focuses on intersection of neuroscience and AI, 10 new faculty positions, 15-year research program. [12]
- USC's Frontiers of Computing (2023): $1B+ initiative, new School of Advanced Computing, AI literacy for all students, includes Institute on Ethics & Trust in Computing. [12]
- Johns Hopkins AI-X Foundry (2023): 80 new faculty slots, 30 cross-disciplinary Bloomberg Distinguished Professors, spans neuroscience to climate resilience. [12]
- Cornell offers research-focused MS in CS (fully funded with stipend) and self-funded one-year MEng in CS with AI concentration. Supports AI for Sustainability (AI4S) and digital agriculture initiatives. [10]
- University of Washington's Professional Master's Programs (PMPs) designed for working professionals, offers MS in AI and ML for Engineering (online). Deep partnerships with Amazon and NVIDIA. Home to Allen Institute for AI (AI2). [10]
- University of Maryland's Artificial Intelligence Interdisciplinary Institute (AIM) launched in spring 2025, awarded $85,000 in 2025-26 Course Development Grants to support seven proposals for new AI-focused courses. UMD and its partners plan to invest over $100 million in the institute over the next 10 years. [5]

**US News Top 10 Undergraduate AI Programs (2026):** [13]
1. Carnegie Mellon University
2. Massachusetts Institute of Technology
3. Stanford University
4. University of California, Berkeley
5. Georgia Institute of Technology
6. University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign
7. The University of Texas--Austin
8. University of Washington
9. Cornell University
10. California Institute of Technology

**National Landscape of AI Degrees in the US (2025 AI Degree Report):** [6]
- 304 universities now offer AI/ML degrees, with 310 master's programs and 193 bachelor's programs (503 total).
- Master's programs grew 167% from 2022 (116 programs) to 2025 (310 programs), adding 64.7 new programs per year on average.
- Bachelor's programs more than doubled from 90 programs in 2024 to 193 in 2025 (114.4% growth).
- 53% of programs are standalone AI degrees, 47% are AI concentrations/tracks within existing degrees.
- The South leads with 38.4% of all AI degrees (193 programs at 113 schools), driven by Texas, Florida, and North Carolina.
- Texas is the national leader with 21 schools offering 39 AI programs (31 master's, 8 bachelor's).
- Florida saw explosive growth from 3 programs in 2022 to 30 in 2025 (900% growth).
- 47% of AI degree-offering universities are R1 institutions; 16% are R2.
- Only 5% of HBCUs (5 schools) offer AI degrees, highlighting a significant equity gap.
- Business schools saw explosive growth from 5 AI programs in 2022 to 68 in 2025 (1,260% increase), mostly MBA in AI programs.
- 51% of master's programs and 16% of bachelor's programs are offered online.
- Online master's programs grew 276% from 2022 (42 programs) to 2025 (158 programs).
- The report recommends universities align AI programs with local industries (e.g., Michigan's robotics and ag-tech) to attract funding and provide employment pipelines.

**Colleges Offering Formal AI Majors (as of August 2026):** [9]
Bentley University, Carnegie Mellon University, MIT, University of Pennsylvania, UC San Diego, Dakota State University, Drake University, Ferris State University, Illinois Institute of Technology, Indiana University-Bloomington, Keiser University, Long Island University, Purdue University (BS and BA options), University of South Florida (starting fall 2025), USC (starting fall 2026), Northwestern University, and Kennesaw State University.

**Key Insight:** "Of the top 10 AI undergraduate programs in the U.S., only MIT and Carnegie Mellon offer formal AI majors. The rest prepare students through computer science programs with tracks, threads, concentrations, or minors to support specialization in AI." [9] "In most cases, computer science remains the more flexible degree. AI majors can be excellent for students with a strong interest in machine learning and intelligent systems, but students should evaluate long-term adaptability and program structure carefully." [9]

**Adelphi University:** Offers a Bachelor of Science in Artificial Intelligence through its College of Arts & Sciences, located in Garden City, New York. The program is STEM-designated, allowing eligible international students to extend their OPT to 36 months. Features small classes of fewer than 25 students, hands-on learning with case studies, and a 3-credit internship option. [10]

#### 1.2 China University AI Programs

**Tsinghua University:**
- Tsinghua University holds the top position in Asia for AI and ranks among the top three globally for Computer Science. [12]
- Tsinghua announced it will establish a new undergraduate school focused on developing talent in artificial intelligence (AI). The university plans to enroll about 150 students in the new school in 2025. [11]
- The new school will emphasize AI's role in education and research, integrating AI with multiple disciplines, and aims to develop a new model for AI-driven education while training students with strong AI literacy, technical expertise, and innovative capabilities. [11]
- Tsinghua has already introduced 117 pilot courses and 147 classes incorporating AI-driven teaching methods, and has developed tools such as intelligent teaching assistants, lesson-planning aids, and automated grading systems. [11]
- The Institute for AI Industry Research (AIR) at Tsinghua University was founded in 2020 by Academician Zhang Yaqin. [16]
- Tsinghua alumni have founded over 1,000 companies, including a dozen unicorns. Notable alumni include Meituan CEO Wang Xing, and China's presidents Xi Jinping and Hu Jintao. About one-third of 2022 undergraduates entered IT/software. [14]
- Tsinghua's "grind culture" is intense: Ph.D. student Felix Gan lives a "996" routine (8 a.m. to 9 p.m., 7 days a week). Students routinely study 7-8 hours daily, with some writing multiple theses. [14]
- In 2024, only ~0.05% of Gaokao test-takers (roughly 1 in 2,000) made it into Tsinghua or Peking University. [14]
- Students use AI tools to accelerate learning (AI tripled one Ph.D. student's research speed), with professors encouraging use while requiring manual validation of final work. [14]
- Preferred employers include Huawei, ByteDance, Tencent, Alibaba, and AI startups. [14]
- "As China is increasingly recognized as sourcing the world's leading AI talent, the name recognition has even more significance than it used to," said Zak Dychtwald, founder of the Young China Group. [14]
- "This is not purely a top-down process — student preferences, labor market signals, and institutional incentives are reinforcing each other, especially in AI," said Zhao Litao, senior research fellow at NUS. [14]

**Peking University:**
- Strong in AI theory, data science, AI ethics, interdisciplinary research. [15]
- Announced plans to expand undergraduate intake by around 150 spots in 2025, with focus on national strategic priorities. [13]
- Undergraduate admission requires HSK Level 6 (>200, writing >65) for Chinese-taught or TOEFL iBT >75 for English-taught, age 17-23. [12]

**Shanghai Jiao Tong University:**
- Engineering-based AI, robotics, machine learning, intelligent systems. [15]
- Shanghai Jiao Tong University's AI research center collaborates extensively with various technology companies to develop innovative solutions. [12]
- Expanding in AI, renewable energy, and integrated circuits. [13]

**Zhejiang University:**
- Strong AI research, links with Alibaba, cloud computing, smart cities. [15]
- Most active Chinese institution in industry-academia AI collaboration papers (321 papers at AAAI and IJCAI 2010-2023). [17]

**Other Top Chinese AI Universities:** [15]
- **Nanjing University** – Machine learning, NLP, cognitive science.
- **University of Science and Technology of China (USTC)** – Research-focused, links with Chinese Academy of Sciences, automation, robotics.
- **Beihang University** – Aerospace AI, UAVs, computer vision, intelligent control.
- **Harbin Institute of Technology (HIT)** – Engineering AI, robotics, pattern recognition, intelligent control.
- **Xidian University** – AI security, signal processing, cybersecurity, biometric systems.
- **Fudan University** – Data science, medical AI, NLP, AI ethics. Fudan University plans to introduce at least 100 AI-related courses in the 2024-25 academic year. [12]

**Key Developments:**
- Several of China's top universities (Tsinghua, Peking, Renmin) have announced plans to expand undergraduate enrollment in 2025, with a sharp focus on national strategic priorities and cutting-edge technologies, particularly AI. [13]
- Both Tsinghua and Peking universities announced plans to expand their undergraduate intake by around 150 undergraduate spots each. [13]
- Renmin University will add over 100 places in AI and related fields. [13]
- The 2025 government work report emphasizes the importance of continuously promoting the 'AI Plus' initiative, aiming to better integrate digital technology with manufacturing and market strengths. [13]
- China in January issued its first national action plan to build a 'strong education nation' by 2035, to help coordinate its education development, improve efficiency in innovation and build a 'strong country.' [13]
- There is a clear trend among leading Chinese universities to actively expand their AI-related academic programs and increase student enrollment. [12]
- Chinese universities actively encourage students to use more AI, contrasting with Western approaches. [9]
- China has built a large AI education and research system. Many universities work with research labs, technology firms, and local government projects. [15]

#### 1.3 AI+X Interdisciplinary Programs

**University of Maryland - Course Development Grants (2025-26):** [5]
UMD's AIM awarded $85,000 in grants for seven new AI courses including:
- "AI Literacy for Community Empowerment" ($25,000 grant) - students collaborate with libraries and nonprofits to promote AI literacy in Maryland communities
- "Advancing Computational Expertise in Neuroscience and Psychology" - A 400-level computational neuroscience course using Python and machine learning
- "Fundamentals of AI-Powered Assistive Technologies" - A 300-level kinesiology course on AI in assistive technologies for disabilities
- "AI and Music—History and Practice" - Exploring AI's intersection with music from historical methods to generative AI
- "Discourse Matters: AI and Humanities Analytics Applications for Japanese Texts"
- "Artificial Intelligence Otherwise" - A 300-level course examining AI through science fiction and social justice
- "AI and the Art of Visual Storytelling" - Integrating AI tools into creative design workflows

**AI + Legal Technology:** [11]
- Legal technology degrees integrating AI emphasize machine learning for contract analysis, predictive analytics, and risk assessment, with 68% of programs updated since 2024 to reflect these trends.
- Graduates with AI-focused legal degrees see a 22% higher employment rate in tech-savvy law firms and compliance roles compared to traditional law graduates as of early 2026 data.
- By 2024, 63% of lawyers reported using AI for legal work, highlighting the demand for graduates skilled in both law and AI technology.
- The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics forecasts a 26% growth in employment for computer and information research scientists from 2023 to 2033.

**Tsinghua's AI+X Integration:** [11]
Tsinghua's new undergraduate school will emphasize AI's role in education and research, integrating AI with multiple disciplines. The university has already introduced 117 pilot courses and 147 classes incorporating AI-driven teaching methods, and has developed tools such as intelligent teaching assistants, lesson-planning aids, and automated grading systems.

**General AI+X Trends:**
- "To create AI systems that truly serve humanity, we need experts from all fields, not just computer science, actively involved in their development." — NYU professor Rumi Chunara. [9]
- A December 2025 New York Times article underscores that colleges nationwide are rapidly expanding AI-driven programs as student demand surges and employers seek graduates with both technical fluency and interdisciplinary training. [9]
- AI degree programs within a School or College of Business went from 5 programs to 68 programs, a 1,260% increase. [6]

#### 1.4 AI Research Institutes and Labs

**US-Based:**
- **MIT CSAIL** - One of the leading AI research labs globally.
- **Stanford HAI** (Institute for Human-Centered AI, 2019) - Interdisciplinary institute across all 7 Stanford schools. [12]
- **Stanford SAIL** (Stanford Artificial Intelligence Lab, since 1963) - Home to Stanford's AI research. [10]
- **UC Berkeley BAIR** (Berkeley Artificial Intelligence Research Lab). [10]
- **University of Washington - Allen Institute for AI (AI2)**. [10]
- **NSF National AI Research Institutes** - 29 institutes connecting over 500 funded and collaborative institutions across the U.S. and around the world. Launched in 2020, funded at about $20 million each over five years. These represent one of the biggest public-private investments to date in AI R&D. [14] By 2024, four funding cohorts had created 27 different institutes located across more than 40 states, with total funding allocation approaching US$500 million. [11]

**China-Based:**
- **Tsinghua AIR** (Institute for AI Industry Research) - Founded in 2020 by Academician Zhang Yaqin. Focuses on AI+IoT, AI+Transportation, AI+Healthcare, BDI Lab, DISCOVER Lab. [16][20]
- **Tsinghua (AIR) - BAAI Health Computing Joint Research Center** (August 2021). [20]
- **Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence (BAAI)** - Partner with Tsinghua AIR. [20]

**European:**
- **UK £300M AI Research Resource** with supercomputers at Cambridge and Bristol. [12]
- **Oxford's Schwarzman Centre/Ethics in AI Institute** (£150M gift). [12]
- **France's Four Interdisciplinary Institutes of AI (3IA)** with €20-30M each; national strategy 2nd phase pledged €2.2B more with emphasis on "trusted AI." [12]
- **Germany's Cyber Valley** - €165M initial funding, links University of Tübingen, University of Stuttgart, Max Planck Institutes, and companies like Amazon/Bosch/Daimler. [12]
- **Swiss National AI Institute (SNAI) (2023)** - Joint ETH Zurich/EPFL initiative, ~CHF 20M initial government backing. [12]

**Canadian:**
- **Mila, Vector Institute, Amii** (over C$200M combined) established Canada as a deep learning powerhouse. [12]
- Amii trains 125,000+ students annually in AI and has reached 1,000+ K-12 teachers across 400+ schools. [4]

---

### 2. Government Policies and Initiatives

#### 2.1 China's "New Generation Artificial Intelligence Development Plan" (2017)

**Core Framework:** [1][2][3][4]
China's "New Generation Artificial Intelligence Development Plan" (AIDP) was issued by China's State Council on July 20, 2017, setting out China's top-level blueprint for AI development. The plan establishes China's goal to become a global AI innovation center by 2030.

**Three-Phase Strategic Goals:**
- **By 2020**: AI industry core >150B RMB, related >1T RMB. Make China's AI industry in-line with competitors.
- **By 2025**: AI core >400B RMB, related >5T RMB. Reach world-leading in some AI fields.
- **By 2030**: AI core >1T RMB, related >10T RMB. China's AI theories, technologies, and applications should achieve world-leading levels, making China the world's primary AI innovation center. [1][2][3]

**Key Focus Areas:**
- Building AI innovation systems, fostering smart economy, developing key technologies (knowledge computing, cross-media reasoning, swarm intelligence, hybrid intelligence, autonomous systems, VR, AI chips, NLP), establishing basic support platforms, and training high-end AI talent. [1]
- The plan involves initiatives and goals for R&D, industrialization, talent development, education and skills acquisition, standard setting and regulations, ethical norms, and security. [2]
- AI is framed as "a strategic technology that will lead in the future." [1]

**China's Position at Launch:**
- China ranked second globally in published scientific papers and patents. Voice and visual recognition technologies were world-leading. However, gaps remained in basic theory, core algorithms, high-end chips, and cutting-edge talent compared to developed countries. [3]

**Implementation Status:**
- The initiative is active, involves multiple ministries, and includes stakeholder consultation mechanisms. [2]
- The plan was issued to all provincial governments, State Council ministries, and directly controlled institutions for implementation. [3]

**2025 Updates:**
- On July 26, 2025, China announced its "Action Plan for Global Artificial Intelligence (AI) Governance," building on President Xi Jinping's October 2023 Global AI Governance Initiative. [5]
- The plan proposes a 13-point roadmap for global AI coordination, with practical steps to implement the 2023 Global AI Governance Initiative. [5]
- China proposed establishing a global AI cooperation organization, an international body designed to foster international collaboration on AI development and regulation, potentially headquartered in Shanghai. [5]
- Since 2017, China has implemented various AI-related regulations including the Data Security Law, Cybersecurity Law, Personal Information Protection Law, and measures targeting AI algorithms and generative AI services. [5]
- The 2025 government work report emphasizes promoting the "AI Plus" initiative to integrate digital technology with manufacturing. [13]

#### 2.2 China's Ministry of Education Policies on AI Education

**K-12 AI Education Policies:**
- In May 2025, the Ministry of Education issued Guidelines for AI education in primary and secondary schools, dividing curriculum by level: primary (imagination and basic cognition), junior high (technical principles), and senior high (systematic thinking and innovation). [6]
- AI literacy changed from "nice to have" to "must have" for K-12 teachers, principals and Party secretaries. [6]
- The MOE's goal: universalize basic AI access in primary and secondary schools by 2030. [7][8]
- A July 28, 2026 notice from the MOE titled "Notice of the Office of the Ministry of Education on Strengthening Artificial Intelligence Education in Primary and Secondary Schools" outlines China's efforts to expand AI education, aiming to make AI education coursework "basically universal" at the K-12 level in China by 2030. [8]
- The notice takes a tiered approach: younger students experience AI in class, while high school students complete creative projects using advanced AI tools. [8]
- The notice cites the need to implement the spirit of the 20th Party Congress, Xi Jinping's speech at the Nationwide Education Conference, and to build a talent reserve for developing "new quality productive forces" (新质生产力). [8]
- Four overall requirements: (1) Persist in cultivating moral people and maintaining correct direction; (2) Persist in taking a people-centered approach and promoting all-round development; (3) Persist in stimulating interest and encouraging exploration; (4) Persist in doing overall planning and advancing steadily. [8]

**Higher Education AI Policies:**
- At the March 2025 Two Sessions, Education Minister Huai Jinpeng called for raising skills in emerging fields. [6]
- Chinese universities actively encourage students to use more AI, not less. [9]
- The MOE white papers are described as "unfunded mandates" that signal priorities but provide no money. [7]

**Implementation Challenges:** [7]
- Local governments bear approximately 85% of public education spending; the central government's ~15% share is delivered primarily through transfer payments.
- Rural areas face a shortfall of 8.5 million computers.
- Only 30.6% of China's population has ever attended high school, which Stanford professor Scott Rozelle notes "is lower than South Africa, lower than Turkey and lower than Mexico."
- The poorest quartile of families in China devotes a staggering 56.8% of income to education.
- Research on China's boarding schools found that 47.3% of boarding school children suffered from acute pessimism, 63.8% said that they felt lonely, 17.6% suffered from depression, and 8.4% exhibited suicidal tendencies.

#### 2.3 US National AI Initiative Act and NSF AI Research Institutes

**National AI Initiative Act (2021):** [13]
- Passed as part of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2021 (signed into law January 2021).
- Represents a coordinated federal strategy for U.S. leadership in AI development, governance, and risk management.
- **Key Framework Components:**
  1. Advance U.S. Leadership in AI R&D: Established the National AI Initiative Office within OSTP, funds AI research institutes, and supports international collaboration. Created the National AI Advisory Committee (NAIAC).
  2. Promote Trustworthy AI Systems: Directs NIST to develop frameworks, standards, testbeds, and guidelines for ethical, transparent, and reliable AI systems.
  3. Prepare the Workforce: Encourages K-12 and higher education AI training, scholarships/fellowships for AI research, and public-private workforce development partnerships.
  4. Coordinate Federal AI Activities: Creates interagency working groups and the National AI Initiative Office.
- Created the National AI Research Resource (NAIRR) Task Force, which released a final report calling for advanced computing resources, curated datasets, and user support for researchers.
- The Act has spurred investments in AI research, job growth, startup support, and cross-sector collaboration.

**NSF National AI Research Institutes:** [11][14][15]
- The National Artificial Intelligence Research Institutes is a U.S. government research and development program, led by the NSF, that funds large, multi-institution research centers dedicated to AI research, education, and workforce development.
- Announced in 2019 with first grants awarded in 2020. It is the largest AI research program funded by the U.S. federal government.
- Each institute receives up to US$20 million over five years.
- By 2024, four funding cohorts had created 27 institutes across more than 40 states, with total funding approaching US$500 million.
- NSF Director Sethuraman Panchanathan called the institutes a "critical component of our nation's AI innovation, infrastructure, technology, education and partnerships ecosystem."
- A 2024 federal R&D report recorded federal investments of US$118.5 million in FY 2023 and US$69 million in FY 2024.
- Currently consists of 29 institutes that connect over 500 funded and collaborative institutions across the U.S. and around the world. [14]

**Selected Institutes by Cohort:**
- 2020: Trustworthy AI in Weather/Climate (Oklahoma), Foundations of ML (UT Austin), Student-AI Teaming (Colorado Boulder), AIFARMS (Illinois), Molecular Discovery (Illinois), IAIFI (MIT), AgAID (Washington State)
- 2021: ATHENA Edge Computing (Duke), ALOE Adult Learning (Georgia State), Resilient Agriculture (Iowa State)
- 2023: TRAILS Trustworthy AI in Law & Society (Maryland), ACTION Cyber Threat Intelligence (UC Santa Barbara), AI-CLIMATE (Minnesota), Exceptional Education (Buffalo)
- 2024: CosmicAI (UT Austin), SkAI (Northwestern)

**NSF Overall AI Investment:** [15]
- NSF has invested in AI research since the early 1960s, providing the technical foundations for today's AI innovations.
- NSF invests over $700 million annually in AI research and development.
- Pioneering work supported by NSF includes: reinforcement learning, neural networks, AI-driven learning, large language models, collaborative filtering, and the Protein Data Bank (which facilitated AlphaFold2).
- NSF announces $1.5B for foundational research to drive scientific breakthroughs.

**White House AI Education Executive Order (April 2025):** [3]
- President Donald J. Trump's April 2025 Executive Order on Advancing Artificial Intelligence Education for American Youth.
- Established the White House Task Force on AI Education, chaired by Michael Kratsios (Director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy), to create public-private partnerships providing AI education resources for K-12 students.
- "As AI reshapes how people learn, work, and communicate, the Trump Administration is committed to ensuring that Americans are equipped to lead the world in harnessing this technology." — Michael Kratsios.

**Major Corporate Commitments (September 2025):** [3]
- **Google**: $1 billion commitment to support education and job training programs in the U.S.
- **IBM**: Will skill 2 million learners by 2028 through its Skillsbuild program.
- **Pearson Education**: Up to 250,000 free vouchers for U.S. high school teachers for Generative AI Foundations certification.
- **Zoom**: $5 million over three years in K-12 education grants.
- **NVIDIA**: $25 million commitment over 5 years for K-12 AI skills and training.
- **Mastercard**: Expanding Kids4Tech™ AI curriculum, committing to reach 1 million U.S. students over five years.
- **Microsoft**: Free AI CoPilot access for every K-12 student; $1.25 million in prizes for Presidential AI Challenge; new LinkedIn Learning AI courses; no-cost AI certifications for community college faculty.
- **Amazon**: AI skills training for 4 million U.S. learners by 2028; AI curricula for 10,000 educators; up to $30 million in cloud/AI credits.
- **OpenAI**: Platform to certify 10 million workers by 2030 in AI tool use; matching with employers.
- **xAI**: $10 million for AI education for underserved youth.
- **Meta**: Over $20 million commitment; partnering with Pearson for military community schools.
- **Adobe**: Free access to AI tools for every K-12 student; free professional development for educators.
- **Dell Technologies**: Premier technology partner for the Presidential AI Challenge.
- **Learning.com**: Multi-million dollar investment to reach 5 million K-12 students with AI literacy curriculum.
- **Arist**: Will train 5 million Americans on AI over 4 years via text message (no app/internet needed).

- **AT&T**: AI literacy resources for 1.3 million students, caregivers, and educators by 2030.

#### 2.4 EU AI Strategy and Education Policies

**AI Literacy Under the AI Act (Article 4):** [2]
- Article 4 entered into application on 2 February 2025, amended via the Digital Omnibus in mid-July 2026.
- It requires AI providers and deployers to ensure AI literacy among their staff, with supervision by national market surveillance authorities starting 2 August 2026.
- The AI Office published Q&A on AI literacy and launched a repository of AI literacy practices, currently featuring over 40 initiatives.

**Key EU Policy Initiatives:** [2]
- **AI Continent Action Plan** (9 April 2025): Aims to expand the EU's AI specialist pool, with European Digital Innovation Hubs (EDIHs) increasing AI skills training.
- **Apply AI Strategy** (October 2025): Supports AI adoption in key sectors with three workforce priorities: (1) AI literate workers for all sectors, (2) sectoral AI experts for digitally intense sectors, (3) active monitoring of AI's impact on the labour market.
- **Union of Skills** (March 2025): Focuses on developing human capital, accompanied by an Action Plan on Basic Skills and a STEM Education Strategic Plan, including a 2030 Roadmap on digital education and an initiative on AI in education.
- The Commission emphasizes supporting SMEs in compliance efforts and working with Member States through the AI Board to facilitate AI literacy implementation.

**Singapore:** [1]
- Since launching the Singapore National AI Strategy (NAIS) 2.0 in December 2023, Singapore has made meaningful progress.
- The National AI Council (NAIC), chaired by Prime Minister Lawrence Wong, was established in February 2026 to provide strategic direction and drive Singapore's AI agenda.

- Over 70 companies across various sectors have chosen to establish AI Centres of Excellence (COEs) in Singapore.
- The $150 million Enterprise Compute Initiative supports companies' AI transformation efforts by facilitating access to cutting-edge AI tools, cloud compute, training, and engineering support.

**South Korea:** [3]
- South Korea adopted an "industry demand-driven" strategy for AI talent development.
- Addresses the challenge of AI talent outflow: ranking 35th out of 38 OECD nations in retention, with a net loss of 0.36 AI specialists per 10,000 people.

- The AI Framework Act (passed 2024, effective January 2026) makes South Korea the second jurisdiction after the EU to introduce comprehensive AI legislation, using a risk-based classification approach.

**Canada:** [4]
- Canada's National AI Strategy: "AI for All" (released 2025-2026), built on three core values: Trust, Opportunity, and Sovereignty.
- Canada's digital sector employs ~800,000 workers and contributes $140B+ to GDP, with 150,000 jobs directly linked to AI.
- Over 3,500 Canadian firms are developing AI, raising $37B+ in venture capital.

- Canada ranked 44th of 47 countries on AI training and literacy, and 42nd of 47 on trust in AI systems.
- Only 24% of Canadians have received any AI training.
- Generative AI alone could add $187B annually to the Canadian economy by 2030.

**Six Pillars of the Strategy:**
1. **Protecting Canadians and Safeguarding Democracy** - Establishing a Canadian AI Safety Institute, mandatory transparency measures.
2. **Empowering Canadians** - Building an AI-skilled nation, goal: create over 250,000 new AI-relevant jobs by 2031.
3. **Powering AI Adoption** - Target: 60% of Canadian businesses (especially SMEs) adopting AI by 2034.
4. **Building the Canadian Sovereign AI Foundation** - Canada needs 5.5 GW of AI compute by 2030, leveraging clean grid (83% renewable/low-emission).
5. **Scaling Canadian Champions** - Unlocking growth capital, using government as anchor customer.
6. **Building Trusted Partnerships** - Signed 20 new economic/defence partnerships, secured nearly $100B in foreign investment commitments.

**Global Context (40 National AI Strategies):** [2]
- GINC analysis (August 2025) examining 40 national AI strategies finds that in 2025, most major economies have refreshed or are updating their AI strategies.
- Five Global Leaders: the US, China, UK, France, and Singapore.

- Regional divergence: EU and Nordic countries focus on trust and alignment with EU AI Act; Indo-Pacific (Japan, South Korea, India, Australia, Taiwan) blends innovation with security; MENA states pursue sovereignty and large-scale investment; BRICS+ emphasizes technological sovereignty; Southeast Asia and LATAM/Sub-Saharan Africa focus on building core capacity.

**Taiwan (Ministry of Digital Affairs):** [1]

- The program was open to all, including undergraduate through doctoral students and professionals.
- The program concluded in December 2025. The experience gained will be integrated to formulate future policies and implementation directions.

### 4. K-12 AI Education

#### 4.1 China's K-12 AI Education

**Policy Framework:** [6][7][8]
- The Ministry of Education's goal: universalize basic AI access in primary and secondary schools by 2030. [7][8]
- May 2025 Guidelines for AI education in primary and secondary schools divide curriculum by level: primary (imagination and basic cognition), junior high (technical principles), and senior high (systematic thinking and innovation). [6]
- July 28, 2026 notice from the MOE: "Notice of the Office of the Ministry of Education on Strengthening Artificial Intelligence Education in Primary and Secondary Schools." [8]
- AI literacy has become a "must have" for K-12 teachers, principals and Party secretaries. [6]
- Four overall requirements: (1) cultivate moral people, (2) people-centered approach, (3) stimulate interest and encourage exploration, (4) overall planning and steady advancement. [8]

**Implementation:** [6]
- Schools are deploying AI tools like DeepSeek-based advisors, AI judges for exam evaluation, and AI counselors for career guidance.
- The "Shicheng Wanxiang" foundation model, built by Beijing Normal University and TAL Education, is being trialed in 60+ Beijing schools.
- TAL Education has sold ~190,000 AI learning machines (March-May 2025, up 70% YoY).
- China's Hangzhou makes AI classes compulsory in schools amid nationwide push. [9]
- Squirrel Ai Learning broke a Guinness World Record with 112,718 students in an online math lesson. [9]

**Risks and Concerns:** [6][7]
- Experts warn over-reliance on AI dulls student inquiry and critical thinking.
- Chu Zhaohui notes AI may strip students of choice by replacing exploration with fabricated solutions.
- "Critical thinking is essential to grasping and mastering AI, avoiding blind dependence that risks creating an 'artificially disabled' generation." [6]
- Concerns about Western-centric bias in AI models and wasteful overspending on redundant tools.
- Rural education faces severe resource depletion: elite schools systematically attract talent from periphery areas, leaving rural schools with teacher shortages (senior teachers are only 6.8% of all teachers in China vs. 26% in the US with 20+ years experience). [7]
- A 2025 study found 82% of rural children aged 6-36 months had at least one developmental delay. [7]
- Funding challenges: MOE white papers are unfunded mandates. Schools are instructed to "strengthen overall planning of funds" but budgets are already stretched thin. [7]
- Rural areas face a shortfall of 8.5 million computers. [7]
- iFlytek's smart classroom software cost one school ¥1,744,000 (~US$254,000). [7]
- At least 63% of primary/secondary students have dealt with spam calls from data leaks. [7]
- The mental health surveillance use case is particularly worrying, as the structure of boarding schooling itself (with 47.3% of boarding students suffering from acute pessimism and 63.8% feeling lonely) is a major source of psychological harm. [7]

**Expert Perspectives:** [6]
- Zheng Yongnian calls for a unified "big innovation system" integrating education, vocational training, and overseas recruitment.
- Xu Fei warns up to 60% of professional knowledge may be obsolete by graduation.
- Zhou Dawang outlines four strategic pillars: learning AI, using AI, creating AI, and protecting AI.
- "Only by gathering forces from government, industry, academia and research, argues Wang, can educational large models leap from 'usable' to 'excellent'." [6]

- According to the OECD's 2024 TALIS survey, 37% of teachers already use GenAI for work-related tasks.
- "When students depend too heavily on GenAI, metacognitive engagement – the mental processes and effort that turns answers into understanding – drops."

### 5. Pedagogical Approaches for AI Talent

#### 5.1 Competition-Based Learning (Kaggle and Others)

**Kaggle Platform:** [15][16][17]
- Kaggle is positioned as "The World's AI Proving Ground," serving a community of 33 million+ AI builders, researchers, and organizations.
- Platform offers: Competitions & Hackathons, Benchmarks, Datasets (728K), Notebooks (1.8M), Models (50,100), and Courses (70+ hours).
- Kaggle accounts for approximately 70% of total prize pools across platforms, with $2.38M in 2024 and $3.718M in 2025 in awarded prizes.
- Total registered users reached 30.4 million, with exponential growth post-2017 (Google acquisition).
- There are 387 Competition Grandmasters and 2,209 Masters.
- Demographic insights: Japan leads in Grandmasters (84) and total gold medals, despite a smaller user base (25,661) compared to the U.S. (395,089 users, 65 Grandmasters), China (52,061 users, 44 Grandmasters), and India (282,294 users, 8 Grandmasters).
- Notable competitions: ARC Prize 2026 (three tracks totaling $2M+ in prizes), Pokémon TCG AI Battle Challenge ($240,000).
- Platforms: U.S.-based platforms account for ~90% of total competition funding. Drivendata focuses on social good, Zindi on African challenges.

**Competitive ML as a Learning Tool:** [19]
- Alexander Guschin (Kaggle Grand Master ranked 5th globally, teacher to over 100,000 students) discusses his journey:
  - "I just spent a lot of time on that... I was skipping most of my lectures and classes at University, I was just doing competitions."
  - "When you solve one dozen of competitions, it's much easier to solve the next dozen."
  - Success requires significant time investment (often 10+ hours per week), careful data exploration, building proper validation, and iterating through dozens of competitions.
  - Forming teams is beneficial for community discussion and learning.
  - "There are some things that almost all competition winners do: they explore data carefully, they try to do EDA, they try to understand the domain, and build a careful validation. The secret trick is just be careful and invest time."

**Teaching Philosophy:** [19]
- Guschin designs courses around real problems (e.g., building a bot/human classifier) where students progressively build solutions from dummy classifiers to full deployed platforms with monitoring.
- Uses competitive elements like leaderboards tracking both ML metrics and technical reliability metrics.
- "I found out that when you teach, you need to figure it out, you need to understand it if you want to come and explain people... the best way to learn something is to teach."
- Generative AI tools like ChatGPT are useful for debugging and productivity but cannot win ML competitions on their own.

**Machine Learning Competitions Ecosystem:** [17]
- MLCs function at the intersection of academic research and industrial application, fostering knowledge exchange, open-source collaboration, and crowdsourced problem-solving.
- Increasingly affiliated with major conferences (e.g., 16 competitions at NeurIPS 2024).
- Historical milestones: Netflix Prize (2006, $1M), Data Science Bowl series, M Competitions (1982-2022), DeepFake Detection Challenge.
- Across 10 platforms, approximately $4-5M USD in prizes awarded annually.

#### 5.2 Open-Source Contributions as Learning

**China's Open-Source AI Strategy:** [18]
- China's open-source approach has resulted in rapid global uptake—Alibaba's Qwen models account for the largest ecosystem on Hugging Face with over 100,000 derivatives.
- Chinese labs have narrowed performance gaps with top Western models despite compute constraints, with DeepSeek R1 and subsequent models approaching frontier performance.
- Chinese models cost a fraction of U.S. prices—Kimi K2.5 costs four times less than OpenAI's GPT-5.2 while achieving similar benchmark scores.
- Beijing has built institutional infrastructure designating data as a formal factor of production and permitting enterprises to carry data assets on their balance sheets.
- The shift toward small, specialized models for industrial deployment plays to China's strengths, as open ecosystems produce these most efficiently.
- The USCC paper argues that U.S. export controls targeting advanced semiconductors for frontier training do not adequately address the physical loop of deployment-driven data creation, meaning China may build AI advantages rooted in its physical economy.
- Beijing's AI+ Initiative, robotics industrial policy, and draft 15th Five-Year Plan all reflect a strategy organized around deployed AI rather than frontier scale.

#### 5.3 Research Mentorship Models

**Tsinghua Research Culture:** [14]
- Many students join research labs early, publish at top-tier CS conferences, and coding is treated as a baseline skill across disciplines.
- Students use AI tools to accelerate learning (AI tripled one Ph.D. student's research speed), with professors encouraging use while requiring manual validation of final work.
- "Professors are telling you use the tools, don't resist the tools, but we do still need to validate our code manually at the end because research requires exact precision." — Felix Gan, Tsinghua Ph.D. student.
- "There's nobody to fix the problem except us. So we have to step up and do the most difficult things, and then other people will follow suit." — Zhixun Tan, Google software engineer and Tsinghua alumnus.

**Small-Scale Elite Programs vs. Mass Education:**
- Tsinghua's new undergraduate AI school will enroll approximately 150 students - a highly selective, small-scale elite program. [11]
- In contrast, the MOE's goal is to universalize basic AI access in primary and secondary schools by 2030 - a mass education approach. [7][8]
- Canada's Amii trains 125,000+ students annually in AI and has reached 1,000+ K-12 teachers across 400+ schools. [4]
- The tension between elite training and mass education is a key theme across all countries.

# AI In Education Statistics (2026): Adoption & Usage Data

## Key Highlights
Global student AI usage jumped from 66% to 92% in 2025, marking the steepest yearly leap on record. The AI in education market is projected to grow from $8.3 billion (2025) to $32.27 billion by 2030 at a 25.9% CAGR, with some projections reaching $136.79 billion by 2035.

## Adoption & Usage
- **K-12 Schools**: 30% of K-12 students use AI tools daily; 53% use AI for homework help. K-12 teacher AI adoption doubled from 25% to 53% between 2023-24 and 2024-25.
- **Teachers**: 60% of US public school teachers used AI in 2024-25. Weekly users save an average of 5.9 hours per week (roughly six weeks of reclaimed time per school year).
- **Higher Education**: 92% of university students used AI tools in 2025 (up from 66% in 2024). 88% of UK university students used generative AI for assessments in 2025. ChatGPT leads with 66% student adoption, followed by Grammarly and Microsoft Copilot at 25% each.
- **College Students**: 64% use AI daily/weekly for coursework help, 60% for checking answers, 54% for editing writing, 54% for summarizing lectures. 61% believe AI tools will become the new normal.

## Benefits
- Harvard physics study (2025): Students using AI tutors learned more than twice as much in less time than peers in active-learning classrooms.
- Enhanced AI tutor showed 127% improvement vs 48% with standard chatbot.
- 90% of educators believe AI improves accessibility and personalized learning; 44% report reduced workload.
- Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat drove 15% increase in passing rates and 12% drop in dropout rates at Miami Dade College.
- Macquarie University students using AI chatbots saw exam scores improve by up to 10%.

## Negative Effects & Risks
- 95% of college faculty fear student overreliance on AI and diminished critical thinking (AAC&U survey).
- 57% of teachers say AI decreases student independent thinking; 52% report decline in critical thinking.
- Nearly 7,000 UK university students formally caught cheating with AI in 2023-24 (triple the previous year).
- 96% of K-12 US teachers received no formal AI training; 85% feel unprepared to manage AI in classrooms.
- Top teacher concerns: Plagiarism (65%), reduced human interaction (62%), data privacy (42%).

## Governance & Policy
- Only 10% of schools and universities have formal AI guidelines (UNESCO survey of 450+ institutions).
- Only 7% of schools worldwide have AI guidance; 40% of those policies are informal.
- Just 19% of institutions with AI policies offer AI skills training.
- All 50 US states plus DC have reviewed or proposed AI-related education laws by mid-2025.

## Market Projections
- North America held 37.5% of global AI education revenue in 2025 (~$3.1 billion).
- Global AI edtech market projected to reach $92.09 billion by 2033.
- 47% of leaders identify AI upskilling as top workforce strategy over next 12-18 months.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
# Global AI Adoption Index (GAIAI) 2026 — Summary

This report by Alice Labs presents the **Global AI Adoption Index (GAIAI) 2026**, a reproducible set of official benchmarks on enterprise AI adoption across the EU, OECD, Canada, US, and UK. It relies exclusively on official statistics from Eurostat, OECD, Statistics Canada, U.S. Census Bureau (BTOS), and UK ONS.

## Key Findings

**EU Enterprise Adoption:** 19.95% of EU enterprises (10+ employees) used AI in 2025, up from 13.48% in 2024. A steep size gap exists: 55.03% of large enterprises vs 17% of small enterprises used AI.

**OECD Adoption:** 20.2% of firms used AI in 2025, up from 8.7% in 2023 — a 132% increase in two years. 57.3% of ICT firms used AI (highest sector concentration), while professional/scientific services reached 36.8%.

**Canada:** 12.2% of businesses used AI in the past 12 months (Q2 2025), doubling from 6.1% a year earlier. 66.7% report no plans to adopt; 78.1% of non-planners cite "AI not relevant."

**United States:** 5.4% of employer businesses reported AI use in the previous two weeks (Feb 2024), up from 3.7% (Sep 2023). Expected use rose to 6.6% by Fall 2024.

**United Kingdom:** 9% of firms adopted AI in 2023, with projected adoption rising to 22% in 2024 based on plans.

**Generative AI:** McKinsey reports 71% of organizations regularly use GenAI (self-report); Eurostat official figure is ~6.5% of EU enterprises. The gap between 20% (official integrated adoption) and ~75% (self-report any-use) is described as the "addressable opportunity."

## Top Barriers
- **Skills/expertise shortage** (EU: 70.89% of enterprises that considered AI but didn't adopt)
- **Perceived irrelevance** (Canada: 78.1% of non-planners)
- **Difficulty identifying use cases** (UK: 39%)

## Spending & ROI
- Worldwide AI spending forecast to reach US $632 billion by 2028 (29% CAGR)
- GenAI spending forecast at US $644 billion in 2025 (76.4% YoY increase)
- Only ~25% of companies have captured significant value from AI investments (BCG)

## Country-Level Rankings (2024 data)
- Denmark: 27.6% (highest EU)
- Sweden: 25.0%, Finland: 24.7%, Belgium: 24.7%, Netherlands: 22.7%, Germany: 20.0%
- France: 10.4%, Italy: 8.2%, Poland: 5.9%
- Non-EU: Japan ~42% (broader basis), Singapore ~44%, Australia ~39%, South Korea ~28%
- China: ~58% for large industrial enterprises only

## Key Insight
The report emphasizes that the 5x variation in adoption rates (5% to 78%) is a **definition gap**, not a measurement error. Different time windows (2 weeks vs 12 months), population frames, and survey methodologies make rates not directly comparable across systems. The recommended rule of thumb: **20% as the official integrated-adoption rate** and **75% as the self-report any-use rate**.
</summary>

# Top 10 AI Tutoring Systems in 2026: Do They Actually Improve Learning Outcomes?

This evidence-based analysis evaluates 10 leading AI tutoring platforms through peer-reviewed research, longitudinal student data, and expert evaluations. With global spending on intelligent tutoring systems projected to reach $3.2 billion in 2026, the analysis prioritizes empirical evidence of learning gains, retention rates, and skill mastery.

## Methodology
Evaluation criteria include: peer-reviewed research with control groups, effect size data (Cohen's d), longitudinal tracking over 6+ months, independent evaluations, adaptive accuracy, and knowledge retention rates.

## The Top 10 Platforms

1. **Carnegie Learning's MATHia** — Built on 30+ years of cognitive science research at Carnegie Mellon University. A 2018 RAND Corporation study found effect sizes of 0.19-0.36. 2025 data from 500+ schools shows students outperform peers by 12 percentile points on standardized assessments. Best for middle/high school math. $50-75/student/year.

2. **Khan Academy's Khanmigo** — GPT-4-powered tutor using Socratic dialogue. 2025 SRI International study showed 23% faster mastery of algebra concepts. A 2026 pilot with 15,000 students showed learning gains equivalent to 2-3 weeks of additional instruction. Free-$9/month.

A 2020 PNAS study found students averaged 5.4× faster learning in certain math topics. 2025-2026 international deployments showed 1.2 grade level improvement in math proficiency. Best for math/science remediation.

4. **Duolingo** — Advanced speech recognition and personalized conversation practice. Learners completing 5 units (~120 hours) achieve proficiency equivalent to 4 college semesters. A 2025 study found adaptive algorithm reduced time-to-proficiency by 34%. Free-$12.99/month.

5. **Century Tech** — Neuroscience-informed learning design. A 2024 UCL Institute of Education study found 18% higher retention rates. Schools reported average grade improvements of 0.4 letter grades. Predictive analytics 87% accurate in forecasting exam performance 8 weeks ahead. £15-25/student/year.

6. **Thinkster Math** — Hybrid AI-human model. 2025 AIR evaluation found effect sizes of 0.42 for elementary students. Students average 1.5 years of mathematical growth in one academic year. $40-75/month.

7. **Cognii** — NLP-powered open-response learning. 2024 Pearson efficacy study found 28% improvement in constructed response quality. 2025 Journal of Educational Psychology research found deeper conceptual understanding through iterative feedback. Institutional pricing.

8. **Querium's StepWise** — Step-by-step problem analysis for STEM. 2023-2024 IES-funded study found pass rates 22 percentage points higher; underrepresented minorities showed 27-point gains. Community college implementations showed 35% fewer course retakes. $30-50/course.

9. **Gradarius/Realizeit** — Symbolic mathematics engine. Arizona State University found 18% higher pass rates and 25% better final exam scores. 2025 meta-analysis placed it among top three for math learning gains, effect sizes averaging 0.31. Institutional pricing.

10. **Photomath Plus** — Camera-based problem recognition with AI tutoring. 2025 Harvard GSE study found 19% improvement in conceptual understanding when using tutoring features. Free-$9.99/month.

## Comparative Analysis

## Critical Success Factors
1. Granular knowledge modeling
2. Formative feedback (not just summative assessment)
3. Metacognitive support
4. Appropriate challenge level (zone of proximal development)
5. Transparency and explainability

## The Verdict
Well-designed AI tutoring systems do improve learning outcomes, with effect sizes (0.25-0.45) comparable to human tutoring. AI tutors excel at well-defined domains but struggle with open-ended creativity, ethical reasoning, and interdisciplinary synthesis. The most effective systems augment human instruction rather than replace it.

This article provides a detailed overview of AI-based Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS), which use artificial intelligence to deliver personalized, adaptive instruction at scale. The piece covers the core components, benefits, limitations, real-world applications, and future of these systems.

### Key Context
- UNESCO projects a global shortage of 44 million teachers by 2030.

### The 4 Core Components of ITS

2. **Student Model** – Tracks individual knowledge, pace, and learning gaps in real time.
3. **Tutoring (Pedagogical) Model** – Selects instructional strategy based on domain + student data.
4. **User Interface Model** – Delivers content, collects responses, and provides feedback.

### Key Benefits
- **Personalized learning at scale** – Benjamin Bloom's 1984 "2-sigma problem" study showed one-on-one tutoring produced ~2 standard deviation improvement. Kurt VanLehn's 2011 meta-analysis found step-based ITS achieved a mean effect size of 0.76 over classroom instruction (vs. human tutoring's 0.79).
- **Immediate, targeted feedback** – Prevents misconceptions from taking hold.
- **Identifying and closing learning gaps** at granular concept levels.
- **Empowering teachers with actionable data** – Class-wide patterns, at-risk learners, etc.
- **Scalability and educational equity** – Closing disparities between well-resourced and under-resourced schools.

### Challenges and Limitations
- **High development cost** – Development-to-instruction time ratios as high as 200:1 (e.g., Carnegie Learning's Cognitive Tutor). LLM-based systems may reduce costs.
- **Limited emotional/social intelligence** – ITS struggle with learner affect (frustration, boredom). Affective Tutoring Systems (ATS) using multimodal signals are emerging.
- **Subject coverage gaps** – Most research concentrated in Mathematics (33%), Language/Literacy (24%), and Science (17%); Humanities underrepresented.
- **Risk of students "gaming" hint systems**, correlating with lower post-test performance.

### Notable Real-World Examples
- **K-12/Higher Ed**: Carnegie Learning's Cognitive Tutor (algebra), AutoTutor (computer literacy via dialogue), ASSISTments (math).
- **Corporate/Military**: SHERLOCK (U.S. Air Force F-15 diagnostics), Cardiac Tutor, GIFT (U.S. Army framework).
- **Generative AI Tutors**: Khan Academy's Khanmigo (GPT-4) grew from 40,000 to 700,000 student users in 2024–25. SchoolAi by Coschool reported 8–11% increases in class averages.

### Future Directions
- **Conversational and Generative AI** – LLM-powered tutors enabling open-ended dialogue and Socratic questioning.
- **Emotional AI** – Detecting learner affect and adapting instruction accordingly.
- **Expanding access** – India's AI adoption in education growing at 25–35% annually, with over 2 million students accessing AI tutoring features by late 2025. The goal is redistributing access to quality learning, not just improving scores.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>

Overall ITS averaged 0.58, compared to human tutoring's median of 0.79., Research has documented ratios of development time to instruction time as high as 200:1 hours for systems like Carnegie Learning's Cognitive Tutor., A randomized controlled trial of GPT-4 as a homework tutor showed improved student engagement and grammar outcomes with minimal content preparation required., India's government reported that AI adoption in education is growing at 25–35% annually, with over 2 million Indian students accessing AI tutoring features by late 2025.

--- SOURCE 15: A systematic review of AI-driven intelligent tutoring systems ... ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12078640

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This systematic review, published in NPJ Science of Learning (2025), examines the effects of AI-driven Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITSs) on K-12 students' learning and performance. The review analyzed 28 studies involving 4,597 students. Key findings include:

**Research Design:** Most studies used quasi-experimental designs with pre/post-tests. Studies were categorized into four control group types: ITS vs. Teacher (8 studies), ITS vs. Non-intelligent tutoring system (5 studies), ITS vs. Modified ITS (11 studies), and No control (4 studies). Half of the interventions lasted less than a week, raising concerns about novelty effects. The longest intervention was 30 weeks.

**Geographic Distribution:** 54% of studies originated from the USA, 27% from Asia (Taiwan, China, Thailand, Korea, Turkey, Saudi Arabia), and 15% from Europe. 82% of studies focused on STEM subjects, with the remainder in language arts.

**Effects on Learning:** ITSs generally showed positive effects on learning and performance compared to traditional teaching, with medium to large effect sizes. Seven out of eight studies comparing ITS to traditional teaching reported significant positive effects. However, when compared to non-intelligent tutoring systems, the positive effects were mitigated. The review notes that the novelty effect may influence short-term results.

**Key Limitations:** None of the included studies addressed AI ethics considerations. The review calls for longer interventions, larger and more diverse sample sizes, and further investigation into ethical implications of AI in education.

**Authorship:** 62% of studies were authored by individuals with educational science backgrounds, 15% from computer science, and 19% from both. Only one study was affiliated with an ITS company.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: AI and Auto-Grading in Higher Education: Capabilities, Ethics ... ---
URL: https://ascode.osu.edu/news/ai-and-auto-grading-higher-education-capabilities-ethics-and-evolving-role-educators

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from The Ohio State University ASC Office of Distance Education, authored by Graduate Research Associate Yuhan Gao (July 15, 2025), examines AI and auto-grading in higher education. It distinguishes between Auto-Grading Tools (AATs), which have existed since the 1960s and assess structured responses like code, multiple-choice, and short answers using static/dynamic analysis, and AI-assisted grading powered by LLMs (e.g., ChatGPT), which can evaluate complex, open-ended assignments like essays. Key strengths and limitations are discussed: AATs excel at objective tasks but struggle with open-ended work; AI grading offers scalability for subjective assessments but introduces ethical concerns around bias, transparency, and fairness. Studies by Flodén (2025) and Wetzler et al. (2024) show AI grading is often unreliable—grading leniently on low-performing essays and harshly on high-performing ones—and produces incorrect facts or references. Universities like Cornell, Purdue, UC San Diego, Florida, Rutgers, and Indiana University widely use platforms like Gradescope. The article advocates for a hybrid model combining human oversight with AI-generated feedback, noting that while human grading also has bias, AI can be systematically refined and audited. Educators remain essential, with AI positioned as a supportive technology, not a replacement. The future of assessment requires a collaborative, multidisciplinary approach to build equitable, reliable, and trustworthy systems.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 4: How Does Gradescope’s AI-Assisted Grading Work? - Apporto ---
URL: https://www.apporto.com/gradescopes-ai-assisted-grading-explained

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Gradescope's AI-assisted grading uses recognition and clustering algorithms to group similar student answers, helping instructors grade faster and more consistently. The AI organizes submissions and suggests answer groups, while instructors review responses, apply rubrics, assign scores, and provide final feedback. Gradescope does not use generative AI to invent scores or feedback; instead, it relies on specialized recognition and clustering algorithms. Student submissions are processed by overlaying them against a blank template, extracting student ink, and isolating answer areas. The system uses OCR combined with recognition models to read English-language handwriting and common math notation. The AI forms answer groups by analyzing individual answers and clustering identical or near-identical responses, but every group must be reviewed and confirmed by an instructor. Instructors grade by question, with student names hidden to reduce bias. Dynamic rubrics can be added or modified mid-grading, with changes applied retroactively. The system supports multiple question types including multiple choice, fill-in-the-blank, math, and programming assignments. Feedback can be applied to entire answer groups simultaneously, with individual adjustments available. Regrade requests are handled within the same grouping logic. The article also compares Gradescope to PowerGrader, which is rubric-first by design.
</summary>

<summary>
Georgia Tech's Design Intelligence Laboratory and NSF's National AI Institute for Adult Learning and Online Education (AI-ALOE) have developed a new version of the virtual teaching assistant named Jill Watson, powered by OpenAI's ChatGPT. The project aims to enhance teaching presence in online education for adult learners. 

**History:** The original Jill Watson launched in 2016 using IBM's Watson platform, answering student questions on discussion forums. An intermediate 2019 version switched to Google's BERT. The latest version uses ChatGPT as the backend and engages in extended conversations based on courseware (syllabi, textbooks, video transcripts, slides, etc.).

**Technology:** The architecture includes three main components: a knowledge base (pre-processed courseware), agent memory (MongoDB database storing interaction history), and a question-answering pipeline. It uses coreference resolution, skill classification (contextual answering, irrelevant, greetings), and ChatGPT prompts with consistency verification via textual entailment.

**Experiments & Results:** In Fall 2023, Jill was deployed in a Georgia Tech OMSCS AI class (600+ students) and a Wiregrass College English class. An A/B experiment randomly divided the OMSCS class into sections with and without Jill access. Key findings:
- Jill's accuracy on synthetic datasets ranged from 75% to 97%, depending on the source (syllabi ~75-80%, textbooks >90%).
- Jill Watson (78.7% pass rate) significantly outperformed OpenAI's Assistant service (30.7% pass rate) on a human-evaluated test.
- Jill enhanced teaching presence (design & organization) and social presence, but no statistically significant impact on cognitive presence was found.
- Students with Jill access had more A grades (66% vs 62%) and fewer C grades (3% vs 7%) compared to the control group.

**Plans:** The team aims to replicate results in more classes (especially introductory computing), explore whether Jill can enhance cognitive presence (critical thinking/deeper understanding), and examine Jill's impact on offloading routine question-answering for teaching teams.

The project is funded by Georgia Tech, NSF (Grants #2112523 and #2247790), and the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation. Core team members include Sandeep Kakar, Pratyusha Maiti, Robert Lindgren, and Karan Taneja.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 10: Jill Watson: A Virtual Teaching Assistant powered by ChatGPT ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2405.11070v1

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper introduces Jill Watson, a conversational Virtual Teaching Assistant (VTA) powered by ChatGPT for online classrooms. Unlike the legacy Jill Watson, which was a question-answering system for course logistics, the new Jill Watson is conversational and answers questions about both course logistics and course content based on multiple large documents (slides, notes, syllabi, e-books). The system uses a skill-based architecture inspired by XiaoIce, requiring no prior training or fine-tuning, and relies entirely on publicly available resources.

Key components include: (1) Coreference Resolution using ChatGPT prompts to resolve references in user queries; (2) Skill Classifier to route queries to appropriate skills (Contextual Answering, Self-awareness, Greeting, Irrelevant); (3) Contextual Answering skill that pre-processes PDF documents into passages, uses Dense Passage Retrieval (DPR) with dual embeddings (clean text and summaries), queries ChatGPT with context batches, and applies textual entailment checks to detect hallucinations; (4) Moderation filters using OpenAI Moderation API and prompts encouraging polite responses.

In evaluations comparing Jill Watson with legacy Jill Watson (LJW) and OpenAI Assistants (OAI-Assist) on 150 questions, Jill Watson achieved a 76.7% pass rate (vs. 26% for LJW and 31.3% for OAI-Assist), with only 5.7% harmful errors (vs. 16.5% for OAI-Assist). In toxicity testing with insult prompts, Jill Watson responded with "I don't know" (IDK) 98% of the time for standard insults and 82% for adapted insults, significantly reducing toxic output. The deployed system had an average response time of 6.8 seconds and demonstrated capabilities including coreference resolution, date-aware answers, self-correction when mistakes are pointed out, and refusal to generate harmful content.

Limitations include reliance on limited context for RAG (cannot answer long-range queries like "Summarize chapter 15"), potential error cascading in modular design, and a trade-off between safety and performance where some answerable questions may be rejected.
</summary>

<summary>
# China K-12 Content & Platform Market Summary (IMARC Group Report)

## Market Overview
The China K-12 content & platform market reached **USD 15,941.44 Million** in 2025 and is projected to reach **USD 45,835.75 Million** by 2034, growing at a **CAGR of 12.45%** during 2026-2034.

## Key Growth Drivers
1. **Government-Led Digital Education Infrastructure**: The Smart Education of China platform has become the world's largest digital education repository. By end of 2023, it connected 519,000 educational institutions, benefiting 18.8 million teachers and 293 million learners, with 36.7 billion cumulative visits. The Ministry of Education declared 2025 the inaugural year of smart education and launched the National Education Digitalization Strategic Plan 2.0 in May 2025.

2. **AI Integration**: AI is enabling personalized adaptive learning experiences with intelligent tutoring, automated grading, and adaptive learning pathways. Major EdTech firms (e.g., TAL Education's MathGPT) have developed proprietary educational LLMs. The government mandated AI education for all K-12 students beginning September 1, 2025, designating 184 schools as AI education bases nationwide.

3. **Blended Learning Adoption**: Cloud-based platforms are proliferating, supporting scalable, cost-effective, accessible digital learning. The Chinese government announced a $52 billion investment in R&D for 2024 (10% increase YoY).

## Key Market Challenges
- **Regulatory Uncertainty**: The July 2021 "Double Reduction" policy banned for-profit tutoring for core academic subjects, forcing major EdTech companies to pivot toward smart hardware, quality education, vocational training, and adult learning.
- **Digital Infrastructure Disparities**: Significant urban-rural gaps persist in broadband access, devices, and technology-capable teachers.
- **Data Privacy & Security**: Strict data sovereignty requirements, parental consent mandates, and concerns over student data misuse create compliance burdens.

## Market Segmentation (2026-2034)
- **By Component**: Content Solutions (digital courseware, e-textbooks, video lectures, test prep, gamified/AR-VR content) and Platform Solutions (LMS, SIS, adaptive learning platforms, collaboration tools)
- **By Subject Area**: STEM, Language & Literature, Social Studies & Humanities, Arts & Music, Physical Education & Health
- **By Deployment Mode**: Cloud-based, On-premises, Hybrid
- **By Grade Level**: Primary (Grades 1-5), Middle (Grades 6-9), High (Grades 10-12)
- **By Learning Model**: Synchronous, Asynchronous, Blended Learning
- **By Business Model**: Subscription-based, Freemium, Pay-Per-Course, Institutional Licensing
- **By End User**: Public Schools, Private Schools, Tutoring/After-school Institutions, Individual Learners & Parents
- **By Region**: North China, East China, South Central China, Southwest China, Northwest China, Northeast China

## Competitive Landscape
Highly dynamic market with established education giants pivoting post-Double Reduction toward AI-powered hardware and quality education. Key recent development: In August 2025, TAL Education's Xueersi AI Thinkie 1-on-1 Super Educational Intelligence received a 4+ rating from the China Academy of Information and Communications Technology, the highest industry level for AI-powered personalized learning products.

This case study, written by Md. Jubair Hasan, provides a comprehensive analysis of Duolingo's rise as a global language learning platform. 1. **Trigger**: Masterful push notifications (e.g., passive-aggressive owl reminders).
2. **Action**: Frictionless engagement (5-minute lessons, mobile-first design).
3. **Variable Reward**: Gamification features (XP, badges, leaderboards, Streak system) using operant conditioning.
4. **Investment**: Sunk cost lock-in (Streak freezes, in-app purchases, social features).

- **Vertical Teams/Pods**: Cross-functional teams focused on single metrics.
- **A/B Testing**: Over 750 tests per quarter.
- **Grease Week**: Ritual for paying down technical debt.

- **Birdbrain**: Proprietary AI personalization engine modeling user proficiency and exercise difficulty.

- **Valuation Volatility**: Stock dropped ~46% from highs despite strong earnings.

This document is Oak National Academy's written evidence submitted to the UK Education Committee's inquiry into the use of Artificial Intelligence and EdTech in Education (May 2026). Oak is a publicly funded arm's length body of the Department for Education (DfE), providing free digital curriculum resources for schools in England.

**Key Points:**

- **AI Tool Launch:** Oak launched Aila, the UK's first public-body generative AI product, in September 2024. Over 60,000 teachers have used it, creating 95,000+ lesson plans and downloading 280,000+ resources.

- **Workload Impact:** Aila users report saving an average of 3 hours per week. Nearly two-thirds of surveyed teachers reported reduced workload.

- **Digital Infrastructure:** Oak advocates for developing a digital, machine-readable National Curriculum, a robust content ontology, and quality-assured source material to ensure AI tools align with the English National Curriculum safely. The DfE is developing a "content store" — a structured repository of curriculum-aligned content.

- **Safety & Ethics:** Aila uses retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) grounded in Oak's trusted content, structured moderation, input threat detection, and human-in-the-loop safeguards. Oak exceeds DfE's Generative AI Product Safety Standards, including filtering for age-appropriate content even though it's teacher-facing.

- **Equity:** Oak's reach is greatest in the most disadvantaged schools (36% more resource downloads in most deprived areas vs. least deprived). The tool supports adaptation for SEND, EAL, and stretch/challenge.

- **Teacher Adoption:** 88% of teachers have tried AI, and 58% report weekly use. Lesson planning is the most common use case (54%). Early career teachers show higher adoption rates.

- **Curriculum Alignment:** Oak has been asked by the DfE to support digitisation of the revised National Curriculum and refresh its own curriculum resources. A refreshed National Curriculum is due in September 2028.

- **Open Licensing:** Oak's content, code, and data are openly available under open licenses (OGL, MIT), with over 100 organisations using Oak's API.

- **Assessment Implications:** AI's expanding role in assessment (AI-assisted marking, continuous assessment, academic integrity challenges) will require robust National Curriculum-aligned infrastructure.

#### 2.1 Global Spending and Evidence

- Global spending on intelligent tutoring systems is projected to reach **$3.2 billion in 2026** [11].
- Benjamin Bloom's seminal 1984 study documented the "2-sigma problem": one-to-one tutoring with mastery learning produced roughly a 2 standard deviation improvement over conventional classroom instruction [14].
- Kurt VanLehn's 2011 meta-analysis found step-based ITS achieved a mean effect size of **0.76** over classroom instruction. Overall ITS averaged **0.58**, compared to human tutoring's median of **0.79** [14].
- A systematic review published in **NPJ Science of Learning (2025)** analyzed 28 studies involving 4,597 students, finding that ITSs generally show positive effects on learning and performance compared to traditional teaching, with medium to large effect sizes. Seven out of eight studies comparing ITS to traditional teaching reported significant positive effects [15].
- **54%** of studies originated from the USA, **27%** from Asia (Taiwan, China, Thailand, Korea, Turkey, Saudi Arabia), and **15%** from Europe. **82%** of studies focused on STEM subjects [15].

- The OECD's Digital Education Outlook 2026 warns that performing tasks with AI doesn't automatically lead to learning; purpose-built educational AI shows sustained improvements [5].
- AI-powered personalized learning increases engagement by up to **60%** and learning efficiency by **57%** [5].
- **75%** of students feel more motivated in personalized AI environments vs. **30%** in traditional classrooms [5].

### 7. KEY INSIGHTS AND TRENDS

**The "Definition Gap" in Adoption Data**: The 5x variation in adoption rates (5% to 78%) is a definition gap, not a measurement error. Different time windows (2 weeks vs 12 months), population frames, and survey methodologies make rates not directly comparable. The recommended rule of thumb: **20% as the official integrated-adoption rate** and **75% as the self-report any-use rate** [2].

**Only ~25% of companies** have captured significant value from AI investments according to BCG's AI Radar 2025 survey — the so-called "AI impact gap" [2].

**Worldwide AI spending** forecast to reach **US $632 billion by 2028** (29% CAGR) [2].

**GenAI spending** forecast at **US $644 billion in 2025** (76.4% YoY increase) [2].

**24.7% of working-age population** in Global North uses generative AI vs. **14.1%** in Global South [5].

**AI tools could add $7.9 trillion** to global economy if AI literacy scales across the workforce [5].

**The demographic cliff** starting in 2026 makes AI adoption a survival issue for higher education, with 15 years of declining traditional-age enrollment and **71% turnover** in entry-level admissions roles [12].

**UNESCO** reports more than **250 million children out of school** and an additional **600 million** failing to reach minimum competency levels [15].
